Navy, and the United States Air Force.

Commanders, staffs, and subordinates ensure their decisions and actions comply with applicable United States,

text. For other definitions shown in the text, the term is italicized and the number of the proponent publication

                                 Introduction

The United States Army Engineer School developed this publication with the joint participation of the approving
Service commands. The test procedures and terminology used in this manual conform to the latest methods and
specifications of the American Society for Testing and Materials (ASTM), the American Concrete Institute, and
the Portland Cement Association. The ASTM source publications are not required for testing specified in this
document as the procedure is fully explained for military personnel use.

This manual is adopted for use by United States Navy and United States Air Force personnel. Certain tests and
procedures prescribed differ in principle or method and are more detailed than counterpart tests that are currently
required by the United States Navy for new construction at Navy installations (including those in forward areas).
The tests in this manual also apply to arctic construction. However, cold-weather effects present different
problems and additional tests will be required for correct evaluation of the materials. These additional tests and
considerations associated with arctic construction are in TM 5-349.

TM 3-34.48-1 and TM 3-34.48-2 should be used in conjunction with each other.

Appendix A contains a metric conversion chart for this manual. A complete listing of preferred metric units for
general use is contained in Federal Standard 376B at <http://www.usaid.gov/policy/ads/300/fstd376b.pdf>.

                                                 Chapter 1

                            General Information

         Military engineers are called on to plan, design, and construct airfields, heliports, and
         roads in joint areas of operations (JOA). In a high operational tempo environment, the
         majority of pavement engineering efforts focus on maintenance, repair, and
         rehabilitation of existing facilities. To ensure that these facilities meet proposed
         requirements, the responsible engineer officer must coordinate closely with appropriate
         ground and air commanders. The engineer relies on information from commanders and
         the operations plan on the weight and traffic frequency of using air or ground vehicles,
         facility life, geographic boundaries governing site selection, and the time available for
         construction. Detailed planning, reconnaissance, and site investigations are often
         limited by the lack of time and the tactical situation. However, when time and security
         permit, the engineer should conduct normal ground reconnaissance and on-site
         investigations. It is important for the engineer to obtain the best site information
         available before entering the design or site selection phases. This manual provides
         guidance on current military pavement engineering practices relative to the JOA.
         Reference publications are provided for additional information beyond the scope of
         this manual.

BASIC PLANNING CONSIDERATIONS

     1-1. Military engineers in the JOA should follow the following guidelines:
              Keep designs simple. Simple designs require minimum skilled labor and specialized materials.
              Use local materials when possible. This eliminates construction delays associated with a long
                  communications and logistics line.
              Use existing facilities when possible. This avoids unnecessary construction.
              Remember that safety factors in design are drastically reduced in the JOA because of time
                  constraints and the inherent risks of war.
              Design for initial or temporary structures. Initial design life is for up to six months, and temporary
                  design life is for up to two years.
              Phase construction to permit early use of the facility while construction and improvements
                  continue.
              Avoid sites with dense brush, timberland, and rolling terrain that require heavy clearing or grading.
              Prevent destruction of natural drainage channels, culverts, and roads. Repairs generally require
                  time and labor far exceeding those needed to prevent damage.

AIRFIELD CONSTRUCTION

     1-2. The planning and construction of Air Force bases in the JOA is a joint responsibility of Army and Air
     Force personnel. A summary of Air Force and Army responsibilities follow.

29 February 2016  TM 3-34.48-1  1-1


---

Chapter 1

AIR FORCE RESPONSIBILITIES

     1-3. The Air Force provides the following support:
              Emergency repair of war-damaged air bases.
              Force beddown of Air Force units and weapon systems, excluding Army base-development
                  responsibilities.
              Construction management of emergency repairs of war damage and force beddown.
              Operation and maintenance of Air Force facilities and installations.
              Crash rescue and fire suppression.
              Material and equipment to perform Air Force engineering missions.

ARMY RESPONSIBILITIES

     1-4. The Army provides the following troop construction support for the Air Force:
              Emergency repair assistance for war damaged air bases that exceed the Air Force organic
                  capability.
              Development of engineering designs, standard plans, and material to meet Air Force requirements.
              Reconnaissance, survey, design, construction, or improvement of airfields, roads, utilities, and
                  structures.
              Rehabilitation of Air Force bases and facilities beyond the immediate emergency recovery
                  requirements of the Air Force.
              Materials and equipment to perform Army engineering missions.
              Construction of temporary standard air base facilities.
              Repair management of war damage and base development, including supervision of Army
                  personnel. The Air Force base commander will set the work priorities.
              Road and airfield construction.

     1-5. Engineer construction units, under the appropriate Army command, have the following
     responsibilities:

              Reconnoiter roads and bridges.
              Recommend traffic-control procedures.
              Construct and install signs and other route-marking materials.
              Regulate traffic at locations where engineer work is being performed.
              Assist vehicles to keep traffic moving on main supply routes regardless of weather, enemy activity,

                  or other difficulties.

ENGINEERING STUDY

     1-6. After the specific requirements for roads, airfields, and heliports have been determined, engineers
     should prepare the facilities for use as soon as possible. In most cases, the need is critical because mission
     accomplishment depends on using certain roads and airfields. To obtain these facilities quickly, an adequate
     investigation of each site and a careful study of the design details are essential. This is explained in greater
     detail in chapter 2.

1-2  TM 3-34.48-1  29 February 2016

                                                 Chapter 2

                 Reconnaissance and Site Selection

         This chapter outlines the location, layout, and design of military roads and airfields.
         Before constructing a road or airfield, the best facility location is determined and the
         essential areas and construction features are formulated. Throughout the
         preconstruction phase, problems can be avoided by a well-planned site selection.

LOCATION FACTORS

     2-1. Construction of a road or airfield initially consists of providing a prepared subgrade and base course
     according to the design criteria. Airfield runways require more transverse areas than roads. Although the
     governing criteria and dimensions for roads and airfields differ, the basic approach to their location and layout
     is the same. Engineers use the following factors to locate and lay out construction projects:

              Mission.
              Existing facilities.
              Location and design.
              Soil characteristics.
              Drainage.
              Geology.
              Topography.
              Earthwork.
              Alignment.
              Obstacle crossings.
              Bridge approaches.
              Ground cover.
              Required areas.
              Material and utility accessibility.
              Marginal material.
              Flight-way obstructions.
              Sunlit slopes.
              Tactical considerations.
              Future expansion.

MISSION

     2-2. Ensuring that a site will fulfill mission requirements is the most important factor in site selection. Lines
     of communication must be built to accomplish a specific mission in the most direct and efficient manner
     possible. Each location factor must be evaluated to support the mission.

EXISTING FACILITIES

     2-3. Use existing facilities. Wartime missions of engineer troops are extensive, and new construction should
     be avoided. Extensive road nets of varying quality and capacity already exist in most areas of the world.
     Where possible, use these road nets to the fullest extent. In many cases, expansion and rehabilitation of
     existing facilities are adequate for mission accomplishment.

29 February 2016  TM 3-34.48-1  2-1


---

Chapter 2

     2-4. Except in highly developed areas, existing airfields are seldom adequate to handle modern, high-
     performance aircraft. However, these airfields can usually be made adequate with minimum rehabilitation.
     Rapid parking expansion can improve the maximum on-ground capability of existing airfields that are
     structurally capable of handling high-performance aircraft. It may serve as a nucleus for larger fields that
     meet the requirements of high-performance aircraft. Helicopters and light planes can often operate from
     existing roads, pastures, or athletic fields.

LOCATION AND DESIGN

     2-5. To the greatest extent possible, the location and design for a facility must provide the best response to
     requirements. Alternative road and airfield plans can be evaluated from the standpoint of total earthwork and
     drainage structure requirements to reduce construction effort.

     2-6. Construct airfields in areas that serve existing and future requirements. Consider the future needs of
     military units and facilities, such as depots and hospitals, when locating roads. Soil type and incumbent
     pavement structure requirements, rock formations, and vegetation should also be considered when locating
     roads. A road segment to be constructed or improved should be evaluated for its contribution to the overall
     network. Similarly, an airfield should be evaluated for its ability to enhance an airfield network.

SOIL CHARACTERISTICS

     2-7. Locate roads and airfields on terrain with the best possible subgrade soil conditions. This will decrease
     construction effort and result in a better facility. The subgrade should be compacted under conditions that
     allow it to support the design loads. Conduct a basic soils investigation before construction to provide the
     data needed to ensure good construction decisions. Refer to TM 3-34.64/MCRP 3-17.7G for soils information
     and TM 3-34.43/MCRP 3-17-7H/NAVFAC MO 330/AFH 32-1034 for soil survey procedures.

DRAINAGE

     2-8. Locate roads in areas that are easily drained and where drainage structures are minimized. Drainage is
     a more critical factor in locating airfields than roads. Because of the wide areas involved in airfield
     construction, water must be diverted completely around the field or long drainage structures that are difficult
     to maintain must be constructed. This topic is further discussed in chapters 6 through 9.

     2-9. Avoid valley low points and depressed areas because they are focal points for water collection. Many
     airfields are constructed across long, gentle slopes because of the relative ease of diverting water around the
     finished installation. If possible, avoid construction on unprotected floodplains and alluvial fans due to flood
     hazard. Alluvial terraces are often ideal locations for airfields. They offer flat expanses that are above the
     river floodplain and are normally protected from flooding.

     2-10. Avoid constructing facilities in high water table areas. Although it is possible to construct subsurface
     structures that will remove part of this moisture, maintaining routes through these areas presents a continual
     problem. If it is impossible to avoid constructing a road or airfield in this type of terrain, the water tables
     must be lowered during construction to reduce the adverse effect of water on the strength of the supporting
     subgrade and base course.

GEOLOGY

     2-11. Before locating lines of communication, carefully analyze the geology of the area. Sizeable quantities
     of rock along a construction project may cause a large removal problem, slow construction, and increased
     construction effort. Engineer troop units require special equipment and training to excavate rock.

     2-12. Rocky outcrops are more common in hilly terrain than in flat or rolling country. In areas where the
     preliminary design indicate that cutting is required to reach final grade, take enough borings or dig enough
     test pits to determine the location of the rock.

2-2  TM 3-34.48-1  29 February 2016


---

                                                                                              Reconnaissance and Site Selection

2-13. Identify the type of rock material for evaluation as a suitable construction aggregate. Determine the
structural orientation of the rock mass to properly design road cuts and ensure rock-slope stability. It is best
to align road cuts perpendicular to the strike in sedimentary rocks. If this is not possible, use safe-slope
ratios. (See figure 2-1.)

                                                Figure 2-1. Safe-slope ratio

TOPOGRAPHY

     2-14. Construct roads and airfields within maximum grade specifications. The specifications depend on the
     facility construction standard. Avoid excessive grades and steep hills when locating these routes. If steep
     hills must be negotiated, the route should run along the side of the hill rather than going directly over it. This
     may result in a longer route, but it is generally more economical and avoids excessive grades.

EARTHWORK

     2-15. The largest single work item during lines of communication construction is earthwork operations. Any
     step that simplifies earthwork operations will decrease the required work and increase job efficiency. When
     cutting and filling on a project, using the material excavated to construct required embankments will
     generally reduce earth handling. This balancing must be within the haul capabilities of available equipment.
     Even though earthwork should be balanced throughout a project, it may be more practical to open a nearby
     borrow pit or establish spoil areas if the haul distance is excessive. Balancing cannot be done where the
     excavated material is not acceptable for use in an embankment.

ALIGNMENT

     2-16. Keep the number of curves and grades at a minimum for efficient traffic flow. Vehicles have difficulty
     in negotiating sharp curves; even gentle curves decrease traffic capacity. Lay routes with minimum curves
     by making the tangent lines as long as possible. Locating long tangents is influenced primarily by the terrain
     and limited by efficient location principles (minimizing earthwork, avoiding excessive grades, obtaining
     suitable fill material). Align runways in the direction of the prevailing wind to optimize aircraft operations.

OBSTACLE CROSSINGS

     2-17. When a route crosses a major obstacle (river, ravine, canal), bridges or crossing structures are required.
     Construction is time consuming and requires materials that may be in short supply. Avoid these obstacles
     when possible by forgoing other location principles to decrease the number of obstacle crossings or using
     existing structures to decrease total work requirements. This may require the strengthening of an existing
     bridge or no bridging work. When possible, the road should not cross a particular obstacle, such as a winding
     river, more than once.

29 February 2016  TM 3-34.48-1  2-3


---

Chapter 2

BRIDGE APPROACHES

     2-18. When locating routes, carefully evaluate construction requirements for approaches to obstacles.
     Construction of approaches over marshes or floodplain areas can cause greater concerns than the obstacle
     crossing itself. Approach conditions may be the prime factor in obstacle crossing and may dictate route
     location. Consider the approach and the obstacle when establishing the optimum route.

GROUND COVER

     2-19. Routes should avoid heavily wooded areas that require extensive clearing. If this is not possible, the
     route should pass through areas having the least vegetation. Strip unsuitable material before beginning
     earthwork.

REQUIRED AREAS

     2-20. Airfields need large areas of relatively flat land to efficiently accomplish the mission. This usually
     restricts the number of sites that can be considered for airfield construction. Advance location and layout will
     avoid cramping necessary facilities. Frequently, the airfield must be spread over a large section to obtain the
     required area. This results in the construction of a complex network of taxiways and service roads. Consider
     the ability to construct this connecting network to appropriate specifications during planning.

     2-21. Roads built on rolling or flat terrain seldom require large, lateral areas. Roads constructed in deep cuts
     or fills require proportionately greater lateral areas to account for slopes.

MATERIAL AND UTILITY ACCESSIBILITY

     2-22. The efficient operation of airfields requires the use of electricity, water, gas, and sewer systems. Locate
     new airfields near existing utility systems to avoid construction of new facilities or long transmission lines.
     A nearby railhead will help the construction effort.

     2-23. Consider the quality and availability of construction materials when locating a facility. Obtain suitable
     base-course materials from existing pits and quarries when possible. Planning and effort are required to open
     a new quarry. The quality and available quantity of materials must meet the construction requirements. The
     proximity of a suitable base-course material source is a critical planning factor.

MARGINAL MATERIAL

     2-24. When planning the location of a project, consider using nearby marginal materials. Using marginal
     materials for subbase and base construction and as an aggregate in pavements is sometimes made possible
     with geotextiles, mechanical stabilization, or admixtures. Often, the use of marginal material is unavoidable.
     When possible, poor-quality material should be excavated and replaced with more suitable material or the
     project should be relocated. When marginal materials must be used, guidance is provided in UFC 3-220-
     04FA.

FLIGHT-WAY OBSTRUCTIONS

     2-25. The safe operation of fixed- or rotary-wing aircraft requires the removal of obstacles above the lines
     specified by design criteria. These criteria depend on the operating characteristics of the aircraft to be
     serviced. For example, most heliports require an approach zone with a 10:1 glide angle (8:1 for short-duration
     operations), whereas heavy-cargo aircraft in the support area require a glide angle as flat as 50:1. To achieve
     this glide angle, it is often necessary to remove vegetation and hills and perform extensive earthwork
     operations far from the airfield. Avoid locations that require extensive work to achieve the necessary glide
     angle. More information regard variables and requirements is provided in UFC 3-260-01, UFC 3-260-02,
     and UFC 3-260-03.

     2-26. A similar clearance is required on runway sides. The specified width must be cleared of obstacles and
     graded according to specifications.

2-4  TM 3-34.48-1  29 February 2016


---

                                                                                                    Reconnaissance and Site Selection

SUNLIT SLOPES

     2-27. If tactical concealment is not required, locate roads on the sunny, exposed sides of valleys or hills,
     particularly in wet or cold areas. This permits the road surface and subgrade to dry rapidly, minimizes icy
     conditions, and makes maintenance easier. Prevailing winds should also be considered when locating roads
     and airfields. Prevailing winds will carry snow, rain, and sand onto the roadway if the orientation of the road
     is undesirable. Protective snow or sand fences should be oriented to account for prevailing winds.

TACTICAL CONSIDERATIONS

     2-28. Frequently, it is necessary to construct temporary roads or heliports or to improve landing strips to
     move personnel and materials. When this is the case, consider the following:

              Locate roads in a defilade position on the reverse side of a hill or ravine to avoid enemy
                  observation and provide cover from direct artillery or mortar fire.

              Take advantage of natural camouflage and concealment when constructing a road or airfield in an
                  exposed area.

              Disperse facilities to minimize bombing effects or strafing attacks when designing an airfield.
                  Airfields in forward areas are prime targets for enemy air and ground attacks. It may be necessary
                  to use ground troops in defensive positions against enemy ground action.

FUTURE EXPANSION

     2-29. Due to the unpredictability of military operations, engineer troops are often required to modify and
     expand previously completed construction. The road that is adequate for current maneuvers may be
     inadequate for future operations. Airfields built for small aircraft with a limited evacuation mission may
     require modification to meet stringent design criteria for high-performance aircraft. Improvement and
     expansion are continuing jobs for military construction.

     2-30. Avoid constructing a road or airfield in a restricted area where there is no possibility of expansion.
     Design basic facilities so that they can be used as part of the expanded facilities. The ability to expand an
     existing route or facility will conserve personnel and material and permit rapid completion of future projects.

RECONNAISSANCE OPERATIONS

     2-31. Reconnaissance operations vary with the operational environment; assigned mission; and size, type,
     and composition of the reconnaissance element. An aerial map or ground reconnaissance is necessary to
     determine the best existing or possible location for a future road or airfield.

MISSION

     2-32. The primary mission of a reconnaissance party is to find a site that meets most of the requirements, to
     recommend a general layout and construction plan, to estimate the work required to construct the facility,
     and to obtain the data needed to determine a completion date and detailed construction schedules. Final
     construction plans and schedules are made with regard to the tactical and logistical situation and the
     construction time available.

     2-33. When the reconnaissance mission is complete, a reconnaissance report serves as the basis for tactical
     plans and construction schedules. The reconnaissance report is submitted by the personnel that conducted the
     investigation. It must be complete, comprehensive, and sufficiently detailed to permit careful analysis.

RECONNAISSANCE-PARTY CAPABILITIES

     2-34. Thorough reconnaissance requires qualified, trained, and experienced personnel. The quality of the
     reconnaissance is directly related to the abilities of the party accomplishing it. This is especially true in
     airfield reconnaissance, which requires broader engineering judgment than other engineer reconnaissance.
     Even a qualified civil engineer with civilian or military experience requires special training for this activity.
     It would be unusual for one person to be proficient in every task that a thorough reconnaissance must include;

29 February 2016  TM 3-34.48-1  2-5


---

Chapter 2

     therefore, the assignment of personnel must provide overall efficiency as a unit. The party must be selected
     with regard to the conditions the unit may encounter.

     2-35. Conditions to be considered include the road net, the general nature of the terrain, the weather, the
     prevalence of land mines, the attitude of the civilian population, and the amount of enemy resistance the party
     may expect. These factors also influence equipment assigned to the party. The equipment should include the
     items necessary for soil and topographic surveys, mobility, security, and good communication. The success
     of the mission depends on proper personnel and equipment. One without the other will not accomplish the
     needed results. If available, a soils or terrain analyst is a valuable member of the reconnaissance party. If an
     analyst is not available, obtain soil samples for later analysis.

RECONNAISSANCE STEPS

     2-36. Reconnaissance steps include planning, briefing, a preliminary study, air reconnaissance, and ground
     reconnaissance.

Planning

     2-37. Planning forms the reconnaissance mission. It involves the coordination of reconnaissance efforts by
     appropriate headquarters, the estimation of needs, and the assignment of a reconnaissance mission. Ground
     and aerial methods should be integrated. This is a responsibility of the engineer brigade, the group, or the
     battalion not the individual reconnaissance party. Reconnaissance missions are based on user requirements
     as governed by ground forces. Maintain close liaison with headquarters to achieve proper coordination.
     Improper coordination results in duplication of effort in some areas and inadequate reconnaissance in other
     areas.

Briefing

     2-38. The briefing tells the reconnaissance party exactly which site or area is to be reconnoitered, what is
     already known about the area or site, and what information the party is expected to obtain. Details concerning
     the time or methods of reporting the information will be included in the briefing. The party must also know
     the type of facility it is reconnoitering. If a site has been tentatively selected or if some information has
     already been determined from a preliminary study, the party must be informed. Otherwise, time and effort
     will be wasted. A soils or terrain analyst should brief the reconnaissance party if such an expert is not able to
     accompany the party. If available, aerial photographs should be used in the briefing.

     2-39. The following information is necessary for a full understanding of a particular reconnaissance mission
     and should be covered in the briefing:

              The general area to be covered if an area reconnaissance is required or the exact location of the
                  site or facility to be investigated for a specific reconnaissance.

              The nature of the proposed facility; the types of vehicles or aircraft expected to use it; the length
                  of time use is anticipated; and the minimum requirements for dimensions, grades, and clearances.
                  These items are covered by the applicable standard layout and specifications published by the joint
                  force commander in the theater. The reconnaissance officer may be familiar with the items, but
                  they should be briefed for reference.

              The anticipated vehicle traffic, aircraft, and personnel to be initially accommodated at the
                  proposed facility. When dealing with airfields, figures are often given in terms of the number and
                  type of aviation units to be assigned to the installation. Strength and equipment figures should also
                  be available for reference.

              The minimum amount of aircraft service, repair facilities, and special requirements needed.
              The expected future expansion of the new facility.
              The expected construction time available for building support facilities.
              Information previously obtained about the proposed project.
              The essential details concerning the report and how, when, and to whom the report should be

                  made.

2-6  TM 3-34.48-1  29 February 2016


---

                                                                                                    Reconnaissance and Site Selection

     2-40. When the reconnaissance party will be away from the parent unit for a lengthy, continued
     reconnaissance, additional instructions must be covered in the briefing. The reconnaissance party is briefed
     on locations for drawing rations, clothing, and equipment replacements; drawing petroleum, oil, and lubricant
     supplies; and service facilities for vehicle maintenance. In addition, they are briefed on the type of
     communication equipment (radio, messenger, television satellite) to arrange.

     2-41. When ground reconnaissance is ordered ahead of forward ground-force elements, the following
     additional information is necessary:

              The friendly-force situation.
              The known enemy-force situation.
              The location of adjacent friendly units.

     2-42. The following information is applicable for parties engaged in air reconnaissance:
              The instructions for alternative and emergency-landing.
              The location of available aviation petroleum supplies.
              The location of the forward flying line.

Preliminary Study

     2-43. A preliminary study consists of studying information obtained during the briefing, conducting a map
     reconnaissance of the area, studying aerial photographs, delineating soil boundaries, assembling other
     available preliminary information, and planning and preparing for the actual reconnaissance.

     2-44. Information sources that may be useful in preliminary planning and the preliminary study of a specific
     mission must be verified by ground reconnaissance. These information sources include—

              Intelligence dossiers that provide planning data and other information on a particular airfield site
                  or route that may already exist. These dossiers are the result of previous reconnaissance or
                  reconnaissance plans and can usually be obtained if adequate coordination is maintained with
                  higher headquarters and other units engaged in reconnaissance. Similarly, reports of aerial
                  reconnaissance that were conducted in anticipation of later ground reconnaissance may be
                  available from adjacent or higher units.

              The Office of the Chief of Engineers and subordinate agencies prepare strategic and technical
                  reports, studies, and summaries on areas of actual or potential military importance. These reports
                  provide the best available data at the time of publication. Topographic, geologic, and soil maps
                  and data on climate and groundwater tables are usually included. The reports may contain
                  information on water supply, construction materials, vegetation, and special physical phenomena.

              Army and Air Force tactical intelligence reports are important, reliable sources of information.
                  Intelligence reports are usually prepared in the interior zone but tactical intelligence reports are
                  field-prepared reports of all-around force elements. They may include facts learned by obtained
                  from detainee interrogations, tactical data, reports, records, and interaction with the local
                  population. Intelligence reports are used to prepare strategic and technical reports.

              Road, topographic, soil, vegetation, and geologic maps published by friendly or enemy
                  governments and agencies are sources of information. Maps showing the suitability of terrain for
                  various military purposes may be of considerable value in planning roads and airfields.

              Aerial photographs show the approximate amount of grading and excavation required, the total
                  area and extent of promising sites, the extent of necessary clearing, the presence of flying hazards
                  (for airfields), and the area and local drainage conditions.

              Topographic maps should be prepared from aerial photographs if time and facilities are available.
              Weather reports published by governmental agencies and the Air Force Air Weather Service are

                  used to determine critical factors for runoff determination, prevailing winds, and cloud cover that
                  will affect construction and future operations.

Chapter 2

              Aeronautical reports and charts provide an overview to help plan aerial reconnaissance.
              Indigenous governmental agencies may provide valuable information on a great diversity of

                  subjects.

Air Reconnaissance

     2-45. Air reconnaissance involves a general study of the topography, drainage, and vegetation of an area.
     Construction problems, camouflage possibilities, and access routes should be visualized. Usually the specific
     ground-reconnaissance procedure is planned by selecting areas that need investigated from the air and
     determining what questions need answered. Air reconnaissance provides valuable negative information by
     eliminating unsuitable sites, but it cannot be solely relied on for positive information.

Ground Reconnaissance

     2-46. While air reconnaissance can effectively reduce the amount of ground reconnaissance, it cannot replace
     ground reconnaissance. Questions that are tentatively answered from the air are verified on the ground. Often,
     ground and air reconnaissance are not separate missions. A continuing air reconnaissance may be interspersed
     with specific ground reconnaissance.

REPORTING

     2-47. The reconnaissance party must always submit the report on time. Reports are submitted for sites
     investigated, even if the reconnaissance party considers the site unsuitable.

     2-48. Full details on the method, place, and time of submitting reconnaissance reports should be included in
     the instructions given to the reconnaissance party. Reconnaissance reports can be submitted in writing or by
     secure telecommunications. A radio report should be followed by a detailed written report. Standard
     reconnaissance reports are preferred. They ensure full coverage of needed information and allow a
     comparative evaluation of two or more sites. Standard formats are helpful in comparing sites that have been
     reconnoitered by different parties. This simplifies the reporting process.

     2-49. Military roads and road networks are classified according to their location and use. They are classified
     according to width, surface, and obstructions.

             Notes.

             1. Terms and formulas approved by the member nations of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization,
             the Southeast Asia Treaty Organization, the United States, the United Kingdom, the Canadian and
             Australian Armies Nonmaterial Standardization Program, and other treaty nations are covered in
             FM 3-34.170/MCWP 3-17.4.

             2. Abbreviations, symbols, and notations used in route reconnaissance may also be used in airfield
             reconnaissance. (See FM 3-34.170/MCWP 3-17.4.) Information given in road reconnaissance
             reports is useful in reporting on access roads to airfield and heliport sites.

Air Reconnaissance

     2-50. An air-reconnaissance team generally consists of two members—the pilot and the engineer observer.
     Having the officer in charge of the ground-reconnaissance party serve as the engineer observer for the air-
     reconnaissance party is advantageous and should be arranged when possible. Time is saved and errors of
     omission are minimized because a report from the engineer observer to the officer in charge of the ground-
     reconnaissance party is unnecessary except as a matter of record. The pilot can also assess the site and make
     the appropriate recommendations.

                                                      Reconnaissance and Site Selection

     2-51. Two-place, fixed-wing aircraft or two-place helicopters are suitable for most air-reconnaissance
     missions. Reconnaissance of enemy-occupied airfields is best accomplished with modified tactical aircraft.
     Effective air reconnaissance should provide the information on—

              Terrain features.
              Obstacle descriptions.
              Lines of communication evaluation.
              Area suitability for various construction types.
              Water sources.
              Construction materials in the area of operations.
              Cover and concealment.

Ground Reconnaissance

     2-52. The composition of the ground-reconnaissance party depends on the scope and extent of the mission,
     nature of the terrain it must traverse, probability of enemy contact, attitude of the civilian population, and
     prevalence of mines in the area to be reconnoitered. See table 2-1 for a list of personnel suitable for an airfield
     reconnaissance.

2-53. Personnel involved should be trained in ground reconnaissance. It is important that the person in charge
and the assistant be well versed in the aspects of reconnaissance.

2-54. Equipment needed to carry out the assigned tasks should be taken. The equipment varies as the
composition of the party varies. A typical list of equipment suitable for the party is listed in table 2-2,
page 2-10.

2-55. Map and air studies are not substitutes for ground reconnaissance; they reduce the amount of ground
effort required. Ground reconnaissance should determine the—

        Estimated grades to be encountered.
        Estimated amount of clearing involved, to include trees, tree stumps, and boulders. Sometimes

        Estimated amount of debris that will be generated during clearing operations. In some cases, the

             trees that are removed may be used in the construction operation. (Clearing operations are
             discussed in chapter 4 of this manual.)

ROUTE AND ROAD RECONNAISSANCE

     2-56. Thorough reconnaissance is essential in the selection of roads. It starts with a study of available maps
     and aerial photographs. Aerial reconnaissance provides valuable information. Detailed information, however,
     can be obtained only by ground reconnaissance. Reconnaissance performed in connection with military lines
     of communication is route reconnaissance. Reconnaissance to check existing roads is road reconnaissance.
     Reconnaissance to determine the location for a new road is location reconnaissance.

ROUTE RECONNAISSANCE

     2-57. Route reconnaissance includes gathering information about roads, bridges, tunnels, fords, waterways,
     and natural terrain features that may affect the movement of troops, equipment, and supplies in military
     operations. Route reconnaissance may be hasty or deliberate.

2-10                                      TM 3-34.48-1                                  29 February 2016


---

                                                                                                    Reconnaissance and Site Selection

     2-58. A hasty route reconnaissance is conducted to determine the immediate trafficability of a specified route
     and is limited to critical terrain data. It may be adequately recorded on a map overlay or sketch and be
     supplemented by reports about various aspects of the terrain.

     2-59. A deliberate route reconnaissance is detailed. It provides the data necessary for a thorough analysis
     and classification of significant features along a route, including repair or demolition procedures, if required.
     An overlay is used to point out exact map locations, and enclosures are attached to the overlay. The enclosures
     include a reconnaissance report that provides a permanent record and ensures that enough detail is recorded.
     The use of these forms is explained in FM 3-34.170/MCWP 3-17.4.

ROAD RECONNAISSANCE

     2-60. Road reconnaissance is conducted to determine the traffic capabilities of existing roads and to provide
     more detailed information than needed for route classification. It may include enough information to develop
     work estimates for improving the road to certain standards of trafficability. DA Form 1248 (Road
     Reconnaissance Report) is used to record this information. (See figure 2-2.) Maps, overlays, and sketches are
     used as needed.

                                              Figure 2-2. River action

2-61. The most important factor in planning military roads is making maximum use of the existing road net.
Subject to the requirements of the tactical plan, the existing road net must be adapted to military use before
undertaking new construction. Existing roads should be surveyed at the earliest opportunity to determine
their condition and capacity. Improving an existing road rather than constructing a new one saves time.

2-62. Periodic road reconnaissance is conducted to obtain information about the road situation in a specific
area. A situation map is prepared and kept current to show the condition of roads, the density of traffic, the
need for maintenance work, and the results of maintenance. Periodic reconnaissance is important during wet
or unusually dry weather to determine the effects of these conditions. Maintenance requirements are based
on periodic reconnaissance and must be coordinated with the agencies using the roads to ensure proper
standards of maintenance and to avoid work on roads that are no longer needed.

29 February 2016  TM 3-34.48-1  2-11

Chapter 2

LOCATION RECONNAISSANCE

     2-63. When a new road is necessary, the first step is location reconnaissance. This requires reconnaissance
     of possible routes to ensure selection of the best route. The main objective of a location reconnaissance is to
     locate a new road that will withstand anticipated traffic and provide the best possible operating conditions.

FORDS, DIPS, CAUSEWAYS, AND BRIDGES

     2-64. Gap crossings are vital to road networks and can absorb a significant proportion of the cost of both
     construction and maintenance. It is important that these structures are appropriate to the category and volume
     of the traffic carried. The success or life of these structures depends very much on the hydraulic design. Fords
     and bed-level causeways, like conventional bridges, may be constructed so that they cause little interference
     with the design flood.

FORDS

     2-65. A ford is a shallow place in a waterway where the bottom, naturally or by human improvement, permits
     the passage of personnel and vehicles. A ford is used instead of a bridge when time limitations, the lack of
     structural materials, the tactical situation, and the terrain configuration make its use necessary and practical.
     An increase in water depth can close a ford for a considerable time. Streams in mountainous and desert
     country are subject to sudden changes in depth. An increase in depth can be sudden and endanger personnel
     or vehicles in the ford. Stream bottoms can be composed of material that requires a lot of effort to make fords
     usable.

Reconnaissance

     2-66. Route reconnaissance should include the selection of possible ford sites. Special emphasis is placed on
     the requirements to be discussed in this section. Ford reconnaissance and required reports are covered in FM
     3-34.170/MCWP 3-17.4.

Requirements

     2-67. The characteristics of a good ford are a slow current (usually less than 2 miles per hour); low, sloping
     banks; good approaches; and a uniformly increasing bottom depth with a firm bottom material. See table
     2-3 for width, depth, and bank slope requirements for fords.

                                         Table 2-3. Requirements for military fords

                Maximum    Maximum width     Type of bottom                              Maximum
                  depth        (one-way                                                  allowable
                   (feet)        traffic)                                                slope on
                                  (feet)                                              approaches*

                           3 (single file) Firm enough to prevent sinking            1:1

      Infantry  3 1/2      7 (column of    Boulders and obstacles                    3:1
                           3s)             removed                                   2:1

      Trucks    2          10              Firm and smooth                           2:1
                                                                                     2:1
      Light tanks 1-3      10              Firm and smooth

      Medium                               Firm and smooth

      Heavy tanks 4-6      12              Firm and smooth

      *Based on the hard, dry surface. If wet and slippery, the slope must be less.

2-68. A desirable location for a ford is in the reach of the stream between bends. At this location, the bottom
depth is constant between the banks with a slight channel in the center. The influence of river action on
possible fording locations is shown in figure 2-2, page 2-11. Because of the increased velocity of the water,

2-12                           TM 3-34.48-1                                          29 February 2016


---

                                                                                              Reconnaissance and Site Selection

bends result in a deep channel that is difficult to improve. In the reach, the center channel is not so deep or
sharp and is readily adaptable for improvement. In addition, the variation in the shape of the banks is not as
pronounced in the reach area as it is at the bend.

2-69. For a natural ford, the bottom material should be hard, durable, and interlocking. These materials resist
erosion and cutting by wheeled traffic. The general terrain determines bottom conditions as follows:

        Mountainous terrain. In mountainous country, sudden freshet floods can transport large boulders
             and stones along the bottom. This material is deposited at the passing of high water or where the
             widening of the stream reduces the velocity. It may be necessary to remove this material before
             traffic can cross the ford.

        Moderate or gentle slope terrain. In terrain of moderate or gentle slopes, the velocity will
             prevent the deposition of fine material. This tendency and the scouring action of water will leave
             a good, firm bottom. The bottom material may be disturbed by traffic and will require protection.

        Slightly sloping or flat terrain. In slightly sloping or flat terrain, streams meander and have a
             low velocity. Sometimes there is a high water table. In such cases, the bottom material may be
             very soft. This requires a completely improved ford with special emphasis on bottom
             requirements. Timber, lumber, matting, gravel, or gabions can be used to improve trafficability.

2-70. A maximum water depth of 2 feet is allowable for truck traffic. (See table 2-3.) To ensure maximum
use of the ford, determine the depth that the stream will flow at frequently recurring times. Estimates of
various depths of flow can be made by direct stream observation as follows:

        Base flow. Base flow is the normal flow that occurs in a stream when there has been no recent
             rain. The depth of this flow is dependent on the quantity of the ground water.

        High water flow. During the year, many rainfalls normally occur that cause flows above the base
             level. The velocity generates slight erosion cut. (See figure 2-3, 2-14) The occurrence of such
             flows prevents vegetation growth. Since these flows can occur with relative frequency during the
             year, the depth of these flows could control the use of the ford. In the event that the depth is greater
             in places than the fording depth of trucks, it may be necessary to fill these gaps with rock or gravel.
             (See table 2-3.) However, such filling might cause the velocity of flow over the ford to be increased
             to the point that vehicles would have difficulty using the ford.

        Flood flow. In the absence of records, it is necessary to check stream banks for evidence of
             floodwater levels. The highest level of flood that occurs within a period of two years is of particular
             interest. The bend of a stream, especially with a high bank on the outside of the bend, would show
             an erosion cut that can be used to determine the flood level. (See figure 2-3.)

Chapter 2

                                            Figure 2-3. Stream cross section

     2-71. Carefully note the height of the bank and the type of soil. This information helps to determine
     construction requirements. Normal stream velocity at the fording site should not exceed 3 feet per second.
     This velocity would, in most cases, occur at low or moderate levels.

     2-72. Make a cross section of a ford location similar to those illustrated in figure 2-2, page 2-11, and figure
     2-3. Include full details on the bank slopes, bottom slopes, bottom variations, and water depth. In addition,
     determine the average velocity of the stream from measurements taken at equal intervals across the stream.
     Record the character of the streambed, to include vegetation density and type, whether or not the channel is
     scoured, and the type of soil. This information determines the value of Manning’s roughness coefficient.

Construction

     2-73. The phases of ford construction are—
              Approach Development. The maximum slopes for ford approaches should be as recommended
                  in table 2-3, page 2-12. Place material cut from the banks off to the side and not in the stream
                  where it may form an obstruction, because traffic will wet the slopes and cause eventual
                  deterioration. Provisions should be made for protecting the surface.
              Bottom Preparation. Ford-bottom preparation will depend on site conditions. Fill short, deep
                  gaps with rock or gravel, preferably retained by wire mesh. Soft, mud bottoms can be improved
                  by first covering the bottom with willow, brush mattresses, or timbers. Second, cover the bottom
                  with metal planking, rock, or coarse gravel. Even a hard and tenacious bottom deteriorates under
                  traffic conditions and requires protective maintenance. Consider the following factors when
                  raising the bottom of the ford:
                   The depth upstream from the ford increases in proportion to the amount of rise of the ford
                        bottom.
                   The flow velocity over the ford increases at an increased fording depth. Vehicles may be
                        difficult to operate and control.

Marking

     2-74. Place marking posts at each end of the ford and at as many intermediate points as necessary. Mark a
     post at each end with an index to indicate depth. Warning notices should be clearly and prominently placed
     to alert drivers that flooding can occur suddenly and without warning.

Maintenance

     2-75. Examine fords after each flooding. Repair scour damage upstream and downstream with riprap.
     Remove boulders and other debris to provide a clear passage for vehicles.

2-14       TM 3-34.48-1  29 February 2016


---

                                                                                                    Reconnaissance and Site Selection

DIPS

     2-76. Dips are paved fords used for the crossing of dry, wide, and shallow arroyos in semiarid regions that
     are subject to flash floods.

Reconnaissance

     2-77. The preferred location of a dip is in the straight run of an arroyo or wash. Determine the width between
     the banks and the top elevation of the banks. In addition, check the area above the dip site to determine if
     ponding will occur and to what level.

     2-78. Determine the type of soil in the banks and bottom for construction requirements. In addition, note the
     size and type of bottom rock. This type of information gives an indication of the volume and velocity of flash
     floods that move or carry large material.

     2-79. Investigate the area, especially the banks, to determine the general flash-flood high watermark. This
     information on the area of the waterway, along with an approximation of velocity as indicated by the rock or
     other debris on the bottom, gives some indication of the volume of flow. This information will be necessary
     if bridging is required.

Construction

     2-80. The subgrade should be of erosion-resistant material or a rock-compacted base, and it should be set
     between the cutoff retaining walls. The pavement should be of concrete or compacted macadam. The general
     construction is shown in figure 2-4. Other factors of importance are as follows:

              The site should be in the reach of the stream and well away from any bends. There is more erosion
                  in bends than in straight stretches. If a very severe flood occurred, a structure placed in a bend
                  might be destroyed.

              The structure should be set at right angles to the flow to reduce scour.
              The structure must be set at true dry-streambed level to avoid scour erosion or silting. Under no

                  circumstances should the structure be set above dry-streambed level.

                  Legend:  inch
                  in       minimum
                  min

                  Figure 2-4. Cross section of dip section

Marking

     2-81. The marking for dips is the same as for fords. Place marking posts at each end and at intermediate
     points, as needed. Mark a post at each end with an index to indicate depth. Warning notices should be clearly
     and prominently placed to alert drivers that flooding can occur suddenly and without warning.

Chapter 2

Maintenance

     2-82. Dips, like fords, must be examined after each flooding. Repair scour damage upstream and downstream
     with riprap, and remove boulders and other debris. When macadam is used, holes may be scoured in the
     roadway. Consider stockpiling rock adjacent to the area for immediate maintenance repair.

CAUSEWAYS

     2-83. When it is essential to keep a roadway open during floods of medium intensity, a raised causeway can
     be used in place of a ford or dip. This type of structure must be well sited, carefully designed to pass the flow,
     and strongly built. It must incorporate a sufficient waterway at streambed level to permit the passage of the
     design volume of flow before the flood level reaches the top of the structure. A typical design is shown in
     figure 2-5.

      Legend:       corrugated metal pipe
      CMP      Figure 2-5. Overflow (causeway)

Construction

     2-84. A sufficient cross-sectional area must be provided to ensure that the flood level will not submerge the
     structure. Consider the following basic elements:

              The size and number of culverts or other elements must be sufficient to pass the flow. When the
                  water elevation upstream and downstream is above the culvert crown, pipe equations should be
                  used for flow design.

              The inverts or lowest parts of the culverts must be set at streambed level.
              The cover over the stream must be sufficient enough to protect the waterway against traffic loads.

     2-85. Protect both the upstream and downstream faces of the embankment against scour and erosion. Heavy
     flooding or overtopping of the structure will require complete protection in the form of a concrete or rock-
     gabion facing. To further prevent excessive scour and erosion, carry the protective facings below the
     streambed and provide them with aprons. Anchor the ends of the structure securely into the banks so that
     there is minimum obstruction to water flow.

     2-86. Provide guardrails to guide and direct traffic. Because the structure can be overtopped, prepare for
     ready replacement of the guardrails.

2-16           TM 3-34.48-1                     29 February 2016


---

                                                                                                    Reconnaissance and Site Selection

Maintenance

     2-87. Inspect the structure for scour or erosion after each flow that causes partial submergence or
     overtopping. Repair any damage immediately, otherwise, at the next heavy flow, the structure could be
     destroyed. Stockpiling heavy rock and gabions at each end of a structure may be required.

BRIDGES

     2-88. This section presents elements of bridge design other than the requirements for structural design.
     Bridges must conform to the requirements of stream hydraulics in the same way as cross-stream structures
     (fords, dips, causeways).

Location

     2-89. The location of a bridge should be away from bends in the straight section or reach of the stream (figure
     2-2, page 2-13). In this location, there are moderate, even depths from bank to bank. The deep channel tends
     to be in the center. Abutments will be placed on the edge of the stream. Because of the even distribution of
     flow, scour and erosion at the stream pier and bank abutments are not expected to be so excessive as to cause
     maintenance problems.

Construction

     2-90. The height of a bridge depends on the flood-flow high watermark. The height of that mark will
     determine the profile or superstructure level of the bridges as follows:

              When the flood-flow high watermark is above the banks, a high profile or high-level bridge must
                  be constructed to keep the superstructure above the flood level. This type of bridge is well above
                  the bank level and may require a considerable length and height of approach.

              When the flood-flow high watermark is below the bank level, a low profile or low-level bridge
                  can be constructed. This type of bridge presents fewer problems than the high-level bridge, since
                  approach ramps will not have to be constructed.

     2-91. The location of bridge abutments depends on an analysis of the flood level and the cross section of the
     stream. (See figure 2-6.) Abutments placed at Point 1A and Point 1B present the most direct solution because
     they are located on high, dry ground. Use of these locations, however, may necessitate more construction
     effort because of the increased length of the bridge. This increased length could result in the need for
     intermediate piers and spans. With this method, the full river waterway will be used for the passage of
     floodwater.

    Legend:
    HW high watermark

                                 Figure 2-6. Waterway cross section at bridge site

29 February 2016  TM 3-34.48-1  2-17


---

Chapter 2

     2-92. Abutments placed at Point 2A and Point 2B would reduce construction time because fewer
     intermediate piers and spans would be required. In addition, the fill in Area 1A-2A and Area 1B-2B could be
     accomplished as the bridge is constructed. As can be seen from figure 2-6, page 2-17, this placement reduces
     the cross section of the waterway. The following techniques could be used to accommodate this reduction in
     an available cross-sectional area:

              The elevation of the bridge superstructure could be raised to account for the rise in the flood level.
                  In this case, use substantial abutments that are well protected against end scour.

              The superstructure elevation could be left substantially at the original level, and approach ramps
                  over Area 1A-2A and Area 1B-2B could be constructed as causeways to allow for flow. Care must
                  be taken to ensure that there is no excessive scour or erosion below the culvert outlet that would
                  affect the roadway.

              The roadway approaches in Area 1A-2A and Area 1B-2B could be depressed below the
                  superstructure level. In this case, the excess flood flow would pass over the roadway approaches,
                  thus relieving the bridge flow. If this action is taken, the roadway may not be usable at all times.
                  Since overflow is anticipated, the construction of these approaches is similar to construction of
                  causeways without the culverts. If the bridge is designed properly with fording depths as outlined
                  in table 2-3, page 2-12, it may be usable during floods under extreme conditions.

              When a depressed roadway or an elevated superstructure is used, the approach to the bridge must
                  have a gentle slope to prevent vehicle impact on the abutment and to ensure traffic visibility.

Drainage

     2-93. The soil behind bridge abutments can become saturated because of rain or other conditions. This
     saturation can take place whether the approach road is at the natural grade of the soil or it is a filled approach.
     When saturation occurs, static hydraulic pressure on the back face of the abutment generates additional
     overturning movement. With wood abutments, this condition is relieved naturally. However, if concrete
     abutments are used, the pressures can be relieved as follows:

              Step 1. Use weep holes to pierce the abutments with bagged gravel backing on the soil side.
              Step 2. Place gravel backing against the lower part of the abutment drained by a perforated pipe

                  at the footing elevation. Set the pipe to drain out at the sides of the abutment.

ENGINEER RECONNAISSANCE

     2-94. Engineer reconnaissance is often conducted in conjunction with deliberate route reconnaissance to
     determine route conditions (including work estimates) and to locate construction materials to improve or
     maintain the route. The types of engineer reconnaissance are general and special. General engineering
     reconnaissance gathers engineering information of a broad nature within the operational area to locate and
     evaluate construction materials, resources, terrain features, and facilities that have engineer implications.
     Special engineer reconnaissance obtains detailed information regarding an investigation of a specific site or
     evaluates the potential use of an undeveloped facility, such as an airport or heliport. DA Form 1711 (Engineer
     Reconnaissance Report) is a required enclosure to the route reconnaissance. (See FM
     3-34.170/MCWP 3-17.4 for additional information.)

AIRFIELD RECONNAISSANCE

     2-95. Airfield reconnaissance differs from road-location reconnaissance in the scope of information. (See
     FM 3-34.170/MCWP 3-17.4 for additional information.) An airfield project involves more personnel,
     machine hours, and material than a road project. Air traffic imposes more severe limitations on its traffic
     facilities than vehicular traffic. Consequently, the site selected must be the best site available.

     2-96. Recent advances in geographic information system technologies allow reconnaissance efforts to be
     conducted in a digital environment. Most data sets used in theaters of interest are archived digitally and can
     be readily loaded into commercial software with relevant features highlighted for analysis. Key design
     parameters can be overlain from data obtained from several map types to create a composite view of the area
     of interest to help with selecting airfield locations or expansions.

2-18  TM 3-34.48-1  29 February 2016


---

                                                                                                    Reconnaissance and Site Selection

PLANNING

     2-97. Tentative airfield sites are selected within enemy territory using map and aerial photograph
     reconnaissance, supplementing data from reports of aerial observers or intelligence sources. These sites may
     be undeveloped potential sites or operating enemy installations. Reconnaissance should begin as soon as
     possible.

     2-98. Most known airfield locations, the geometry, and the civilian population attitude are contained within
     digital archives that can be readily queried for an area of interest. It is recommended that the planning team
     access the required geographic information systems for an area of interest to direct future air and ground
     reconnaissance.

     2-99. For an undeveloped potential site, the object of the reconnaissance is to verify or amend tentative
     selections and layouts and estimate the material, equipment, and troop requirements for the construction
     planned. If it is a captured enemy airfield, a decision to use the captured field or develop a completely new
     site is needed. Estimates for the engineering effort necessary to restore the airfield may also be required.

     2-100. New airfields added to an area where friendly aircraft are operating can be developed as follows:
              Select the best available map of the area where a new airfield will be located. Draw a 5 mile
                  diameter circle around existing airfields, and shade them. Note high-tension, electric transmission
                  lines and shade a 2 mile wide strip centered on these lines. Locate and shade similar obstructions
                  on the map. Assault or hasty airfield selection is discussed in TM 3-34.48-2. This exercise can
                  now be performed in a digital environment expeditiously. Most archived aerial maps contain
                  layers of information grouped according to features of interest (power lines, roadways, streams,
                  railways) that can be turned on or off to allow rapid viewing of potential hazards.
              Confine the study for a potential airfield to the unshaded parts of the map. Look for sites of
                  sufficient area (preferably flat with good natural drainage, unobstructed air approaches, and
                  accessibility to routes of communication). Assign the most likely sites to reconnaissance parties
                  for appropriate air and ground investigation.

SELECTING A RUNWAY LOCATION

     2-101. An airfield siting template is a convenient way to select a runway location that meets glide-angle
     requirements at a site. (See figure 2-7, page 2-20.) This template can be drawn on acetate or heavy cellophane
     to place on a map. The template indicates specifications for flight way, horizontal approach, and glide angle.
     When placed on the map, the template shows landforms and natural or manufactured obstacles that are in or
     above the plane of the glide angle.

     2-102. Digital geographic information system environments allow similar airfield sighting from a
     computer. For elevation information, the ready availability of digital satellite terrain elevation data imagery
     can provide topography at a coarse scale to allow rapid determination of potential airfield sites.

     2-103. For example, a hill within the approach zone at a distance of 8,000 feet from the end of the overrun
     with an elevation of more than 160 feet above the end of a proposed runway is in a 50:1 glide angle. (See
     figure 2-7.) This runway location would be unsuitable according to the specifications. The template is a useful
     tool for the reconnaissance officer and the preliminary planning group. Prepared templates can measure
     distances in feet, yards, miles, and kilometers by placing gradations along the edges.

      ft       Figure 2-7. Sample airfield-siting template

PROCEDURES FOR AIRFIELD AIR RECONNAISSANCE

     2-104. While en route to a site or general area, the engineer notes open borrow pits, large construction
     material stockpiles, rail and road access to the site, and errors on the maps that have been studied. The pilot
     plays an important role on the reconnaissance team. Besides chauffeuring the engineer officer, the pilot
     considers approaches, mental hazards, and physical obstructions related to tactical aircraft that may use the
     proposed installation. A pilot familiar with operational requirements and the performance characteristics of
     tactical aircraft is valuable.

     2-105. The engineer observer assesses possible construction problems at a potential site. The engineer
     selects tentative sites and directs questions to the ground reconnaissance party. The engineer receives the
     pilot’s suggestions concerning flying related characteristics of the sites investigated and modifies estimates
     according to these recommendations.

     2-106. To be effective as an engineer observer, the officer should possess the following qualifications:
              Knowledge of road and airfield requirements and construction procedures.
              Experience in airfield work.
              Immunity to airsickness. An airsick officer cannot effectively accomplish air reconnaissance. A
                  tendency to become airsick is greatly enhanced by the continual concentration on a particular site
                  and the steep turns and maneuvers essential to continued observation.
              Proficiency in map reading. Upon approaching a designated or tentatively selected site for
                  reconnaissance, the normal altitude for the first circuit is approximately 300 feet. Nothing more
                  than orientation can be accomplished in this circuit. Sometimes a site tentatively selected during
                  an area search can be eliminated during this circuit or the next few passes.

2-20           TM 3-34.48-1                                 29 February 2016


---

                                                                                                    Reconnaissance and Site Selection

     2-107. Similar second and third passes are flown. Obstructions, main slopes, and general features are noted
     during these circuits. The pilot begins to formulate an estimate of flying related characteristics of the field.
     Pinpoints for the ends of the runway are made on the map but additional trips should be flown across the area
     if necessary.

     2-108. After the runway has been selected, an initial low pass is made at about 50 yards to one side of the
     proposed centerline. A second pass in the opposite direction is flown on the other side of the centerline. Both
     of these flights should be made at a constant air speed so that the runway length can be estimated by
     multiplying the air speed by the average flight time.

             Note. The length is usually overestimated when flying at low air speeds if a strong wind is blowing
             along the centerline. This can be decreased if the distances obtained by two passes in opposite
             directions along the centerline are averaged (assuming that the wind is constant).

     2-109. A final circuit is then flown at approximately 200 feet. During this trip, the ends and centerline of
     the runway are given a final check, and the pilot completes the appraisal of the fields flying suitability.

     2-110. In departing, the observer reviews dispersal areas and checks access roads again. Additional passes
     over the site are made if questions arise as a result of this last check. An air reconnaissance report format
     similar to figure 2-8, page 2-22, may be used.

     2-111. An area reconnaissance proceeds with an inspection of other possible sites. Complete notes must be
     kept to avoid reviewing sites that have been already checked. However, reinvestigation of the final site
     selected and selected alternative sites may sometimes be necessary.

PROCEDURES FOR AIRFIELD GROUND RECONNAISSANCE

     2-112. The ground-reconnaissance phase is preceded by map and air reconnaissance to discover what
     specific sites and questions warrant ground investigation.

     2-113. The reconnaissance party should properly record the general condition of roads and bridges, the
     location of usable or repairable railheads, the locally available materials and equipment, and potential water
     points to be investigated on the ground. When reconnaissance of a definite site is involved, a more detailed
     observation of the access route should be made. A check must be made of bridge capacities, overhead
     clearances, features that might hinder the movement of construction equipment to the site, and the suitability
     of railheads and sidings for use in construction. A detailed report of the quantity and quality of materials
     available at quarries, pits, and stockpiles must be prepared.

     2-114. When the site to be surveyed is reached, the most likely locations for a runway must be investigated.
     If the terrain is open enough to permit good observation, these locations may be quickly determined.
     Locations for runways are traversed by vehicle or on foot. A rough survey of each selected runway is carried
     out immediately and ideally conducted with global positioning system referenced positions. Lengths are
     paced, critical slopes are measured with a clinometer, and directions are determined with a magnetic compass.

     2-115. The type of soil is noted and observations of a few samples are made. A preliminary check of a
     possible runway can be made in 15 minutes if the country is reasonably clear and open.

2-116. Soil type plays a critical role in the design and construction of a runway, taxiway, or apron. It
determines what the required level of effort will be to improve the natural ground. It also determines the
suitability of the surrounding soils to provide sufficient bearing strength to withstand the structural loads of
the intended aircraft.

2-117. Expedient soil evaluations can be performed, and the rapid soils analysis kit that is tailored to
evaluate soils in contingency aircraft operations can be used. These techniques can be conducted within 1 to
2 hours. (See TM 3-34.43/MCRP 3-17-7H/NAVFAC MO 330/AFH 32-1034) and United States Army

2-22       TM 3-34.48-1                                         29 February 2016


---

                                                                                              Reconnaissance and Site Selection

Engineer Research and Development Center, Geotechnical and Structures Laboratory (ERDC/GSL) TR-08-
3 for additional information.)

2-118. If the area is rough and is not sufficiently open to permit a quick selection of runway locations, a
detailed search must be made on foot. The reconnaissance officer, accompanied by necessary personnel,
follows the centerline of the area for the runway and dispersal areas. The reconnaissance officer notes the
obstacles (gullies, rocky outcrops, swampy areas) that cannot readily be eliminated on a large-scale map or
sketch. Examination of the results discloses possible runway locations.

2-119. The best runway location is selected by considering these centerline investigations with prevailing
wind direction; air approaches; glide angles; groundwater conditions; and discharge areas for collected
runoff, clearing, grubbing, and earthwork. If a suitable runway does not exist, a negative site report on the
site is submitted.

2-120. Once the selection of a potential runway is made, a careful and detailed walk of the runway centerline
is made to recheck its suitability. Stakes are driven at each end of the runway, and prominent features are
properly referenced to expedite the runway location by construction unit surveyors.

2-121. The reconnaissance party survey sergeant stakes out the centerline of the runway and runs a ground
profile at the centerline and each shoulder line. Levels are taken at 500-foot intervals and at intermediate
breaks or slope changes. In a flat area, this interval may be increased to as much as 1,000 feet. If an alternative
runway is selected, a similar survey is conducted for that runway if time permits. The soils analyst conducts
a field investigation of the soil conditions at the site. Refer to chapter 10 of this manual for more information
about soil conditions.

2-122. Previously acquired information is checked for accuracy at the site. Errors, including discrepancies
on the maps and mistakes, are included in the report. (See figure 2-9, page 2-24, for a sample report of aerial
photograph interpretations format.)

2-123. When possible, local inhabitants are interviewed to check information already obtained and to obtain
more information. Several opinions should be obtained. Questions should be phrased to provide the best
comparison of answers. The information must be weighed carefully with regard to the credibility of each
person questioned.

2-124. The reconnaissance of a designated site should be accomplished in one day unless hostile forces
delay the work. A specific reconnaissance of a captured enemy airfield is somewhat different. Detailed
information about existing facilities and their condition is desired. (See figure 2-10, page 2-25, for a sample
reconnaissance report of a captured enemy airfield format.) A structural strength of the supporting layers will
add tremendous value to the survey through the use of a dynamic cone penetrometer. (See TM 3-34.43/MCRP
3-17-7H/NAVFAC MO 330/AFH 32-1034 for additional information.)

     2-125. When reconnaissance parties are operating at a considerable distance from the headquarters directing
     the reconnaissance, it is imperative that an initial report reaches headquarters without delay. Submit
