                                                 Chapter 3

                 Surveys and Earthwork Operations

         Construction surveys are initiated when new construction is necessary. These surveys
         provide data for earthwork estimation (including the estimation method to use) and
         information for the mass diagram. The finished survey books should be filed with the
         construction project records of the operations and training officer (United States
         Army). The earthwork operation is one of the most important construction aspects in
         road and airfield construction. Earthwork requires the greatest amount of engineering
         effort from the standpoint of personnel and equipment. Therefore, planning,
         scheduling, and supervision of earthwork operations are important in obtaining an
         efficiently operated construction project.

CONSTRUCTION SURVEYS

     3-1. Construction surveying is the orderly process of obtaining data for various phases of construction
     activity. It includes the following surveys: reconnaissance, preliminary, final location, and construction
     layout. The reconnaissance and preliminary surveys are used to determine the best location. The remaining
     surveys are conducted after a location has been established.

     3-2. The purpose of construction surveys is to control construction activities. The number and extent of
     surveys conducted is governed by the time available, the construction standard desired, and the availability
     of personnel and materials. In the combat zone, roads and airfields are constructed with minimum preplanning
     and construction control activities. However, extensive surveys may be conducted for a deliberate project in
     the communications zone. The quality and efficiency of construction is directly proportional to the number
     and extent of surveys and other preplanning activities. The principles and techniques of field surveying are
     discussed in detail in TM 3-34.55. The equipment used for the surveys can be manual, automated, and global
     positioning system surveying equipment. There are off the shelf software packages that provide the ability to
     support the raw survey data and develop a three-dimensional geometric design model and a set of
     construction drawings.

     3-3. After completing a thorough construction survey, transfer the design information from the computer
     software to automated survey equipment and then to the field on construction stakes. These stakes are the
     guides and reference markers for earthwork operations. Mark the stakes so that the construction conforms to
     the planned line and construction crews properly interpret the grade of the road or airfield and the information
     on the stakes.

RECONNAISSANCE

     3-4. The reconnaissance survey provides the basis for selecting acceptable sites and routes and furnishes
     information for use on subsequent surveys. If the location cannot be selected on the basis of the
     reconnaissance survey, it must be determined by the preliminary survey.

PRELIMINARY

     3-5. The preliminary survey is a detailed study of a location tentatively selected on the basis of
     reconnaissance, survey information, and recommendations. It consists of running a traverse along a proposed
     route, recording topography, and plotting results. For roads, it may be necessary to conduct several
     preliminary surveys if the reconnaissance party has investigated more than one suitable route. Establish,
     station, and profile the route centerline with horizontal and vertical control points. Take cross-section
     readings to allow rough calculations of the earthwork involved. Sometimes cross sections may be taken

29 February 2016  TM 3-34.48-1  3-1


---

Chapter 3

     during the reconnaissance survey if the conditions warrant. If the best available route has not been chosen,
     select it at this time.

     3-6. An airfield survey establishes controls, notes terrain features, measures glide-angle clearance, makes
     soil profiles, and investigates drainage patterns and approaches. Accurately establish the final centerline
     during this survey.

FINAL LOCATION

     3-7. As time permits, conduct a final location survey. Establish permanent benchmarks for vertical control
     and well-marked points for horizontal control. These points are called hubs because of the short, square stake
     used; hub stakes are 2 inches by 2 inches. On most surveys, the hub is driven flush with the ground, and a
     tack in the top of the stake marks the exact point for angular and linear measurements. A flat guard stake—
     extended above the ground and driven in at a slope so that the top is over the hub—indicates the hub location.
     The guard stake is about 3/4 inch by 3 inches.

Horizontal Control

     3-8. The purpose of horizontal control is to accurately determine horizontal locations for the various
     facilities of an engineering project. Establish permanent, well-marked points for horizontal control and
     reference them at the site before construction begins. On a large facility, establish a grid network and use it
     for this control. Tie the network into the military grid system in the particular area, if such a system has been
     established. On an airfield, place control points beyond the clear zone. These points define the centerline of
     the runway and other important sections of the airfield.

     3-9. As taxiways and other facilities are laid out, establish and reference new control points. In laying out
     the centerline, place target boards at each end of the runway so that the surveyor can make frequent checks
     on alignment while the line is being staked out. Target boards may be set up on a line that requires precision
     alignment. Reference control stakes, and replace them if they are disturbed or lost. Locate the target board
     just beyond the outermost control point stake.

Vertical Control

     3-10. Vertical control methods determine the difference in elevation between points. If available, establish a
     level reference surface or datum from a known benchmark. Differences in elevation, with corrections, are
     subtracted from or added to this assigned value, resulting in elevation of the points. Take the benchmark
     system datum from a known elevation or barometer reading or make an arbitrary assumption for establishing
     relative elevation differences.

CONSTRUCTION LAYOUT

     3-11. The construction layout survey is the final preconstruction operation. It provides alignments, grades,
     and locations that guide construction operations. The survey includes determining exact placement of the
     centerline; laying out curves; setting remaining stakes, grades, and shoulders; staking out necessary
     structures; laying out culvert sites; and performing other work required to begin construction. Continue this
     survey until construction is completed.

CONSTRUCTION STAKES

     3-12. Use construction stakes for centerline, slope, offset, shoulder, grade, reference, ditch, culvert,
     intermediate, and temporary benchmarks. The stakes should be approximately 1 inch by 3 inches by 2 feet.
     Use finished lumber when possible. If it is not possible to use finished lumber, use small trees or branches
     blazed on both sides and cut to length. Finished grade stakes and temporary benchmarks are 2 inches by 2
     inches by 12 inches. Place stakes using a three- to five-person crew equipped with manual or automated
     survey equipment or a real-time kinematic global positioning system, an ax, sledgehammer, and machete.

3-2  TM 3-34.48-1  29 February 2016


---

                                                                                                     Surveys and Earthwork Operations

     3-13. The primary functions of construction stakes are to indicate facility alignment control elevations, guide
     equipment operators, and eliminate unnecessary work. They also determine the clearing width required by
     indicating the cut and fill limits at right angles to the centerline of a road.

     3-14. Mark and place construction stakes to conform to the planned line and grade of the proposed facility.
     Use colored marking crayons to mark the stakes. Use a uniform system so that the construction crew can
     properly interpret the information on the stakes. Construction stakes indicate the—

              Stationing or location of a part of the facility in relation to its starting point. If the stake is located
                  at a critical point (such as a point of curvature, point of intersection, or point of tangency of a
                  curve), note this on the stake.

              Cut or fill height from the existing ground surface to the top of the subgrade for centerline stakes
                  or to the shoulder grade for shoulder or slope stakes.

              Horizontal distance from the centerline to the stake location.
              Side-slope ratio used on slope stakes.

     3-15. The number and location of stakes used differ between roads and airfields. A typical set of construction
     stakes consists of a centerline stake and two slope stakes, and it is referred to as a three-point system. Point
     one is the centerline of the facility. Points two and three are the construction limits of the cut and fill at right
     angles to the centerline.

CENTERLINE OR ALIGNMENT

     3-16. The centerline or alignment (hub) stakes are placed on the centerline of a road or airfield and indicate
     its alignment, location, and direction. (See figure 3-1.) They are the first stakes placed, and they must be
     located accurately. These stakes are used as reference points in locating the remaining stakes. Centerline
     stakes are placed at 100-foot intervals. On rough ground or sharp horizontal and vertical curves, place the
     stakes closer together. Stake the point of curvature, point of intersection, and point of tangency on horizontal
     curves. On vertical curves, stake the point of vertical curvature, the point of vertical intersection, the point of
     vertical tangency, and the low point or high point of the curve.

                  Legend:  centerline
                  ℄

                           Figure 3-1. Centerline stakes

3-17. Place centerline stakes with the broad sides perpendicular to the centerline. The side of the stake that
faces the starting point is the front. Mark the front of the stake with a symbol for centerline and point of
curvature, point of intersection, or point of tangency if applicable. On the front, mark the distance from zero
or the starting point in 100-foot stations and the fractional part of a station if used. For example,
6 + 5422 marked on a stake indicates that it is 654.22 feet from the origin of the facility and is known as the
station of this point. Stations are used in locating sections of construction and in preparing reports.

29 February 2016           TM 3-34.48-1                   3-3


---

Chapter 3

     3-18. Place the amount of cut or fill required at the station on the reverse side of the stake. A cut is marked
     with a C, and a fill is marked with an F. A centerline stake placed at Station 78 + 00 and requiring a fill of
     6 feet to bring this station up to the final grade line would be placed as shown in figure 3-1, page 3-3.

     3-19. The cut or fill amount indicates the difference between the final grade line and the ground line where
     the stake is placed. A point on the stake is seldom used as the line of reference to the final grade.

     3-20. To prevent misinterpretation of the cut or fill amount, decimal parts of a foot are written smaller, raised,
     and underlined. (See figure 3-1.) Facing the direction of increasing stations, the centerline forms the dividing
     line between the right and left sides of the area to be graded. When facing either side of the centerline, it is
     customary to refer to the areas as the right or left side.

SLOPE

     3-21. Slope stakes define the limits of grading work. (See figure 3-2.) When used in read work, they can be
     used as guides to determine the clearing width necessary. The area to be cleared usually extends 6 feet beyond
     the slope stakes. Set slope stakes on lines perpendicular to the centerline (one on each side), at points where
     the cut and fill slopes intersect the natural ground surface. Stakes at points of zero cut or fill are placed sloping
     outward from the centerline.

     Legend:  center
     C        centerline
     ℄

     Figure 3-2. Marking and placing slope stakes

     3-22. Sloping stakes outward allows equipment to work up to the stake without removing it. The slope
     indicates the direction of the centerline of the road, and equipment operators can read the stakes easier. Place
     slope stakes at 100-foot intervals on tangents and at 50-foot intervals on horizontal or vertical curves. When
     a sharp break in the original ground profile occurs, it should be staked.

     3-23. The front of a slope stake is the side facing the centerline. On this side of the stake, mark the difference
     in elevation between the natural ground elevation at this point and the finished grade at the edge of the
     shoulders. Under this figure, place another figure that indicates the horizontal distance from the centerline of
     the road to the slope stake. Place the station number on the other side of the stake. Below the station number,
     indicate the appropriate slope ratio. Figure 3-2 shows the proper markings for a slope stake in a typical
     situation.

3-4           TM 3-34.48-1                         29 February 2016


---

                                                                                                     Surveys and Earthwork Operations

OFFSET

     3-24. Equipment used on a cut or fill section may destroy or remove many of the grade (centerline, shoulder,
     or slope) stakes. To prevent loss of man-hours and repetition of survey work, caution construction crews to
     protect grade stakes when possible. Place offset stakes beyond construction limits to avoid resurveying
     portions of the road to relocate these stakes. Figure 3-3 shows offset stakes used to relocate the original
     stakes.

                                   Figure 3-3. Marking and placing offset stakes

     3-25. Place offset stakes on a line at right angles to the centerline of the facility. From these, the slope stakes
     can easily be located. After relocating a slope stake, relocate the centerline stake by measuring toward the
     centerline of the road the horizontal distance indicated on the slope stake, and place the new centerline stake
     at that location.

     3-26. An offset stake contains the information given on the original slope stake plus the difference in
     elevation and horizontal distance from the original slope stake to the offset stake. Mark the offset distance
     on the front of the stake, and circle it to indicate that it is an offset reference. If the offset stake is at a different
     elevation from the slope stake, the cut or fill value must be increased or decreased by the difference in
     elevation. An offset stake placed at a horizontal distance of 10 feet from and 1 foot above the right slope
     stake would be placed and marked as shown in figure 3-3. The surveyor and grade supervisor coordinate on
     the meaning of the markings, regardless of the type of marking used.

FINISH-GRADE

     3-27. Use wooden stakes (2 inches by 2 inches) with the tops colored red or blue for finish-grade stakes.
     Finish-grade stakes, also called blue tops or red tops, indicate the final grade elevation of the completed
     facility. They are used when the grade is within inches of the final elevation. Do not use these stakes in
     combat road construction except in areas with steep slopes. This type of stake normally requires a guard stake
     to protect it and indicate its location. On large projects, it may be impractical to use guard stakes with each
     finish-grade stake.

     3-28. There are no markings on finish-grade stakes other than the color on the top. These stakes may be set
     for use with the top of the stake exactly at the finished grade or with the top of the stake above the finished
     grade. This is decided by the surveyor and construction foreman.

29 February 2016  TM 3-34.48-1  3-5


---

Chapter 3

     3-29. With the final-grade stakes set and marked at a predetermined distance above the finished grade, stretch
     a string between two stakes across the work area, and use a graduated ruler or stick to check the elevation.
     On an airfield layout, place these stakes along the centerline, edge of pavement, intermediate lines, shoulder
     lines, and ditch slopes. For roadwork, place the stakes along the centerline and the edge of the shoulder; they
     may or may not be placed on the slopes.

REFERENCE

     3-30. Many hubs marking the location of highways and airfields are uprooted or covered during construction.
     They must be replaced, often more than once, before construction is complete. As an aid in relocating a point
     that may become hidden by vegetation, or as a means of replacing points that may have been destroyed,
     measurements are made to nearby permanent or semipermanent objects. This process is known as referencing
     or witnessing a point. On many surveys, permanent objects may not be available as reference points. In such
     cases, additional stakes may be driven. These stakes are approximately 2 inches by 2 inches by 18 inches.

     3-31. There are no markings on a reference stake. A point can be referenced by a known distance and a
     known angle or by two known distances. A transit must be used in the first case and may be used as an
     advantage in the second case. The method of using two known distances can be used when a transit is not
     available. Place two points at measured distances from the point to be referenced. Use two tapes to relocate
     the original point or stake. Hold the zero end of one tape on one reference point and the zero end of the other
     tape on the other reference point. The point of intersection of the two tapes at the respective distances gives
     the location of the point in question.

     3-32. To be of most value in replacing a missing station or point, the reference stakes will be less than 100
     feet from the point and, if possible, the arcs should intersect at approximate right angles. Place the stakes
     outside the construction limits, and indicate their location by blazing trees or additional stakes. Normally, the
     location of the reference stakes can be obtained from the surveyor’s notebook.

CULVERT

     3-33. Culvert stakes are located on a line parallel to, and offset by a few feet from, the centerline. The
     information required on the culvert stakes includes the distance from the stake to the centerline, the vertical
     distance to the invert, and the station number. Once the survey crew has finished staking out the culvert, the
     construction supervisor can place the pipe accurately by using batter boards.

BENCHMARKS

     3-34. Vertical control of a road or airfield must be maintained during construction. To do this, points of
     known elevation must be established. Obtain elevations from permanent monuments, known as benchmarks,
     established by geodetic surveys. From these benchmarks, run a line of levels and set temporary benchmarks.
     On small projects, running the levels from a point of assumed elevation frequently sets the temporary
     benchmarks. This is especially true of construction in combat areas.

     3-35. Usually, temporary benchmarks are placed at 500- to 1,000-foot intervals and are placed off the limits
     of construction. Stakes 2 inches by 2 inches, solidly placed in the ground, may be used for this purpose.
     However, a nail driven into a tree, a manhole cover, or a pipe driven into the ground may also be used.
     Frequently, reference points serve as temporary benchmarks. Temporary benchmarks are set before
     centerline stakes are set because vertical control must be established before construction begins.

EARTHWORK ESTIMATION

     3-36. Earthwork computations involve calculating earthwork volumes, determining final grades, balancing
     cuts and fills, and planning the most economical haul route for material. How exact earthwork computations
     are depends on the extent and accuracy of field measurements, which are controlled by the time available
     and the type of construction involved. To plan a schedule, the quantity of earthwork and the soil and haul
     conditions must be known so that the most efficient type and quantity of earthmoving equipment can be
     chosen and the appropriate time allotted.

3-6  TM 3-34.48-1  29 February 2016


---

                                                                                                     Surveys and Earthwork Operations

     3-37. When time is critical, earthwork quantities are estimated very roughly or not at all. When time is not
     critical, higher construction standards are possible, and earthwork quantities are estimated and controlled by
     more precise methods.

FUNDAMENTAL VOLUME DETERMINATION

     3-38. The volume of a rectangular object may be determined by multiplying the area at one end by the length
     of the object. This relationship can be applied to the earthwork determination by considering road cross
     sections at the stations along the road as the end areas and the horizontal distance between cross sections as
     the lengths. The end areas of the cross sections must be computed before volumes can be calculated. If a
     three-dimensional computer software package is used in the road or airfield design, volume determinations
     are calculated using the survey and design data.

END-AREA DETERMINATION METHODS

     3-39. When the construction area centerline has been located, measurements are taken in the field to compute
     the required quantities of cut or fill. A cross-sectional view of the land is plotted from these measurements.
     The cross sections are taken on vertical planes at right angles to the centerline. Where the ground surface is
     regular, cross sections are taken at every full station (100 feet). Where the ground is irregular, they must be
     taken at intermediate points as determined by the surveyor. (See figure 3-4 for a typical cross section.)

                  Legend:  centerline
                  ℄

                           Figure 3-4. Typical fill cross section

3-40. Plot ground elevations from the surveyor’s notes. Make a sectional template of the subgrade that shows
the finished subgrade and slopes plotted to the same scale as the cross sections. Superimpose the template on
the cross section, and adjust it to the correct centerline elevation. Trace the template and extend the side
slopes to intersect the original ground. If the section involves cut and fill, draw the appropriate lines of each
template. When the sections are complete, begin the end-area measurements and determine the volume. Of
the several satisfactory methods of measuring the end areas, only the trapezoidal, stripper, double-meridian
(triangular), and planimeter methods will be described in this manual. The method chosen will depend on the
time available, the accuracy desired, the available equipment, and the engineer’s preference.

Trapezoidal

     3-41. The trapezoidal method is widely used to determine end areas. The computations are tedious, but the
     results are accurate. In using the trapezoidal method, the area of a cross section is obtained by dividing the
     cross section into triangles and trapezoids, computing the area of each part separately and taking the total
     area of the verticals to the ground line to divide the cross section into two triangles and two trapezoids. (See
     figure 3-5, page 3-8.) Make the assumption that the ground is perfectly straight between these selected points
     on the ground line. While this is not usually correct, the assumption is within the accuracy normally required.

Basic Formulas

     3-42. Before the area of the cross section can be computed, the basic formulas for the computation of the
     areas of triangles and trapezoids must be understood. If a line is drawn from one of the vertices of a triangle
     perpendicular to the side or base opposite this vertex, the line formed represents the altitude of the triangle.
     (See figure 3-6.) The area of a triangle can be expressed as the product of one-half the base multiplied by the
     altitude. This relationship is expressed by the following formula:

                          𝐴𝐴 = 0.5𝑏𝑏ℎ

     where—     base
     b =        altitude
     h =

                Legend:   base
                b         altitude
                h

                Figure 3-6. Triangle base and height dimension locations

     3-43. A trapezoid is a four-sided figure having two sides parallel but not equal in length. (See figure 3-7.) If
     a perpendicular line crosses the two parallel sides of the bases, the distance between the two bases along this
     perpendicular line is the altitude of the trapezoid. The area of a trapezoid can be expressed as the average
     length of the bases multiplied by the altitude. This relationship can be expressed by the following formula:

                          𝐴𝐴 = 0.5(𝑏𝑏1 + 𝑏𝑏2)ℎ

     where—     base
     b =        altitude
     h =

Area Computation

     3-44. The first step in computing areas by the trapezoidal method is to break the cross-sectional area into
     triangles and trapezoids by drawing verticals. (See figure 3-5.) Determine the area of these small figures
     using the appropriate formula.

     3-45. To determine the appropriate dimensions, the notes taken by the surveyors must be known. The cross-
     section notes taken in the field are in fractional form. The number below the line indicates the horizontal
     distance from the centerline to that point on the ground. The number above the line indicates the ground
     elevation of that point. Points on the grade line of the proposed road are written in a similar manner and are
     obtained by computations from the final grade line to be established. (See figure 3-8.) Thus, the note 32.0

                                                                                                                                                                                               21

     indicates that the point is at elevation 32.0 and 21 feet from the centerline of the road. If the cross section is
     divided into triangles and trapezoids by erecting verticals, obtain notes for the centerline, shoulders, and end
     slopes to solve for the area.

                Figure 3-8. Cross-section cut showing distances and elevations

3-46. To solve the triangles and trapezoids formed, consider the bases of these figures to be vertical and the
altitudes to be horizontal. Vertical bases are found by subtracting elevations, and horizontal altitudes are
found by subtracting horizontal distances from the closest vertical in the direction of the centerline.

Stripper Method

     3-47. The stripper method is a variation of the trapezoidal method. (See figure 3-9.) To use this method,
     measure (graphically) the lengths, and multiply the sum by the constant width. The distance between vertical
     lines may be a value, but it must be constant throughout the cross-section area. In rough terrain, the vertical
     lines should be closer together to ensure greater accuracy.

              Figure 3-9. Fill cross section arranged to show the stripper method

   3-48. One of the easiest and most convenient ways to measure the vertical lines is with a strip of paper or
   plastic. Lay the strip along the vertical lines, adding the lines to get a total. The strip will show the sum of
   the vertical lines in the same scale that the cross section is plotted. This figure, multiplied by the width, will
   give the area of the cross section.

   3-49. Inaccuracies result when a triangle or trapezoid falls within the limits of the width or when the area is
   curved. However, the method is rapid, and the accuracy is adequate under urgent conditions. Figure 3-10
   shows a typical cross section with a stripper marked to show the total length of the vertical lines and the
   width. The stripper indicates that the sum of the vertical lines is 21.7 feet (the width is 10 feet). Applying
   these figures to the formula, then—

                               𝐴𝐴 = 𝑤𝑤(Σ𝑏𝑏)

Double-Meridian Triangle

     3-50. The double-meridian triangle method gives a more precise value for a cross-section area than the
     stripper method. However, it involves more time. With this method, the area is subdivided into two series of
     trapezoids using the elevations of adjacent points and their projections on the centerline (the distances). (See
     figure 3-11.)

        Legend:                     centerline
        ℄

                  Figure 3-11. Cross-section area by the double-meridian method

29 February 2016                    TM 3-34.48-1                                 3-11


---

Chapter 3

     3-51. These trapezoids have bases equal to the horizontal distance of the respective points from the centerline
     and heights equal to their differences in elevation. Where the difference in elevation is plus, the area of the
     trapezoid is plus. Where the difference in elevation is minus, the area of the trapezoid is minus. The
     component areas are added algebraically. Because this procedure uses the sum of the bases of the trapezoid,
     the area obtained is double the true area and must be divided by 2. The following steps for the computation
     are simple arithmetic—

              Step 1. Subtract the adjoining elevations.
              Step 2. Multiply by the distance from the centerline.
              Step 3. Add the multiplied results and list plus and minus quantities.
              Step 4. Add these quantities.
              Step 5. Divide by 2.

     3-52. The steps for completing the procedure for the double-meridian triangle method follow:
              Step 1. Start at the centerline ground or grade elevation, whichever is lower. (This is Point A. See
                  figure 3-11, page 3-11.) Work from the centerline in a clockwise direction to the left (Point A, B,
                  C, D, E, and F) and counterclockwise to the right (Point A, G, H, I, and F) to the centerline ground
                  or grade elevation, whichever is higher (Point F).
              Step 2. Working from point to point, multiply the difference in elevation between each adjacent
                  pair of points by the sum of their distance from the centerline. Point F to Point A is not considered
                  because the sum of their distances from the centerline is zero. Going from a lower to a higher
                  elevation gives a plus quantity, while going from a higher to a lower elevation gives a minus
                  quantity. Place plus quantities in one column and minus quantities in another column.
              Step 3. Divide the algebraic sum of the plus and minus quantities by 2 to obtain the cross-section
                  area in square feet. In sections with cut and fill, treat each part as a separate section.

Computer-Aided Design

     3-53. Very accurate measurements can be made if cross sections are digitized using computer-aided design.
     Cross sections are placed on a digitizing pad; points are plotted into the computer; and with one command,
     the area is calculated.

VOLUME DETERMINATION METHODS

     3-54. An engineer can accomplish the necessary earthwork computations by using one of the following
     methods of volume determination:

 Average end-area method.
 Prismoidal formula method.
 Average-depth-of-cut-or-fill method.
 Grid method.

Average End Area

3-55. The average-end-area method is most commonly used to determine the volume bounding two cross
sections or end areas of a prismoid. The volume is measured in cubic yards (1 cubic yard equals 27 cubic
feet). Use the following formula:

                    𝑉𝑉 = 𝐴𝐴1 + 𝐴𝐴2 × 𝐿𝐿
                                        2  27

where—  area
A =     distance between end sections A1 and A2 in feet
L =     volume in cubic yards
V =

3-56. If cross sections are taken at full 100-foot stations, the volume in cubic yards between successive cross
sections in square feet may be found using the following formula:

                                                     𝑉𝑉 = 1.85 (𝐴𝐴1 + 𝐴𝐴2)

3-57. In either form, the formula is only accurate when A1 and A2 are approximately the same shape. The
greater the difference in shape between the two end sections, the greater the possibility of error. However,
the method is consistent with field methods in general. In most cases, the time required for a more accurate
method is not justified.

Prismoidal Formula

3-58. The prismoidal method is used where the end areas differ widely in shape or a more exact method of
computing volume is needed. Its use is very limited because it requires more time than the average-end-area
method and gives greater accuracy than what is required for most road and airfield construction. The
prismoidal formula is—

rather than averaging the areas of A1 and A2.

Average Depth of Cut or Fill

     3-60. With the centerline profile and final grade established, earthwork could be estimated with the average-
     depth-of-cut-or-fill method. Estimate the average depth of cut or fill between 100-foot stations and obtain the
     volume of material from table 3-1, page 3-14. The accuracy of this method depends on the care given in
     establishing the centerline profile, the instruments used, and the accuracy of field reconnaissance. However,
     the volumes obtained by this method are generally adequate for most military construction.

3-61. The centerline profile of a road is typical of the entire transverse section because of narrow widths.
Because of the greater width required on an airfield runway, the centerline profile may be misleading due to
the typical conditions across the entire transverse width at that point. Therefore, earthwork quantities for
airfields should be estimated mainly from cross sections. In the absence of sufficient time, the average-cut-
or-fill method is better than none. Before using table 3-1, determine the—

             44 feet.

        Quantity to be added to the figure in column 2 if the width of the base or top of the fill is an odd
             number of feet.

        Quantity to be added if the slope ratio on the sides is 1.5:1 or 2:1.

     3-62. To use table 3-1 use the following steps:
              Step 1. Find the row in column 1 with the correct average amount of cut or fill.
              Step 2. Move horizontally to the right, and find the correct figure under the appropriate width of

                  proportionately.

Grid

     3-63. When the quantity of material within the limits of the cut sections is not enough to balance the fill
     sections, material must be borrowed. The most convenient method is to widen the cuts adjacent to the fills
     where the material is needed. Compute the volume by extending the cross sections. If this is not possible,
     locate borrow pits at another area. The grid method is a convenient method of computing the borrow material
     available in a borrow pit.

     3-64. In this method, stake out the area with a system of squares, referencing points outside the limits of
     work. The dimensions of the squares depend on the roughness of the original terrain, the anticipated
     roughness of the final surface, and the accuracy desired. Rougher terrain requires smaller dimensions to get
     accurate results. The squares must be sized so that no significant breaks in the original ground surface or in
     the pit floor exist between the corners of the square or the edges of the excavation and the nearest interior
     corner.

     3-65. By taking elevation readings at the stakes before and after excavation, data is obtained to compute the
     volume of borrow taken from the pit. Figure 3-12 shows a borrow pit with 25 squares staked. To identify the
     various intersecting points, label lines in one direction with numbers and in the other direction with letters.
     Thus, the intersection of lines C and 3 would be labeled C3.

Chapter 3

FACTORS INFLUENCING EARTHWORK CALCULATIONS

     3-72. On many projects, one objective of the paper location study is to design the grade line so that the total
     cut within the limits of the work equals the total fill. The uncertain change in the material volume makes this
     difficult. It is usually more economical to haul excavated material to the embankment sections, eliminating
     borrow and waste.

Shrinkage

     3-73. Shrinkage has occurred when 1 cubic yard of earth, as measured in place before excavation, occupies
     less than 1 cubic yard of space when excavated, hauled to an embankment, and compacted. The difference is
     due to the combined effects of the loss of material during hauling and compaction to a greater-than-original
     density by the heavy equipment used to make the embankment.

     3-74. Shrinkage is small in granular materials, such as sand and gravel, and is large in ordinary earth
     containing appreciable percentages of silt, loam, or clay. Shrinkage is very high (possibly 70 percent) for
     shallow cuts containing humus, which is discarded as unsuitable for embankments. These shallow cuts
     (usually 4 to 8 inches deep) are called stripping.

     3-75. Loose and swell refer to a condition that is the reverse of shrinkage. The earth assumes a larger volume
     than its natural state when stockpiled or loaded into a truck. This factor ranges from 10 to 40 percent swell
     and is usually uniform for a given material.

     3-76. Shrinkage varies with changes in the soil constituents, changes in moisture content, and the type of
     equipment used. Consequently, a percentage allowance assumed in design may eventually prove to be 5
     percent or more in error. A common shrinkage allowance is 10 to 30 percent for ordinary earth.

     3-77. Settlement refers to subsidence of the completed embankment. It is due to slow additional compaction
     under traffic and to gradual plastic flow of the foundation material beneath the embankment.

Net Volume Calculation

     3-78. Compute the volume of cut and fill and the net volume between two points on the construction project.
     The net volume is the difference between the volume of cut and the volume of fill between two specified
     stations. The net volume may apply to the entire project or to a few stations. Net volume may be described
     as in-place, compacted, or loose. Table 3-2 provides conversion factors used to find the net volume.

Earthwork Volume Sheet

     3-79. The earthwork volume sheets allow for systematically recording this information and making the
     necessary calculations. They provide a means of tabulating earthwork quantities for use in the mass diagram
     discussed later in this chapter. The earthwork volume calculation sheet (see figure 3-15, page 3-20) is divided
     into columns for recording and calculating information as follows:

              Stations (column 1). List station cross-sectional areas that have been plotted. Normally, these
                  areas are taken at full stations and at intermediate stations that are required to fully represent the
                  actual ground conditions and earthwork involved.

              End area cut (column 2). Record the computed cross-sectional areas of cut at each station. These
                  areas may be computed by one of the commonly used methods, depending on the degree of
                  accuracy required.

              End area fill (column 3). Complete column 3 in the same manner as column 2, except show
                  cross-sectional areas of fill.

              Volume of cut (column 4). Complete the volume of cut material between adjacent stations and
                  record it in column 4. The most common method for computing volumes is the average-end-area
                  method (or the earthwork table based on this method).

             Note. This volume represents the volume of cut between the stations and the volumes reflected as
             in-place yardage.

              Volume of fill (column 5). Complete column 5 in the same manner as column 4, except show fill
                  volumes. Fill volumes reflect compacted yardage rather than in-place yardage.

              Stripping fill cut (column 6). Before actual earthmoving operations begin, remove the layer of
                  humus or objectionable material that lies on the ground surface.

             Note. This layer varies in depth but is usually 4 to 6 inches deep. This material must be wasted
             because it is not satisfactory to place in an embankment. Indicate the volume between stations of
             this humus material over sections of cut in column 6.

              Stripping fill (column 7). Before an embankment can be constructed, the same layer of humus
                  must be removed and the volume replaced with satisfactory material. Indicate the volume of this
                  material between stations over sections of fill.

              Net cut (column 8). Indicate the volume of cut material between stations that is available for the
                  embankment. Column 8 is column 4 minus column 6 because the total cut must be decreased by
                  the amount of material wasted in stripping, including the organic material.

              Adjusted cut (column 9). One cubic yard of material in its natural, undisturbed state occupies
                  approximately 1.25 cubic yards when removed and placed in a truck or stockpile. The same cubic
                  yard, when placed in an embankment section and compacted, occupies a volume of approximately
                  0.9 cubic yards. In planning operations, convert these various volumes to the same state so that
                  the comparisons can be made. Changes in volume of earthwork are discussed in this chapter. (See
                  table 3-2 for conversion factors.) Column 9 is column 8 multiplied by the appropriate conversion
                  factor (0.9 in this case) to convert it from in-place yardage to compacted yardage.

              Total fill (column 10). Indicate the amount of compacted material required between stations to
                  complete needed embankments. Column 10 is column 5 plus column 7 plus the amount necessary
                  to replace the quantity removed by stripping. This figure represents the fill required to achieve the
                  original ground line.

              Algebraic sum (column 11). Column 11 is the difference between column 10 and column 9. This
                  indicates the volume of material that is available (plus) or required (negative) within the station
                  increment after the intrastation balancing has been done.

              Mass ordinate (column 12). Column 12 indicates the total of column 11 starting at Station
                  0 + 00. While passing through a stretch where cutting predominates, this column increases in
                  value. While passing through a stretch where embankment is required, this column decreases.

MASS DIAGRAM

     3-80. The first step in planning earthmoving operations is to estimate the earthwork quantities involved in
     the project. With these estimates, the engineer can prepare detailed plans for economical and efficient
     completion of the earthmoving mission.

     3-81. The mass diagram is one method of analyzing earthmoving operations. This diagram can tell the
     engineer where to use certain types of equipment, the quantities of materials needed, the average haul
     distances, and the average slope for each operation when combined with a ground profile. This permits the
     preparation of detailed management plans for the entire project. The mass diagram is not the complete answer
     to job planning, and it has limitations that restrict its effectiveness for certain types of projects. However, it
     is one of the most effective engineer tools and is easily and rapidly prepared.

CONSTRUCTION

     3-82. Using column 1 (station) and column 12 (mass ordinate, cumulative total) of a completed earthwork
     volume sheet, a mass diagram can be plotted. (See figure 3-16.) Plot the mass diagram on scaled graph paper
     with the stations indicated horizontally, and the mass indices (column 12) denoted vertically. Connect the
     plotted points to complete the mass diagram. Positive numbers are plotted above the zero datum line, and
     negative numbers are plotted below.

Properties

     3-83. Figure 3-17 shows a typical mass diagram with the actual ground profile and final-grade line of the
     project plotted. They use the same horizontal axis (stations). The ground profile is placed above the mass
     diagram to facilitate the calculation of the average grade the equipment will work. The horizontal axis is the
     only thing these graphs have in common.

Chapter 3

     3-84. The mass diagram is a running total of the quantity of earth that is in surplus or deficient along the
     construction profile. If more material is being cut than filled at one station, it is a cut operation at that station.
     The quantity or volume of surplus material will be increasing as cutting operations continue through the
     station, producing an ascending mass diagram curve line. In figure 3-17, page 3-21, Stations A to B and
     Stations D to E are cutting operations. The total volume for the cut at Stations A to B is obtained by projecting
     the points on the curve line at Stations A and B to the vertical axis and reading the volume.

     3-85. If more material is being filled than cut at one station, it is a fill operation at that station. The deficient
     material quantity or volume will be increasing as filling operations continue through the station, producing a
     descending mass-diagram curve line. In figure 3-17, Stations B to D are filling operations. The total volume
     for the fill at Stations B to D is obtained by projecting the points on the curve line at Stations B and C to the
     vertical axis and reading and adding the volumes above and below the zero datum line.

     3-86. The maximum or minimum point on the mass diagram where the curve changes from rising to falling
     indicates a change from cut to fill (or vice versa). This is referred to as a transition point. On the ground
     profile, the grade line crosses the ground line at the transition point, as illustrated at Stations B and D.

     3-87. When the mass diagram crosses the datum line or zero volume, as at Station C, there is exactly as much
     material filled as there is material cut or zero volume excess or deficit at that point. The section of the mass
     diagram, from the start of the project at Station A to a point of crossing the zero volume line, is known as a
     node. Each crossing point on the zero volume line indicates another node. The last node may or may not
     return to the zero datum line. Nodes are numbered from left to right.

     3-88. The final position of the mass diagram line (above or below the datum line) indicates if the project was
     predominately a cut or fill operation. In figure 3-17, where the mass diagram ends at Station E, the operation
     was a cutting operation; that is, surplus material was generated by cutting and must be hauled away (waste
     operation). Borrow operations occur when the final position of the mass diagram is below the zero volume
     line.

Project Analysis

     3-89. Once the basic properties of the mass diagram are understood, the engineer can conduct a detailed
     analysis to determine where dozers, scrapers, and clump trucks will operate. This is accomplished by using
     balance lines. A balance line is a line of specific length drawn horizontally, intersecting the mass diagram in
     two places. The specific length of the balance line is the recommended working or maximum haul distance
     for different pieces of equipment. The term maximum haul distance is used because operating equipment
     beyond this point would not be efficient. The maximum haul distances (balance-line lengths) are up to 300
     feet for a dozer; 301 to 5,000 feet for a scraper; and 5,001 feet to several miles for a dump truck.

     3-90. These lengths are measured using the horizontal scale (stations measured in hundreds of feet). Always
     use the maximum haul distance (length) of each piece of equipment, provided the project or node is at least
     that length. Start excavating each node with the dozer, followed by the scraper and dump truck.

     3-91. Figure 3-18 shows a balance line drawn on a portion of a mass diagram. If this were a dozer balance
     line, the distance between Stations A and C would be 300 feet.

     3-92. The cut equals the fill between the ends of the balance line. The mass line returns to exactly the same
     level, indicating that the input and the expenditures of earth have been equal. In figure 3-18, this occurs
     between Stations A and C, indicating an exact balance of earthwork.

     3-93. In figure 3-18, the vertical line labeled Q measures the quantity of material made available by cutting
     between Stations A and B. This is also the amount of embankment material required between Stations B and
     C. This is described as the balanced quantity of earthwork. If equipment was used to do the balanced
     earthwork between Stations A and C, the maximum distance that earth would have to be moved would be
     the length of the balance line AC.

     3-94. In accomplishing balanced earthwork operations between Stations A and C, some of the haul distance
     would be short, while some would approach the maximum haul distance. The average haul distance is the
     length of the horizontal line placed midway between the balance line and the top or bottom point (transition
     point) of the curve and is found by dividing the vertical distance of the quantity in half.

Chapter 3

     3-97. The mass diagram is a useful indicator of the amount of work expended on a project. By definition,
     work is the energy expended in moving a specified weight a given distance. It is the product of weight
     multiplied by the distance. Because the ordinate of the mass diagram is in cubic yards (which represents
     weight) and the abscissa is in stations or distance, an area on the mass diagram represents work. If equipment
     is used to do the balanced earthwork between the ends of the balance lines as drawn, the work expended is
     equal to the area between the mass line and the balance line. (See figure 3-20.)

                                    Figure 3-20. Work in earthmoving operations
     3-98. Another item calculated from the mass diagram is average grade. This value is used when computing
     equipment scheduling and use. Figure 3-21 illustrates a portion of the mass diagram where the average grade
     has been determined.

                               Figure 3-21. Balance lines for equipment efficiency

APPLICATION

     3-99. The mass diagram is used to find the cost of a project in terms of haul distance and yardage, to locate
     the areas of operation for various types of equipment, to establish the requirements for borrow pits and waste
     areas, and to provide overall control of required earthmoving operations. However, the means used to analyze
     the mass diagram will follow the same principles regardless of the end result desired. The analysis of the
     mass diagram is based on the proper location of balance lines.

3-24  TM 3-34.48-1  29 February 2016

                                                                                              Surveys and Earthwork Operations

3-100. Because the lengths of balance lines on a mass diagram are equal to the maximum or minimum haul
distances for the balanced earthmoving operation between their end points, they should be drawn to conform
to the capabilities of the available equipment. Equipment planned accordingly will operate at haul distances
that are within its best range of efficiency.

3-101. Figure 3-21 illustrates a portion of a mass diagram where two balance lines have been drawn: 300
feet for dozer capabilities and 5,000 feet for scraper capabilities. The following job analysis can be made
from the diagram:

        Use dozers between Stations C and E. The maximum haul distance is 300 feet; the average haul
             distance is the horizontal bisector shown. The amount that will be cut between Stations C and D
             and filled between Stations D and E is the length of the indicated vertical lines.

        Use scrapers for cutting from Stations A to C and filling from Stations E to G. The minimum and
             maximum haul distances are 301 and 5,000 feet. The average haul distance is the horizontal line
             midway between the balance lines. The vertical line indicates the amount of earthwork.

3-102. To determine the average grade for the scraper or dozer work area, use the following steps:
        Step 1. Draw a horizontal line through the work area that roughly divides the area in half on the
             profile. (See figure 3-22.) This is a rough estimate.
        Step 2. Extend a vertical line from the end points of the average haul line up through the project
             profile. (See figure 3-23, page 3-26.) These lines are referred to as the average haul vertical.
        Step 3. Draw a final line connecting the intersecting points of the lines drawn in Steps 1 and 2.
             This line represents the average grade.
        Step 4. Determine the average change in elevation (vertical distance between the cut and fill).
        Step 5. Calculate the average grade using the following equation:

Placement of Balance Lines to Minimize Work

     3-103. Because the area between the apex of the mass diagram and the balance line is a measure of the work
     involved in the balancing operation, the size of these areas should be decreased if possible. However, the
     method used to minimize the area depends on the shape of the mass diagram and the number of adjacent
     nodes that can be used.

     3-104. If two nodes are adjacent, work is minimized when two balance lines are drawn as one continuous
     line with the balance lines equal in length. Each balance line must be within the maximum efficient haul
     distance for equipment. The best placement of balance lines on the portion of a mass diagram would be equal
     lines. (See figure 3-24.) Only one balance line (CH) may be needed if it is within efficient haul distance
     specifications. The quantity of materials (in yards) involved is indicated by line Q, and the work involved
     would be the area above line CH.

           Note. The best placement of balance lines would be lines AE and EF.

           Legend:  quantity of material
           Q

                    Figure 3-24. Minimizing work with two nodes

between CH and DG and increased by the size of the area between BD and C. This would result in a savings
because the increase is less than the decrease for the same amount of earthwork balanced. This decreasing

     process will continue by raising the lines to the point where one equals the other, or until the point where AE
     equals EF.
     3-106. If there is an even number of adjacent nodes, work is reduced when the balance lines are one
     continuous line (AB + CD + EF = BC + DE + FG). (See figure 3-25.) The length of each balance line must
     be within equipment maximum haul capabilities as defined earlier.

                         Figure 3-25. Minimizing work with an even number of nodes
     3-107. If there is an odd number of adjacent nodes, work is decreased when the balance lines are one
     continuous line, and AB + CD + EF - (BC + DE) equals the limit of efficient haul or approximately 1,000
     feet. (See figure 3-26.) Balance lines must be within equipment limits.

                         Figure 3-26. Minimizing work with an odd number of nodes

Calculation of Earthwork Not Within Balance Lines

     3-108. It is usually impossible to place balance lines so that the entire amount of earthwork on a project can
     be balanced. Some part of the mass line will be outside the balance lines. This material must be wasted or
     borrowed. If the portion not within balance lines is ascending (cutting), there is waste; if it is descending
     (filling), there is borrow. (See figure 3-27.) Concentrate necessary borrow and waste operations in one
     general area.

                                Figure 3-27. Waste and borrow on a mass diagram

Analysis Format

     3-109. The simplest and most practical method of tabulating the results of a mass diagram is to write the
     quantities and distances on the diagram. (See figure 3-28, page 3-28.) It is also possible to extract information
     from the mass diagram and put it in a format that effectively controls the operation. One method is to prepare
     a mass diagram analysis sheet. (See figure 3-29, page 3-28.)

                                                                                                     Surveys and Earthwork Operations

MASS DIAGRAM LIMITATIONS

     3-110. The mass diagram has many limitations that preclude its use in earthmoving operations. At best, it
     is merely a guide indicating the general manner in which the operation should be controlled. An attempt to
     get exact quantities and distances from it may be misleading, but it is a good starting point.

     3-111. The mass diagram is most effective when used to plan operations along an elongated project (road,
     airfield runway, taxiway). The haul distances are along the centerline or parallel to it. However, if the project
     becomes relatively wide compared to its length, movement of earth may be transverse as longitudinal,
     resulting in longer, transverse haul distances and invalidating the mass diagram analysis.

     3-112. The mass diagram is used to analyze the balancing potential within one phase of a project. For
     instance, the mass diagram may indicate that the best balancing of a certain portion of a runway will require
     a haul distance of 2,200 feet along the site. It may be better to balance yardage with an adjacent taxiway
     where the haul distance will be 1,200 feet. The mass diagram can deal with the runway or the taxiway, not
     both simultaneously.

     3-113. The mass diagram assumes that material excavated in the cut sections is acceptable for use in the
     embankment sections. This is not necessarily true. However, unacceptable quantities can be eliminated from
     the earthwork table.

     3-114. The mass diagram is applicable to projects needing balanced earthwork. Balancing eliminates the
     double handling of quantities. If there is a short distance between an acceptable borrow pit and an
     embankment section, it may be more economical to use the borrow pit instead of a long balancing operation.
     This can be determined by a work or economy study.

                                                 Chapter 4

                  Clearing, Grubbing, and Stripping

         Land clearing is the removal and disposal of vegetation, rubbish, and surface boulders
         embedded in the ground. In the JOA, land clearing includes the removal and disposal
         of mines, booby traps, and unexploded bombs. Grubbing is the uprooting and removal
         of roots and stumps. Stripping is the removal and disposal of unwanted topsoil and sod.
         Clearing, grubbing, and stripping are accomplished by using heavy engineering
         equipment. Hand- or power-felling equipment, explosives, and fire are also used.
         Factors that determine the method used are the acreage to be cleared, the type and
         density of vegetation, weather conditions, the effect of the terrain on equipment
         operation, the availability of equipment and personnel, and the time available for
         completion. For best results, a combination of methods is used in a sequence of
         operations. Clearing, grubbing, and stripping are the same in road and airfield
         construction. In airfield construction, the areas to be cleared are usually larger than
         road construction, the number of personnel and amount of equipment used are
         correspondingly greater, and the disposal of unsuitable materials requires more
         detailed planning and longer hauls.

FOREST TYPES AND ENVIRONMENTAL CONDITIONS

     4-1. Clearing, grubbing, and stripping operations differ in every climatic zone because each zone has
     different forest and vegetative types. Forests are not uniform in type, growth, and density within climatic
     zones. Soils, altitudes, water tables, and other factors vary widely within each zone.

     4-2. The general nature of a forest is determined from records of the principal climatic factors, precipitation,
     humidity, temperature, sunlight, and the direction of the prevailing winds. The nature and action of climatic
     factors during the growing season determine the amount and types of forests. From these records, a general
     interpretation of the forests in an area can guide detailed reconnaissance. The climate classifications of
     forests are temperate, rain, monsoon, and dry.

TEMPERATE FORESTS

     4-3. Temperate forests contain softwood and hardwood trees. Hardwoods are dominant where soil is old,
     deep, and fertile. Softwoods are dominant where soil is young, shallow, and less fertile. The density of growth
     in these forests varies with topography and local climate conditions. Bogs are common in cold region,
     softwood forests. Bogs present a hazard to construction equipment during clearing operations. Root systems
     vary according to geologic conditions and tree species. The types of root systems typical of various tree
     species are listed in table 4-1, page 4-2.

                                Clearing, Grubbing, and Stripping

RAIN FORESTS

     4-4. Rain forests occur in tropical climates where rainfall is heavy throughout the year. They consist of tall,
     broad-leaved trees that grow as high as 175 feet. The trees have umbrella-like foliage that permits little
     sunlight to penetrate. The undergrowth consists of thick vines that cling to the trees for support and grow to
     great heights. Where sunlight reaches the forest floor, the undergrowth is dense and varied. Because of
     continual precipitation, the root systems are on or near the ground surface and spread in a lateral pattern
     around the base of the trees.

MONSOON FORESTS

     4-5. Monsoon forests occur in climates of heavy seasonal rains with strong, warm winds. The forests are
     dense, with varied species of hardwoods that are moderate-sized, broad-leaved, and have shallow root
     systems. The undergrowth is very dense with shrubs, vines, and plants.

DRY FORESTS

     4-6. Dry forests occur in arid and tropical regions where there is little precipitation. The forests are scrub
     or savanna. Scrub forests usually consist of broad-leaved hardwoods with dense thickets along watercourses.
     In open areas, there are scattered growths of low, thorny, stunted shrubs and stunted trees that usually have
     long, tough taproots that are difficult to remove. Savanna forests are in more humid, dry-forest regions. These
     forests are park-like with large trees widely and uniformly spaced. Savannas usually have continuous
     coverings of small grasses.

GEOLOGIC AND PERMAFROST CONDITIONS

     4-7. An investigation of the geologic conditions of a forest can help when estimating the density and depth
     of tree root systems. The investigation should be concerned with hardpan, marshy, and permafrost conditions.

HARDPAN OR ROCK

     4-8. Where a forest is closely underlain by hardpan or rock, the tree roots branch and remain near the
     surface. This growth is easy to uproot. Where the soil is firm and the hardpan or rock is deep, the trees form
     large, deep taproots that make uprooting difficult.

INUNDATED, MARSHY, AND BOGGY AREAS

     4-9. In these areas, trees have thick, wide-spreading, and shallow root systems near the surface of the
     ground.

PERMAFROST

     4-10. In northern regions where permafrost occurs, the root systems of trees are similar to those in hardpan
     or rock. Where the permafrost is near the surface, roots branch out and lie close to the surface. Taproots
     develop where permafrost is deeper.

PREPARATION

     4-11. Taking time to understand the site conditions before committing equipment and personnel to a clearing,
     grubbing, and stripping task will allow mission planners to provide the best available resources to the given
     tasks. These preparations can be very critical to planning and executing mission timelines for what is typically
     the first in a series of construction activities.

RECONNAISSANCE AND PLANNING

     4-12. The types of trees, vegetation, soil, and terrain encountered while clearing the land must be determined
     as accurately as possible from climatic and geological maps, intelligence reports, the surface, and aerial and
     ground reconnaissance (refer to chapter 2 of this manual for more detailed information).

29 February 2016  TM 3-34.48-1  4-3


---

Chapter 4

     4-13. After the information has been verified, estimate the quantity of work, select the available equipment,
     determine the number of personnel needed, and plan a sequence of operations to complete the clearing rapidly
     and efficiently. In clearing operations, the decisive factors controlling the method of clearing are the type and
     amount of equipment and the time available for completion.

TIMBER CRUISING

     4-14. Timber cruising is performed to estimate the diameter, height, and number of each tree species in an
     area. It is used to determine the quantity of usable timber or to estimate the amount of work required in
     clearing. A sample forested area (usually 10 percent of the total forested area) is cruised, and the result is
     applied to the entire area. The sample size may be increased or decreased. In small areas, a 100-percent cruise
     is usually made.

     4-15. In timber cruising for land clearing, record the tree diameters at breast height, taken at 4 1/2 feet above
     the ground, and record the species and number of trees. This information is used to plan the clearing operation
     and select the type of equipment most efficient for the tree sizes and species.

CLEARING CONSIDERATIONS

     4-16. Properly executed site clearing operations require careful consideration of the effects of this activity
     on the site and surrounding mission area. The following paragraphs discuss the most prominent of these
     potential considerations.

PERMAFROST

     4-17. Clearing of ground cover over permafrost that is near the freezing point may result in thawing of
     material, causing considerable ground-surface subsidence.

SAFETY

     4-18. Careful consideration must be given to the safety of personnel and equipment during clearing
     operations. Protective, tractor-mounted cabs should be used when extensive clearing operations are
     anticipated. Protective cabs permit greater flexibility in clearing operations and increase operator efficiency.
     With this protection, damage to the dozer is reduced and continuous production results.

     4-19. Proper supervision and planning can help prevent accidents caused by falling trees, uprooted stumps,
     stump holes, and rough or broken terrain during the clearing operation. Equipment used in clearing should,
     if practical, be equipped with heavy steel plating for protection of the undercarriages. This will prevent
     stumps, logs, and boulders from damaging vulnerable equipment parts.

CAMOUFLAGE

     4-20. To provide cover and concealment (camouflage) for the construction site, do not remove standing trees
     and brush outside the designated cleared area unless necessary. When uprooting trees with bulldozers, take
     care to control their fall to avoid breaking surrounding trees.

TIMBER SALVAGE

     4-21. Trim timber useful for logs, piles, and lumber, and stockpile it for future use in bridge, culvert, and
     other construction applications. Push or skid this timber into a salvage area where it can be moved to a
     sawmill with little difficulty.

TEMPORARY DRAINAGE

     4-22. Phased development of the drainage system in the early stages of clearing, grubbing, and stripping is
     essential to ensure uninterrupted construction. Delays caused by flooding, subgrade failures, heavy mud
     conditions, and the subsequent immobilization of construction equipment can be eliminated by careful
     development of the drainage system before (or concurrent with) other construction. Use original drainage

4-4  TM 3-34.48-1  29 February 2016


---

                                                                                                      Clearing, Grubbing, and Stripping

     features as much as possible without disturbing natural grades. Slope drainage ditches downhill to allow
     water runoff.

     4-23. Fill holes left by uprooted trees and stumps with acceptable soil, and compact the ground to prevent
     the accumulation of surface water. Use dozers and graders for this work. Slope the ground toward drainage
     ditches to prevent ponding on the surface. Backfill existing ditches at the latest possible time to permit the
     best use of the existing drainage.

DISPOSAL

     4-24. Use waste areas or burning to dispose of cleared materials. The choice of method depends on the type
     of construction, environmental concerns, location, threat, and time available. Generally, the material is
     pushed and skidded off the construction site and into the surrounding timber to speed disposal and keep the
     area cleared for equipment operation. To dispose of material as rapidly as possible, assign specific units of
     equipment to accomplish this concurrently with clearing and grubbing. The disposal method should be
     consistent with the methods of camouflage, salvage, and drainage used for clearing. Cleared material can be
     disposed of by using it as fill material in revetments around hardstands when protective measures are needed.

Waste Areas

     4-25. In airfield construction, consideration must be given to the areas used for disposal of construction
     waste. Waste material must not become an obstruction or hazard to air traffic. Approach and takeoff slopes
     must be considered when forming disposal areas.

Dumps Adjacent to Work Areas

     4-26. In forward combat areas where saving time is essential, the quickest and most convenient method of
     material disposal is to pile the materials adjacent to the work area. Study construction plans to determine
     where the least interference will be located.

Off-Site Areas

     4-27. If construction debris cannot be piled up without causing drainage or other potential work impacts to
     the main project, it may be necessary to clear some adjacent land to dispose of the debris. Locate this clearing
     as close to the main project as possible to shorten the hauling distance. Use the same methods to clear disposal
     areas that are used in clearing work areas.

Burning

     4-28. Do not use fire for clearing land unless suitable equipment and sufficient personnel are not available
     for other methods of clearing. When burning is required, closely follow recommended procedures from
     headquarters.

     4-29. Under favorable tactical conditions, brush and timber debris may be burned. To limit the likelihood of
     detection because of smoke, keep fires burning as hot as possible and do not push new material into the fire
     rapidly. Do not permit fires to burn at night unless tactical conditions are extremely favorable and approval
     has been obtained from headquarters.

Fire Control

     4-30. Before starting a fire, create a firebreak by stripping the area around the debris to be burned. If burning
     large areas, establish firebreaks on each side as a precaution against shifting winds. Maintain a fire guard
     over the fires as an additional safety measure. In dry weather, hand shovels, water buckets, and other
     expedient firefighting equipment should be available to extinguish fires caused by flying sparks. Burning
     greatly reduces disposal volume, but large debris piles produce large fires that can be difficult to control once
     ignited. Be aware of the weather and wind conditions before burning debris. Gusty winds can spread fire into
     neighboring forests, resulting in uncontrollable fires.

29 February 2016  TM 3-34.48-1  4-5


---

Chapter 4

Burn Pits

     4-31. The most satisfactory method for burning large quantities of brush and timber is to burn them in a pit
     or trench dug by a bulldozer or scraper. The sides of the pit reflect the heat back into the fire, producing a
     very hot fire. Burning will be rapid and complete. Push the material into the pit with a bulldozer. Start the
     fire with limbs and small brush to get a good bed of coals. Gradually increase the size of the material as the
     intensity of the fire increases. Get as little dirt as possible into the pit because it smothers the fire and fills the
     pit. A Soldier should be detailed to tend the fire and ensure that the pile is kept compact. This method cannot
     be used in swampy areas where groundwater will seep into the trench.

Log Piles

     4-32. If burn pits are not desirable, burn logs by loosely piling them so that the heat and flames can pass
     through. It is always best to start the fire with brush. After a large bed of coals is formed, add a few logs at a
     time to maintain a good blaze.

     4-33. To burn green, wet logs, it may be necessary to use fuel oil or diesel to furnish enough heat to dry out
     the logs and start the burning process. Pile the logs parallel, one on top of the other. A pipe with drilled or
     cut holes carries the fuel oil to the center of the pile. Once the pile is burning well, the fuel is stopped and the
     pipe is removed. Care must be taken to avoid ground contamination.

     4-34. Fuel oil is also a quick and convenient means of starting brush fires, particularly if the brush is green
     and wet. If pushing material into the pile while the pipe is being used, bury the outside end of the pipe. This
     protects it from damage from tractor grousers and bulldozer blades.

Clearing and Piling Stumps

     4-35. In preparing stumps for burning, remove as much dirt as possible from the roots. Dirt on the roots will
     retard combustion and smother the fire. When the stumps are pushed out, leave them with the roots exposed
     to the sun and wind so that the dirt will dry quickly. Scrubbing with the side of the bulldozer blade will knock
     off much of the dry dirt. Pile the stumps as close together as possible with the trunks pointing toward the
     center of the pile. Keep the stumps together after they start to burn. This procedure will speed up burning.

AIRFIELD APPROACH ZONES

     4-36. Obstructions that extend above the glide angle must be removed. Although glide-angle requirements
     may be met by topping trees, it is best to fell or uproot trees that extend above the glide angle. Demolished
     material may be left in place if conditions allow. Airfield glide angles and approach zones are further
     discussed in TM 3-34.48-2.

PERFORMANCE TECHNIQUES

     4-37. The following paragraphs describe recommended techniques for clearing, grubbing, and stripping
     activities. Many times, equipment and personnel resources dictate which technique is used, but using the
     following guidance can significantly increase productivity.

CLEARING WITH EQUIPMENT

     4-38. The use of engineer equipment is the most rapid and efficient clearing method. Unusually large trees,
     stumps, and terrain that decrease the maneuverability of equipment and increase maintenance requirements
     limit the use of equipment. This type of equipment includes bulldozers, tree-dozers, tractor-mounted units,
     tractor-mounted clearing units, winches, power saws, rippers, and motor graders. In addition, pioneer tools
     are used for some clearing operations. Table 4-2 summarizes the limitations and proper applications of
     engineer equipment in clearing operations. Use production rates of equipment under normal operating
     conditions for determining the total time required for the job. Clearing rates are discussed in TM
     3-34.62/MCRP 3-17.7I.
