Chapter 4

Bulldozer

     4-39. When clearing an area in dry or temperate forests, the bulldozer is most efficient for removing small
     brush, trees, and stumps up to 6 inches in diameter. Although more time and effort are required, bulldozers
     can also remove trees up to 30 inches in diameter when tractor-mounted clearing units and power saws are
     not available. Because of its ability to push, move, and skid felled trees and brush, the bulldozer is the primary
     unit of equipment in clearing operations.

     4-40. When clearing with bulldozers, the sequence of operations depends on the type of trees, the terrain,
     and planned construction. After establishing the boundaries of the area to clear, select spoil areas for disposal
     of cleared material based on the shortest haul, a downgrade slope, effective camouflage, and general
     accessibility.

     4-41. Start clearing at the disposal area and move in each direction away from it. Use one or two bulldozers
     to clear small trees and brush, and use another pair of dozers to remove larger trees and stumps bypassed by
     the other units. If necessary, add more bulldozers for a third cycle of operation to take care of the heaviest
     removals.

     4-42. Move the cleared material to the spoil area by skidding, pushing, or pulling. Disposal should be done
     with uprooting and removing. It is best to have a separate crew assigned for disposal.

     4-43. Multiple operations are possible when other types of equipment are available, using each type where
     it is most effective. For example, use power saws to fell large trees. Use clearing units to uproot large stumps
     and work in areas inaccessible to dozers. Use bulldozers to clear, stockpile, and dispose of light material. The
     operational methods used by bulldozers in clearing depend on the size of the trees. The methods briefly
     discussed below are discussed fully in TM 3-34.62/MCRP 3-17.7I.

Small Trees (Six Inches or Less in Diameter) and Brush

     4-44. In clearing small trees and brush, operate the bulldozer with the blade straight and digging slightly. It
     may be necessary to back up occasionally to clear the blade. The cleared material can be pushed into
     windrows for later removal or pushed off to one side of the area to be cleared.

Medium Trees (Six to Twelve Inches in Diameter)

     4-45. To push over medium trees, set the blade of the bulldozer as high as possible to gain added leverage.
     (See figure 4-1.) As the tree falls, the bulldozer is backed up quickly to clear the roots. With the blade lowered,
     the bulldozer travels forward again and digs the roots free by lifting the blade. The felled tree is ready for
     removal to the spoil areas.

     Figure 4-1. Bulldozer removing medium-size trees

4-8  TM 3-34.48-1                                      29 February 2016


---

                                                                                                      Clearing, Grubbing, and Stripping

Large Trees (Twelve or More Inches in Diameter)

     4-46. Removing large trees is much slower and more difficult than clearing brush and small trees. (See figure
     4-2.) First, gently and cautiously probe the tree for dead limbs that could fall. Then, position the blade high,
     and center the blade for maximum leverage. Determine the direction of fall before pushing the tree over; the
     direction of lean is usually the direction of fall. If possible, push the tree the same as a medium tree. If the
     tree has a large, deeply embedded root system, use the following steps:

              Step 1. Make a cut deep enough to cut some of the large roots on the side opposite the direction
                  of fall. Use a V ditch cut around the tree, tilted downward laterally toward the tree roots.

              Step 2. Cut side two.
              Step 3. Cut side three.
              Step 4. Build an earth ramp on the same side as the original cut to obtain greater pushing leverage.

                  Then, push the tree over. As the tree starts to fall, reverse the tractor quickly to get away from the
                  rising root mass. After felling the tree, fill the stump hole so that water will not collect in it.

             Note. The roots on the fourth side may need to be cut also.

                      Figure 4-2. Four steps for removing large trees with a bulldozer

Tree-Dozer, Tractor-Mounted Unit

     4-47. The tree-dozer is a tractor with a blade that splits and slices large trees. A sharp projection on the left
     side of the blade splits the trees, while the cutting edge shears them off at ground level. A steel canopy and a
     guide bar control the direction of falling trees and protect the operator.

29 February 2016  TM 3-34.48-1  4-9


---

Chapter 4

     4-48. The tree-dozer is a simple, efficient piece of equipment used for military land-clearing operations. It
     does not disturb the soil to a noticeable degree. It provides—

              Clear fields of fire and security around cantonments, airfields, and other facilities.
              Right-of-way clearance to desired depths along roads and railroads, thereby reducing enemy

                  capability of ambush.

     4-49. Before committing a tractor equipped with a tree-dozer mount, investigate soil conditions in the area
     to determine if the soil can support the equipment. Use the tree-dozer mounting to make cuts through
     forestland but not heavy swampland. Shear trees at ground level; sweep them into piles or windrows, and
     dispose of them. One tractor equipped with a tree-dozer mounting can clear approximately 1 to 2 acres per
     hour depending on the tree density and size. Use one of the following clearing methods: counterclockwise,
     clockwise, steep-slope, or level terrain.

Counterclockwise Method

     4-50. When the tractor can move forward almost continuously, it shears anything in its path to ground level.
     Fast production can be obtained by laying out long areas (200- to 400-feet wide) that can be cut from the
     outside toward the center in a counterclockwise direction. The cut material then slides off the trailing (right)
     end of the tree-dozer mounting and leaves the uncut area free of fallen debris. The windrows are placed
     lengthwise on the borders of the areas. Sweeping with the tree-dozer mounting forms the final debris piles.
     Sweep one blade width at a time. Work from the center of each area, at a right angle to the border. (See figure
     4-3.)

                                         Figure 4-3. Counterclockwise method

Clockwise Method

     4-51. Again, long areas are laid out in 200- to 400-foot widths, but the cutting is done from the center toward
     the sides in a clockwise direction. This allows the cut material to fall toward the center, which becomes the
     windrow site. The piling is done with the tree-dozer mounting. (See figure 4-4.) When windrowing, the
     operator keeps the cutting edge on the ground while pushing into the windrow and raises it when backing
     away. This allows accumulated soil to sift away and lessens soil deposits in the windrow.

4-10  TM 3-34.48-1  29 February 2016


---

                                                  Clearing, Grubbing, and Stripping

                                         Figure 4-4. Clockwise method

Steep-Slope Method
4-52. On extreme slopes, rapid production is obtained by working in a semicircular pattern, from left to right,
at approximate right angles to the windrow. (See figure 4-5.) If the terrain is steep, the windrows should be
on the contour, and the tractor should work from the uphill side and push downhill to the windrow.

                  Figure 4-5. Steep-slope method

29 February 2016  TM 3-34.48-1                    4-11


---

Chapter 4

Level-Terrain Method
     4-53. Where the vegetation is dense and small, cutting and windrowing simultaneously can obtain the highest
     production. Work from left to right at a 90° angle to the windrow, with the trailing edge of the tree-dozer
     working against the uncut material. This prevents cut material from sliding off the moldboard and allows the
     cut material to accumulate on the moldboard.

     4-54. When the moldboard is filled, the operator should stop the tractor and deposit the cut material. The
     operator should then reverse to the starting point and repeat the operation to the right, reducing the time lost
     in backing up. (See figure 4-6.) When the tractor reaches the previously cut material, the operator should
     deposit cut material and form another windrow.

                                             Figure 4-6. Level-terrain method

     4-55. The operator works in patches, from inside to outside, in a counterclockwise direction and at right
     angles to the windrows. (See figure 4-6.) Sweeping and piling the resulting debris can be accomplished faster
     when tractors are used in teams traveling abreast.

Winches

     4-56. Towing winches mounted on tractor-dozers or trucks are limited in use for clearing because of their
     small capacities.

Tractor-Mounted Winch

     4-57. Use tractor-mounted winches for uprooting trees and stumps up to 24 inches in diameter, hoisting and
     skidding felled trees, and extricating mired equipment. On the tractor-dozer unit, the winch is mounted in the
     rear and is directly geared to the rear power take-off on the tractor. The line pull developed varies with the
     size of the tractor, the speed at which the winch is operated, and the number of layers of rope on the drum.
     The line pull of a tractor-mounted winch is about one-half the pull of a standard tree- and stump-pulling unit.

Truck-Mounted Winch

     4-58. As an expedient, truck-mounted winches can be used on trees up to 6 inches in diameter. Their
     capacities are too limited for heavy work. Their best use is for skidding felled trees and logs to a disposal
     area if the haul road is sufficiently cleared for trucks to operate.

4-12  TM 3-34.48-1  29 February 2016


---

                                                                                                      Clearing, Grubbing, and Stripping

Felling Equipment

     4-59. Felling can be done with hand tools or power equipment. Axes, two-man saws, shovels, pick-mattocks,
     and machetes are used to chop or saw down standing timber; dig and uproot stumps; and slash grass, vines,
     and undergrowth. Hand clearing is usually slow and difficult for military requirements unless explosives or
     mechanical methods are used. This clearing method can be used with good results when labor is plentiful,
     forests are dense, and the terrain is rough. Powered equipment, such as chain saws and circular saws, are
     primary felling equipment.

Ripper

     4-60. In land clearing, the ripper helps bulldozer removal operations and tree- and stump-pulling units. The
     ripper cuts and breaks tree roots and loosens boulders from the ground. The short depth of shank penetration
     limits the rippers use to shallow root systems. Before stripping operations, the ripper is used to loosen and
     break up frozen soil or organic material for easier removal by graders or scrapers.

Grader

     4-61. The grader is used to cut grass and weeds, remove small brush, and clear the area of dead vegetation.
     The terrain must be level and free from boulders and trees. Graders, used with rippers and bulldozers, can
     windrow the cleared material for removal by other equipment. The grader is extremely limited in most
     clearing operations.

CLEARING WITH EXPLOSIVES

     4-62. Explosives may be used to fell standing trees, uproot entire trees and stumps, and remove and dispose
     of large boulders. Explosives, however, have several disadvantages. The sound of explosives can travel
     farther than the sound of construction equipment. In loose soil, the initial charge may be entirely expended
     in compacting the soil under a tree or stump; a second charge may be required to remove it. Often, deep
     taproots are only broken by explosives and have to be removed by hand. Also, explosives take time to place
     and create large craters that require borrow excavation and compaction to backfill. In spite of these
     disadvantages, it is still sometimes necessary to use explosives to clear an area where the terrain precludes
     or seriously impedes the operation of heavy equipment. Refer to FM 3-34.214//MCRP 3-17.7L for the correct
     application of explosives and demolitions.

Trees and Stumps

     4-63. Methods of tree and stump blasting vary with the size and condition of the tree, root structure, and
     ground conditions. Figure 4-7, page 4-14, shows the methods of placing charges to blast stumps with different
     root structures. Refer to table 4-1, page 4-2, for the root system type for several tree species in temperate
     forests.

     4-64. The size of the charge required depends on the strength of the explosive available; the size, variety,
     and age of the tree or stump; and soil conditions.

     4-65. Various tool types (pinch bars, earth augers, spoons) can be used when drilling holes for the charge.
     Wood augers can be used for taproots. For loading and tamping, a smooth, wooden pole about 5 feet long
     and 1 1/2 inches in diameter can be used (for example, the handle from a long-handled shovel; the crook of
     the blade end provides a good grip). Holes must be tamped firmly with earth to retain the full force of the
     explosion.

29 February 2016  TM 3-34.48-1  4-13


---

Chapter 4

                      Figure 4-7. Stump-blasting methods for different root structures

Boulders

     4-66. When boulders cannot be used in an embankment or fill, they must be removed from the construction
     area. Blasting is a quick and easy method of dislodging boulders. Mud-capping, blockholing, or snakeholing
     may be used (refer to FM 3-34.214//MCRP 3-17.7L or TM 3-34.85/MCRP 3-17A for additional information).
     Refer to TM 3-34.65/NTRP 4-04.2.12/AFMAN 10-903 for quantities and types of explosives used and details
     regarding blasting rock.

REMOVAL OF SURFACE ROCKS

     4-67. Surface rocks must be removed in certain types of construction. The following are the three methods
     used in this operation: hand, bulldozer, and crane or scoop loader. The choice of method depends on the
     situation.

Hand

     4-68. When there is sufficient time and personnel, rocks are picked up and loaded into hauling units by hand.
     This method is slow and used in military construction as an expedient.

Bulldozer

     4-69. The bulldozer is the most commonly used engineer equipment for moving rocks to a fill or disposal
     area. The rocks may be windrowed by bulldozers for later removal by scrapers or shovels and trucks. If the
     distance is short, bulldozers may push them to the designated disposal area.

4-14       TM 3-34.48-1  29 February 2016


---

                                                                                                      Clearing, Grubbing, and Stripping

Crane or Scoop Loader

     4-70. Clearing surface rock by this method alone is possible, but it is slow. If the rocks are first windrowed
     or moved into piles by bulldozers or graders, the shovel loads trucks quickly and efficiently. The rocks can
     then be hauled long distances for disposal.

STRIPPING

     4-71. Stripping consists of removing and disposing of the topsoil and sod that cannot be used as subgrade,
     foundation under a fill, or borrow material. Examples of this material are organic soils, humus, peat, and
     muck. Unsuitable soil must be removed to a depth where compaction and thickness requirements are satisfied.
     Stripping is done concurrently with clearing and grubbing by using bulldozers, graders, scrapers, and
     sometimes shovels. Good topsoil and sod should be stockpiled for later use (dust control, erosion control,
     camouflage).

REMOVAL OF STRUCTURES

     4-72. An airfield construction site may be acceptable except for obstructions (houses, railroads, power lines)
     on the proposed site or near the operation of aircraft. The primary selection of a site involves compromises.
     The survey party often selects a site where limited clearing of structures will be necessary before full-scale
     operations can take place.

Power Lines

     4-73. Power lines obstructing forward area construction or glide angles should be removed. Sometimes the
     lines may be needed intact and a different approach to the airfield must be used. If the lines cross the runway,
     relocate the lines around the nearest end of the runway. As a last resort, underground installation may be used
     if armored underground cable or conduit is available that will adequately insulate the lines. In support area,
     power lines that are not in an approach zone or high enough to extend into the glide angle when located in
     an approach zone may be marked with suitable warning lights.

Roads and Railroads

     4-74. In general, roads and railroads near airfields are not obstructions if traffic does not interfere with
     aircraft approach or takeoff. Do not destroy paved main highways or railroad lines because they may be
     required for ground operations. It is desirable to have the airfield located near a good road or railroad so that
     supplies can be transported to the site.

Buildings

     4-75. Buildings may be completely demolished with explosives or heavy equipment, leaving no salvage.
     Buildings may also be torn down in a way that conserves usable material or allows them to be relocated.

REMOVAL OF BURIED EXPLOSIVES

     4-76. Mines, booby traps, unexploded ordnance, and other buried explosives must be located and removed
     or neutralized before construction operations begin. Check reports and data on the area to locate and identify
     explosives.

     4-77. Establish the boundaries of the construction area, and then make a visual search of the most likely
     places for explosives. They are usually near existing structures, houses, and roads; in disturbed ground
     hollows where the earth has visibly settled; and under stockpiles, pickets, or stakes placed in unnatural
     locations. If time allows, thoroughly investigate the area with mine detectors or by probing methods.

     4-78. The safety of personnel and equipment is primary during the removal of mines. The speed of clearance
     is secondary. When possible, use trained explosive ordnance disposal detachments especially when the size
     of the bomb precludes detonation in place.

29 February 2016  TM 3-34.48-1  4-15


---

Chapter 4

     4-79. The method of mine and unexploded ordnance removal is a command decision. For a minefield with
     booby traps or other antipersonnel devices, it is best to destroy the mines in place by explosives or mechanical
     means. Unexploded ordnance may be disarmed by ordnance personnel and then manually removed from the
     area and disposed. If ordnance personnel are not available, destroy the device in place.
     4-80. Surface mines or bomblets may be pushed from an area using a drag chain or bulldozer. If devices are
     destroyed in place, resulting holes and craters must be filled and compacted with acceptable material using
     bulldozers or graders. (See TM 3-34.62/MCRP 3-17.7I for additional information.)

4-16  TM 3-34.48-1  29 February 2016

                                                 Chapter 5

                     Subgrades and Base Courses

         This chapter discusses the functions of the subgrade, subbase, and base courses. It also
         covers material selection and construction procedures. Refer to chapter 12 of this
         manual for the determination of the base- and surface-course thickness for roads and
         expedient construction methods in the JOA. Refer to TM 3-34.48-2 for similar
         information on classes of airfields and heliports and commonly used types of surface
         materials. For additional information on soil, compaction, and the California bearing
         ratio (CBR) requirement, refer to TM 3-34.64/MCRP 3-17.7G and TM 3-34.43/MCRP
         3-17-7H/NAVFAC MO 330/AFH 32-1034.

DESIGN CONSIDERATIONS

     5-1. Pavement structures may be rigid or flexible. In rigid pavements, the wearing surface is made of
     cement. A rigid pavement made of cement will have great flexural strength, act as a beam, and bridge minor
     irregularities that may occur in the base of the subgrade it rests upon.

     5-2. Other types of pavements are classified as flexible. In a flexible pavement, a distortion or displacement
     occurring in the subgrade is reflected in the base course and continues upward into the surface course.
     Flexibility denotes the tendency of courses in this type of structure to conform to the same shape under traffic.

     5-3. Flexible pavements are used almost exclusively in the JOA for road and support area airfield
     construction. They are adaptable to most situations, and they fall within the construction capabilities of the
     combat heavy engineer battalion and its support units. In most cases, the hot-mixed asphalt job mix formula
     is designed with the Marshall method, using the Marshall impact hammer. For road and street projects, the
     Superpave gyratory compactor may be used if available. Rigid pavements are generally not suited to
     construction requirements (unless the materials are readily available) and are not discussed in detail in this
     manual. (See TM 3-34.43/MCRP 3-17-7H/NAVFAC MO 330/AFH 32-1034 for additional information.)

FLEXIBLE-PAVEMENT STRUCTURE

     5-4. A typical flexible-pavement structure is shown in figure 5-1, page 5-2. It illustrates the terms used in
     this manual that refer to the various layers. The layers shown in figure 5-1 are not present in every flexible
     pavement. For example, a flexible-pavement structure may consist of an asphaltic-concrete surface, a base
     course, and the subgrade. The design of flexible pavements must include a thorough investigation of the
     subgrade conditions; borrow areas; and sources of select, subbase, and base materials.

TESTS

     5-5. Military engineers should classify soils according to TM 3-34.64/MCRP 3-17.7G, and then select
     representative samples for detailed tests. Detailed tests determine compaction characteristics, CBR values,
     and other properties needed for designing the flexible-pavement structure. Subbase and base-course materials
     are tested for compliance with specification requirements for gradation, liquid limit (LL), plasticity index
     (PI), and CBR values. When tests are completed, limiting conditions in the subgrade and subsoil must be
     determined. Materials are selected for each layer based on their characteristics (gradation, LL, PI, and CBR
     values).

29 February 2016  TM 3-34.48-1  5-1


---

Chapter 5

             Note. Layers and coats are not present in every flexible-pavement structure. Intermediate courses may
             be placed in one or more lifts. Tack coats may be required between the intermediate courses and under
             the surface course. A prime coat may be required between the highest aggregate surface and the first layer
             of asphalt.

                                    Figure 5-1. Typical flexible-pavement section

LOAD DISTRIBUTION

     5-6. Flexible-pavement design is based on the principle that the magnitude of stress induced by a wheel
     load decreases with depth below the surface. Consequently, the stresses induced on a given subgrade material
     can be decreased by increasing the thickness of the overlying layers (subbase, base, and surface courses).
     Figure 5-2 shows the distribution of a single-wheel load on two sections of flexible pavement, one with a
     thick flexible-pavement structure and one with a thin flexible-pavement structure. In both cases, the subgrade
     is the foundation that eventually carries the load applied at the surface. Figure 5-2 demonstrates that the stress
     magnitude on the subgrade decreases as the flexible-pavement structure is thickened. On the left diagram,
     the flexible-pavement structure is thick, the load at the subgrade level is spread over a wide area, and the
     stress on the subgrade is low. On the right diagram, the structure is thin, the load at the subgrade level is
     confined to a much smaller area, and the stress on the subgrade level is significantly higher. The pattern of
     decreasing stress with increasing depth is the basis of the conventional flexible-pavement design in which
     subgrade materials of low-bearing capacity are covered with thick flexible-pavement structures.

     5-7. The distribution of pressures under a multiple-wheel assembly is shown in figure 5-3. Multiple-wheel
     assemblies are beneficial because the stress distributions produced by the tires do not overlap to a large degree
     at shallow depths. This is illustrated at line A-A in figure 5-3. Therefore, multiple-wheel assemblies are
     beneficial on thin flexible-pavement structures constructed on subgrades with high-bearing capacity.

5-2        TM 3-34.48-1  29 February 2016

                  Figure 5-2. Distribution of pressures under single-wheel loads

approx

Figure 5-3. Distribution of pressures produced by multiple-wheel assemblies

5-8. The tire-contact area and tire pressure affects the intensity of stress at a given point in a flexible
pavement. The major difference in stress intensities caused by variation in tire pressure occurs near the
surface. Consequently, the surface course (pavement or a well-graded crushed aggregate) and base course
are seriously affected by high tire pressures.

SUBGRADES

     5-9. Using information from a deliberate soil survey as outlined in TM 3-34.43/MCRP 3-17-7H/NAVFAC
     MO 330/AFH 32-1034, consider the following factors when determining the suitability of a subgrade:

              General characteristics of the subgrade soils.
              Depth to the bedrock.
              Depth to the water table.
              Compaction that can be attained in the subgrade.
              CBR values of uncompacted and compacted subgrades.
              Weak or soft layers or organics in the subsoil.
              Detrimental frost action or excessive swell susceptibility.

29 February 2016  TM 3-34.48-1                                                    5-3


---

Chapter 5

GRADE LINE

     5-10. Classify the subgrade soil according to the Unified Soil Classification System (USCS) as described in
     TM 3-34.64/MCRP 3-17.7G, and consider the previously listed factors to determine the suitability of a
     subgrade material. When locating the grade line of a road or airfield, consider the suitability of the subgrade,
     the depth to the water table, and the depth to bedrock. Generally, the grade line should be established to
     obtain the best possible subgrade material consistent with the design parameters. Simplicity of construction
     must also be considered.

COMPACTION

     5-11. Compaction normally increases the strength of subgrade soils. The typical procedure is to specify
     compaction according to recommended requirements. (See figure 5-4.) A specification block should be used
     to determine limits for density and moisture content.

     Notes.
     1. A cohesive soil is one with PI less than 5.
     2. A cohesionless soil is one with a PI greater than or equal to 5.
     3. Percent compaction is a percent of the maximum density at CE 55.
     4. Each layer shown will not necessarily be used in the final design.
     5. The minimum compacted layer thicknesses are 4” for a road and 6” for an airfield.

     Legend:

     CBR      California bearing ratio

     CE       compactive effort

     PI       plasticity index

         Figure 5-4. Recommended compaction requirements for support areas

     5-12. Compaction is relatively simple in fill sections because the layers are subjected to construction
     processes and can be compacted during construction. Compaction is more difficult in cut sections. During

5-4           TM 3-34.48-1                                                                 29 February 2016


---

                                                                                                            Subgrades and Base Courses

     construction, compaction must be obtained to a depth where the natural density of material will resist further
     consolidation under traffic.

     5-13. Specific requirements for minimum depth of subgrade compaction for cohesive (clayey) and
     cohesionless (sandy) soils for road designs are described in chapter 12 of this manual. This same information
     for airfield designs is described in TM 3-34.48-2.

Typical Cases

     5-14. Cohesionless soils (except silts) can be compacted from the surface with heavy rollers or very heavy
     vibratory compactors. Cohesive soils (including silts) cannot be compacted in thick layers. In cut areas
     consisting of cohesive soils, it may be necessary to remove the subgrade material and replace it with
     sequential lifts capable of being compacted to the required density. Initially, replace material in 6-inch lifts
     and adjust the lift thickness up or down as necessary to determine the minimum compactive effort.
     Compaction of cohesive soil is best achieved with penetrating rollers, such as tamping or sheepsfoot rollers.

     5-15. Compare the native subsoil compaction with compaction requirements for the subgrade as described
     in chapter 12 of this manual and TM 3-34.48-2 to determine if consolidation of the subsoil is likely to occur
     under the design traffic load. If consolidation is likely to occur, compact the subsoil or design a thicker
     flexible-pavement structure to prevent subsoil consolidation.

     5-16. Cohesive materials, including those of relatively low plasticity that show little swell tendency, should
     be compacted at the optimum moisture content determined from the density-moisture curves developed for
     that soil using the modified proctor test per UFGS-32 11 16.16. Cohesionless, free-draining materials should
     be compacted at moisture contents approaching saturation.

Special Cases

     5-17. Although compaction normally increases soil strength, some soils lose stability when scarified and
     rolled. Some soils shrink excessively during dry periods and expand excessively when they absorb moisture.
     Special treatment is required when these soils are encountered. The following paragraphs describe the soils
     in which these conditions may occur and suggested methods of treatment.

Soils That Lose Strength

     5-18. The soil types that decrease in strength when remolded are generally in the USCS CH, MH, and OH
     groups. They are soils that have been consolidated to a high degree by alternate cycles of wetting and drying
     or by geologic overburden loads. They have developed a definite internal structure with a high strength when
     left undisturbed. Scarifying, reworking, and rolling these soils in cut areas will reduce the soils load-bearing
     capacity.

     5-19. When these soils are encountered, obtain CBR values for the soil in undisturbed and disturbed
     conditions. Compact the removed soil to the design density at the design moisture content. Other samples
     should be compacted to the design density across the range of specified moisture contents. If the undisturbed
     value is higher than the laboratory test results, no compaction should be attempted, and construction
     operations should be conducted to produce the least possible soil disturbance. Since compaction should be
     avoided in these cases, the required depth of compaction may govern the total thickness design above the
     subgrade instead of the CBR method. (See UFC 3-260-02 for additional information.)

Silts

     5-20. The bearing capacity for silts, very fine sands, and rock flour (predominantly USCS ML and SC
     groups) is good if properly compacted within the specified moisture range. Compaction of silt, very fine
     sand, and rock flour in a high water table area can pump water to the surface. The material becomes very soft
     and loses a considerable amount of load bearing capacity. This condition can also develop when silts and
     poorly draining, very fine sands are compacted at a high moisture content. Compaction reduces air voids so
     that the available water fills the void space. Therefore, it is difficult to obtain the desired density in these silts
     and very fine sands at moisture contents greater than optimum.

29 February 2016  TM 3-34.48-1  5-5


---

Chapter 5

     5-21. Water from a wet, spongy silt subgrade often enters the subbase and base during compaction through
     capillary action. This additional moisture will have detrimental effects on bearing capacity and frost
     susceptibility. If the source of water can be removed, it is usually not difficult to dry these deposits. These
     soils usually crumble easily and scarify readily. If the soils can be dried, normal compaction effort should be
     applied. However, removing the source of water is often difficult and, in some cases, impossible in the
     allotted construction period.

     5-22. In areas with a high water table, drying is not possible until the water table is sufficiently lowered.
     Compaction operations will continue to cause water to be pumped to the surface. Areas of this nature are best
     treated by replacing the soil with subbase and base materials or with a dry soil that is not adversely affected
     by water.

     5-23. Do not disturb the subgrade where drainage is not feasible or a high water table cannot be lowered.
     Also, do not disturb the subgrade where soils become saturated from sources other than high water tables and
     cannot be dried, such as construction during wet seasons. Compaction of lifts during wet periods can cause
     fines from the subgrade to contaminate the upper layers of the flexible-pavement structure.

     5-24. The pumping and detrimental actions previously described should be anticipated when silts or very
     fine-sand subgrades are located in areas with a high water table. Pumping action limits the ability to obtain
     the desired compaction in the immediate overlying material.

Swelling Soils

     5-25. Soils are characterized as swelling if they display a significant increase in volume with the addition of
     moisture. These soils can cause trouble in a region where construction is accomplished during a dry season
     and the soils absorb moisture during a subsequent wet season. If the moisture content of the compacted soil
     increases after compaction, the soil will swell and produce large uplift pressures. This action may result in
     unacceptable differential heaving of flexible pavements. For military construction, swelling soils are placed
     at moisture contents that will not result in more than a 3-percent change in volume if soil moisture is later
     increased.

     5-26. Preswelling is a common method for treating subgrade soils with expansive characteristics. The soil
     should be compacted at a moisture content where a 3-percent or greater swelling has occurred. This reduces
     the impact of future expansion. Proper control of moisture content is the most important item to remember
     for swelling soils.

SELECTION OF SUBGRADE AND SUBSOIL DESIGN CALIFORNIA BEARING RATIO VALUES

     5-27. The CBR test described in TM 3-34.43/MCRP 3-17-7H/NAVFAC MO 330/AFH 32-1034 includes
     procedures for conducting tests on samples compacted in test molds (design density and soaked for four days)
     and for taking in-place CBR tests on undisturbed samples. These tests estimate the CBR that will develop in
     the prototype structure. Where the design CBR is above 20, the subgrade must also meet the gradation and
     Atterberg limit requirements for a subbase. (See table 5-1.)

     5-28. Subgrades can be stabilized mechanically (by adding granular materials), chemically (by adding
     chemical admixtures), or with a stabilization expedient (sand-grid, matting, or geosynthetics). Stabilization
     with chemical admixtures (lime, Portland cement, fly ash) is generally costly but may prove to be
     economically feasible, depending on the availability of the chemical stabilization agent in comparison with
     the availability of granular material. Chemically stabilized layers should be designed according to the criteria
     presented in TM 3-34.64/MCRP 3-17.7G.

5-29. If mechanical stabilization is used and the stabilized material meets the gradation and Atterberg limit
requirements in table 5-1, it can be assigned a subbase CBR rating. If it does not meet the requirements for a
subbase, the material must not be considered a select material.

5-30. A stabilization expedient may provide significant time and cost savings as a substitute to other means
of stabilization or low strength fill. The most popular manmade stabilizers are sand grid, matting, and various
types of geosynthetics, especially geotextiles. Matting and sand grid are expedient methods of stabilizing
loose sands for unsurfaced road construction. Geotextiles and other geosynthetics are primarily used to
reinforce weak subgrades, maintain the separation of soil layers, and control drainage through the road or
airfield design. The availability of these materials must be weighed with the considerable time savings for
use of expedients in combat construction.

FROST SUSCEPTIBILITY

     5-31. In areas subjected to seasonal freezing and thawing, subgrade materials may exhibit frost heave and
     thaw weakening. Table 5-2, page 5-8, lists the frost-susceptibility ratings of soils. Materials with F3 and F4
     classifications are extremely frost-susceptible, especially if the water table is less than 5 feet below the top
     of the subgrade. Silty soils are particularly susceptible and their CBR value may be less than 1 during thawing
     periods. The thaw period and resulting degraded soil strength may last from one to four weeks. Emphasis
     must be placed on reducing traffic loads during this period to help reduce the possibility of damage.

     5-32. Select and subbase materials that are subjected to freezing and thawing may exhibit detrimental frost
     effects. Although these materials generally are not affected by excessive frost heave, they may lose up to
     50 percent of their strength during thawing conditions. This is especially true of materials that have more
     than 20 percent fines (particles passing the number 200 sieve). Materials categorized as F1, F2, F3, and F4
     in table 5-2, are unsuitable as base or subbase materials in seasonal frost and permafrost areas. Materials
     categorized as F1 and F2 may be suitable as a select material in seasonal frost and permafrost areas, provided
     the plasticity meets the requirements of table 5-1.

SELECT MATERIALS AND SUBBASE COURSES

     5-33. When designing flexible pavements, locally available materials may be used between the subgrade and
     base course. These layers are designated in this manual as select materials or subbases. Those with design

                                                                                                            Subgrades and Base Courses

     5-34. Where the CBR value of the subgrade, without processing, is in the range of 20 to 50, select materials
     and subbases may not be needed. However, the subgrade cannot be assigned a design CBR value greater than
     20 unless it meets the gradation and plasticity requirements for subbases.

     5-35. Where subgrade materials meet plasticity requirements but are deficient in grading requirements, it
     may be possible to treat an existing subgrade by blending in stone, lime rock, sand, or similar materials to
     produce an acceptable subbase and raise the design CBR value.

Select Materials

     5-36. Select materials will typically be locally available as coarse-grained soils (gravels and sands) although
     fine-grained soils in the ML and CL groups may be used in certain cases. Consider limestone rock, sandstone
     rock, coral, oyster shells, ashes, cinders, caliche, and disintegrated granite when evaluating sources of select
     material. To qualify as a select material, a material must meet the gradation and Atterberg limit requirements
     established in table 5-1, page 5-7. A maximum aggregate size of 3 inches will aid in meeting aggregate
     gradations.

Subbase Materials

     5-37. Subbase materials may consist of native coarse-grained soils or blended and processed soils. Limestone
     rock, sandstone rock, coral, oyster shells, ashes, cinders, caliche, and disintegrated granite may be used as
     subbases when they meet the requirements in table 5-1. The existing subgrade may meet the requirements
     for a subbase course, or it may be possible to modify the existing subgrade to produce a subbase. Do not mix
     native or processed materials unless the unmixed subgrade meets the LL and PI requirements for subbases.

     5-38. A suitable subbase may be formed using material that is stabilized with commercial admixtures.
     Portland cement, hydrated lime, fly ash, and bituminous materials are commonly used. The plasticity of some
     materials can be decreased by adding lime or Portland cement, enabling them to be used as subbases.

Compaction

     5-39. Select and subbase materials can be processed and compacted using normal compaction procedures.
     Specify compaction according to the criteria described in figure 5-4, page 5-4.

SELECTION OF DESIGN CALIFORNIA BEARING RATIO

     5-40. CBR tests are usually conducted on remolded samples. However, where existing similar construction
     is available, conduct CBR tests on material in place when it has attained its maximum expected water content
     or on undisturbed, soaked samples. The procedures for selecting test values described in the section on
     subgrades also apply to select and subbase materials. To be used as a select or subbase, the material must
     comply with the requirements indicated in table 5-1, page 5-7, including CBR value, gradation, and Atterberg
     limits. If a material meets the requirements for gradation and Atterberg limits for the next higher design CBR
     category, but the material CBR value does not meet the maximum design CBR for that category, assign the
     material a CBR design value equal to the measured CBR results. For example, a material with a measured
     CBR value of 37 that meets the gradation and Atterberg limit requirements for a CBR 40 subbase should be
     used as a CBR 37 subbase. Conversely, if the material failed to meet the CBR 40 subbase requirements
     (gradation and Atterberg limits) but met the CBR 30 subbase requirements, it would be used as a CBR 30
     subbase not a CBR 37 subbase.

     5-41. Some native materials develop satisfactory CBR values but do not meet the gradation requirements in
     table 5-1. These materials may be used as select or subbase materials, if supported by adequate in-place CBR
     tests on construction projects using the materials that have been in service for several years.

     5-42. The CBR test is not applicable for evaluating materials stabilized with chemical admixtures. These
     chemically stabilized soils must be assigned an equipment CBR value based on the type of admixture and
     method of application. (See TM 3-34.64/MCRP 3-17.7G.) Ratings as high as 100 can be assigned to these
     materials when proper construction procedures are followed.

Chapter 5

BASE COURSE

     5-43. The purpose of a base course is to distribute the induced stresses from the wheel load so that the load
     will not exceed the available strength of the underlying soil layers. When the subgrade strength is low, the
     stress must be reduced to a lower value or a thicker base is needed. When the subgrade strength is high, a
     thinner base course will provide adequate stress distribution. Because the stresses in the base course are
     always higher than in the subgrade, the base course must have higher strength. (See figure 5-5).

         Figure 5-5. Distribution of stress in base courses and effects of subgrade strength
                                                 on base course thickness

     5-44. The base course is normally the highest quality structural material used in a flexible-pavement
     structure, having CBR values near the CBR standard material (crushed limestone). Base courses are always
     cohesionless materials and are normally processed to obtain the proper gradation.

REQUIREMENTS

     5-45. Give careful attention to the selection of materials for base courses. The materials should be dense and
     uniformly graded so that no differential settlement occurs. For continuous stability, base courses must meet
     gradation and plasticity requirements.

Gradation

     5-46. Normally, a material used as a base course must meet the gradation requirements outlined in table 5-3,
     table 5-4, and table 5-5 (depending on the type of material). Determine gradation of the proposed material
     using mechanical analysis. If strict adherence to gradation requirements is not feasible, a safe rule of thumb
     is to avoid using materials that have more than 15 percent fines (particles passing the number 200 sieve).

Plasticity Index and Liquid Limit

     5-47. In addition to the gradation requirement, a base-course material must meet the same PI and LL
     requirements for a subbase material. (See table 5-1, page 5-7.) Material with a LL greater than 25 or a PI
     greater than 5 should not be used as a base course.

Chapter 5

Compaction

     5-48. Base-course material must be capable of being compacted to meet the requirements given in figure 5-4,
     page 5-4. When constructing a base course, lift thickness must be designed on its ability to attain the required
     density. Lift thickness is dependent on the type of material, the compaction equipment used, and the method
     of construction.

5-49. The CBR of the finished base course must conform to that used in the design. The total compacted
thickness must equal that obtained from the flexible-pavement design curves. Table 5-6 shows nine material
types commonly used as base courses for roads and airfields. A typical design CBR is given for each type of
material. Laboratory CBR tests to determine design CBR values are not necessary.

MATERIALS

     5-50. Natural, processed, and other materials are used for base courses. Descriptions of these materials
     follow.

Natural

     5-51. A wide variety of gravels, sands (gravelly and sandy soils), and other natural materials (lime rock,
     coral, shells, some caliches) can be used alone or blended as a suitable base course. Sometimes natural
     materials require crushing or removal of oversized material to maintain gradation limits. Some natural
     materials may be suitable for use as a base course by mixing or blending them with other materials.

Sand and Gravel

     5-52. Many natural deposits of sandy and gravelly materials make satisfactory base-course materials. Gravel
     deposits differ widely in the relative proportions of coarse- and fine-grained material and in the character of
     the rock fragments. Blending materials from two or more deposits can often produce satisfactory base
     materials. Uncrushed, clean, washed gravel is normally not suitable for a base course because there are not
     enough fine sands present. Fines act as a binder and fill the voids between coarser particles.

Sand and Clay

     5-53. Natural mixtures of sand and clay of varying thicknesses are often located in riverbed deposits. Often,
     there are great variations in the proportions of sand and clay from the top to the bottom of the deposit.
     Depending on the proportions of sand and clay, these deposits may also provide suitable base-course

5-12                            TM 3-34.48-1                                  29 February 2016


---

                                                                                                            Subgrades and Base Courses

     materials. With proper proportioning and construction methods, satisfactory results can be obtained with
     sand-clay soils.

     5-54. Deposits of partly disintegrated rock that consist of fragments of rock, clay, and mica flakes should not
     be confused with sand-clay soils. The mica flakes make the deposit unsuitable for use as a base course.
     Mistaking these deposits for a sand-clay soil may result in base-course failure.

Processed

     5-55. Processed materials are made by crushing and screening rock, gravel, or slag. A properly graded,
     crushed rock base-course material produced from sound, durable rock makes the highest quality base
     material. Existing quarries, ledge rock, cobbles, gravel, talus deposits, coarse mine tailings, and similar hard
     and durable rock fragments are typical sources of processed materials. Table 5-3, page 5-11, shows the
     common rock types that are suitable for base-course material. Generally, rock that is hard enough to require
     blasting during excavation makes suitable base-course material.

     5-56. Base courses made from processed materials can be divided into the following general types:
              Stabilized. In a stabilized base course, material ranging from coarse to fine is mixed to meet the
                  gradation requirement given in table 5-4, page 5-11. The mixing process can be accomplished in
                  advance (at a processing plant) or during the placing operation. Because the aggregates produced
                  in crushing operations or obtained from deposits are often deficient in fines, it may be necessary
                  to blend in selected fines to get a suitable gradation. Screenings, crusher-run fines, or natural clay-
                  free soil may be added for this purpose.
              Coarse-graded. A coarse-graded type of base course is composed of crushed rock, gravel, or slag.
                  When gravel is used, 50 percent of the material by weight must have two or more freshly fractured
                  faces, with the area of each face equal to at least 75 percent of the smallest midsectional area of
                  the piece.
              Macadam. The term macadam is usually applied to construction in which a coarse, crushed
                  aggregate is placed in a relatively thin layer and rolled into place. Fine aggregate or screenings are
                  placed on the surface of the coarse aggregate layer and rolled and broomed into the coarse rock
                  until it is thoroughly keyed in place. Water may be used in the compacting and keying process.
                  When water is used, the base is termed water-bound macadam. The crushed rock used for
                  macadam base courses should consist of clean, angular, durable particles that are free of clay,
                  organic matter, and other unwanted material or coating. A hard, durable, crushed aggregate can
                  be used, provided the coarse aggregate is one size and the fine aggregate will key into the coarse
                  aggregate. Aggregates for macadam-type construction should meet the gradation requirements
                  given in table 5-5, page 5-11.

Other

     5-57. In some JOA areas, deposits of natural sand and gravel and sources of crushed rock are not available.
     This has led to the development of base courses from materials that normally would not be considered. These
     include caliche, lime rock, shells, cinders, coral, iron ore, rubble, and similar materials. Some of these
     materials are weak rock that crush or degrade under construction traffic to produce composite base materials
     similar to those described in the preceding paragraphs. Others develop a cementing action that results in a
     satisfactory base.

     5-58. These materials cannot be judged on the basis of the gradation limits used for other materials. Rather,
     they are judged on the basis of service behavior. Strength tests on laboratory samples are not satisfactory
     because the method of preparing the sample seldom replicates the characteristics of the material in place. The
     PI is a reasonably good criterion for determining the suitability of these materials as base courses. As a
     general rule, a low PI (≤5) is a necessity. However, observation of these types of base materials in existing
     roads and pavements is the most reliable indicator of whether they will be satisfactory.

Coral

     5-59. Coral is commonly found along tropical ocean coastlines. Coral is normally very angular and, as such,
     its greatest asset as a construction material is its bonding properties. These properties vary based on the

29 February 2016  TM 3-34.48-1  5-13


---

Chapter 5

     amount of volcanic impurities, the proportion of fine and coarse material, and the age and length of exposure
     to the elements. Proper moisture control, drainage, and compaction are essential to obtain satisfactory results.
     Avoid variations of more than 1 percent from optimum moisture content. Uncompacted and poorly drained
     coral is susceptible to high capillary rise, resulting in too much moisture and loss of stability. Sprinkling with
     a seawater or sodium chloride (salt) solution promotes bonding when rollers are used. Coral should cure for
     a minimum of 72 hours after compaction is complete.

Caliche
     5-60. Caliche is a by-product of chemical weathering processes. It is composed of limestones, silts, and clays
     cemented together by lime, iron oxide, or salt. Caliche has been used extensively in arid regions as a base
     material because of its ability to recement when saturated with water, compacted, and given time to cure.
     Caliche varies in content (limestone, silt, and clay) and degree of cementation. It is important that caliche of
     good, uniform quality is obtained from deposits and that it be compacted within a specified moisture range.

     5-61. After caliches have been air-dried for 72 hours, the LL of the material passing the No. 40 sieve should
     not exceed 35, and the PI should not exceed 10. For base-course material, caliches should be crushed to meet
     the following gradations:

              Percent passing a 2-inch sieve: 100.
              Percent passing a number (No.) 40 sieve: 15 to 35.
              Percent passing a No. 200 sieve: 0 to 20.

     5-62. Stripping should be used to remove undesirable material from surface deposits of caliche.

Tuff
     5-63. Tuff and other cement-like materials of volcanic origin may be used for base courses. Tuff bases are
     constructed the same as other base courses except that the oversize pieces are broken and the base is
     compacted with sheepsfoot rollers after the tuff is dumped and spread. The surface is graded, and final
     compaction and finishing are accomplished.

Rubble
     5-64. The debris or rubble of destroyed concrete/masonry buildings may be used in constructing base
     courses. Jagged pieces of metal and similar objects must be removed: large pieces of rubble should be broken
     into 3-inch pieces or smaller.

                                                  DANGER

                    When using rubble in a tactical environment, use caution. Rubble
                    may contain mines or booby traps.

Bituminous Base
     5-65. Bituminous mixtures are frequently used as base courses beneath high-use bituminous pavements,
     particularly for support area airfields carrying heavy traffic. Bituminous bases may be advantageous when
     locally available aggregates are relatively weak and have poor quality, when mixing plant and bituminous
     materials are readily available, or when a relatively thick structure is required for traffic.

     5-66. When a bituminous base course is used, it is placed in lifts no more than 3 1/2 inches thick. If a
     bituminous base is used, the binder and leveling courses may be omitted, and the surface course may be laid
     directly on the base course.

SELECTION

     5-67. Selection of the type of base-course construction depends on the materials and equipment available
     and the anticipated weather conditions during construction. A complete investigation should be made to

5-14  TM 3-34.48-1  29 February 2016


---

                                                                                                            Subgrades and Base Courses

     determine the location and characteristics of natural materials suitable for base-course construction. Base
     courses of untreated natural materials are less affected by adverse weather and normally require less technical
     control. Untreated bases are relatively easy and fast to build and are preferred to bituminous or cement-
     stabilized types. This is true even where suitable admixture materials for such construction are readily
     available, but is not true in many areas of the world.

SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS FOR SEASONAL FROST AND PERMAFROST CONDITIONS

     5-68. Since base-course materials are near the surface of the road or airfield, the amount of strength lost
     during thawing periods will have a strong influence on the life of the facility. If possible, the materials listed
     in table 5-2, page 5-8, as nonfrost susceptible or frost susceptible (frost group S1 or S2) should be used as
     base courses in seasonal frost and permafrost areas.

CONSTRUCTION OPERATIONS

     5-69. Construction operations for roads and airfields include fine grading; hauling, placing, and spreading;
     blending and mixing; watering base materials; compacting; and finishing. These tasks are organized
     according to the construction schedule and quality control plan for the project.

Fine Grading

     5-70. The subgrade is fine graded to achieve the desired cross section established by final grade stakes.
     Before placing select material, subbase, and base course, the subgrade should be compacted to attain the
     required density. Ruts and other soft spots should be corrected.

Hauling, Placing, and Spreading

     5-71. Placing and spreading material on the prepared subgrade may begin at the point nearest the borrow
     source or at the point farthest from the source. The advantage of working from the nearest point to the source
     is that haul vehicles can be routed over the spread material, which will compact the base and avoid damage
     to the subgrade. An advantage of working from the point farthest from the source is that hauling equipment
     will further compact the exposed subgrade. Also, this practice will not overwork the base course, which can
     cause unwanted segregation. This method also reveals weak spots in the subgrade so that they can be
     corrected before placement of the base courses and interferes less with spreading and compaction equipment.

     5-72. The self-propelled aggregate spreader is preferred for placing a base course. If a self-propelled spreader
     is not available, base-course material can be spread using towed spreaders, scrapers, or dump trucks. If
     equipment capable of spreading the aggregate in even lifts is not available, the material can be initially
     dumped in long windrows and subsequently spread with graders, dozers, or front-end loaders.

     5-73. Lift thickness should be based on the ability to compact the material to the required density. A good
     rule of thumb is to initially place the base course in 6-inch lifts. After testing the compacted density, increase
     or decrease the lift thickness as necessary to meet the project requirements.

Blending and Mixing

     5-74. Materials to be blended and mixed should be spread on the road, runway, or taxiway in correct
     proportions, with the finer material on top. Fold the fine material into the coarser aggregate with the grader
     blade. If available, dry mix the material using blades, disks, harrows, or rototillers, leaving the material in
     windrows. When a grader is used, thoroughly mix the materials by blading the windrows of materials from
     one side of the area to the other, with the blade of the grader set to give a rolling action to the material. The
     coarse and fine aggregates can also be mixed in mechanical plants (mobile or stationary) or on a paved area
     with graders and bucket loaders. Proportionally distribute the coarse and fine aggregates by weight or volume
     in quantities so that the specified gradation, LL, and PI requirements are attained after the base has been
     placed and compacted. Mixing operations should produce uniform blending.

     5-75. When mechanical mixing is used, place the coarse and fine aggregates in separate stockpiles or
     adjacent windrows to permit easy proportioning. When bucket loaders are used, place the fine- and coarse-

29 February 2016  TM 3-34.48-1  5-15


---

Chapter 5

     aggregate portions in adjacent windrows on a paved area. Blade the windrows together to meet the
     requirements specified for the project.

Watering Base Materials

     5-76. As in subgrade-compaction operations, obtaining the specified compacted density requires that the
     material be placed and compacted at a moisture content inside the specification block. The moisture content
     of the base material at the site can be obtained by a nuclear density meter, a speedy moisture tester, or by
     expedient methods. Given the on-site moisture content, the engineer in charge can calculate exactly how
     much water to add or if the base needs to be aerated to achieve the specified moisture content range.

     5-77. A truck-mounted water distributor can control watering. Asphalt distributors should not be used
     because the pump lubrication system is not designed for water. A container capable of movement and gravity
     discharge of water may be used as an expedient water distributor.

Compacting

     5-78. Base-course compaction must produce a uniformly dense layer that conforms to the specification
     block. Compact base-course material with vibratory or heavy, rubber-tired rollers. Maintain moisture content
     during the compaction procedure within the specified moisture-content range. Compact each layer through
     the full depth to the required density. Measure field densities on the total sample. Use a test strip to determine
     which rollers are most effective and how many roller passes are necessary to achieve the desired compaction.
     The quality of the finished flexible pavement is a direct result of the care and judgment used when
     constructing the base course. Base-course layers that contain gravel and soil-binder material may be
     compacted initially with a sheepsfoot roller and rubber-tired rollers. Rubber-tired rollers are particularly
     effective in compacting base materials if a kneading motion is required to adjust and pack the particles. Base
     courses of crushed rock, lime rock, and shell are compacted with vibratory, steel-wheeled, or rubber-tired
     rollers. Select the equipment and methods on each job to suit the characteristics of the base material. When
     using rollers, begin compaction on the outside edges and work inward, overlapping passes by one-half of a
     roller width.

Finishing

     5-79. Finishing operations must closely follow compaction, resulting in a crowned, tight, and water-shedding
     surface free of ruts and depressions that would inhibit runoff. Use the grader or finishing compacted aggregate
     bases. Blade the material from one side of the runway, taxiway, or road to the middle and back to the edge
     until the required lines and grades are obtained. Before final rolling, the bladed material must be within the
     specified moisture-content range so that it will consolidate with the underlying material to form a dense,
     unyielding mass. If this is not done, thin layers of the material will not be bound to the base, and delamination
     may result. Final rolling is done with rubber-tired and steel-wheeled rollers.

ASPHALT CONCRETE COMPACTION

     5-80. Asphalt compaction for the base course and the asphalt concrete layer requires that the asphalt in place
     be compacted to some percentage of the laboratory density. Typically, density specifications require that field
     densities should be 98 to 100 percent of laboratory densities. Laboratory density should be determined
     according to the ASTM on standard test method for bulk specific gravity and density of no-absorptive
     compacted bituminous mixtures.

     5-81. The Army and Air Force allow two methods of compacting asphalt paving mixtures in the laboratory:
     the Marshall method and the Gyratory Testing Machine (GTM) method. The procedures for conducting the
     Marshall mix design tests are described in CRD-C 649-95. The procedure for gyratory compaction is given
     in CRD-C 651-95 or the standard testing method for the ASTM Standard Test Method for Compaction and
     Shear Properties of Bituminous Mixtures by Means of the United States Corps of Engineers GTM. The
     exceptions are as follows:

              Use 4-inch diameter molds, not 6-inch molds, when Marshall Stabilities and flows are to be
                  determined.

        Use the mixing and compaction temperature requirement as given in United States Army Corps
             of Engineers (USACE) CRD-C 649-95.
