5-83. In the event that an airfield pavement is to be subjected to aircraft with tire pressures of 230 pounds
per square inch or more, the GTM method is mandatory for Army airfield pavements. The GTM method is
preferred, but not mandatory for Air Force airfield pavements. If the GTM method is used for design, it
should also be used for control testing. If the GTM method cannot be used for control testing, the Marshall
apparatus can be used by developing a correlation between the GTM and Marshall specimens for the job mix.
Care should be taken to ensure that excess breakage of the aggregate particles does not occur during Marshall
compaction. Additional information is presented in UFC 3-250-03.

SPECIAL PROCEDURE FOR MACADAM BASES

     5-84. Macadam base-course construction procedures are discussed in the following paragraphs.

Preparing Subgrade

     5-85. If a macadam base course is constructed on a material with high plasticity, there may be base
     infiltration of fine materials. This can be prevented with a blanket course of fine material, such as crusher
     screenings or 3 to 4 inches of sand. The blanket course should be lightly moistened and rolled to a smooth
     surface before spreading the coarse macadam aggregate. A membrane or a geotextile fabric may be used
     instead of the blanket course.

Spreading

     5-86. Macadam aggregate must be placed and spread carefully to ensure that hauling vehicles do not add
     objectionable material to the aggregate. Care is necessary when placing the aggregate at the point nearest the
     source and when routing hauling vehicles over the spread material. If the compacted thickness of the lift is
     4 inches or less, spread the loose macadam aggregate in a uniform layer of sufficient depth to meet
     requirements. For greater compacted thickness, apply the aggregate successively in two or more layers.
     Spreading should be from dump boards, towed aggregate spreaders, or moving vehicles that distribute the
     material in a uniform layer. When more than one layer is required, construction procedures are identical for
     each layer.

Compacting

     5-87. After spreading, immediately compact the coarse aggregate the full width of the strip by rolling it with
     a steel-wheeled roller. Rolling should progress gradually from the sides to the middle of each strip in a crown
     section and from the low side to the high side where there is a transverse slope across the road, runway, or
     taxiway. Continue rolling until there is no creep or wave movement of the aggregate in front of the roller;
     this indicates that the aggregate is stable. Do not attempt rolling when the subgrade is softened by rain.

29 February 2016                TM 3-34.48-1                                                       5-17


---

Chapter 5

Applying Screenings

     5-88. After the coarse aggregate has been thoroughly stabilized and set by rolling, distribute sufficient
     screenings (fine aggregates) to fill the voids in the surface. Roll continuously while screenings are being
     spread so that the jarring effect of the roller will cause the screenings to settle into surface voids. Spread
     screenings in thin layers by using hand shovels, mechanical spreaders, or moving trucks. Do not dump the
     screenings in piles on the coarse aggregate. If necessary, use hand or drag brooms to distribute screenings
     during rolling.

     5-89. Do not apply screenings too thick because they will bridge over the voids and prevent the direct bearing
     of the roller on the coarse aggregate. Continue spreading, sweeping, and rolling until screenings cannot be
     forced into the voids. Start sprinkling the surface with water after the screenings have been spread. Sprinkling
     causes the screenings to be flushed down into the voids of the aggregate. The surface is then rolled. Do not
     saturate; it will soften the subgrade.

     5-90. Continue sprinkling and rolling until a mixture of screenings and water forms, fills the voids, and
     gathers in a small wave before each roller. When a section of a strip has been rolled thoroughly, allow it to
     dry completely before performing additional work.

FINISHED SURFACES

     5-91. The base-course surface determines the smoothness of the finished pavement. If the finished base does
     not conform to the specified grade when tested with a 12-foot straightedge, the finished pavement also will
     not conform. The base surface should be smooth and conform to specified design requirements.

     5-92. When tested with a 12-foot straightedge applied parallel and perpendicular to the centerline of the
     paved area, the surface of the base course should not show deviation in excess of 3/4 inch for roads and
     airfields (for propeller-type aircraft) or 1/8 inch for jet aircraft. Correct a deviation in excess of these figures,
     remove material to the total depth of the lift, and replace with new material and compact as specified above.

SLUSH ROLLING

     5-93. The purpose of slush rolling (rolling with enough water to produce a slushy surface) is to achieve
     compaction when conventional methods fail. Slush rolling should only be permitted on a free-draining, cured
     base course. Slushing requires a considerable amount of water on the surface. The quantity varies with the
     type of material, the temperature, and the humidity. If the surface is mostly satisfactory but has some large
     areas that require slushing, slush only the rough areas. Slushing brings fines to the top and creates voids. In
     general, slush rolling should not be used on a high-quality base-course material. It should be used only when
     required by the specifications or when conventional compaction methods have failed.

Applying Water

     5-94. Engineers must calculate a water application rate in terms of gallons per square yard to allow the water
     distributor operator to accurately apply water. A reasonable estimate for applying water to a 6-inch lift is
     0.5 to 1.0 gallon per square yard. The rollers must follow immediately behind the water truck to achieve the
     desired results because the roller should carry a wave of water ahead of it as it passes over the base course.

Rolling Equipment

     5-95. Use pneumatic-tire, vibratory, or steel-wheeled rollers to obtain a smooth finish on the base course.
     Continue rolling until compaction has been obtained.

Finishing

     5-96. There are usually small rivulets or ridges of fines left on the surface after slushing is completed. Where
     these are excessive or when the thickness of the blanket of fines is excessive, sprinkle the surface with water
     and hone (dress lightly) with a grader blade. This delicate operation requires a good operator and a sharp,
     true blade. Follow the grader immediately with a pneumatic roller to reset the surface.

5-18  TM 3-34.48-1  29 February 2016


---

                                                                                                            Subgrades and Base Courses

WET ROLLING

     5-97. Base courses require a final surface finish. The final finish should be obtained immediately after final
     compaction or proof rolling. For less critical base courses or where deemed necessary by the project engineer,
     wet rolling and slush rolling may be used to obtain the final finish. Both methods have strong points, and the
     job may require a combination of the two in some cases.

Applying Water

     5-98. Wet rolling does not require the large amount of water demanded for slush rolling, and the base course
     does not need to go through the curing period required by the slush-rolling method. Apply enough water to
     the base course to raise the moisture content of the upper 1 to 2 inches of the base course to approximately
     2 percent above the minimum moisture content. The percent of moisture will vary with the type of material
     and is a matter of judgment by the project quality control manager.

Finishing

     5-99. Finish the surface by having the grader blade lightly cut the final surface. The light blading will loosen
     the fines; the coarser particles of the base course will be carried along by the blade to form a windrow at the
     edge of the section being finished. This coarse aggregate can be evenly distributed over the area and
     incorporated into the surface of the base by a steel-wheeled roller closely following the grader. Additional
     water may be required, and rolling by the steel-wheeled and pneumatic-tire rollers must be continued until a
     smooth, dense surface is obtained. This method can also be used to correct minor surface irregularities in the
     base course.

QUALITY CONTROL

     5-100. Quality control is essential to the success of a project. Although visual inspection is important, it is
     not, by itself, sufficient to control the construction of the courses described in this chapter. Depending on the
     type of base, control tests will include determinations of gradation, mixing proportions, plasticity
     characteristics, moisture content, field density, lift thickness, and CBR values. These tests are described in
     detail in TM 3-34.43/MCRP 3-17-7H/NAVFAC MO 330/AFH 32-1034. Before starting construction, a
     detailed quality control plan should be developed that addresses testing procedures, frequency, location, and,
     most importantly, remedial actions.

SOIL STABILIZATION

     5-101. This chapter presents an introduction and discussion of soil stabilization for improving the structural
     quality and workability of soils used for base courses, subbase courses, select materials, and subgrades for
     pavements. It is applicable to the elements responsible for Army, Air Force, or Navy pavement construction.
     Stabilized soils can often be adequate for airfields, traffic pavements, and parking and storage areas where
     an all-weather surface is required, yet traffic does not justify a higher-strength pavement. Surface treatments
     are also used to provide dust control. The most widely recognized form of stabilization is compaction, which
     improves the mechanical stability of most soils. However, compaction alone is often not sufficient to meet
     project requirements.

     5-102. Stabilization is the process of blending and mixing materials with a soil to improve the soil strength
     and durability. The process may include blending soils to achieve a desired gradation or mixing commercially
     available additives that may alter the gradation, change the strength and durability, or act as a binder to
     cement the soil. For details refer to UFC 3-250-11 and TM 3-34.64/MCRP 3-17.7G.

29 February 2016  TM 3-34.48-1  5-19


---

Chapter 5

USES

     5-103. Pavement design is based on the premise that specified levels of quality will be achieved for each
     soil layer in the pavement system. Each layer must—

              Resist shearing within the layer.
              Avoid excessive elastic deflections that would result in fatigue cracking within the layer or in

                  overlying layers.
              Prevent excessive permanent deformation through densification.
              Control dust.

     5-104. As the quality of a soil layer is increased, the ability of that layer to distribute the load over a greater
     area is generally increased enough to permit a reduction in the required thickness of the soil and surface
     layers.

Improve Soil Quality

     5-105. Stabilization is commonly used for better soil gradation, reduction of the PI or swelling potential,
     and increased durability and strength. Stabilized pavement surfaces can be used for many common
     applications (roads, airfield facilities, construction platforms). Stabilized pavements generally do not provide
     the durability of asphalt or concrete surfacing.

Reduce Surface Pavement Thickness

     5-106. A soil layer’s tensile strength and stiffness can be improved by using additives and can reduce the
     thickness of the stabilized layer and overlying layers within the pavement system. Procedures for designing
     pavements that use stabilized soils are presented in UFC 3-250-01FA. Before a stabilized layer can be used
     to reduce the required thickness in the design of a pavement system, the stabilized material must meet the
     durability requirements of various types of additive stabilization and the minimum strength requirements.
     Generally, as the percent of fines and the PI increase, pulverization becomes more difficult and it is harder
     to obtain uniform distribution of the stabilizing additive. For these types of soils, preprocessing or
     pretreatment with other additives may be necessary. For example, fine-grained soils may be pretreated with
     lime to aid in their pulverization, making the mixing of a bitumen or cement additive more successful.

METHODS

     5-107. The two general stabilization methods are mechanical and additive. The effectiveness of stabilization
     depends on the ability to obtain uniformity in blending the various materials. Mixing in a stationary or
     traveling plant is preferred. However, other means of mixing (scarifiers, plows, disks, graders, rotary mixers,
     and reclaimer/stabilizers) have been satisfactory.

     5-108. The soil stabilization method is determined by the amount of stabilizing required and the conditions
     encountered on the project. An accurate soil description and classification are essential for selecting the
     correct materials and procedure. TM 5-822-14/AFJMAN 32-1019 lists the most suitable treatments for
     various soil types to stabilize the soil for different objectives and contains detailed descriptions of proper
     construction techniques

Mechanical

     5-109. Mechanical stabilization is accomplished by mixing or blending two or more gradations of material
     to obtain a mixture that meets the required specifications. These materials may be blended at the construction
     site, a central plant, or a borrow area. The blended material is spread and compacted to the required density
     by conventional means. If the mixture does not meet the specifications after blending, an additive may be
     necessary for stabilization. Compaction is also a form of mechanical stabilization.

Additive

     5-110. Additive refers to a manufactured commercial product that, when added to the soil in the proper
     quantities, will improve the quality of the soil layer. Additives may stabilize the soil by chemical, physical,

5-20  TM 3-34.48-1  29 February 2016


---

                                                                                                            Subgrades and Base Courses

     or a combination of the two (physicochemical). Chemical stabilizers include lime, acids, and enzymes that
     cause a chemical change in the soil, such as ion-exchange or covalent reactions. Physical stabilizers include
     bitumens that bind the soil by adhesion and fibers that bind by mechanical friction and interpenetration.
     Physicochemical stabilizers, such as lignosulfonates and lime-cement-fly ash (LCF), may bind soil particles
     together and induce chemical changes in the soil (pozzolonic reactions). Selecting and determining the
     percentage of additives depend on the soil classification and the degree of improvement in the soil quality
     desired. Smaller amounts of additives are usually required to alter soil properties (gradation, workability,
     plasticity) than to improve strength and durability sufficient to permit a thickness-reduction design. After the
     additive has been mixed with the soil, ding and compacting are achieved by conventional means.

MODIFICATION

     5-111. Soil modification refers to the stabilization process that results in the improvement in some property
     of the soil but does not, by design, result in a significant increase in the soil’s strength and durability. Soil
     modification usually results in something less than a thoroughly cemented, hardened, or semihardened
     material. This type of stabilization may be accomplished by—

              Compacting.
              Blending mechanically.
              Adding cementing material in small amounts.
              Adding chemical modifiers.

     5-112. Cement and lime modifiers (cement-modified soils and lime-modified soils) are used in quantities
     too small to provide high strength cementing action. They reduce the plasticity of clay soils. Calcium chloride
     or sodium chloride are added to the soil to retain moisture and control dust, to hold fine material for better
     compaction, and to reduce frost heave by lowering the freezing point of water in the soil.

STABILIZER TYPES

     5-113. This section discusses the different types of stabilizers available and provides some limited
     information on the soil types appropriate for the stabilizer type. Stabilizers are broadly classified as traditional
     and nontraditional, referring mostly to historical use. It must be noted that there is no one-size-fits-all solution
     for stabilization. Soils are notoriously variable even within classification types and may have different
     chemistry that would negate the use of some stabilizers. It must be emphasized that each soil/stabilizer
     combination should be treated on a case-by-case basis.

Traditional Stabilizers

     5-114. Traditional stabilizers generally rely on pozzolanic reactions and cation exchange to modify and/or
     stabilize. Although pozzolanic processes are slow, some amount of pozzolanic strength gain may occur
     during the primary reactions, caution exchange, and flocculation/agglomeration. Extent of this strength gain
     may vary with soils depending on the differences in their mineralogical composition.

Cement

     5-115. Cement can be used to modify and improve the quality of the soil or to transform the soil into a
     cemented mass with increased strength and durability. Cement can be used effectively as a stabilizer for a
     wide range of materials; however, the soil should have a PI of less than 30. For coarse-grained soils, the
     amount passing the No. 4 sieve should be greater than 45 percent. The amount of cement used depends on if
     the soil is to be modified or stabilized.

Lime

     5-116. Experience shows that lime will react with many medium-grained soils, moderately fine-grained
     soils, and fine-grained soils to produce decreased plasticity, increased workability, reduced swell, and
     increased strength. Soils classified according to the USCS as CH, CL, MH, ML, OH, OL, SC, SM, GC, GM,
     SW-SC, SP-SC, SM-SC, GWGC, GP-GC, ML-CL, and GM-GC should be considered as potentially capable

29 February 2016  TM 3-34.48-1  5-21


---

Chapter 5

     of being stabilized with lime. Lime should be considered with soils having a PI of greater than 10 and more
     than 25 percent of the soil passing the No. 200 sieve.

Fly Ash

     5-117. Fly ash, when mixed with lime, can be used effectively to stabilize most coarse-grained soils and
     medium-grained soils; however, the PI should not be greater than 25. Soils classified by the USCS as SW,
     SP, SP-SC, SW-SC, SW-SM, GW, GP, GP-GC, GW-GC, GP-GM, GW-GM, GC-GM, and SC-SM can be
     stabilized with fly ash.

Bituminous

     5-118. Most bituminous soil stabilization has been performed with asphalt cement, cutback asphalt, and
     asphalt emulsions. Soils that can be stabilized effectively with bituminous materials usually contain less than
     30 percent passing the No. 200 sieve and have a PI of less than 10. Soils classified by the USCS as SW, SP,
     SW-SM, SP-SM, SW-SC, SP-SC, SM, SC, SM-SC, GW, GP, SW-GM, SP-GM, SW-GC, GP-GC, GM, GC,
     and GM-GC can be effectively stabilized with bituminous materials, provided the above-mentioned gradation
     and plasticity requirements are met.

Combination

     5-119. Combination stabilization is specifically defined as lime-cement, lime-asphalt, and LCF
     stabilization. Combinations of lime and cement are often acceptable expedient stabilizers. Lime can be added
     to the soil to increase the soils workability and mixing characteristics and reduce its plasticity. Then, cement
     can be mixed into the soil to provide rapid strength gain. Combinations of lime and asphalt are often
     acceptable stabilizers. The lime addition may prevent stripping at the asphalt-aggregate interface and increase
     the mixture stability.

Nontraditional Stabilizers

     5-120. Nonstraditional stabilizers for military use generally consist of either polymers or fibers. Polymers
     stabilize similarly to a solid surface product whereas fibers are added to base material and intertwine with it
     to effectively bond materials more rigidly.

Polymers

     5-121. Polymer emulsions (sometimes referred to as latex) used for soil stabilization are generally vinyl
     acetate or acrylic-based polymers suspended in water by surfactants. They typically consist of 45 to
     50 percent polymer content by weight. Analogous to latex paint, the emulsion cures primarily by water loss.
     The polymers used for soil stabilization typically have excellent tensile and flexural strength, adhesion to soil
     particles, and resistance to water. These materials have a shelf life which is up to two years, in proper storage.
     Polymer emulsions should not be mixed with gray or salt water for dilution.

Fibers

     5-122. There are numerous fiber types available. For soil stabilization, a combination of availability, fiber
     properties, and cost per performance pares the fiber type to polypropylene. These fibers are low-cost,
     available in different lengths and diameters, and have been extensively tested. Monofilament, fibrillated, and
     tape fibers are available. Testing has shown that monofilament and tape fibers are more efficient for rapid
     stabilization. Fibrillated fibers may require extensive mixing to effectively defibrillate the fiber for maximum
     efficiency.

     5-123. The most important fiber property for soil stabilization is fiber length. Longer fibers generally result
     in improved performance but hamper construction. The longer fibers are more difficult to mix and
     considerable balling may occur, diminishing efficiency. Testing of different fiber lengths has shown that fiber
     lengths from 3/4 inch to 1.5 inch results in good soil improvements with minimal balling.

     5-124. Soil type is of a secondary role in fiber selection. Polypropylene fibers mixed into soil without
     adhesives (cement) rely exclusively on mechanical interlock, friction, and fiber entanglement between soil

5-22  TM 3-34.48-1  29 February 2016


---

                                                           Subgrades and Base Courses

particles to anchor the fiber in place. Thus, a high-surface area fiber, such as tape fiber, may be more efficient
in a fine-grained clay soil than in a coarse-grained soil, such as gravel, where fewer soil grains are in contact
with the fiber.

Other

     5-125. There are a variety of other nontraditional soil stabilization and modification additives available
     from the commercial sector (acids, lignin derivatives, enzymes, tree resin emulsions, silicates). These
     additives vary widely in their chemical composition and mechanism of action, may be in liquid or solid form,
     and are often touted to be applicable for most soils. Research studies in this area have demonstrated that
     many nontraditional soil additives have little to no benefit for granular soil types. Sandy and gravelly soils
     are often problematic for stabilization, requiring a binder (such as a cement or asphalt emulsion) to provide
     cohesion between soil grains. Medium- and fine-grained soils are likely to benefit most from other
     nontraditional stabilizers. However, these must be treated on a case-by-case basis.

Nontraditional Combinations

     5-126. Blends of soil with polymer emulsions and hydraulic cements or with fibers and hydraulic cements
     have shown promise in laboratory testing and field demonstrations. A synergism exists between emulsions
     and hydraulic cement as the water in the emulsion hydrates the cement and the polymer adds flexibility,
     durability, and strain resistance to the soil cement, increasing the cracking resistance. The use of fibers is also
     very attractive due to their ability to improve the resistance of soil to deformation and resist the tensile stresses
     that lead to cracking. Fibers have been found to be more efficient than polymer emulsion on a weight-to-
     weight basis of comparison. However, fibers may be difficult to use because they tend to ball when graded
     and may be difficult to place in windy situations.

TIME REQUIREMENTS FOR TESTING

     5-127. The more thorough a testing program, the more assurance there is for the long-term success of the
     project. Time is often of primary concern to a military engineer—particularly in a tactical situation—and the
     rapid completion of a project may override the requirement for a complete series of laboratory tests. (See
     table 5-1, page 5-7.) Because of this, the method presented allows for a rapid or expedient approximation
     with a more precise laboratory determination of the type and quantity of stabilizer. An estimate for testing
     time is presented in table 5-8.

                  Expedient     Any               None

STABILIZER SELECTION AND CONCENTRATIONS

     5-128. When selecting a stabilizer additive, many factors must be considered. These factors, design criteria,
     and the selection and mixing of stabilizers can be found in TM 5-822-14/AFJMAN 32-1019 and TM 3-34.48-
     2. If lime is used as a preliminary additive to reduce the PI or to alter the soil gradation before adding a
     primary stabilizing agent, such as bitumen or cement, the designs lime content is the minimum treatment

29 February 2016                TM 3-34.48-1                                   5-23


---

Chapter 5

     level that will achieve the desired results. For nonplastic and low PI materials where lime alone is generally
     not satisfactory for stabilization, adding fly ash may produce the necessary reaction.

     5-129. Several factors need to be considered in the selection of a stabilizer, including environmental
     conditions, availability and cost of stabilizers, logistical considerations, equipment available, soil type, and
     the strength and durability needed for the desired application. For in-depth details about the data needed for
     stabilizer selection, see TM 5-822-14/AFJMAN 32-1019. In general, the higher amount of fines in the soil,
     the harder it is to stabilize. Thus, clays can be difficult to stabilize. Lime may be needed to reduce the
     plasticity and increase friability of high-plasticity clay before cement is added. For sandy and gravelly soils,
     some type of binding agent (cement or emulsion) is necessary to bind the particles together.

     5-130. To select the proper stabilizer type for a particular soil, perform a sieve-analysis test to determine
     gradation and fines content and an Atterberg-limits test according to the procedures given in this manual.
     The selection of a stabilizer begins with a classification of the soil type. (See figure 5-6.) Use figure 5-6 to
     classify the soil. Table 5-9 is then used to make an initial selection of appropriate stabilizers for the soil type,
     and table 5-10, page 5-26, is used to choose an appropriate stabilizer dosage level.

                          Figure 5-6. Gradation triangle for soil classification

5-131. The environmental conditions present at the stabilization site may need special consideration. In
particular, temperature will be the most critical factor that influences the curing time. When temperatures are
below 45 degrees Fahrenheit, curing times will be significantly increased. In general, for every 20 degrees
Fahrenheit temperature decrease, curing time doubles. For example, for 3 percent type III cement, one day
of cure time is needed at 75 degrees Fahrenheit, and two days is needed at 55 degrees Fahrenheit. The curing
time may be offset by increasing the stabilizer concentration from 3 to 6 percent for a one day curing time at
55 degrees Fahrenheit.

5-132. The amount of stabilizers used varies with the particular soil type and the expected durability needed
for the mission. In TM 5-822-14/AFJMAN 32-1019, stabilizer amounts are determined by specific tests and
criteria. Given the constraints of a rapid deployment scenario, there is not enough time to perform mix design
tests with various stabilizers and amounts to determine if those specific criteria are met. If time allows, it is
always best to perform a strict mix design according to TM 5-822-14/AFJMAN 32-1019. However, the
suggested stabilizer amounts given in table 5-9 and table 5-10, pages 5-25 and 5-26, should provide
acceptable performance.

(a) All of these stabilizers require a polymer emulsion surface coating of 0.25–1 gallon/square yard
    (1:2 dilution with water) for weatherproofing. Reapplication of surface coating may be necessary
    depending on traffic and conditions.

(b) Monofilament polypropylene fiber used in combination with stated stabilizers—length and denier
    will vary depending on soil type. In general, the finer the soil, the more fiber surface area (length
    and shape) is needed to interact with the soil-stabilizer matrix.

(c) In some cases, intermediate and high plasticity clays may require stabilizer amounts
    significantly higher than suggested.

EXPEDIENT STABILIZATION

     5-133. Usually, the military engineer needs soil improvement quickly in the JOA with a minimum of
     logistics and stabilization material. In this case, the best stabilizer of choice is cement. It is found around the
     world, will stabilize a wide variety of soils, and can be used for surface pavements. However, common
     Portland (Type I) cement is not a rapid-cure material and may take up to seven days to provide enough
     strength to support large loads, such as cargo aircraft. It provides limited durability and can fail by cracking
     and surface raveling, which may endanger aircraft with foreign object debris. Cement is extremely heavy due
     to its high specific gravity, placing a further logistical burden on the military planner. Using less cement
     reduces the logistical burden at the expense of durability. For expedient and temporary structures, suggested
     amounts of cement for common soils are given in table 5-10. Many of the concerns about cement can be
     reduced by incorporating monofilament polypropylene fibers into the soil cement mix and waterproofing the
     soil cement surface. Using monofilament fibers between 3/4 and 2 inches can—

              Increase the load bearing capacity so that large loads can be handled in three days (sometimes less
                  depending on the temperature).

              Reduce the foreign object debris potential by bonding to the soil cement and creating a mat-like
                  composite.

              Be used with high-early strength cement (Type III) so that large loads, such as C-130 and C-17
                  aircraft, can be placed on the structure within 24 hours of construction.

5-26                                   TM 3-34.48-1                              29 February 2016


---

                                                                                                            Subgrades and Base Courses

     5-134. Construction with fibers is conducted similar to cement stabilization; calculate the correct spacing
     of the fiber bags to achieve the desired concentration of fiber the same as with cement. Use of a reclaimer or
     stabilizer for soil mixing is mandatory. Fiber concentrations between 0.1 and 0.5 percent, based on the weight
     of soil, have shown to be successful. For most soils, fiber concentrations above 0.5 percent have demonstrated
     decreased density compared to lower fiber contents, which may decrease durability. Stabilization depths of
     6 inches are recommended and can be used for soils above CBR 8 to 10 percent. Stabilization of more than
     one lift is typically not practical in expedient situations. A balance between fiber length and constructability
     must be maintained. Longer fibers improve soil engineering characteristics to a larger degree but are harder
     to use because balling and tearing out of the soil occur during grading. Grading soil fiber cement is extremely
     difficult and should only be attempted, if absolutely necessary, within an hour or two of compaction. If an
     area needs smoothing during compaction, stop compaction, grade, and recompact. Typically, the fiber will
     ball up in front of the grader blade, rip out of the soil, and leave large surface scars and tears. In practice, this
     is best accomplished by preparing, compacting, and grading the surface to final elevation immediately before
     stabilization.

     5-135. Measurement of density for fiber-stabilized materials can be accomplished in the laboratory but is
     not possible in the field. Nuclear density devices give false readings because the fiber and sand-cone
     measurements give large errors due to problems excavating the fiber-stabilized soil. If laboratory
     measurements of density can be determined, the highest fiber content that produces equal density to a
     nonfiber stabilized specimen should be chosen.

     5-136. If laboratory data is unavailable for optimum water content, use the following guidelines for cement
     stabilization:

              For cement amounts less than 5 percent, use a water content of 1 percent above the optimum for
                  unstabilized soil.

              For cement contents above 5 percent, use a water content of 2 percent above the optimum for
                  unstabilized soil.

     5-137. Generally, it is best to compact cement-stabilized soil slightly on the wet side of optimum to provide
     extra water for hydration of the cement.

     5-138. For the low stabilizer amounts suggested in table 5-10 it is necessary to cap the surface of the soil
     with a waterproofing agent, such as a polymer emulsion designed for soil stabilization. This prevents water
     from entering the stabilized soil matrix and reducing its strength. It will also prevent fiber pullout from the
     surface and provide dust control. The minimum rate of application is suggested at 0.25 gallons per square
     yard and must be reapplied as necessary depending on traffic. For airfield structures, application rates as high
     as 1 gallon per square yard may be used if the soil will accept that application rate. Bituminous emulsions
     can also be used, but polymer emulsions are more durable under traffic. Note that synthetic fluids used for
     dust control should not be applied to cement-stabilized surfaces because they reduce the strength and
     durability to traffic.

     5-139. If logistics allow, stabilization according to TM 5-822-14/AFJMAN 32-1019 is recommended.
     However, if testing facilities are not available, the high dosage rates suggested for stabilizers can be used if
     logistics allow and the structure may become a long-term use facility in the future. Fibers can be used with a
     stabilizer. For a stabilized soil to be used as a pavement surface, it should be treated with a polymer or
     bituminous emulsion to extend its durability.

WEATHER

     5-140. Hot, dry weather is preferred for bituminous stabilization. When asphalt cements are used for
     stabilization, proper compaction must be obtained. If thin lifts of asphalt-stabilized material are being placed,
     the air temperature should be 40 degrees Fahrenheit and rising, and the compaction equipment should be
     used immediately after lay-down operations. Adequate compaction can be obtained at freezing temperatures
     if thick lifts are used. When cutbacks and emulsions are used, the air and soil temperatures should be above
     freezing. Heavy rains on mixed, uncompacted material may be detrimental.

29 February 2016  TM 3-34.48-1  5-27

Chapter 5

FROST AREAS

     5-141. While bituminous, Portland cement, lime, and combinations of LCF stabilization are the most
     common additives, other stabilizers may be used for pavement construction in areas of frost design with
     approval. Approving agencies for are as follows:

              Headquarters, Department of the Army (DAEN-MPE-D), Washington, DC 20314 for Army
                  projects.

              Headquarters, Air Force Engineering and Services Center (AFESC/DEM), Tyndall Air Force
                  Base, FL 32401 for Air Force projects.

              Headquarters, Naval Facilities Engineering Command, Alexandria, VA 22330 for Navy or Marine
                  Corps projects.

Limitations

     5-142. In frost areas, stabilized soil should be used in a single layer or layers comprising one of the upper
     elements of a pavement system and directly beneath the pavement surfacing layer. The structural advantage
     in reducing the required thickness of the pavement system compensates for the added cost of stabilization.
     Treatment with a lower degree of chemical stabilization should be used in frost areas with caution and after
     intensive tests because weakly cemented material has less capacity to endure repeated freezing and thawing
     than firmly cemented material. A possible exception is using a low level of stabilization to improve a soil
     that will be encapsulated within an impervious envelope as part of a membrane-encapsulated soil-layer
     pavement system. A soil that is unsuitable for encapsulation due to excessive moisture migration and thaw
     weakening may be made suitable by using a moderate amount of stabilizing additive. Materials that are
     modified by a small amount of chemical additive to improve certain properties of the soil without significant
     cementation should also be tested to determine if the desired improvement is durable through repeated freeze-
     thaw cycles. The improvement should not be achieved at the expense of making the soil more susceptible to
     ice segregation.

Construction Cutoff

     5-143. For materials stabilized with cement, lime, or LCF (strength increases with curing time), it is
     essential that the stabilized layer be constructed early in the season to allow strength to develop before the
     first freezing cycle begins. The rate of strength gain is substantially lower at 50 degrees Fahrenheit than at
     70 degrees Fahrenheit or 80 degrees Fahrenheit. Chemical reactions will not occur rapidly for lime-stabilized
     soils when the soil temperature is less than 60 degrees Fahrenheit and is not expected to increase for one
     month. Chemical reactions will also not occur rapidly for cement-stabilized soils when the soil temperature
     is less than 40 degrees Fahrenheit and is not expected to increase for one month. In frost areas, it is not always
     sufficient to protect the mixture from freezing during a 7-day curing period, as required by the applicable
     guide specifications. A construction cutoff date before the onset of freezing conditions may be essential.

DRYING OF WET SOILS

     5-144. Executing earthwork under wet conditions is one of the perpetual challenges of engineering. Proper
     compaction and engineering properties of soils are highly dependent on moisture content, yet nature seldom
     provides natural materials at the ideal moisture content. Experience teaches the field military engineer that
     attempting to subvert the fundamental laws that describe the effect of moisture content on construction and
     engineering properties of soils and aggregates leads to frustration and failure. These wet soils may be due to
     temporary weather conditions, such as thawing of frozen soils or rainfall, or to permanent situations, such as
     a high water table. Drying soils by conventional methods, such as spreading or disking, is likely to be slower
     and more weather dependent than military operations can tolerate.

     5-145. When it is necessary to work with soils that are wetter than desired, chemical drying may be used to
     deal with isolated wet spots or, if necessary, more extensive areas of wet soils.

     5-146. The chemical of choice for drying is quicklime (oxides of calcium and magnesium). Depending on
     the source, it is further defined as high-calcium quicklime, magnesian quicklime, or dolomitic quicklime;
     each is adequate for drying. The oxides hydrate with water and chemically bind water in the soil into a new

5-28  TM 3-34.48-1  29 February 2016


---

                                                                                                      Subgrades and Base Courses

form of hydrated lime. This reaction releases considerable heat (is exothermic), which evaporates more water
and reduces the moisture content of the soils. Because this reaction is very avid and exothermic, it is effective
for drying soils down to freezing temperatures.

5-147. Lime is a generic term used to cover a variety of materials. Only quicklime is effective for drying
soils. Hydrated lime has already combined with water and will not draw moisture into new chemical forms.
It will have certain chemical reactions (cation exchange) with some clay minerals that will make them less
plastic and easier to dry by conventional methods, but this is much different from the avid drying of quicklime
that is not related to soil type. Calcium carbonate is sometimes marketed as agricultural lime and has no value
for engineering stabilization or drying uses.

5-148. A product that contains free quicklime can be used as a drying agent. The more quicklime it contains,
the more effective it will be as a drying agent. Portland cement, fly ash (particularly high calcium Class C
ashes), and kiln dust are examples of common industrial materials with significant quicklime content that can
be used for soil drying. Their effectiveness for drying is directly dependent on the free quicklime content.

                                                 Chapter 6

                         Storm Drainage Design

         Inadequate water drainage is the most common cause of road and airfield failure.
         Therefore, drainage is a vital consideration in planning, designing, and building
         military roads and airfields. It is important during construction and operation.

DESIGN CONSIDERATIONS

     6-1. The objective of storm drainage design is to provide safe passage for vehicles or the operation of
     facilities during a design storm event. The drainage system is designed to collect storm water runoff from the
     pavement surface and adjacent areas, convey it along and through the adjacent areas, and discharge it to an
     adequate receiving body without causing adverse on-site or off-site impacts.

     6-2. Storm water collection systems must be designed to provide adequate surface drainage. Surface
     drainage is important for traffic safety. Rapid removal of storm water from the pavement minimizes
     hazardous conditions that can result in hydroplaning. Surface drainage is a function of transverse and
     longitudinal pavement slope, pavement roughness, inlet spacing, and inlet capacity.

     6-3. Storm water conveyance systems (storm drain piping, ditches, channels, pumps) provide an efficient
     mechanism for conveying design flows from inlet locations to the discharge point without surcharging inlets
     or otherwise causing surface flooding. Erosion potential must also be considered in the design of open
     channels or ditches used for storm water conveyance.

     6-4. The design of appropriate discharge facilities for storm water collection and conveyance systems
     includes consideration of storm water quantity and quality. Local, state, and federal regulations often control
     the allowable quantity and quality of storm water discharges. To meet these regulatory requirements, storm
     drainage systems usually require detention or retention basins and other best management practices for the
     control of discharge quantity and quality.

     6-5. Comprehensive criteria for surface drainage design of military transportation facilities and civilian
     airport pavements are contained in UFC 3-230-01 (using the document is optional, but familiarization is
     encouraged).

CONSTRUCTION

     6-6. Commanders and construction supervisors must ensure continuous maintenance of the drainage system
     during military road or airfield construction. The construction drainage system is temporarily established to
     prevent construction delays and structural failure before completion. Generally, long delays will result if
     drainage is not continuously emphasized by the command.

     6-7. Construction drainage must be completed before it is needed. When a storm begins, it is too late to
     start drainage work. Construction drainage measures used during different phases of construction are
     discussed below.

PRELIMINARY MEASURES

     6-8. An on-site investigation of the system and tributary area is a prerequisite for a study of drainage
     requirements. Information regarding the capacity, elevations, and condition of existing drains will be
     obtained. Topography; size and shape of the drainage area; extent and type of development; profiles, cross-
     sections, and roughness data on pertinent existing streams and watercourses; and possible ponding area
     locations will be determined.

29 February 2016  TM 3-34.48-1  6-1


---

Chapter 6

     6-9. Thorough knowledge of climatic conditions and precipitation characteristics is essential. Adequate
     information on soil conditions (types, permeability, vegetative cover, depth and movement of subsurface
     water, depth of frost) will be secured. Outfall and downstream flow conditions (including high water
     occurrences and frequencies) must be determined. The effect of base drainage construction on local facilities
     and local requirements will be evaluated.

     6-10. Where diversion of runoff is proposed, downstream conditions leading to unfavorable public relations,
     costly litigations, or damage claims will be avoided. Agreements needed to obtain drainage easements or
     avoid interference with water rights will be determined during design and accomplished before construction.
     Possible adverse effects on water quality due to drainage disposal in waterways involved in water supply
     systems will be evaluated.

Environmental Considerations

     6-11. Environmental considerations include the National Environmental Policy, the United States Army
     Environmental Quality Program, the United States Air Force Environmental Quality Program, the United
     States Navy Environmental Quality Program, the environmental impact analysis, and environmental effects
     of surface drainage systems.

National Environmental Policy

     6-12. The National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (Public Law 91-190), approved 1 January 1970, sets
     forth the policy of the Federal government, in cooperation with state and local governments and other
     concerned public and private organizations, to protect and restore environmental quality. The National
     Environmental Policy Act states, in part, that Federal agencies have a continuing responsibility to use
     practical means, consistent with other essential considerations of national policy, to create and maintain
     conditions under which man and nature can exist in productive harmony. Federal plans, functions, and
     programs are to be improved and coordinated to—

              Preserve the environment for future generations.
              Assure safe, healthful, productive, and aesthetically pleasing surroundings.
              Attain the widest beneficial uses of the environment without degradation, risk to health or safety,

                  or other undesirable consequences.
              Enhance the quality of renewable resources and approach the maximum attainable recycling of

                  depletable resources.

     6-13. Federal agencies, in response to the National Environmental Policy Act, must be concerned with the
     impact of their activities on technical and economic considerations and the environment.

United States Army Environmental Quality Program

     6-14. AR 200-1 outlines the Army fundamental environmental policies, management of its programs, and
     its various types of activities. One of which, water resources management, includes minimizing soil erosion
     and attendant pollution caused by rapid runoff into streams and rivers. The overall goal is to plan, initiate,
     and carry out actions and programs in a manner that minimizes adverse effects on the quality of the human
     environment without impairment of the Army mission. A primary objective is to eliminate the discharge of
     pollutants produced by Army activities. Provision of suitable surface drainage facilities is necessary in
     meeting this objective.

United States Air Force Environmental Quality Program

     6-15. AFPD 32-70 outlines Air Force policy in compliance with the National Environmental Policy Act
     executive orders and Department of Defense directives. Procedures outlined in AFPD 32-70 are similar to
     those described for Army installations. AFI 32-7061 establishes 32 CFR 989 as the controlling document on
     environmental assessments and statements for Air Force facilities.

6-2  TM 3-34.48-1  29 February 2016


---

                                                                                                                      Storm Drainage Design

United States Navy Environmental Quality Program

     6-16. The Navy environmental quality initiative is a comprehensive initiative focused on maximizing the
     use of pollution prevention to achieve and maintain compliance with environmental regulations. The
     environmental quality initiative is a fundamental part of the Navy environmental strategy called assess,
     implement, manage and measure to achieve sustained compliance and operational readiness through
     environmental excellence.

Environmental Impact Analysis

     6-17. ATP 3-34.5/MCRP 4-11B presents recommended procedures for use by Army personnel in preparing
     and processing environmental impact assessments and environmental impact documentation. The procedures
     list the step-by-step actions considered necessary to comply with the requirements of the National
     Environmental Policy Act and subsequent guidelines.

Environmental Effects of Surface Drainage Systems

     6-18. Arctic or subarctic facilities could have beneficial or adverse environmental impacts affecting water,
     land, ecology, and socioeconomic (human and economic) considerations. Despite low-population density
     and minimal development, the fragile nature of the ecology in the arctic and subarctic has attracted the
     attention of environmental groups interested in protecting these unique assets.

     6-19. Effects on surrounding land and vegetation may cause changes in various conditions in the existing
     environment (surface water quantity and quality, groundwater levels and quality, drainage areas, animal and
     aquatic life, land use). Proposed systems may also have social impacts on the community, requiring relocation
     of military and public activities, open space, recreational activities, community activities, and quality of life.

     6-20. Environmental attributes related to water could include erosion; aquifer yield; flood potential; flow or
     temperature variations (the latter affecting permafrost levels and ice jams); biochemical oxygen demand; and
     content of dissolved oxygen, dissolved solids, nutrients, and coliform organisms. These are among many
     possible attributes to be considered in evaluating environmental impacts, beneficial and adverse, including
     affects on surface water and groundwater.

Reconnaissance

     6-21. Before construction starts, preliminary area reconnaissance should disclose features that require
     advance drainage planning and operations. These features include—

              Springs and seepage on hillsides that may indicate perched or high water tables detrimental to
                  cuts.

              Trees adjacent to dry- or low-flow streams that could receive their root water from a groundwater
                  table flowing near the surface. Compacted fills across these areas could change the movement of
                  the flow.

              Vegetation or cover that could increase surface runoff if removed during the clearing and grubbing
                  phase of construction.

              Level areas with good vegetation and adjacent slopes. These areas may indicate a shallow
                  groundwater table with capillary water movement and may require intercepting subsurface
                  drainage.

              Streams that should be checked for normal high water and flood indicators.

29 February 2016  TM 3-34.48-1  6-3


---

Chapter 6

Protective Measures

     6-22. Controlling runoff during construction can be costly. The following measures help maintain
     satisfactory drainage during construction:

              Make maximum use of existing ditches and drainage features. Where possible, grade downhill to
                  allow economical grading and take advantage of natural drainage.

              Use temporary ditches to help construction drainage. Ensure that efforts are made to drain
                  pavement subgrade excavations and base courses to prevent detrimental saturation. Carefully
                  consider the drainage of construction roads, equipment areas, borrow pits, and waste areas.

              Be aware of areas where open excavation can lead to excessive erosion. The discharge of turbid
                  water to local streams will require temporary retention structures.

              Hold random excavation to a minimum.
              Sod or seed finished surfaces immediately.
              Plan timely installation of final storm drain facilities and backfilling operations to allow maximum

                  use during construction.

Area Clearing

     6-23. Considerations for clearing for the purpose of adequate drainage is discussed below. Natural drainage
     patterns is always preferred.

Existing Drainage

     6-24. Clear excess vegetation from streams. This increases the velocity and quantity of flow. Widening the
     stream can increase the flow. Bends and meanders can be cut to straighten the stream. Use care in making
     major alignment changes because they can change the hydraulic characteristics of the stream. Changes can
     adversely affect other parts of the stream.

Vegetation Removal

     6-25. Military projects may require the removal of vegetation from large areas. Consider the following
     factors with regard to construction stripping:

              Select a disposal area that will not interfere with or divert the drainage pattern of surface runoff.
                  If the drainage pattern is disturbed, the stripped material may form a barrier resulting in ponding
                  and may otherwise effect adjacent areas.

              Be aware that removing the vegetation from an area can lead to excessive surface runoff and
                  erosion. This could lead to silting of channels and flooding of low areas.

              Consider that serious bank erosion due to surface runoff may occur if vegetation adjacent to the
                  banks of streams or ditches is removed. To avoid this, it may be necessary to leave the vegetation
                  or to provide a berm with a chute.

              Control runoff sediments in large, cleared areas to prevent failure of other structures and possible
                  adverse environmental effects. This is more of a concern in permanent construction than in
                  wartime JOA construction.

Clearing, Grubbing, and Stripping

     6-26. Clearing, grubbing, and stripping include filling holes and back dragging or grading to a slight slope.
     This will ensure proper runoff and prevent water from collecting and saturating the subgrade. If filling and
     grading is not done, the advent of rain will make it necessary to strip off wet soil until dry soil is reached to
     start the fill. Some ditching may be required to direct the surface flow to an outlet point.

6-4  TM 3-34.48-1  29 February 2016


---

                                                                                                                      Storm Drainage Design

Fill

     6-27. When placing fill, exercise firm control over the project to prevent adverse affects from improper
     drainage procedures. Consider the following factors:

              The fill section must be rolled smooth at the end of each working day to seal the surface. No area
                  should be left that can hold standing water.

              The fill surface must be free of ruts caused by trucks and other equipment. These depressions
                  collect rain and saturate the subgrade. The surface must be crowned to discharge runoff quickly.

              When the fill area is large, it may be necessary to create swales (depressed areas) to conduct
                  surface runoff to discharge outlets.

              To allow fill to proceed, it may be necessary to install temporary culverts in the fill area in places
                  other than final design locations. After the fill area has reached design depth, the design culverts
                  can be properly trenched in place.

Ditching

     6-28. Use interception ditches during construction to collect and divert surface runoff before building the
     designed system. Before construction, conduct a site investigation of the general layout consistent with the
     work plan. When interception ditches cannot be made part of the design drainage, consider removing the
     ditches by backfilling and compacting.

     6-29. Locate interceptor ditches on hillsides and at the foot of the slope to intercept and divert runoff from
     the construction site. Make these ditches part of the final drainage system if possible. Roadside ditches are
     required during each construction stage and should be placed at design locations.

     6-30. During construction, use deep ditches for subsurface drainage. They intercept groundwater flow. (See
     figure 6-1.) If groundwater flow must be intercepted but ditching is not possible, modify the ditch into a
     subsurface drainpipe system.

                                            Figure 6-1. Deep interceptor ditch

     6-31. Ditching may be required in swamp areas to continue drainage ditches to an outlet point or drain the
     area. Engineers may use explosives in some cases since the soil may not be capable of supporting construction
     equipment. Draglines should also be considered. Timber or steel mats can be used to provide a firm
     foundation and support equipment during the operation.

Culverts

     6-32. Culverts are required during construction to allow surface runoff. If streams must be diverted to allow
     the construction of permanent culverts, use temporary culverts in the construction area. Never close natural
     drainage channels even if they are dry. If the channels are closed, surface runoff from sudden storms could
     cause a serious problem. These conditions must be anticipated. Construction drainage must keep pace with
     the construction project.

29 February 2016  TM 3-34.48-1  6-5


---

Chapter 6

DRAINAGE HYDROLOGY

     6-33. The design capacity of surface drainage systems should economically drain the facilities with
     consideration to the mission and importance of the particular facility and environmental impacts. The degree
     of protection provided by the drainage system is determined according to the type of traffic, the volume of
     traffic, and the necessity for uninterrupted service. Although the degree of protection should increase with
     the importance of the facility, minimum requirements must be adequate to avoid operation hazards. The
     possibility of a severe accident due to inadequate drainage offsets the cost difference between adequate and
     inadequate drainage facilities.

     6-34. To protect important facilities, the use of design storm frequencies above minimum criteria can be
     justified. In some designs, portions of the drainage system are based on as high as a 50-year design frequency
     to prevent loss of life and to reduce the likelihood of flooding a facility essential to operations.

PRECIPITATION

     6-35. Rainfall is the moisture delivery mechanism of primary concern to most military drainage designers.
     Snowmelt may be of greater concern in colder climates or in the design of reservoirs in milder regions. These
     concerns are beyond the scope of this manual, but they are included in TM 5-852-7/AFM 88-19. The amount
     of rainfall that evaporates depends on the surface temperature of ground features, air temperature, wind speed,
     and relative humidity. Evaporation occurs while rain is falling to the ground and after it lands on vegetation
     and other ground cover.

     6-36. Rainfall may be intercepted by vegetation. Large quantities of water can be trapped in the leaf canopy
     of trees and plants. Rain does not reach the soil until the holding capacity of the vegetation canopy is
     exceeded.

     6-37. A significant portion of water that strikes the soil soaks into the ground. This process is called
     infiltration. The rate of absorption and the quantity of water absorbed depends on the soil type, vegetation,
     terrain slope, and the soil moistness before the rain. Storm water runoff begins to accumulate when the rate
     of rainfall exceeds the rate of infiltration.

     6-38. Before overland water flow can begin its downhill motion, it must be deep enough to overcome
     obstacles to its movement. Detention is the amount of water required to fill depressions on the surface of the
     earth. Except by infiltration or evaporation, no water can leave a depression until the holding capacity of the
     depression has been exceeded.

     6-39. Evaporation, interception, infiltration, and detention are moisture losses. Runoff is precipitation minus
     these moisture losses.

STORMS

     6-40. Storms can deliver a large quantity of water to the earth in a short period of time. For that reason, the
     study of storms is an important part of the study of drainage hydrology. This section discusses storms in
     terms of duration, frequency, and intensity. It also describes procedures for determining maximum storms.
     The five main types of storms are—

              Thunderstorms. Thunderstorms are local atmospheric disturbances of short duration and a high
                  average rate of rainfall (intensity). They are characterized by thunder, lightning, torrential rain,
                  and sometimes hail. Thunderstorms tend to govern the design of drainage for small areas.

              Moderate storms. Moderate storms cover large areas for several hours with moderate intensity.
                  These storms develop greater total precipitation than thunderstorms. The moderate storm normally
                  controls the design of drainage structures for medium-sized basins.

              Long-duration storms. Long-duration storms often have several peaks of high rainfall. They may
                  last several days and develop very large amounts of precipitation at relatively low average rates
                  of rainfall. With a low average rate of rainfall, these storms have little or no impact to small- or
                  medium-sized drainage basins, but they normally control the design of drainage structures for
                  large basins.

6-6  TM 3-34.48-1  29 February 2016


---

                                                                                                                      Storm Drainage Design

              Monsoons. Monsoons are seasonal winds of the Indian Ocean and southern Asia. These winds
                  blow from the south from April to October and from the north during the rest of the year. Heavy
                  rains usually characterize the April-to-October season. This rain is not normally continuous; it
                  rises to a peak and then subsides in a cyclic fashion.

              Tropical cyclones. Hurricanes and typhoons are storms caused by severe cyclonic disturbances
                  over a wide area. Precipitation is normally heavy and long.

Duration

     6-41. Duration is the length of time that a storm lasts. After many years of observation, hydrologists have
     determined that a storm of long duration usually has low intensity. In contrast, a high-intensity storm usually
     has a short duration. Figure 6-2 shows typical storm hydrographs developed by the National Weather Service.
     Time, usually measured in hours, is depicted horizontally. The amount of rain for each unit of time is
     measured vertically in inches. The total amount of precipitation is the area of the graph.

                  Figure 6-2. Typical storm hyetographs

29 February 2016  TM 3-34.48-1                           6-7


---

Chapter 6

Design Life Versus Actual Structure Life

     6-42. The design life of a structure is the period of time during which the item is expected by its designers
     to work within it specified parameters; in other words, the life expectancy of the item. It is the length of time
     between placement into service of a single item and that items on-set of wear-out.

Design Storm Frequency

     6-43. For airfields and heliports, a minimum two-year storm event is required unless a waiver is obtained.
     This event will have no encroachment of runoff on taxiway and runway pavements (including paved
     shoulders). After this design storm frequency is specified, computations must be made to determine the
     critical duration of rainfall required to produce the maximum runoff rate for each area. This depends on the
     slope and length of the overland flow. Another important aspect of the design is minimizing ponding during
     rain events. Ponding is the accumulation of water around an inlet structure during a rain event. Typically,
     ponding will be limited around the apron inlets so that it does not exceed 4 inches.

     6-44. For areas other than airfields, such as developed portions of military installations (roadways,
     administrative, industrial, housing areas), the design storm is based on rainfall of a 10-year frequency.
     Potential damage or operational requirements may warrant a more severe criterion; in certain storage and
     recreational areas, a lesser criterion may be appropriate. With concurrence of the using Service, a lesser
     criterion may be employed in regions where storms of appreciable magnitude are infrequent, and large
     expenditures for drainage are not justified based on damage or operational capabilities. An additional design
     consideration is the spread of water around inlets. Spread is the width of the water on the paved surface
     measured perpendicular to the curb face.

Surface Runoff from Storms Exceeding Design Storm

     6-45. The design storm frequency alone is not a reliable criterion of the adequacy of storm drain facilities. It
     is advisable to investigate the probable consequences of storms more severe and less frequent than the design
     storm before making final decisions regarding the adequacy of proposed drain-inlet capacities. Surface runoff
     from storms greater than the design storm will be disposed of with the minimum damage to the airfield or
     heliport. The center 50 percent of runways, the center 50 percent of taxiways serving these runways, and
     helipad surfaces along the centerline should be free from ponding resulting from storms of a 10-year
     frequency and intensity determined by the geographic location. For areas other than airfields and heliports,
     check with the appropriate local regulatory agency for guidance on design storm requirements.

     6-46. For the two-year frequency storm, the probability of having a storm equaling or exceeding the value
     in any one year is 0.5 (two out of four times). The design storm frequency for JOA construction is normally
     two years. If construction with a longer estimated life is desired, the appropriate design storm should be
     specified in the authorizing directive.

     6-47. As with any statistical method of describing essentially random, natural events such as weather, there
     is a degree of uncertainty. The two-year design storm occurs every two years on average, but it is not
     guaranteed to occur every two years. Statistically, the probability of a storm equal to or greater than the two-
     year design storm occurring within a two year time period is 75 percent (three out of four times). Details of
     the statistics involved can be found in hydrology textbooks.

WEATHER DATA

     6-48. If there is extensive rainfall and rain-rate records for the location of interest and if hydrologists have
     examined those records statistically to formulate intensity-duration tables, those tables can be obtained
     through the Air Force staff weather officer. The staff weather officer is normally located at the division level.

     6-49. Within the United States, the data generally comes from the National Weather Service, directly or
     through the Air Force. Overseas, the staff weather officer may be able to obtain data from local government
     sources, but it may take considerable time to obtain. However, it is unlikely that such pinpoint data is
     available in many overseas JOA locations. When weather data is not available, use rainfall isohyetal maps.
     Isohyetal maps have contours of equal rainfall intensity just as topographic maps have contours of equal

RUNOFF

     6-56. Precipitation supplies water to the surface, but evaporation, interception, and infiltration begin to draw
     water at the start of the storm. Eventually, if the storm is strong enough, vegetation and other surface
     characteristics (depressions and soil) will become saturated, allowing water to flow freely over the surface.
     This condition is called runoff and is usually measured in cubic feet per second. Runoff begins sometime
     after the beginning of precipitation and may continue long after precipitation ends.

     6-57. The total quantity of runoff from a given area, after it is collected in channels and streams, is the flow
     estimate used to design area drainage structures.

     6-58. Transpiration and evaporation also draw from the water supplied by precipitation. However, these are
     relatively small losses and will not usually affect military drainage design. Estimating runoff will be
     discussed later in this chapter. Once the runoff has been determined, necessary ditches and culverts can be
     designed.

HYDROGRAPH

     6-59. Stream-water flow may originate from surface runoff, groundwater, or both. Runoff reaches the stream
     as overland flow. Groundwater flow results from side-bank seepage and springs. The hydrograph depicts the
     fluctuations of flow with regard to time.

     6-60. The elements of a hydrograph are base flow, lag time, peak flow time of concentration (TOC), and
     flow volume. Each stream will have its own characteristic hydrograph with widely varying values for the
     elements. A typical stream-flow hydrograph is shown in figure 6-5, page 6-12.

BASE FLOW

     6-61. The base flow of a stream depends on the amount of groundwater that seeps into the stream and its
     tributaries from the banks and the flow from permanent springs and swamps. Depending on the area, climate,
     and groundwater level, it may flow at a fairly constant rate. Conversely, the flow may fluctuate widely or
     even cease completely for periods of time.

LAG TIMES

     6-62. When precipitation begins over an area, there is an initial period where the loss factors induced by
     interception, infiltration, and detention take effect before surface runoff takes place. Stream flow will increase
     only when these initial losses have been satisfied and surface runoff begins. This is known as initial lag time.

---

Chapter 6

           Legend:       hour
           hr            inch
           In
                    Figure 6-5. Typical hydrograph

6-63. The length of this lag time is influenced by vegetation and other terrain characteristics. For example,
a grass-covered parking area will have a longer initial lag period than an asphalt parking lot of the same size.
A second lag time occurs between the time that the storm reaches its peak precipitation rate and the time that
the stream reaches its maximum flow. The length of this secondary lag time is influenced by the size of the
area drained. In small- and moderate-sized drainage areas, there will be slight differences between storm
peak and stream peak.

PEAK FLOW

     6-64. The peak of the hydrograph is the maximum stream flow that will occur during a particular storm. In
     general, peak flow is generated when the entire drained area is discharging its runoff. Peak flow is read
     directly from the maximum ordinate of the hydrograph. This flow determines the size of the drainage
     structures required at the basin outlet.

CONCENTRATION TIME

     6-65. The TOC is the time it takes a drainage basin to begin contributing runoff to the stream. Assuming
     uniform rainfall, the hydrograph peaks at that point. TOC is critical to the drainage engineer since it
     determines the duration of the storm that will demand the most from the drainage system—the storms critical
     duration.

FLOW VOLUME

     6-66. The area under the curve of the hydrograph indicates the total flow (in cubic feet) that results from a
     particular storm. It is used to determine ponding times when it is practical to use culverts with submerged
     inlets.

6-12                TM 3-34.48-1                    29 February 2016

                                                                                                                      Storm Drainage Design

HYDROGRAPHY CONSTRUCTION

     6-67. A hydrograph is constructed by measuring a streams rise and fall and the times related to these changes
     in flow. When constructing a hydrograph—

              The base flow must be measured when there have been no recent storms. A field reconnaissance
                  must be made for this measurement.

              The peak flow is estimated using the hasty runoff estimation presented in this chapter.
              The general shape of the hydrograph curve will be similar to that shown in figure 6-5.

DESIGN DATA REQUIREMENTS

     6-68. Before designing a drainage system, survey the various types and sources of drainage-related
     information. The survey should include, as a minimum, information concerning the area topography,
     meteorological records, soil characteristics, and available construction resources.

     6-69. Give special attention to the vicinity of the proposed facility and the presence of any topographical
     features that may contribute runoff to the project area. The completed facility will often interfere with the
     natural drainage of the site. Therefore, when analyzing the effects of the surrounding terrain—

              Identify areas that contribute runoff to the site.
              Determine the general size and shape of the contributing areas.
              Determine the natural direction of surface-water flow, the slope of the land, and the type and extent

                  of natural ground cover.
              Locate natural channels that can be used to move runoff within the project area or to divert it away

                  from the work site.

     6-70. Gather information on general climatic conditions, seasonal variations in rainstorms, and intensity and
     duration of representative storms. This data can then be applied to the location of the proposed facility.

     6-71. Obtain soil data from soil and geological maps, aerial photographs, or site tests performed by soil
     analysts. Soil data deals with the horizontal and vertical extent of soil types, the elevation of the groundwater
     table, and the drainage characteristics of the soil. The most important drainage characteristic of a soil is its
     permeability. Permeability limits the rate that the rainfall infiltrates the ground, which greatly influences the
     presence and movement of subsurface water.

     6-72. Make an initial investigation of the time, materials, equipment, and labor available to build a drainage
     system. Without a sufficient quantity of these essentials, the construction of an adequate system is impossible.

DESIGN PROCEDURES

     6-73. Designing a drainage system involves numerous assumptions and estimates. The degree of protection
     to be provided is directly related to the importance of the established time-use period. The general location
     of the facility will be determined by its functional requirements.

     6-74. The drainage system must be planned and designed for the predetermined location of the facility. There
     are three basic procedures in drainage structure design:

              Determine the area (usually in acres) contributing runoff to the facility.
              Estimate the quantity of runoff for which the facility will be protected.
              Design the drainage system to carry the estimated runoff.
