Chapter 6

DETERMINE THE AREA CONTRIBUTING RUNOFF

     6-75. When developing a tentative layout for a drainage system, identify locations within the site that
     requires drainage structures because of topographical or manufactured features. This is best done from a
     topographic map of the area or a sketch of the project site.

     6-76. Next, determine the acreage of the areas that contribute runoff to these required drainage structures.
     An analysis of existing channels is helpful to establish locations for required structures. Upon completion,
     this tentative plan should be field checked at the project site.

Establish Drainage-Structure Locations

     6-77. The initial step in developing a drainage-structure layout is to establish the location of the required
     drainage structures. Generally, placement will be controlled by the topography. For example, a fill section
     that crosses a valley will require one or more culverts to permit the flow of storm runoff down the valley. A
     depression or enclosed area will require ditches or culverts at various points to remove accumulated rainfall.

     6-78. Figure 6-6 shows an airfield with required culverts and open channels or ditches. At Point A the
     elevation is 65 feet, while at Point B the elevation is 55 feet. Culverts and ditches must be laid to carry water
     from high to low elevations. The alignment of these culverts and ditches should be as straight and smooth as
     possible. Sharp bends in ditches or near culverts will cause erosion. Not shown on this sketch are the standard
     ditches constructed along the sides of military roads and airfields.

Delineate Watersheds

     6-79. After initially locating drainage structures, define the boundaries of the areas (or watersheds)
     contributing runoff to each of them. This process is known as delineation. Delineation is performed in the
     following six simple steps:

              Step 1. Locate existing or proposed drainage structures on the topographic map or sketch.
              Step 2. Identify and mark terrain high points.
              Step 3. Draw arrows representing water flow away from these high points. These arrows must

                  always be perpendicular to the contour lines because water flows downhill.
              Step 4. Continue drawing the arrows until they converge on the culvert or the end of the ditch.

                  Runoff will flow parallel to a road or airfield when it is intercepted by side (or interceptor) ditches.
              Step 5. Draw delineation lines. These lines will run from high point to high point, indicating where

                  the flow of surface runoff separates. Delineation lines are located so that flow arrows cannot cross
                  them. Flow arrows cross delineation lines at culverts or ditches. (See figure 6-7 and figure 6-8,
                  page 6-16.)
              Step 6. Since each cover or soil type will have an effect on the basin, if there are multiple types
                  of cover in the basin, each cover or soil type must be delineated and measured according to its
                  respective cover type. (See figure 6-9, page 6-16.)

                  Note. Delineation lines are drawn between opposing arrows.

                  Figure 6-7. Delineation of roads and airfields

Determine Drainage System Size

     6-81. After delineating the watershed, determine its size in acres. Make this measurement carefully since the
     size directly influences the calculation of runoff from the watershed at peak flow. Use an accurate method of
     measurement. A planimeter (measures the area of a plane figure while a mechanically coupled pointer
     traverses the figure perimeter) is quite accurate and should be used if available. However, several other
     methods are suitable for field estimation.

Counting-Squares Method
     6-82. To make a hasty approximation of an area, transpose the outline of the watershed to graph paper or
     another suitable grid. Count the number of whole squares, and estimate the values of the partial squares.
     Multiply the total number of counted squares by the number of counted square feet represented by a single
     square. Then convert this measurement into acres (1 acre equals 43,560 square feet). (See figure 6-13.)

Stripper Method
     6-84. The stripper method is a variation of the geometric-shapes method. (See figure 6-15.) Approximate the
     area by drawing a series of lines that are equal distance (a stripper width of 1 inch) across the delineated area,
     measure the lines, and total. This method is more applicable for field estimations.

land, the acreage can be found by multiplying the total of the length (in inches) by the stripper width (in
inches) by the map scale (in feet per inch) by 2 and dividing the product by 43,560 feet per square acre.

ESTIMATE THE QUANTITY OF RUNOFF

     6-86. Drainage systems must be designed to accommodate the peak flow generated by runoff from
     contributing watersheds during the design storm. Many techniques are available for determining the peak
     flow, but most are too complex for general field use. This manual discusses the most common method for
     estimating runoff—the rational method.

DESIGN DRAINAGE STRUCTURES FOR MAXIMUM RUNOFF

     6-87. To accommodate peak flow of the design storm, design structures must provide a sufficient cross-
     sectional area and longitudinal slope for passing storm runoff. If ponding or flooding of adjacent areas must
     be prevented, the design must be for peak flow. However, the water velocities generated at peak flow must
     not be so great that they cause damage to the drainage structure or excessive erosion and scouring to the
     protected facility.

     6-88. Determine the capacity of drainage structures by calculating the runoff from contributing drainage
     areas. Specific procedures for designing open channels and culverts are discussed later in this chapter.

ESTIMATE RUNOFF USING THE RATIONAL METHOD

     6-89. The rational method is used to estimate the expected peak storm runoff at a given drainage basin outlet.
     Much of the input to the formula is based on judgment. Therefore, it is imperative that sound engineering
     judgment be used to determine the input data.

ASSUMPTIONS

     6-90. The rational method is based on the following underlying assumptions and limitations:
              The area is not greater than 1,000 acres and is regular in shape with a homogeneous cover and soil
                  type.
              The entire drainage area is contributing runoff to the outlet point when peak runoff is obtained.
              The design rainfall intensity is uniform over the entire drainage area (rainfall is uniform over time
                  and space).
              No active streams drain the area. If an active stream drains the basin, use the hasty method. (See
                  TM 3-34.85/MCRP 3-17A for additional information.)

Runoff Coefficient Variable

6-94. The runoff coefficient accounts for losses from precipitation. The runoff coefficient variable is the
decimal fraction of the amount of water expected to run off relative to the amount of precipitation. It can be
expressed as the ratio—

runoff coefficient variable also appears in the table for manufactured surfaces and wooded areas. An area of
SP soil (a pervious, sandy soil with a slope less than or equal to 2 percent) with turf has a runoff coefficient
variable factor of 0.10; that is, 10 percent of the rain falling on this soil will run off. The remaining 90 percent
becomes lost to runoff through infiltration and other factors. At the other extreme, an asphalt pavement has
a runoff coefficient variable of 0.95. Five percent of the rain falling on the asphalt will be lost. The remaining
95 percent is expected to become runoff.

Chapter 6

Runoff Coefficient Variable Versus Slope

     6-96. As terrain becomes steeper, water flows sooner and more rapidly. This allows less time for infiltration
     to occur and results in a larger runoff coefficient variable for natural cover or soil categories. For this reason,
     when the average slope of an area exceeds 2 percent, an adjustment must be made.

     6-97. Table 6-2, page 6-23, has three columns representing different slope conditions and their corresponding
     runoff coefficients. Use the column that corresponds with the average slope percentage.

     6-98. The runoff coefficient variable for turfed soil is different from the runoff coefficient variable for bare
     soil. The turf (grass or other ground cover) exerts a drag on water that causes a slower flow and provides
     more time for infiltration to occur. Therefore, a lower runoff coefficient results. Denuded soil (the turf or
     cover has been removed from the soil) requires an increased runoff coefficient variable because a swifter
     flow results in less time available for losses to occur. If one cover type has more than one flow path, average
     the slopes and use the appropriate column.

                                                  Example

 Average the slope for flow paths 1A and 1B. Given—
 Flow path slope 1A = 2.3%
 Flow path slope 1B = 1.9%.

                                                  2.3% + 1.9%
                                                          2 = 2.1% 𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠

Nonhomogeneous Areas

     6-99. An assumption made when using the rational method is that there is a homogeneous cover and soil
     type throughout the area. Quite often this is not the case, especially in areas where humans have exerted their
     influence on the topography.

     6-100. If one soil and cover type is predominate in at least 80 percent of the area, the area is considered a
     simple area, and the runoff coefficient variable for the predominant soil and cover type is used. If no one soil
     and cover type is predominate in 80 percent of the area, the area is considered a complex area. The runoff
     coefficient variable must be weighted in a complex area. The runoff coefficient variable is adjusted to account
     for the runoff coefficient variable proportions contributed by each subarea. For example, a complex area has
     two subareas: one with average turf and the other with bare soil. The bare soil slope does not affect how fast
     (or slow) water runs off the turfed area or how much of the water soaks into the turfed area. The converse is
     also true. The slope of the turfed area does not affect the speed or amount of water that runs off the bare soil
     area. Table 6-2 shows the runoff coefficient variables for slopes with and without turf.

     6-101. Multiply the runoff coefficient variables by the area (in acres) that the runoff coefficient variables
     affect, total the products, and divide by the total acreage. Expressed mathematically, the formula is—

           𝐶𝐶 = 𝐶𝐶1𝐴𝐴1 + 𝐶𝐶2𝐴𝐴2 + 𝐶𝐶3𝐴𝐴3 + ⋯ 𝐶𝐶𝑛𝑛𝐴𝐴𝑛𝑛
                      𝐴𝐴1 + 𝐴𝐴2 + 𝐴𝐴3 + ⋯ 𝐴𝐴𝑛𝑛

where—

C1A1 = runoff coefficient variable and area for first subarea

C2A2 = runoff coefficient variable and area for second subarea

Intensity Variable

     6-102. As explained previously in this chapter, rainfall intensities can be determined from pinpoint source
     data or isohyetal maps. The former method provides more accurate results if reliable data are available. The
     task of calculating the critical duration for any given drainage area is detailed here.

Drainage Area Variable

     6-103. The drainage area is the area that contributes storm water runoff to the culvert or ditch being
     designed. It must be calculated in acres.

                                                                                                                      Storm Drainage Design

TIME OF CONCENTRATION

     6-104. Under the assumptions listed at the beginning of this section and with the intensity-duration
     relationships presented earlier, only one particular storm will give a maximum discharge for a given area.
     This particular storm is the one that rains over the entire area being drained for a period of time just long
     enough to fill the outlet with runoff from segments of the area at the same time. This time is called the area
     TOC. A storm with a shorter duration than this TOC would not last long enough for the runoff from the more
     distant segments of the area to reach the outlet. The outlet would only be filled with the runoff from nearby
     segments. Therefore, runoff would not be maximized.

     6-105. In figure 6-16, the area below the 10-minute line will drain in 10 minutes or less. Runoff from the
     area between the 10- and 20-minute lines will drain in 10 to 20 minutes. Similarly, the runoff from the area
     between the 20- and 30-minute lines will drain in 20 to 30 minutes. After 30 minutes, the entire area is
     draining. Therefore, the TOC at the outlet for this area is 30 minutes.

                                              Figure 6-16. TOC, regular area

     6-106. If a storm of 20-minute duration sweeps over the area in a uniform fashion, only a fraction of the
     total area inside the 20-minute boundary simultaneously contributes runoff to the outlet at the end of the
     storm. Runoff from the upper third of the area reaches the outlet after the rainfall has ceased and after much
     of the lower acreage has finished contributing runoff. If a 30-minute storm sweeps over the same area in a
     uniform fashion, the entire area contributes runoff to the outlet in the 30-minute time frame.

     6-107. If a storm with a longer duration than the TOC occurs, the drainage designer can ascertain (using
     the standard intensity-duration curve) that the intensity will be less than the intensity of the 30-minute storm.
     Examination of the rational-method equation reveals that since the runoff coefficient and area would not
     change as intensity decreases, the quantity must decrease as well. The critical-storm duration must then be
     equal to the contributing area TOC.

Determine Area Time of Concentration

     6-108. Determine the area TOC by determining representative flow paths. A flow path is the path that a
     typical drop of water will follow from the time it hits the ground until it reaches the area outlet. The flow
     path is representative because drainage areas are not as regular in shape as the area in figure 6-16. The path
     selected must be representative of the time most of the area will be contributing water to the outlet point.
     Establishing representative flow paths is based on experience and judgment (trial and error).

     6-109. Unlike the area depicted in figure 6-16, the area in figure 6-17, 6-26, is irregular as most natural
     areas will be. In irregular areas, it is critical that the flow paths chosen represent the time required for most
     of the area to drain. The area below the 10-minute line will drain in 10 minutes or less. The area between the
     10- and 20-minute lines will drain in 10 to 20 minutes (and so forth up to the 40-minute line). Flow lines a,
     b, and c are determined, and 90 percent of the total area (90 acres) lies below the 30-minute line and will

6-113. After the representative flow paths have been established, estimate the time it will take for water to
reach the outlet if it travels along the established path. To do this, determine (through observation) the nature
of the surface cover and the slope of the flow path. Slope affects the velocity of the water—the steeper the
slope, the faster the water runs. Water travels faster over pavement than across a grassy area of the same
slope because grass slows the water flow. Water travels slower over bare soil than over pavement, but water

     travels faster over bare soil than over grass. Water flow in a ditch is more rapid than overland flow over
     turfed, bare, or compacted gravel surfaces.

Estimate Flow Time for Single Covers

     6-114. After establishing the location, the cover, and the slope of a flow path, figure 6-18 is used to estimate
     the travel time along the flow path. It is important to understand what the illustration is depicting and how to
     use it properly. There is a series of curves, each with linear and curvilinear portions. The slope of the curve
     indicates the velocity at a given point along the flow path. In the curvilinear portion, the slope is initially zero
     and gradually increases until the flow becomes constant. This represents the fact that water initially moves
     slowly and begins to pick up speed as its accumulated depth increases. Initially, the water flows slowly in a
     laminar- or sheet-flow manner and gradually becomes turbulent (and faster) as it progresses downhill. At
     some point, the turbulent-flowing water reaches a steady-state velocity. It is apparent that the slope and
     slickness of the flow path dictate how quickly the transition occurs from slow-moving laminar flow to rapid,
     fully developed turbulent flow.

Note. It is valid to interpolate between percent slope curves.

Select Design Time of Concentration

     6-119. Establish several trial flow paths that are thought to be representative of the area and determine a
     travel time for each path. Compare the time it takes for water to travel along each of the flow paths chosen.
     If the times are within a few minutes of each other, select the longest time as the area TOC. If the times are
     not within a few minutes of each other, analyze the area completely. New flow paths may be needed to
     determine which of the times is representative of the bulk of the area draining. The largest representative
     time is chosen as the design TOC.

RATIONAL METHOD APPLICATION

     6-120. Application of the rational method of estimating drainage varies according to the type of drainage
     area. One type is a single, independent area that does not receive any drainage from an upstream area. Another
     type is a dependent or successive area that receives runoff from another area.

Single Areas

     6-121. The rational method of estimating single areas is simple and straightforward if it is done
     methodically. If followed step-by-step, the estimate will be as valid as the judgments that are made. The
     steps, listed in the proper order, are as follows:

              Step 1. Delineate the area to determine the area contributing runoff to the project location. (Refer
                  to Delineating Watersheds.)

              Step 2. Delineate subareas by soil or cover type. (Refer to Step 6, Delineating Watersheds.)
              Step 3. Determine the acreage for each basin and subarea. (Refer to Determining Drainage System

                  Size.)
              Step 4. Classify the drainage basin as simple or complex. A simple watershed has one cover or

                  soil type over 80 percent of the total area. A complex watershed has no single cover or soil type
                  covering at least 80 percent of the total area.
              Step 5. Determine representative flow paths. (Refer to Determining Time of Concentration.)
              Step 6. Divide flow paths into two sections: laminar and ditch flow. As a rule of thumb, use
                  500 feet plus or minus 200 feet as a point where laminar flow will change to ditch or steady-state
                  flow. Generally, overland flow concentrates into natural rivulets or channels after roughly 500 feet
                  of travel. This distance may vary up to several hundred feet, depending on factors such as soil

29 February 2016               TM 3-34.48-1                                                        6-29


---

Chapter 6

                type, vegetation, and slope. It is best to visually investigate on-site for evidence of channeling and
                take measurements as needed. However, since in this example it is not possible to visually
                investigate the drainage area, clues to determine when overland flow (sheet flow) ends and ditch
                flow begins must come from topographic information. Some clues may be the beginning of uphill
                swales or flow paths that converge into a swale. This convergence may take place in a valley
                where multiple paths meet.

            Step 7. Determine the slope of each section of flow path. (Refer to Determining Time of
                Concentration.)

            Step 8. Determine the average slope of the basin or each subarea based on flow paths. Define the
                slope as being less than or equal to 2 percent, greater than 2 percent and less than 7 percent, or
                equal to or greater than 7 percent.

            Step 9. Find the runoff coefficient variable of the basin or each subarea based on soil or cover
                type and slope from table 6-2, page 6-23. Select the runoff coefficient from the appropriate column

                                                                                                                      Storm Drainage Design

Successive Areas

     6-122. Up to this point, the drainage areas discussed have been single, independent areas (simple or
     complex). These independent areas do not receive runoff from an upstream area. Some drainage systems,
     however, consist of a series of drainage areas with upstream areas discharging runoff into lower areas. The
     areas receiving this runoff are called dependent areas. The runoff accumulates and increases in its passage
     through the system.

     6-123. Sometimes, two or more areas discharge runoff into the same dependent downstream area. These
     contributing areas are called parallel areas.

     6-124. Unfortunately, the increase in runoff is not the simple summation of the peak runoff for each
     individual area. Individual peak flows are acted upon by various factors, including storage and peak-flow
     reduction, while in the drainage network. Also, the peak flow from upstream areas and the peak flow from
     downstream-dependent areas will probably not arrive at the lower outlet simultaneously. Hence, the total
     peak flow must be less than the total of the individual peak flows.

Time of Concentration Calculation

     6-125. Because peak flow accumulates in successive areas, calculating the TOC for those areas is different
     from the method used for single, independent areas. To estimate the amount of the accumulated runoff with
     some precision, a procedure has been developed to recalculate TOC for each of the successive drainage areas
     as water travels downstream. Naturally, as TOC increases, rainfall intensity decreases.

     6-126. The term TOC must be modified to reflect calculation differences when considering two areas (such
     as an upstream area and a downstream area). (See figure 6-21.) The maximum travel time from the most
     hydraulically remote representative points to the outlet area is defined as TOC. The maximum representative
     flow time for runoff originating from an area to arrive at the outlet is defined as inlet time.

                  Legend:  ditch time
                  DT       time of concentration
                  TOC

                  Figure 6-21. Schematic example for successive areas

     6-127. The TOC at the outlet upstream in area W is given as TOCW, which equals inlet time W for this
     independent area. The ditch time or transit time through area X from outlet W to outlet X is DTW-X. The total
     of these two elements (TOCW and DTW-X) is inlet timeW-X. To a designer engaged in sizing the culvert that
     serves as outlet W, the TOC would simply be—

                                                         𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑊𝑊 = 𝑖𝑖𝑖𝑖𝑖𝑖𝑖𝑖𝑖𝑖 𝑡𝑡𝑡𝑡𝑡𝑡𝑡𝑡𝑊𝑊

     6-128. When sizing culverts that occur further down in successive areas (for instance, the culvert at outlet
     X), the designer requires the time it takes water to arrive from the most hydraulically remote location, which
     might be in area X or area W. To determine this maximum representative time (TOCX), the designer must
     compare the travel times for runoff origination in both areas.

     6-129. The travel time for water originating in area W and arriving at outlet X is equal to the inlet time at
     area W (the same as TOCX since area W is dependent) plus the transit time as the water flows in a ditch
     through area X. This composite time, called inlet timeW-X must be compared to the time for water that
     originates in area X or inlet timeX. TOCX, the maximum representative time for water to arrive at outlet X, is
     the larger time value identified in the comparison.

Successive Area Runoff Estimation

     6-130. The modified definition of TOC is applied in estimating runoff for successive areas. This calculation
     requires collection of certain essential data and application of the principles used for single areas,
     appropriately modified, to determine the desired quantity. The required steps are as follows:

              Step 1. Delineate every subarea in the series of areas.
              Step 2. Determine the intensity of the two-year, 60-minute rainfall.
              Step 3. Determine the area, runoff coefficient, and inlet time. For each subarea, determine the

                  area, runoff coefficient variable (corrected for slope and weighted as necessary), and inlet time.
              Step 4. Determine the ditch time (or transit time).

     6-131. For each dependent subarea, the ditch time is determined from the upper outlet to the lower outlet
     using culvert flow (assume 300 feet per minute in the absence of more precise data).

     6-132. To determine the specific quantity, start at the uppermost subarea and proceed downstream, working
     systematically. Subarea W is upstream from subarea X (refer to figure 6-21, page 6-35). Use the following
     steps:

              Step 1. Determine the subarea TOC. Use the following equations for—
                   An independent subarea—
                                                                  𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑊𝑊 = 𝑖𝑖𝑖𝑖𝑖𝑖𝑖𝑖𝑖𝑖 𝑡𝑡𝑡𝑡𝑡𝑡𝑡𝑡𝑊𝑊
                   A dependent area—
                                                     𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑇𝑊𝑊 = 𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑ℎ 𝑡𝑡𝑡𝑡𝑡𝑡𝑡𝑡𝑊𝑊−𝑋𝑋
                        Compare inlet timeX and inlet timeW-X, and select the larger value of TOCX.

              Step 2. Adjust the intensity 60-minute, two-year to intensity TOC, two year.
              Step 3. Calculate the quantity for subarea W. Use the following equation:

                                                                 𝑄𝑄𝑊𝑊 = 𝐶𝐶𝑊𝑊𝐼𝐼𝐼𝐼𝐼𝐼𝐼𝐼𝑋𝑋𝐴𝐴𝑊𝑊

Chapter 6

DESIGN COMPUTER PROGRAMS

     6-133. Many private and public domain software products are available for the analysis and design of
     various components of storm drain systems. These products range from simple computational tools for
     specific components of the storm drain system to complex programs that can analyze complete storm drain
     systems using interactive graphical interfaces. The computer hardware and software industry is rapidly
     changing. New and more advanced applications software is developed each year. For public sector software,
     user support is minimal or nonexistent if the software is obtained directly from the government. Private
     vendors sell many of these packages and may offer user support. The following three programs may be useful
     in the analysis and design of drainage systems for urban areas. While these programs represent a start for
     most projects, many programs are available that may better suit a specific project.

Technical Release-55 Program

     6-134. Technical Release (TR)-55 is a hydrology program that implements Natural Resources Conservation
     Service methods for calculating TOC, peak flows, hydrographs, and detention basin storage volumes. It is
     useful for urban drainage situations where detailed hydrograph routing procedures are not warranted. The
     program, now compatible with Windows™ operating systems, incorporates the procedures outlined in
     TR-55. TR-55 contains simplified procedures to calculate storm runoff volume, peak rate of discharge,
     hydrographs, and storage volumes required for storm water reservoirs. The procedures are applicable in small
     urbanizing watersheds in the United States.

     6-135. TR-55 is extremely easy to use with interactive menus that prompt the user for specific inputs.
     Several screens of input are normally required before an analysis can proceed. Help screens assist the user in
     successfully performing an analysis.

Technical Release-20 Program

     6-136. TR-20 is a comprehensive hydrology program that implements Natural Resources Conservation
     Service methods for generating and routing runoff hydrographs in a multibasin watershed. The program
     provides hydrographic analyses of a watershed under present conditions and various combinations of land
     cover or use and structural or channel modifications using single rainfall events. Output consists of runoff
     peaks, flood hydrographs, time of occurrence, and water surface elevations at a cross section or structure.
     Subarea surface runoff hydrographs are developed from storm rainfall using a dimensionless unit hydrograph,
     drainage areas, times of concentration, and runoff curve numbers. Hydrographs can be developed, routed,
     added, stored, diverted, or divided to convey floodwater from the headwaters to the watershed outlet. TR-20
     is useful for large watersheds where detailed hydrograph routing is warranted.

Hydrologic Modeling System

     6-137. The Hydrologic Engineering Center Hydrologic Modeling System is a flood hydrograph package
     developed by USACE. The Hydrologic Modeling System model, like TR-20, is designed to simulate the
     surface runoff response of a river basin to precipitation by representing the basin as an interconnected system
     of hydrologic and hydraulic components. Each component models an aspect of the precipitation-runoff
     process within a portion of the basin. A component may represent a surface runoff entity, a stream channel,
     or a reservoir. Representation of a component requires a set of parameters that specify the particular
     characteristics of the component and mathematical relations that describe the physical processes. The result
     of the modeling process is the computation of stream flow hydrographs at desired locations in the river basin.
     It is useful for large watersheds where detailed hydrograph routing is warranted.

     6-138. Hydrologic Modeling System simulates a river basin as a group of subareas interconnected through
     channel routing reaches and confluences, and the program performs hydrologic calculations on a user-
     specified time step for a single storm (soil moisture recovery during dry spells is not included). Hydrologic
     Modeling System is used to generate discharge, not water surface elevations (although it does calculate
     normal depth). The Hydrologic Engineering Center River Analysis System model is typically used in
     conjunction with Hydrologic Modeling System to determine water surface profiles through detailed hydraulic
     computations.

                                                 Chapter 7

                          Open-Channel Design

         An open channel is a conduit with a free-water surface used to transport water. The
         ditch, an open channel cut into the soil, is the most common. The ditch can be lined
         along the bottom from bank to bank.

FACTORS

     7-1. The size, shape, method of construction, and location of a ditch are determined by its purpose. These
     factors, once determined, will influence the design capacity and maintenance requirements.

LOCATION

     7-2. The main types of ditches used in road and airfield construction are—
              Interceptor. An interceptor ditch is generally located on a hillside above a roadway or other
                  feature requiring protection. Its function is to intercept runoff and direct the flow to a more
                  desirable location. It is usually located above side hill cuts to prevent erosion of the cut.
              Side ditch. A side ditch is located along the side of a road. It collects runoff from the road and
                  adjacent areas and transports it to a culvert or diversion ditch.
              Diversion. When the topography allows, a diversion ditch is built to transport water away from
                  roadways or airfields. It can be used in conjunction with interceptor and side ditches to transport
                  water between culverts or to divert an existing stream channel around a project.

CROSS SECTION

     7-3. The location and peak quantity of runoff expected will determine the ditch cross-sectional area
     required. The most common shapes of cross sections—triangular (symmetrical and nonsymmetrical),
     trapezoidal, and segmental—are shown in figure 7-1, page 7-2.

     7-4. In the JOA, the shape of a ditch is dictated, to a great extent, by the choice of engineer equipment
     available for construction. Two items of equipment are uniquely suited for speedy ditch excavation: the motor
     grader and the wheeled tractor-scraper. Other equipment that can be used to excavate a ditch section include
     the backhoe; bulldozer; front-end loader; trenching machine; and a crane equipped with a dragline, clamshell,
     or shovel front. However, production rates for these items are low compared to the grader or scraper so they
     are more likely to be used.

     7-5. Triangular or V ditches are commonly installed to handle flows up to 60 cubic feet per second. The
     road grader is well designed to quickly excavate the necessary cross section to handle this flow, provided
     that the ditch is built in soil rather than rock. Grader efficiency drops significantly when cross sections of
     larger dimensions are required.

     7-6. For flows larger than 60 cubic feet per second, the trapezoidal ditch is commonly specified. A wheeled
     scraper can excavate the flat bottom and midsection of this ditch rapidly, and the side slopes can be dressed
     back by subsequent passes of a road grader. Smaller bottom widths can be provided using the previously
     mentioned equipment, including the road grader with its blade turned to a high angle. Production rates will
     be much lower for the grader than those of the wheeled scraper.

29 February 2016  TM 3-34.48-1  7-1


---

Chapter 7

                                             Figure 7-1. Ditch cross sections

     7-7. The 60 cubic feet per second guideline is flexible. If a scraper is not available to excavate a ditch
     carrying 100 cubic feet per second, a grader is used to construct an oversized V ditch rather than using low-
     production-rate equipment to construct a trapezoidal ditch.

     7-8. The segmental-ditch shape results when explosives are used to create the ditch. This technique is often
     used when the terrain is too soft to support excavating machinery. Ditches cut by hand will often bear this
     shape as well.

SIDE-SLOPE RATIOS

     7-9. Ditches have two sides and two associated side-slope ratios. Side slope is the slope of the channel bank,
     normally expressed as a ratio of feet horizontal to feet vertical. For example, a side-slope ratio of 3:1 is 3 feet
     horizontal to 1 foot vertical. When the sidewalls on opposite sides are inclined equally, the ditch is called
     symmetrical. Nonsymmetrical ditches have two different side slopes.

     7-10. The designer selects appropriate side-slope ratios. The selection is critical to ensure that the ditch serves
     its purpose. Ditch sidewalls that are too steep invite excessive erosion and are likely to cause the ditch to clog
     with sediment. If the side slope is too severe, a serious accident could occur if a vehicle runs into the ditch
     and becomes entrapped or overturns. Only one side slope is required for symmetrical ditches. For clarity, the
     terms front slope or ditch slope and back slope are used to differentiate between the dissimilar slopes. (See
     figure 7-2 for an illustration.)

     7-11. The sidewall of a roadside ditch located adjacent to the shoulder is called the front slope of the ditch.
     The far slope, called the back slope, is simply an extension of the cut face in an excavation. The following is
     applicable only in shallow ditches in relatively flat terrain:

              Roadside ditches may be cut nonsymmetrical at 3:1 (front slope) and 1:1 (back slope).
              Diversion ditches may be cut symmetrically at 1:1.
              Ditches subject to cross traffic may be cut symmetrically at 3:1 or more gently.

FLOW TYPES

     7-13. Several flow types are associated with open channels. Some of these types occur simultaneously in
     the same channel. An understanding of these flow types and their interrelationship is essential to the effective
     design of drainage systems.

     7-14. An open-channel flow has a free surface and no hydraulic pressure. Some examples of open-channel
     flow include ditches, canals, streams, and culverts not flowing full. Empirical formulas with experimentally
     derived coefficients are used in designing an open channel. These hydraulic formulas reflect certain hydraulic
     theories and assumptions governing design analysis of free-flow channels.

     7-15. A steady flow is assumed in an open channel with a uniform depth during the design period. Changes
     in flow are generally slow, and errors that may be introduced by this assumption are not significant.

     7-16. A continuous flow is assumed according to the principle of the conservation of mass.

     7-17. A uniform flow is assumed when the depth of water throughout a channel is constant in dimension and
     slope. This means that the slope of the water surface is the same as the slope of the channel bottom. This
     assumption is essentially correct for channels of moderate slope and length. Flows in ditches, canals, and
     rivers are uniform, but flows over spillways or waterfalls are not uniform.

     7-18. The strength of viscosity forces and the thickness of moving fluid determine if channel flow is turbulent
     or laminar.

7-4                        TM 3-34.48-1                                                                   29 February 2016


---

                                                                                                           Open-Channel Design

7-19. Turbulent flow is assumed for purposes of open-channel design. This flow type occurs when viscosity
forces are relatively weak and the individual water particles move in random patterns within the aggregate
forward-flow pattern.

7-20. Laminar flow occurs when viscosity forces are predominate and fluid particles move in smooth,
parallel paths. An example of this type of flow is honey poured from a container; honey has high-viscosity
strength compared to water. The only type of laminar flow considered in this manual is sheet flow, which
occurs where depth is extremely shallow. It is assumed that the flow in natural and designed channels will
be steady, continuous, uniform, and turbulent.

EQUATIONS

     7-21. This section discusses open-channel design equations. Because of the variables and assumptions to be
     made, trial techniques are required to determine the shape and depth of a particular channel before a final
     solution is reached.

VELOCITY OF FLOW

     7-25. Many ditches with differing side slopes and cross-sectional areas of flow will carry the same rate of
     runoff on a similar longitudinal slope. In each case, the velocity of flow will be different. Since excessive
     velocity in a ditch will cause erosion and possible damage to adjacent structures, it must be contained within
     limits. Table 7-3 lists the maximum permissible velocities, depending on soil and other factors.

7-26. The following applies to velocity relationships:
        As a slope increases, velocity increases.
        If the quantity of runoff increases and the area remains constant, velocity increases.
        If Manning’s roughness coefficient increases, velocity decreases.
        If velocity increases, erosion increases.

HYDRAULIC RADIUS

     7-27. The hydraulic radius is the area of the ditch water cross section divided by its wetted perimeter. (See
     figure 7-4, page 7-8.) It relates the surface area of friction resistances with the volume of water being carried
     by the ditch. The hydraulic radius can be calculated using an electronic calculator. (See figure 7-5, page
     7-8.)

CONSIDERATIONS

     7-28. There are certain factors known for each ditch being designed. These factors affect the design details.
     The location, peak flow, effect of the terrain on the slope, and soil type or materials used to line the ditch
     have a bearing on the channel design.

LOCATION

     7-29. The ditch location determines the general shape of the ditch and the side slopes to be used in its design.

7-8                                             TM 3-34.48-1                       29 February 2016


---

                                                                                                                       Open-Channel Design

QUANTITY OF RUNOFF

     7-30. Designers must know the quantity of runoff that the channel will have to carry. Usually, this is
     estimated using the rational method for runoff determination. However, it may also be estimated based on
     knowledge of the slope, the diameter, and the type of culverts used to discharge into the channel. The quantity
     of runoff also determines the type of ditch section (triangular or trapezoidal) to be used. This depends on if
     the quantity of runoff is greater than or less than 60 cubic feet per second.

SLOPE

     7-31. The terrain will determine the slope. In general, the slope used will be the natural ground slope. Small
     modifications of the slope can be made for short ditch sections.

DITCH LINING

     7-32. The ditch lining determines the velocity and roughness coefficient or resistance factor. Table 7-3, page
     7-7, gives maximum erosion velocities for each type of soil and lining. The lower velocity on the chart
     indicates that the velocity erosion will start to occur in some portion of the ditch. At the high velocity value,
     the entire length of the ditch will probably be eroding.

     7-33. Table 7-3 also provides Manning’s roughness coefficient, which represents the friction resistance of
     the ditch, channel, or stream for various soil types and linings. Use the average roughness coefficient value
     for design purposes.

TECHNIQUES

     7-34. Once design considerations have been examined, the interactive design procedure can begin.

STEPS

     7-35. The steps used in design are—
              Step 1. Determine the peak volume of storm water runoff. Using the rational method, calculate
                  the area contributing flow to the ditch. Find the quantity of runoff using the appropriate formula.
              Step 2. Determine the slope in feet per foot. If the slope is already known as a percentage, it may
                  be converted to units of feet per foot by dividing by 100.
              Step 3. Select trial values for the roughness coefficient and velocity. From table 7-3, select the
                  roughness coefficient and velocity values for the soil type of the ditch. The initial trial velocity
                  should be held to 1 foot per second below the high value. Usually, the channel will be carrying
                  less than design flow, reducing the velocity and making sedimentation likely. If a high value is
                  chosen for the design velocity, the water will remove this deposited material during peak flow
                  without causing extensive damage to the channel.
              Step 4. Determine the hydraulic radius. Use the nomograph or equation to find the hydraulic radius
                  of the ditch using the slope, Manning’s roughness coefficient, and velocity. Call this RM to
                  distinguish it from the radius value, Rt, used in appendix B.
              Step 5. Determine the ditch cross section type. For quantity of runoff greater than 60 cubic feet
                  per second, use a trapezoidal ditch. For quantity of runoff equal to or less than 60 cubic feet per
                  second, use a triangular ditch. The location determines if the ditch is symmetrical or
                  nonsymmetrical.
              Step 6. Select the appropriate hydraulic radius for the desired ditch cross section. (See appendix
                  B, tables B-1 through B-9, pages B-9 through B-17.) Select table by identifying the table title with
                  the appropriate tentative side-slope ratios. Locate the value of Rt (hydraulic radius found using the
                  tables in appendix B) that corresponds with Rm (hydraulic radius found using Manning’s equation),
                  and find the cross-sectional area and ditch depth corresponding to Rm and Rt. If the exact value of
                  Rm is not available in the table, use the next smaller Rt value listed in that column.

           where—  area
           AW =    quantity of runoff

           The area and velocity are determined in Steps 6 and 3. If the calculated quantity is—

            No more than 5 percent greater than the design quantity, the ditch selected can be used.

            More than 5 percent greater than the design quantity, reduce the velocity and repeat Steps 4
                through 7.

            Smaller than the design quantity by more than 5 percent, increase the velocity. However, do
                not make it any larger than the maximum velocity permissible for the soil or lining. (See table
                7-3, page 7-7.)

            Less than the 95-percent limit of the design quantity, the cross section must be increased by
                flattening the side slopes or by increasing the bottom width (if a trapezoidal section is used).

            Step 8. Provide freeboard (the additional ditch depth over what is required to carry the design
                flow). Add 0.5 foot to the water depth for freeboard. This added depth enables the ditch to carry
                the design capacity, even with sediment in the ditch bottom. The total depth, including freeboard,
                will be the cutting depth and the set ditch grade depth.

                                       Example

Design a ditch to carry a peak volume of storm water runoff equaling 47.3 cubic feet per second from
a culvert to a stream that is 289 feet from the outlet of the culvert. The ditch invert (or bottom)
elevation at the outlet of the culvert will be 7.0 feet above sea level. The ditch invert will be
constructed above the stream high watermark at an elevation of 5.5 feet above sea level. The ditch
lining will be bare (unturfed) GMd soil, as excavated. (See table 6-6, page 6-39, and table 7-3, page
7-7). Use the equation—

(Nomograph and table method) The solution of a ditch problem is a trial technique in which several
values of velocity are used. Use a table to tabulate the results. (See table 7-4, page 7-14.) Follow
these steps:

            Step 1. Select a ditch. Since design flow is less than 60 cubic feet per second, the
                ditch should be triangular. The channel is not a roadside ditch; it should be
                symmetrical. Select side slopes for a 3:1 triangular ditch for the first trial. (This assumes
                that periodic vehicular crossings are expected.) These factors can be changed if the
                ditch design is not suitable. Enter the information in the ditch selection column on the
                ditch design work sheet.

            Step 2. Select the velocity. The erosion velocity for the soil is 3 to 5 feet per second.
                This means that at 3 feet per second the soil in the ditch may begin to erode, and at 5
                feet per second the whole ditch will erode. It is preferable not to exceed the velocity
                maximum of 5 feet per second, and the best choice is usually 1 feet per second lower
                than the velocity maximum, which is 4 feet per second. Enter this figure on the work
                sheet.

      • Step 7. Determine if the ditch is appropriate. This process describes a symmetrical,
           triangular ditch in GMd soil, with a slope of 0.0052 feet per foot and 3:1 side slopes. It carries
           45.5 cubic feet per second runoff with a water depth of 1.9 feet and a velocity of 4.2 feet per
           second. Since the velocity in the ditch is greater than 3 feet per second, the ditch can be
           considered self-cleaning and requires little maintenance. Peak runoff will remove any silt
           buildup from the channel bottom. With velocity = 4.2 feet per second, there may be some
           erosion of the ditch, but it should not be a significant maintenance problem. The shape,
           lining, and slopes are acceptable.

      • Step 8. Determine the cutting depth. The water level in the ditch should be at least 0.5 foot
           below the edge of the ditch as a safety factor. Accordingly, the cutting depth is the water
           depth plus 0.5 foot of freeboard. Use the following equation to calculate cutting depth:

                                          𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶 𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑ℎ = 𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑ℎ + 𝑓𝑓𝑓𝑓𝑓𝑓𝑓𝑓𝑓𝑓𝑓𝑓𝑓𝑓𝑓𝑓𝑓𝑓

Using the rutting depth just calculated, cutting depth = 1.9 + 0.5 = 2.4 feet. Since there are 2.5 feet
(8.0 − 5.5 = 2.5) of available cutting depth at the end of the ditch, the design is acceptable.

Conclusion. Use this ditch.

SPECIAL CHANNELS

     7-36. Some facilities will have special channels where surface runoff will be intercepted and removed. These
     channels are similar to open channels except that they tend to be very wide and shallow. To determine runoff
     capacity (in cubic feet per second) in this type of channel, open channel hydraulics must be modified.

Gutters

     7-37. Gutters are shallow, paved drainage channels used in more permanent construction adjacent paved or
     hard-surfaced areas. They provide positive removal of runoff, protection for easily eroded soils adjacent to
     the pavement, and prevent softening of turf shoulder areas commonly caused by a large volume of runoff
     from adjoining pavements.

     7-38. A cross section of a typical runway gutter is shown in figure 7-8, page 7-16. This gutter conforms to
     United States Air Force safety requirements and design charts of that particular gutter. Safety and operational
     requirements for fast landing speeds make it desirable to provide a continuous, longitudinal grade in the
     gutter. Close conformity to the runway gradient requires the use of sump inlets (drop inlets covered by
     gratings). A sufficient number of inlets should be provided in the gutter to prevent the depth of flow from
     exceeding 3 inches.

Median Channels

     7-39. Channels will be placed down the center of medians, dual roads, runways, taxiways, and similar
     structures. These channels will be symmetrical but wide and shallow. The input flow into such channels is
     from surfaced and unsurfaced areas adjacent to the channel. The flow can be determined by the rational
     method. Since the factors of slope, roughness coefficient, flow, and the general width are known, the depth
     can be determined by trial using the flow equation or nomograph for flow in open channels.

Berms

     7-40. The uncontrolled inflow from drainage areas adjacent to open channels has been a source of numerous
     erosion failures. Combating this problem requires special consideration during the design of the surface
     drainage system. Local runoff inflow can be particularly detrimental. Because of normal irregularities in
     grading operations, runoff becomes concentrated and causes excessive erosion as it flows over the sides of
     the channel. Constructing a berm (a raised lip that is usually made of earth) prevents this problem. (See figure
     7-9.) Place the berm at the top edge of the channel. The berm prevents inflow into the channel except at
     designated points where an inlet—properly protected against erosion—is provided.

     7-41. Where excavated material is wasted, such as a levee or dike parallel to the channel, frequent openings
     through the levee to permit inflow to the channel are needed. A suitable berm allows a minimal amount of
     excavated material to flow back into the channel. This prevents sloughing from the spoil bank into the
     channel.

     7-42. Runoff from the area is determined by the rational method. This runoff is collected and conveyed by
     the channel formed by the berm. The factors of quantity, roughness coefficient, slope, and width are used to
     solve for depth by the trial method.

CONSTRUCTION AND MAINTENANCE

     7-43. Ditch construction normally requires a grader or scraper. Sometimes they are used together. Depending
     on the location, other factors must be considered in designing and building ditches. Interceptor ditches should
     be set on grades, allowing quick removal of water without erosion. When the grade is not sufficient to permit
     quick water removal, the ditch may require an asphalt or concrete lining. Berms may be constructed on the
     downhill side of interceptor ditches to prevent overflow and excessive erosion of the downhill slopes. (See
     figure 7-9.)

     7-44. Abrupt changes in the normal flow pattern of a ditch will induce turbulence and cause excessive
     erosion. These conditions usually develop at channel transitions, junctions, and storm drain outlets.
     Accordingly, special attention must be given to these locations during design.

     7-45. Channel maintenance problems exist in drainage systems. The basic design of the ditch must consider
     these maintenance problems before they arise. Therefore, designers must have a thorough understanding of
     the two basic ditch maintenance problems: sedimentation and erosion. When used together, channel
     protection and ditch shape control maintenance problems effectively.

SEDIMENT CONTROL

     7-46. Water flowing over land tends to carry sediment into open channels. When channel velocity is 3 feet
     per second or less, sediment can be deposited in the channel. Since most storms are less intense than the
     design storm, the channel bottom may accumulate a large volume of loose sediment. When peak flow does
     occur, the velocity should be great enough to scour the channel bottom clean of loose sediment. If the
     sediment is not removed, it will compact and gradually reduce the depth of the ditch. At peak flow, the ditch
     may overflow and cause damage to adjacent structures if the channel is not cleaned out; therefore, the channel
     should be kept clean through maintenance.

     7-47. When designing channels, keep peak velocity flow above 3 feet per second. The channel is self-
     cleaning at this velocity. A higher velocity is preferred, but the velocity must not exceed the maximum
     velocity for the soil. (See table 7-5, page 7-18.) When the soil type requires a maximum allowable velocity
     less than 3 feet per second, sedimentation will be a maintenance problem. One solution is to line the ditch
     with asphalt or concrete. This reduces the coefficient of friction, increasing the velocity. When sedimentation
     is expected and linings cannot be used, increase the allowable freeboard to eliminate overflow.

EROSION CONTROL

     7-48. Water flowing through open channels is turbulent. This turbulence increases as the velocity increases.
     Velocity and turbulence erode and carry away channel soil, which endangers nearby structures (roads,
     bridges, culverts) and the channel. In addition, the eroded material may be deposited in areas within the
     channel that will cause damage. In these cases, channel maintenance and repair will be a constant concern.

     7-49. Erosion occurs when the velocity of flow exceeds the velocity at which channel soil erodes. (See table
     7-5 for maximum velocities.) Lowering the velocity below the soil-erosion velocity can prevent erosion. This
     can be accomplished by lining the natural channel material with a more erosion-resistant material or by
     reducing the side slopes. Table 7-6 shows recommended side slopes. Erosion should be considered and
     accounted for in the design of channels.

7-50. Reducing the hydraulic radius will decrease the velocity. This decrease in hydraulic radius can be
accomplished by increasing the wetted perimeter in relation to the area. This can be accomplished by
widening the ditch, flattening the side slopes, or widening the bottom. This increases the wetted perimeter
without materially increasing the area. The required changes in ditch design are determined by the trial
approach since the amount of runoff must be retained while reducing the velocity.

7-51. Erosion must be controlled to maintain an effective and clear drainage system with a minimum of
maintenance and to reduce hazardous dust conditions. Proper design of side slopes in cut and fill sections
(based on the type of soil) will reduce the need for extensive erosion control measures; however, additional
control is usually required. Most methods of control are based on dissipating the energy of the water,
providing an erosion-resistant surface, or some combination of these techniques. This section ways to reduce
or eliminate the erosive force of water.

7-52. Terracing is a control measure designed to dissipate the energy of overland flow in nonuse areas.
Turfing, paving, gunite lining, and placing riprap are control methods designed to cause turbulence and to
increase retardation, thereby dissipating the energy of flow in open channels (ditches, pipe outfalls). In cases
where riprap will be eroded, the use of gabions is a speedy and relatively inexpensive means of dissipating
energy.

Terracing

     7-53. A terrace is a low, broad-based earth levee constructed approximately parallel to the contours of the
     topography. A terrace intercepts and holds the water until it infiltrates the soil or moves it as overland flow
     to a suitable discharge point. A hardy, vigorous turf should be planted to hold the disturbed soil in place.
     Vertical spacing and longitudinal gradients of terraces are given in figure 7-10, page 7-20.

Lining the Channel

     7-54. Lining the bottom and sides of the channel can control erosion. Channel lining materials include grass
     or turf, pavement, and riprap.

Turfing

     7-55. Natural linings (grass, turf) take considerable time to grow or effort to place. Because of this, they are
     seldom used in the JOA. Ditches are protected by placing strips of sod (held in place by wooden boards or
     stakes) perpendicular to the flow path at intervals along the ditch. (See figure 7-11.)

Paving and Gunite Lining

     7-56. When design and construction are done properly, paving the ditch with asphalt or concrete will prevent
     erosion. Because of the low roughness coefficient values of different types of pavement, velocity may
     increase too much, causing erosion where the pavement ends. Special protection, such as a stilling basin or
     rock lining, may be required to slow the velocity before allowing the flow to continue into the natural soil
     channel. Because of the low roughness coefficient values of pavement, it can be used effectively to increase
     flow velocities if they are too low, thus preventing deposition.

     7-57. Ditches having grades in excess of 5 percent usually require paving or a gunite lining. Where a slope
     equals or exceeds 5 percent, paving must be extended downslope at least to the point in the ditch that the
     erosive energy of the water is controlled or absorbed without erosion damage. Paving with asphalt or concrete
     provides superior erosion-resistant linings in gutters, ditches, and outfall structures.

     7-58. Gunite lining of ditches controls erosion effectively. Gunite is a mixture of cement and sand with water
     added just before the mixture is sprayed from a high-pressure nozzle onto the surface being protected. The
     gunite lining is formed over steel mesh placed over the bottom and sides of the ditch. Gunite is sprayed to a
     thickness of 1 to 1 1/2 inches, with the steel mesh located midway in the thickness. Human resources, time,
     and material and equipment expenses usually limit the use of paving or gunite linings to the most demanding
     conditions in JOA airfield construction.

7-20       TM 3-34.48-1  29 February 2016

                                          Figure 7-11. Erosion-control checks

Placing Riprap

     7-59. Riprap lining involves placing rocks or rubble in the bottom and on the sides of the ditch to prevent
     soil erosion and undesirable meandering. Rocks should be hand-placed in at least two layers and compacted
     individually. Riprap prevents erosion and decreases velocity in the channel because of its high roughness
     coefficient value. Riprap also helps prevent erosion when making transitions from paved to soil ditches or
     from other high-velocity ditches to those where lower velocity is required.

     7-60. Riprap protection should be provided adjacent to hydraulic structures (drop structures, energy
     dissipaters). When placed on erodible surfaces, it prevents scour at the ends of the structure. This protection
     is required on the bed and banks for a sufficient distance to establish velocity gradients and turbulence levels
     at the end of the riprap. The expansion allows the flow to expand and dissipate its excess energy in turbulence
     rather than directly on the channel bottom and sides. Riprap has been known to fail from—

              Movement of the individual stones from a combination of velocity and turbulence.
              Movement of the natural bed material through the riprap, resulting in slumping of the blanket.
              Undercutting and leveling of the riprap from scour at the end of the blanket.

     7-61. Consideration must be given to the selection of an adequate size of stone, use of adequately graded
     riprap, provision of a filter blanket, and proper treatment of the end of the riprap blanket. The stone size
     selection required for protection with Froude numbers (the ratio of inertial forces to gravity forces) and depths
     of flow in the channel is shown in figure 7-12, page 7-22. Two curves are given. One is for riprap subjected
     to direct flow or adjacent to hydraulic structures (side inlets, confluences, energy dissipaters) where
     turbulence levels are high. The other is for riprap on the banks of a straight channel where flows are relatively
     quiet and parallel to the banks.

7-65. A well-graded mixture of stone sizes is preferred to a relatively uniform size of riprap. A recommended
gradation is shown in figure 7-14, page 7-24. In certain locations, the available material may dictate the
gradation of riprap to be used. The gradation should resemble the recommended mixture as closely as
possible. Consider increasing the thickness of the riprap blanket when locality dictates using gradations with
a larger percentage of small stone than shown by the recommended plot. If the gradation of the available
riprap is such that movement of natural material through the riprap blanket would be likely, place a filter
blanket of sand, crushed rock, gravel, or synthetic cloth under the riprap. The usual blanket thickness is 6
inches, although a greater thickness is sometimes necessary.

7-66. An ideal riprap design would provide a gradual reduction in riprap size until the downstream end of
the blanket blends with the natural bed material. Unless this is done, turbulence caused by the riprap is likely
to develop a scour hole at the end of the riprap blanket. However, the extra effort required to provide gradual
reduction in riprap size is seldom justified. Double the thickness of the riprap blanket at the downstream end
to protect against undercutting and unraveling. An alternative is a rubble blanket of constant thickness and
suitable length, dipping below the natural streambed to the estimated depth of the bottom scour.

Gabions

     7-67. Gabions are large, steel, wire-mesh baskets, usually rectangular and variable in size, designed to solve
     erosion problems at a low cost. Widely used in Europe, gabions are now accepted in the United States as a
     valuable and practical construction and maintenance tool. They can be used in place of sheet piling, masonry
     construction, or cribbing.

Description and Assembly

     7-68. Gabions are supplied from manufacturers in flat, folded bundles. For ease in handling and shipping,
     the number of gabions per bundle varies according to the size of the gabions. The box gabion is a rectangular
     cage or basket formed of woven, hexagonal, galvanized steel, wire mesh with 4- to 8-inch openings and
     divided by diaphragms into cells. To assemble, remove a single gabion from the bundle and unfold it on a
     hard, flat surface to straighten unnecessary creases and kinks. Fold the front, back, and end panels to a right
     angle to form a box. (See figure 7-15.) Securely lace the vertical edge and diaphragms
     with binding wire.

7-24                TM 3-34.48-1                                    29 February 2016


---

                                Open-Channel Design

                                         Note. Gabion ends and diaphragms will be lifted into a
                                         vertical position and laced to form a box.

                                           Figure 7-15. Assembly of a gabion

Installation

     7-69. Before placing the gabions, make the ground surface relatively smooth and even. Place the assembled
     gabions in position singly or wired together in groups suitable for handling. It is convenient to place the
     gabions front-to-front and back-to-back to expedite the stone-filling and lid-lacing operation. Lace the basket
     along the perimeter of contact surfaces. Where there is more than one course of gabions, the base of the
     empty gabions placed on top of a completed row must be tightly wired to the latter. (See figure 7-16, page
     7-26.)

     7-70. When using 3-foot-high gabions, place them empty and lace for approximately 100 linear feet. Anchor
     the first gabion firmly and apply tension to the other end with a come-a-long ratchet or by other means to
     achieve the proper alignment. Anchoring can be accomplished by partially filling the first gabion with stone.
     While the gabions are being stretched, inspect the corners to ensure that the lacing is secure and the corners
     are closed. Keep gabions taut while they are being filled with stone.

     7-71. Where water, soil, and atmospheric conditions allow, galvanized wire mesh can have a life of 40 years
     or more. For soils and water showing a hydrogen (pH) factor of less than 7 or more than 12, plastic-coated
     wire must be used to form gabions.

Filling Procedures

     7-72. The best filling material is one that allows flexibility in the structure and, at the same time, fills the
     gabion compartments with a minimum of voids and maximum weight. Ideally, the stone should be small,
     just slightly larger than the size of the mesh (usually 4 to 8 inches). The stone should be clean, hard, durable,
     and resistant to weathering and frost action. Use the following steps when performing the filling operation:

              Step 1. Fill the gabionsto a depth of 1 foot.
              Step 2. Place one connecting wire in each direction and loop around two meshes of the gabion

                  wall. (See figure 7-16.)
              Step 3. Repeat this operation twice or until the gabion is filled; then fold the top shut and wire it

                  to the ends, sides, and diaphragms.
              Step 4. Pack the stone inside the compartment as tight as practical.
              Step 5. Protect the vertical diaphragm during the filling operation, temporarily place rebars and

                  lace them along the upper edges.

     7-73.

7-74. Some manual stone adjustment is required during the filling operation to prevent undue voids. Fill the
gabion slightly overfull and allow for subsequent settlement; then lace the lid down with binding wire to the
tops of the sides and to the tops of the diaphragm panels. Since it is necessary to stretch the lid to fit the sides
exactly, use a short crowbar or special tool designed for this purpose.

7-75. The strong interconnection of the units in a gabion structure is an important feature. It is essential that
the lacing be done properly. Adjoining gabions are wired together by their vertical edges. Empty gabions,
stacked on filled gabions, are wired to the filled gabions at the front and back.

7-76. Gabions may be filled by almost any type of earth-handling equipment (payloader, crane, conveyor,
modified concrete bucket). The use of rounded stone, if it is available, reduces the possibility of damage to
the galvanized wire during mechanical filling. When the depth of the water is too great for the gabions to be
filled on site, fill them at a dry location nearby and place them underwater by crane or barge.

Maintenance and Repair
     7-77. Maintenance and repair are simple procedures; therefore, gabions are inspected at least once a year.
     Holes can be patched with small panels of mesh, and broken wires can be repaired. (See figure 7-17.)

                                          Figure 7-17. Repairing a broken wire

Thickness

     7-78. The thickness of gabions may be calculated by considering the gradient of the channel, the steepness
     of its slope, the type of material forming the banks and bed, and the curvature of its course. A 12-inch-deep
     lining is suggested for channels having reasonably straight alignment, side slopes of less than 35°, and a flow
     velocity of about 10 feet per second. (See figure 7-18.) Use an 18-inch gabion lining for curved channel
     sections with a side slope of 45°. Use 36-inch stepped-back gabion protection for sharper side slopes. For a
     steep channel slope, a combination of lining and weirs may be required.

                  Legend:  design high water level
                  DHWL     feet
                  ft       inch
                  in

                  Figure 7-18. Typical channel lining using gabions

7-79. In the case of easily erodible soil, a layer of filter material or permeable membrane of cloth woven of
synthetic fibers is required. The gabion should be filled with stone small enough to allow at least two
overlapping layers. In designing a gabion-lined channel, the roughness factor or coefficient in Manning’s
formula may be assumed to be between 0.025 and 0.030. If the gabions are grouted, the roughness factor can
be assumed to be between 0.012 and 0.018. Gabion-lined channels may be designed using Manning’s
equation and the procedures for open-channel design.

Chapter 7

Uses

     7-80. Gabions can be used in the following ways:
              Protective and antierosion structures on rivers (revetments, groins, spurs).
              Other antierosion structures (weirs, drop structures, check dams).
              Channel linings.
              Seashore protection.
              Low-water bridges or fords.
              Culvert headwall and outlet structures.
              Bridge abutments and wing walls.

     7-81. Culvert inlets and outlets are often modified by using transition structures to reduce entrance losses
     and inhibit erosion. Therefore, gabions are most commonly used for headwalls and outlet aprons.

     7-82. Headwalls or wing walls are designed to protect the slopes of an embankment against scour,
     to increase culvert efficiency by providing a flush inlet as opposed to projecting one, to prevent disjointing
     of sectional-pipe culverts by anchoring the inlet and outlet, and to retain the embankment slope.
     These structures are built in a variety of shapes: straight, L-shaped, flared, and warped. A typical plan
     using a headwall and an outlet apron with a culvert is shown in figure 7-18, page 7-27. Straight headwalls
     are generally used on small, roadside culverts under driveways and in small channels having a low approach
     velocity. They are also recommended where there is a tendency for lateral erosion to develop at the outlet.

     7-83. An apron is often required at the outlet of a culvert to reduce the outlet velocity and thereby inhibit
     scour. Gabions are well adapted for use here because of their roughness, flexibility, and durability.
     (See figure 7-19.) Table 7-7 shows the gabion protection required for various outlet velocity ranges.

                                                                                                                       Open-Channel Design

Culvert Outlets

     7-84. Most culverts operate under free outfall conditions (no control of tailwater), and the discharge
     possesses kinetic energy in excess of that occurring naturally in the waterway. This excess kinetic energy
     must often be dissipated to control damaging erosion. The extent to which protective works are required for
     energy dissipation depends on the amount of excess kinetic energy and the characteristics of the material in
     the outlet channel. In general, scour occurs at average velocities in excess of about 1.5 feet per second in
     uniform-graded sand and cohesionless silts, 2.5 feet per second in well-graded sand, 3.0 feet per second in
     silty sand, 4.0 feet per second in clay, and 6.0 feet per second in gravel. These velocities should be used only
     as a general guide.

     7-85. If possible, study local material to determine its erosion tendencies before a decision on the degree of
     protection is required. The study should consider the following types of outfalls offering three degrees of
     protection:

              Plain outlets provide no protective works and depend on natural material to resist harmful erosion.
              Transitions provide little or no dissipation on the works themselves, but result in a spreading of

                  the effluent jet to approximate the cross-section flow of the natural channel, thus reducing the
                  concentration of energy before releasing the flow to the outlet channel.
              Stilling basins result in dissipation of energy on the protective works.

Plain Outlets

     7-86. If the discharge channel is in rock or a material highly resistant to erosion, special erosion protection
     is not required. This type of outlet should be used only if the material in the outlet channel can withstand
     velocities about 1.5 times the velocity in the culvert. At such an outlet, side erosion from eddy action or
     turbulence is more likely to prove troublesome than bottom scour.

     7-87. Cantilevered culvert outlets may be used to discharge a free-falling jet onto the bed of the outlet
     channel. As a result, a plunge pool will be developed. The depth and size of the plunge pool depend on the
     energy of the falling jet at the tailwater and the erodibility of the bed material.

Transitions

     7-88. Outlet headwalls and wing walls serve the dual purpose of retaining the embankment and limiting the
     outlet transition boundary. Erosion of embankment toes can be traced to eddy attacks at the ends of the walls.
     A flared transition is effective if it is proportioned so that eddies induced by the effluent jet does not continue
     beyond the end of the wall or overtop a sloped wall.

     7-89. As a guideline, it is suggested that the product of velocity and flare angle not exceed 150°. For example,
     if effluent velocity is 5 feet per second, each wing wall may flare 30°. If velocity is 15 feet per second, the
     flare should not exceed 10°. Unless wing walls can be anchored on a stable foundation, a paved apron
     between the wing walls is required. Special care must be taken in the structure design to preclude
     undermining.

     7-90. A newly excavated channel may be expected to degrade. Proper allowance for this action should be
     included in establishing the apron elevation and depth of cutoff wall. Warped end walls provide excellent
     transitions that result in the release of flow in a trapezoidal cross section that approximates the cross section
     of the outlet channel. A warped transition is made at the end of the curved section to reduce the possibility
     of overtopping as a result of superelevation of the water surface. A paved apron is required with warped end
     walls. Riprap is usually required at the end of a transition-type outlet.

Stilling Basins

     7-91. At culvert outlets where a high concentration of energy or easily eroded materials makes excessive
     erosion likely, a stilling basin or other energy-dissipating device is required. For JOA construction, riprap or
     simple, concrete stilling basins are usually required. There are many types of energy-dissipating devices
     (hydraulic-jump basins, roller buckets, flip buckets, impact-energy-dissipating devices, stilling wells). In
     unusual cases involving major structures, the use of a special type of device should be considered. Three
     types of dissipaters that may offer a solution are the hydraulic-jump stilling basin with details developed at

29 February 2016  TM 3-34.48-1  7-29


---

Chapter 7

   the Saint Anthony Falls Hydraulic Laboratory, the impact-energy dissipater with details developed at the
   hydraulic laboratory of the Bureau of Reclamation, and stilling wells. These dissipaters are beyond the scope
   of JOA construction. Design procedures are not included in this manual.

Installing Check Dams

     7-92. Decreasing the slope can also reduce the water velocity in a channel. However, except for local
     variations, building ditches at slopes other than that of the surrounding ground is impractical. One method
     for decreasing the slope is to install check dams or weirs. (See figure 7-20.)

     7-93. Check dams should be considered when the slope ranges between two and eight percent. Channels
     with slopes of two percent or less generally do not require extensive erosion controls. With slopes in excess
     of eight percent, it is usually more economical to pave the ditch with asphalt or concrete than to build check
     dams.
