     7-95. The spacing between check dams is 100 feet. To prevent erosion of the channel sides at the check dam,
     a weir notch is built in the center of the dam. The weir notch must be designed to carry the flow in the ditch.
     Weir-notch dimensions for various flow rates are given in table 7-8, page 7-32.

Maintenance

     7-96. Erosion is a common problem with check dams. It usually occurs when the weir notch is too small or
     is clogged with debris so that water flows over the top of the dam. Scour begins on the area exposed to the
     hydraulic jump. If allowed to continue long enough, the erosion will extend to the area around the dam. (See
     figure 7-21, page 7-32.) If this occurs, there will be more damage caused to adjacent structures than if the
     dam had never been installed.

     7-97. Some protection usually takes the form of an extended horizontal or sloping apron. Anchoring the sides
     and bottom into at least 2 feet of compacted material can also prevent scour. Then place riprap along at least
     4 feet of the downstream channel. These construction techniques will prevent scour and undercutting

                                                 Chapter 8

                               Culvert Design

         A culvert is an enclosed waterway used to pass water through an embankment or fill.
         The flow in a culvert depends on several factors (lining, slope, headwalls, wing walls,
         downstream conditions). Accordingly, culvert types and construction procedures are
         discussed before considering culvert hydraulics and design features.

CULVERT TYPES AND DESIGNS

     8-1. There are several factors to consider when selecting and installing culverts for subsurface drainage. In
     this chapter, several common culvert types are presented along with considerations for when to use each type
     in design. Also discussed in this chapter are the parameters for proper design and installation of culverts.

PIPE SELECTION, BEDDING, AND BACKFILL

     8-2. A drainage pipe is defined as a structure (other than a bridge) to convey water through a trench or
     under a fill or other obstruction. The selection of a suitable construction conduit will be governed by the
     availability and suitability of pipe materials for local conditions with due consideration of economic factors.
     When alternate designs are advantageous, each system will be economically designed for full capacity, best
     slope, least depth, and proper strength; installation provisions will be made for each material involved. When
     field conditions dictate the preference of one pipe material to another, the reasons will be clearly presented
     in the design analysis.

     8-3. Consider life cycle cost factors in selecting the type of pipe to be used in construction. The factors
     include strength under maximum or minimum cover being provided, pipe bedding, backfill conditions,
     anticipated loadings, length of pipe sections, ease of installation, resistance to corrosive action by liquids
     carried or surrounding soil materials, suitability of jointing methods, provisions for expected deflection
     without adverse effect on the pipe structure or on the joints or overlying materials, and cost of maintenance.
     Although it is possible to obtain an acceptable pipe installation to meet design requirements by establishing
     special provisions for several materials, usually just one or two materials will economically meet individual
     requirements for a proposed drainage system.

     8-4. Department of Defense has approved the use of plastic pipe for low volume roadway applications.
     However, plastic pipe is not approved for use under airfield pavement except for subsurface water collection
     and disposal.

     8-5. Corrugated metal pipe (CMP) with any percentage of bituminous coating will not be installed where
     solvents will enter the pipe. If solvents are expected, polymeric coated corrugated steel pipe is recommended.

     8-6. The selection of culvert materials to withstand deterioration from corrosion or abrasion will be based
     on these specific considerations. Rigid or plastic pipes are preferable where industrial wastes, spilled
     petroleum products, or other substances harmful to bituminous paving and coating in CMP are apt to be
     present. Typically, concrete pipe should not be used where soil is more acidic than pH 5.5 or where the fluid
     carried has a pH less than 5.5 or higher than 9.0. High density polyethylene pipe is unaffected by acidic or
     alkaline soil conditions. Concrete pipe can be engineered to perform very satisfactorily in the more severe
     acidic or alkaline environments. Type II or Type V cements should be used where soils and water have a
     moderate or high sulfate concentration. High-density concrete pipe is recommended when the culvert will be
     subject to tidal drainage and saltwater spray. Where highly corrosive substances are to be carried, the resistive
     qualities of vitrified clay pipe or plastic-lined concrete pipe should be considered.

     8-7. Corrugated steel pipe will be galvanized and will generally be bituminous coated for permanent
     installations. Bituminous coating or polymeric coating is recommended for corrugated steel pipe subjected

29 February 2016  TM 3-34.48-1  8-1


---

Chapter 8

     to stagnant water; where dense decaying vegetation is present to form organic acids; where there is
     continuous wetness or continuous flow; and in well-drained, normally dry, alkali soils. Polymeric-coated
     pipe is not damaged by spilled petroleum products or industrial wastes. Corrugated aluminum alloy pipe,
     fabricated in the same shapes and sizes as corrugated steel pipe, shows corrosion resistance in clear granular
     materials even when subjected to sea water. Corrugated aluminum pipe will not be installed in soils that are
     highly acid (pH less than 5), are alkaline (pH greater than 9), in metallic contact with other metals or metallic
     deposits, where known corrosive conditions are present, or where bacterial corrosion is known to exist. Also,
     it will not be installed in material classified as OH (organic clays of medium to high plasticity, organic silts)
     or OL (organic silts and organic silty clays of low plasticity) according to the USCS (see UFC 3-220-10N on
     Soil Mechanics). Although bituminous coatings can be applied to aluminum alloy pipe, these coatings do not
     provide adequate protection (bituminous adhesion is poor) under these corrosive conditions. Suitable
     protective coatings for aluminum alloy have been developed but are not economically feasible for culverts
     or storm drains. When considering a coating to use, performance data from users in the area can be helpful.
     Performance history indicates various successes or failures of coatings and their probable cause; these
     histories are available from local highway departments.

PERMANENT CULVERTS

     8-8. Materials for permanent-type installations include nonreinforced concrete, reinforced concrete,
     corrugated steel, plastic, corrugated aluminum alloy, and structural plate steel pipe.

Corrugated-Metal-Pipe Culverts

     8-9. CMP is commonly used in military construction because it is commercially available in numerous
     shapes, lengths, and diameters. For JOA construction, CMP is made of an aluminum and steel alloy. It comes
     in nested half sections that are 2-foot lengths when assembled. It is available in the diameters and gauges
     listed in table 8-1. The minimum diameter recommended is 18 inches for lengths up to 20 feet and 24 inches
     for the other lengths. Small diameters may become clogged with debris and are difficult to maintain.

                                                   Table 8-1. Sizes of CMP

            Diameter    Gauge  Thickness (inches)
             (inches)
                           8           0.179
           12, 18, 24,    10           0.135
           30, 36, 42,    12           0.105
           48, 60, 72     14           0.075
                          16          0.0598

     8-10. Specific construction techniques are employed when placing CMP. A retaining wall called a headwall
     is placed at the upstream end of the culvert. Headwalls are always used upstream; they are desirable but not
     mandatory for the downstream end. The headwall supports the soil mass at the end of the culvert and helps
     to protect against erosion.

     8-11. CMP joints must be overlapped so that water flowing through the culvert passes over the joint, not into
     it. Failure to properly overlap the pipes allows the water to force through the joints and into the fill. Joints
     must be sealed, preferably with caulk or bituminous material. If the joints are not sealed, voids may be
     generated around culverts, causing the fill to collapse. To increase the velocity for a greater quantity of flow,
     line the culvert with asphalt. Commercial CMP is available with asphalt linings.

     8-12. CMP has flange-type fittings that are easily fastened together by nuts and bolts that come with the
     sections. Vise grips and a ratchet set make assembly faster and easier.

High-Density Polyethylene Pipe

     8-13. High-density polyethylene (HDPE) pipe is commonly used in construction because it is readily
     available in numerous corrugation types, lengths, and diameters. Type C HDPE pipe comes with corrugation
     on the inside and outside. Type S HDPE pipe comes with a smooth interior and a corrugated exterior. Type

8-2                     TM 3-34.48-1               29 February 2016


---

                                                                                                                                  Culvert Design

     D HDPE pipe has a smooth inside with a spiral type of corrugation. Pipe sizes range from 4 inch inside
     diameter to 72 inch inside diameter. External diameters range from 5 to 80 inches. For detailed information
     on installation of HDPE culverts, contact the U.S. Army Geotechnical and Structures Laboratory at ERDC
     USACE, in Vicksburg, MS at (601) 636-3111 or by e-mail at ERDCinfo@usace.army.mil.

Concrete-Pipe Culverts

     8-14. When available, precast concrete pipe should be used for culverts instead of CMP. It has two
     advantages over CMP. First, it is stronger and requires less cover than CMP to support the same load. Second,
     the interior surface of concrete pipe is smoother (roughness coefficient equals 0.013) than CMP (roughness
     coefficient equals 0.024). Because of these advantages, concrete pipe of the same diameter and slope as CMP
     will carry a higher flow.
     8-15. Concrete pipe is fabricated in circular and noncircular cross sections. It is available in many lengths
     and widths. Seal joints between the sections to prevent excessive leakage and subsequent weakening of the
     fill section. Substantial headwalls are required at each end to prevent separation at the joints. Start assembly
     downstream and work upstream, ensuring that male ends point downstream.

Concrete-Box Culverts

     8-16. Consider concrete-box culverts where the full area of the waterway must be used. One advantage is
     that the box can be designed to withstand external loads with little or no cover. Box culverts are especially
     adaptable to rock sites since the bottom of the culvert can be placed directly on the rock.
     8-17. Concrete-box design requires knowledge of construction techniques for reinforced concrete structures.
     Box culverts can be precast, but construction in the JOA may require that they be cast in place.

EXPEDIENT CULVERTS

     8-18. Expedient field-type culverts are built of material available on-site (logs, oil drums, sandbags filled
     with a sand-cement mixture). Some examples of culverts built of these materials appear in figure 8-1; figure
     8-2, page 8-4; and figure 8-3, page 8-4. Expedient culverts built and sized properly should serve until
     permanent structures can be built. For evaluating hydraulics, end areas equivalent to CMP can be used for
     similar slopes.

                                                Figure 8-1. Oil-drum culvert

CULVERT CONSTRUCTION

     8-19. Proper placement is one of the most important factors during culvert construction. It is a major
     contributor to survival of the culvert under adverse conditions. Some things to consider when placing culverts
     are alignment, slope, depth of fill, compaction, length, and erosion control.

Alignment

     8-20. The relationship of the culvert to the streambed is of major importance. Improper location can cause
     the stream to seek an alternative path other than the culvert. This could quickly close a road or airfield to
     traffic. To lessen this effect, use the alignment techniques shown in figure 8-4.

8-4  TM 3-34.48-1                                                               29 February 2016


---

                                                                                                                            Culvert Design

8-21. Place the culvert directly in the streambed to maintain an existing drainage pattern. (See view A of
figure 8-4.) If the channel hydraulics are not changed, the stream will not change directions even though it
may be diagonal to the fill.

8-22. Prevent the stream from shifting course at the culvert inlet or outlet. Sometimes a structure will cut
across a stream meander, which leads to uncertainty when placing the culvert in the streambed. (See view B
of figure 8-4.) In this case, it is best to cut a new channel to lead the stream away from the structure. The old
streambed must be filled and dammed with erosion-resistant material at the junction of the old and new
channels. The dam can be built of sandbags, logs, riprap, or similar material.

8-23. Provide a smooth transition into and out of the culvert. A structure may cut across a bend of the stream
with a straight run of the stream through the structure. (See view C of figure 8-4.) If the bend is close to the
structure, it is preferable to recut the stream as shown and lay the culvert in the new streambed. Care should
be taken to fill in and dam the entrance to the old streambed and the junction of the two streambeds, as
described above.

                  Figure 8-4. Culvert alignment

29 February 2016  TM 3-34.48-1                   8-5


---

Chapter 8

     8-24. Move the water past the project as quickly as possible. When the channel flows parallel to the structure,
     erosion will eventually occur. To prevent erosion, dig a new channel that routes the flow through the culvert
     and away from the structure. (See view D of figure 8-4.) Again, be sure to fill and dam the old streambed at
     the junction point.
     8-25. The alignment of ditch relief culverts is shown in figure 8-5, page 8-6. The amount of flow and the
     slope of the ditch determine the spacing between culvert inlets. On a road with a 5-percent grade, relief
     culverts should be spaced 500 feet apart. On an 8-percent grade, spacing should be reduced to 300 feet.

                                              Figure 8-5. Ditch relief culverts

Slope

     8-26. Culverts should be installed with the invert of both the inlet and the outlet of the culvert at streambed
     or channel elevation. The invert is the lowest point in the internal cross section of an artificial channel
     or the bottom of the culvert. The normal grade of the culvert can be modified by the following two techniques:

              Drop-inlet technique. Drop inlets can be used to lower the culvert inlet. This will reduce the slope
                  of the culvert. (See view A in figure 8-6.)

              Outlet-above-grade technique. The culvert outlet can be raised to reduce the slope of the culvert.
                  (See view B in figure 8-6.)

     8-27. For culverts to be self-cleaning, flow velocity should be at least 3 feet per second. To achieve this
     velocity, the culvert should not be set on less than a 0.5 percent grade, if practical. To prevent excessive outlet
     velocity, the culvert grade should not exceed 2 percent.
     8-28. In general, free-falling outlets and culverts with slopes of more than 2 percent will require outlet
     erosion protection. In mountainous country where there are excessive stream slopes or in fills across dry
     valleys, culverts may have to be set at grades other than the terrain or streambed slope. In the JOA, it may be
     advisable to accept the erosion problem and install the culvert with a slope for an excess of 2 percent. This
     will prevent a blockage caused by debris passing through the pipe.

8-6  TM 3-34.48-1  29 February 2016


---

                                                              Culvert Design

                                Figure 8-6. Changing the normal grade of a culvert

Depth of Fill

     8-29. The distance measured from the culvert invert to the edge of the shoulder or top of the fill is the depth
     of fill. (See figure 8-7.) The depth of fill must be equal to or greater than the total of the cover and the pipe
     diameter. Otherwise, a smaller diameter culvert or a drop inlet must be used. For a road culvert made of
     CMP, the largest diameter allowable must equal two-thirds the minimum fill depth.

Legend:                             depth of fill
D                 Figure 8-7. Culvert specifications for CMP

Compaction

     8-30. The depth of the compacted soil from the top of the culvert (crown) to the finished construction grade
     is called cover. The culvert and the surrounding compacted soil must have sufficient strength to carry the
     compacted soil backfill (dead loads) and the wheel and impact loads (live loads) of the traffic. Live loads are
     more damaging than dead loads on culverts under shallow cover, and dead loads are more damaging than
     live loads on culverts under deep cover. Accordingly, minimum protective cover and maximum permissible

29 February 2016  TM 3-34.48-1                                8-7


---

Chapter 8

     depths of backfill must be included in design considerations for culverts. During construction, provide
     adequate additional cover to protect the culvert from damage in places where heavy construction equipment
     will be crossing frequently.

     8-31. The minimum cover required to protect the culvert pipe against live loads will depend on the type of
     load. For road culverts, the minimum cover is one-half the diameter of the culvert or 12 inches, whichever is
     greater. The cover over culverts used in airfields must be specifically designed for the heaviest aircraft using
     the facility. Table 8-2 lists characteristics of United States aircraft. Use this table to determine the landing-
     gear configuration, wheel loads, and culvert weight type. This allows the selection of the proper fill
     requirements category in table 8-3, page 8-10, or table 8-4, page 8-11.

     8-32. Table 8-3 and table 8-4 provide the cover requirements for culverts under airfields. These tables are a
     series of charts based on aircraft load and gear configurations. A culvert weight type and pipe diameter is
     identified in each chart. Use linear interpolation for the incremental diameters not listed. These charts are
     good for 5,000 pounds more than listed. For example, the chart 60,000-pounds single-wheel is good for
     single-wheel loads up to and including 65,000 pounds.

Bedding (Foundations)

     8-36. The minimum bedding depth for pipe culverts is one-tenth the diameter of the pipe. (See figure
     8-7, page 8-7.) The bedding is formed and shaped to fit the bottom of the culvert. In addition, the foundation
     is cambered (curved slightly upward) along the culvert centerline to allow for settlement and ensure tightness
     in the joints. (See figure 8-8.) The invert elevation should not increase as the flow proceeds downstream.

                            Figure 8-8. Elevation of center section of culvert

8-37. Culverts are constructed on firm, well-compacted foundations. The composition of the soil on the
bottom of the stream should be determined. Good granular material will be required to form a proper
compacted and shaped bed. If a stream bottom is composed of poor material (organic matter, muck, silt, large
material that could puncture the CMP), remove and replace the material. The depth of material to be removed
will depend on information obtained from borings. Provide cradle footings when the bearing strength of the
soil is completely inadequate and uneven settlement is expected.

8-38. These footings may require piling. (See figure 8-9, page 8-14.) Footings used for timber culverts can
also be adapted for various types of culverts and soils. (See figure 8-10, page 8-14.)

compacted soil for bedding the culvert. (See figure 8-11.)

                                                                                                                                  Culvert Design

Backfill

     8-40. Use caution when backfilling around the culvert. The backfill supports the culvert against soil pressure
     generated by surface loads. (See figure 8-6, page 8-7.) The soil selected should be placed in well-compacted
     layers kept at the same elevation on both sides of the culvert. If hand-operated, air-operated, or other
     mechanical tampers are used, compact in 6-inch layers. If logs are used, hand tamping or another expedient
     method is used. Compact the soil in 4-inch layers. Compact from the culvert bed material to 12 inches or
     one-half the diameter above the top of the culvert (whichever is greater).

Length

     8-41. Culvert length is determined by the width of the embankment or soil mass through which the culvert
     carries water. Culverts that do not include a downstream headwall must be long enough to extend a minimum
     of 2 feet beyond the toe of the embankment to prevent erosion.

Headwalls, Wing Walls, and Aprons

     8-42. Headwalls and aprons are constructed to guide water into the culvert, prevent or control erosion, reduce
     seepage, hold the soil in place, and support the culvert ends. Headwalls close to a road should not protrude
     above shoulder grade and should be at least 2 feet outside the shoulder so that it does not present a traffic
     hazard.

     8-43. Use headwalls on the upstream end of culverts. If possible, use a headwall on the downstream end too.
     When concrete pipes are used, headwalls are mandatory at each end. Headwalls, upstream and downstream,
     should have wing walls or retaining walls set at an angle to the headwall. This supports the fill, and directs
     water flow to prevent erosion. The upstream wing wall guides the water into the culvert and improves culvert
     hydraulics. The downstream wing wall, combined with an apron, reduces the velocity of the stream and
     lessens outlet erosion. Headwalls and wing walls should be reinforced concrete or mortared stone. Refer to
     the TM 5-302 series of manuals for standard designs. These structures can be made of expedient material
     (lumber, logs, sandbags). (See figure 8-12, page 8-16.) For speedy construction in the JOA, sandbags filled
     with a soil and cement mixture may provide the best headwall possible.

     8-44. When headwalls are not used on the downstream end, the culvert should project beyond the toe of the
     fill by at least 2 feet. Use riprap to protect the projecting area culvert riprap. (See figure 8-13, page 8-16.)

Erosion Control

     8-45. Culverts discharging into open channels should have antiscour protection to prevent erosion. Two types
     of channel instability can develop downstream from culvert and storm-drain outlets. These conditions are
     gully scour and scour hole. (See figure 8-14, page 8-17.) Predict the type of scour for a given field situation
     by comparing the original or existing channel slope or drainage basin downstream of the outlet to what is
     required for stability.

     8-46. Gully scour is expected when channel flow exceeds what is required for stability. It begins downstream
     where the channel is stable and progresses upstream. (See the top portion of figure 8-14.) If sufficient
     differential in elevation exists between the outlet and the stable channel, the outlet structure will be
     completely undermined. Erosion of this type may be considerable, depending on the location of the stable
     channel section relative to the outlet in the vertical and downstream directions.

     8-47. A scour hole or localized erosion is expected if the downstream channel is stable. (See the bottom
     portion of figure 8-14.) The severity of damage anticipated depends on existing conditions or those created
     at the outlet. Sometimes the extent of the scour hole may be insufficient to produce instability of the
     embankment or structural damage to the outlet. However, flow conditions can produce scour that erodes the
     embankment and causes structural damage to the apron, end wall, and culvert. (See figure 8-15, page 8-17.)

                                                                  Culvert Design

                  Figure 8-14. Types of scour at culvert outlets

                                                 Figure 8-15. Outlet erosion

     8-48. Erosion is best controlled by two methods: velocity reduction and channel protection. Reducing the
     slope of the culvert reduces the velocity. This solution may require a larger pipe since it changes the capacity
     of the culvert.

     8-49. Headwalls, wing walls, or channel linings can absorb the energy of flowing water and reduce its
     velocity to acceptable levels. When wing walls are not provided, line the stream bank and bottom for some
     distance downstream with riprap or other material. Ditch linings were discussed in chapter 7.

CULVERT DESIGN

     8-50. The hydraulic load on a culvert is the amount of water that will flow to the culvert inlet, as direct-
     surface or channel-stream flow. Surface flow is determined by the rational method and the channel-flow
     method that was discussed earlier.

Hydraulics of Culverts

     8-51. Culvert quantity of flow is the amount of water the culvert will carry in a unit of time. This capacity is
     expressed in cubic feet per second. For a particular culvert of known size, shape, and interior roughness, the
     discharge capacity is controlled by one or more of the following factors:

              Height of the water above the culvert inlet.
              Hydraulic gradient of the culvert.
              Length of the culvert.
              Elevation of the tailwater at the culvert outlet.

     8-52. The type of inlet is generally not considered in military culvert design. However, it should be
     remembered that the discharge capacity of a culvert would be increased by a smooth, transition type of inlet

29 February 2016  TM 3-34.48-1                                    8-17


---

     with headwalls and wing walls. For construction in the JOA, the culvert should have a design capacity
     sufficient to pass the peak runoff from the design storm.

     8-53. The hydraulic gradient of a culvert is one of the culvert discharge capacity controls. It can be
     satisfactorily estimated as the slope in feet per foot. The gradient is calculated by dividing the head on a
     culvert by the culvert length. (See figure 8-16.) The head is the difference in elevation between the—

              Ends of a culvert if the inlet and the outlet are not submerged.
              Water surface directly above the inlet and the top of the outlet if the inlet is submerged and the

                  outlet is not submerged.
              Water surface directly above the inlet and the outlet if the inlet and outlet are submerged.

Critical Slope

     8-57. For a given culvert size and head, the discharge capacity of the culvert will increase as the hydraulic
     gradient increases. This continues until the hydraulic gradient becomes equal to or greater than the critical
     slope. As the hydraulic gradient is increased beyond the critical slope, culvert discharge remains constant.

Box-Culvert Flow Design

     8-60. Flow characteristics of box culverts may be different from pipe culverts, even those with the same
     slope, lining, and inlet and outlet conditions. Flow quantity can be determined as previously noted for the
     conditions of inlet and outlet water elevations.

     8-61. Assuming that the water elevation of the inlet is at the top of the box and the outlet is free flowing, the
     difference in inflow characteristics between pipe and box culverts of the same material and slope is negligible.
     Computing the cross-sectional area required for a pipe and designing a box of the same material, slope, and
     cross-sectional area can determine box-culvert sizes.

     8-62. When the water elevation is above the top of the box inlet, use the nomograph in figure 8-17. In this
     case, make trial solutions until there is correlation between the box size and ponding depth.

Submerged-Inlet Pipe Culvert Design

8-63. Submerging the culvert inlet results in ponding. The elevation of the pond surface—which determines
the depth of submergence—is a function of the extent of the pond, the structure safety requirement, and the
time it takes to empty the pond. The runoff rate, the pond volume, and the culvert-flow rate determine these
factors. This is derived using the following steps:

 Step 1. Determine the rate of runoff (quantity) the culvert must drain or, in the case of ponding,
     the inlet drain capacity.

 Step 2. Determine the length of the culvert.

 Step 3. Determine the head on the culvert.

        Step 4. Determine the size and type of pipe or box culvert required to handle the quantity of flow.
        (See figure 8-16, page 8-18.) To use table 8-7 enter the nomograph at the intersection of the length
        for the type and size of culvert (for example, Point A in the nomograph). (See figure 8-17.) Extend
        the line horizontally to the turning-point line (Point B in the nomograph), and extend the line to
        the culvert head in feet (Point C in the nomograph). Find the discharge quantity in cubic feet per
        second for the pipe selected at the intersection with the discharge line.

 Step 5. Compute the discharge velocity in feet per second. Use the following equation:

Unsubmerged-Inlet Pipe Culvert Design

     8-64. The steps to be applied to the design of these culverts are determined as follows:
              Step 1. Determine the rate of runoff. Use the area that the culvert must drain. This will be the
                  required capacity of the culvert.
              Step 2. Determine culvert use (road or airfield).
              Step 3. Calculate the critical dimensions from the cross sections. (See figure 8-18.) Determine
                  the length in place and the fill critical.
              Step 4. Determine the largest pipe for the fill. Begin from the cross section at the outside edge of
                  the shoulder. Consider available pipes and adequate cover. The maximum culvert diameter is equal
                  to two-thirds of the minimum fill for roadway loadings. (See figure 8-18.) The cover required for
                  culvert protection is equal to one-half the diameter of the culvert or 12 inches (whichever is
                  greater). (See table 8-2, page 8-9, for runways and taxiways sustaining aircraft wheel loads, and
                  see table 8-3, page 8-10, or table 8-4, page 8-11, for wheel loads and minimum cover required.)
              Step 5. Determine the culvert capacity and outlet velocity. Use values based on culvert material
                  and slope. (See table 8-7, page 8-19.)
              Step 6. Determine the number of culvert pipes required. Divide the area runoff by the pipe
                  capacity. Round up to the next whole number.
              Step 7. Determine the order length. The order length is calculated by multiplying the number of
                  pipes times the length in place times a waste factor of 1.15. (See Step 3 for the length in place and
                  Step 6 for the number of pipes.)
              Step 8. Determine the maximum permissible discharge velocity. Calculate the maximum velocity
                  that the culvert outlet will discharge into the channel lining using table 7-3, page 7-7. Determine
                  the correct pipe to use. Apply the following criteria to calculations:
                   Ensure that the outlet velocity is equal to or less than the maximum velocity of the discharge.
                        If the outlet velocity exceeds the soils, the outlet must be protected against erosion.
                   Use the least number of culvert pipes possible to carry the flow and still be consistent with
                        the above criteria.

PONDING AREAS

     8-65. Ponding is the accumulation of runoff at the inlet of a drainage structure resulting from the inability of
     the system to discharge more of the runoff than the rated capacity of the structure. Military drainage structures
     in the JOA are designed to discharge the runoff based on the two-year design storm that, by definition, is
     expected to be equaled or exceeded at least once in the design period. Thus, a storm more severe than the
     design storm may occur and generate excessive runoff, overloading the drainage structures. In anticipation
     of this event, areas around drainage structure inlets are designed to accommodate a certain amount of
     ponding.

     8-66. In some cases, a system may not be able to take care of the runoff from the design storm due to
     limitations in culvert cover and space, terrain conditions, time, materials, or other conditions. To provide for
     this, include sufficient ponding areas in the original plan to prevent flooding of vital areas. The ponding areas
     store excess runoff until the intensity of the storm decreases and the structure can handle the flow.

     8-67. When possible, military drainage systems are designed to pass the runoff from the design storm without
     ponding. However, some provision for ponding may be made in areas where flooding for a period of time
     will not affect the facility operational status.

     8-68. The following specifications are generally adhered to in ponding area design for military installations:
              The edge of the pond must be at least 75 feet from the edge of the pavement when used for runway
                  and taxiway design.
              The depth of the pond will be determined by the porosity of the fill, the amount of freeboard
                  required to prevent overtopping of the road, the height of the headwall and wing wall, and the time
                  allowed for the pond to empty when a pond is used with road fills or embankments. When ponding
                  is anticipated, the adjacent fill side slope should be made less steep to prevent the sloughing of
                  saturated fill.
              The pond must be drained before damaging infiltration of the subgrade can occur. The actual time
                  during which ponding is allowable will depend on the soil type and soil condition in the ponding
                  area and the embankment. In general, this period will be no more than four hours from the start of
                  the storm.

     8-69. In designing ponding areas, the following assumptions are made to simplify the calculations and to
     retain satisfactory accuracy:

              A culvert discharges its design capacity before runoff starts to accumulate at the inlet and form a
                  pond.

              An increase in the head due to ponding does not increase the discharge capacity of the culvert.

     8-70. The determination of permissible volume, the preparation of runoff curves, and the soil analysis must
     be done before designing ponding areas to meet the above specifications and assumptions.

RUNOFF CURVES

     8-74. To determine the amount of water that an area will contribute to a pond, a cumulative runoff curve
     must be plotted. For example, an area has 33.3 acres, consisting of 23.3 acres of impervious soil and 10 acres
     of paved surface. The weighted C value is 0.75, the TOC is 13 minutes, and the location intensity is 2.2
     inches per hour for a 1-hour storm with a two-year frequency. Prepare a cumulative runoff curve based on
     the data given. Ponding may be required to reduce the culvert size.

Tabulation of Data—Rational Method

     8-75. The data required to plot a cumulative runoff curve using the rational method is shown in
     table 8-9. Each column is prepared as follows:

              Column 1 is a tabulation of time in minutes. A similar combination of time increments can be used
                  if enough properly spaced points are obtained to plot a smooth curve. The cumulative runoff curve
                  is constructed by plotting time in minutes (column 1) against volume in cubic feet (column 6).

              Column 2 is the product of the runoff coefficient (as determined by using the rational method) and
                  the area in acres.

              Column 3 is the intensity in inches per hour for each one of the minute values of column 1. These
                  values are obtained from the standard intensity-duration curve number 2.2 in figure 6-4, page
                  6-10. The value of 2.2 is the location intensity, in inches per hour, of the 1-hour, two-year storm
                  as specified in the given conditions.

              Column 4 is the rate of runoff in cubic feet per second for the entire interval of time shown in
                  column 1. It is obtained by multiplying columns 2 and 3.

              Column 5 is the time in seconds given in column 1.
              Column 6 is the quantity of water supplied to the pond for the time given in column 1. For the first

                  five minutes of rainfall, the quantity of water entering the pond is given by—
                   Column 6 = (column 4) (column 5).
                   Column 6 = (163) (300) = 48,900 cubic feet.

ANALYSIS FOR PONDING

     8-79. The safe volume for ponding is 100,000 cubic feet with a 4-hour limit on ponding time. Reduce the
     flow past the outlet point by using a single culvert and allowing ponding at the inlet.

     8-80. A 30-inch CMP culvert (roughness coefficient = 0.024) on a 1.2-percent slope discharges 24 cubic feet
     per second. (See table 8-7, page 8-19.) Assuming that the pipe always discharges at the rated capacity, the
     cumulative discharge is a straight-line function for a time interval with a line passing through the origin.

     8-81. Continue the straight lines so that it intersects the cumulative runoff curve. At the point of intersection,
     the cumulative runoff will equal the cumulative amount of water passed by the culvert. From then on, there
     will be no ponding. Determine if the ponding area is large enough, based on how long the pond will exist
     behind the inlet. The greatest vertical distance between the cumulative runoff curve and the 30-inch
     cumulative discharge volume is line P. (See figure 8-23.) Line P represents the maximum volume of water
     ponded behind the 30-inch culvert.

     8-82. Measuring line P by the vertical scale indicates that the maximum ponding volume will be 115,000
     cubic feet. At 42 minutes, the cumulative supply curve shows that 175,000 cubic feet of water was supplied
     to the pond by the rainstorm. At the end of 42 minutes, the 30-inch culvert has theoretically discharged 60,000

                                                                                                                                  Culvert Design

     cubic feet. Therefore, the difference between the quantity supplied (175,000 cubic feet) and the quantity
     discharged (60,000 cubic feet) is 115,000 cubic feet, which must still be in the pond.

     8-83. Since the safe ponding volume is 100,000 cubic feet, a 30-inch CMP is unsatisfactory. Calculating for
     a 36-inch culvert, the pond volume will be 75,000 cubic feet with a pond time of 95 minutes. Since the safe
     ponding volume of 100,000 cubic feet and the 4-hour limit on the ponding time are not exceeded, the 36-inch
     culvert is satisfactory. In addition, the excess volume of 25,000 cubic feet will be available for storms that
     may exceed the design storm.

ADVANTAGES OF PONDING

     8-84. Although ponding is an added safeguard against the effects of storms more severe than the design
     storm, its primary use is as an economic measure. Ponding allows reductions in the culvert pipe size necessary
     to handle runoff. However, if additional pipe or other construction is required for ponding, check the
     additional cost against the savings in reduction of pipe size. Ponding appreciably reduces pipe sizes for areas
     that have a short TOC. For a longer TOC, ponding has little or no effect on pipe sizes. The area available for
     ponding often restricts the use of ponding as an economical option. This area should be sufficient to satisfy
     the requirements of the design storm. It should also have enough reserve capacity to take care of storms more
     intense than the design storm. Facilities for ponding should be coupled with initial grading operations, if
     possible, to secure the most efficient use of personnel and equipment.

DROP INLETS AND GRATINGS

     8-85. Drop inlets are vertical entrances to a culvert or a storm drain. They may be used to lower the elevation
     of the culvert inlet below ditch elevation. This is done when fill does not provide sufficient cover or when
     discharge velocity is erosive and can only be controlled by changing the slope. For storm drains (underground
     culverts or conduits designed to carry surface runoff), drop inlets are used to collect surface runoff from
     paved and turfed areas, street gutters, and ditches. (See figure 8-24, page 8-34.)

     8-86. A framework of bars, or a perforated plate called a grating, passes the storm runoff into a drop inlet.
     The grating serves as a filter and a cover for the inlet. Gratings are shown in figure 8-25, page 8-34.

CONSTRUCTION OF DROP INLETS AND GRATINGS

     8-87. Drop inlets should always be protected with grating. An expedient grating can easily be fabricated
     using reinforcement bars welded together. These gratings should be spaced to readily admit debris that will
     pass unobstructed through the culvert. A drop inlet may be constructed of concrete, brick, timber, or CMP
     sections. Inlet grating should be fabricated of steel bars, steel plate, cast iron, or reinforced concrete with
     adequate strength to withstand the anticipated load. The loads may range from the weight of debris collected
     over the grating to vehicle or aircraft wheel loads.

     8-91. A grating opening should be at least 18 inches long and placed parallel to the direction of flow. The

MAINTENANCE OF DROP INLETS AND GRATINGS

     8-92. Drop inlets and gratings require continuous maintenance because debris collects at the openings. A
     maintenance schedule must be established to check and clean debris from the inlets and gratings. If these
     openings are not kept clean, a pond could form at the inlet, resulting in damage to nearby structures. This
     damage consists of subgrade saturation by the pond or direct flooding of adjacent areas. Periodic maintenance
     of drop inlets should include removing the cover and inspecting and cleaning the chamber.
     8-93. Expedient drop inlets must be covered with bars. (See figure 8-26.) If the box is left open, it will fill
     with debris and make cleaning difficult, especially if a pond has developed.

SUBSURFACE DRAINAGE

     8-94. When surface failures prove that natural subsurface drainage is inadequate, it becomes necessary to
     determine if a subsurface drainage system is needed, and if so, what type to install.

8-36           TM 3-34.48-1                            29 February 2016

CRITERIA

     8-95. Generally, subsurface drainage may be divided into three classes. These classes are base drainage,
     subgrade drainage, and intercepting drainage.

Base Drainage

     8-96. Base drainage generally consists of subsurface drainpipes laid parallel and adjacent to pavement edges
     with pervious material joining the base and the drain. (See figure 8-26.) Base drainage is required where frost
     action occurs in the subgrade beneath the pavement and where ground water rises to the bottom of the base
     course through natural conditions or ponding of surface runoff. If pavement becomes temporarily inundated
     and there is little possibility that the water will drain from the base into the subgrade, base drainage is
     required. Table 8-11 establishes the criteria for this situation.

                                        Table 8-11. Base drainage criteria for K

                 Less than 8                                              1 x 10-5 fpm
                 From 8 to 25
                                                                          1 x 10-6 fpm
                    Over 25                                               1 x 10-7 fpm

Note. Capillary action is related inversely to permeability. A soil with K = 10-7 is more prone to capillary action than soil with
K = 10-8.

Legend:

fpm                            feet per minute

8-97. Base drainage is also required at the low point of longitudinal grades in excess of 2 percent where the
subgrade coefficient of permeability is less than 1 times 10-3 feet per minute. The coefficient of permeability,
a property of each soil type, is defined as the discharge velocity at a unit hydraulic gradient. The coefficient
of permeability is determined experimentally with a laboratory test or an actual field test of the soil involved.
The coefficient is expressed in units of velocity, such as feet per minute or centimeters per second. Base
drainage is required if the subgrade coefficient of permeability is smaller than the coefficient of permeability.

Subgrade Drainage

     8-98. Subgrade drainage is required for permanent construction when seasonal fluctuations of groundwater
     may be expected to rise to less than 1 foot below the bottom of the course. See figure 8-27, age 8-38, for

Intercepting Drainage

     8-99. Intercepting drainage is required when water seeping into a pervious layer will raise the groundwater
     locally to a depth of less than 1 foot below the bottom of the base course. This condition is often encountered
     in thin and pervious soil layers, in exposed rock cuts, or in seepage from springs. A typical intercepting
     drainage section is shown in figure 8-29, page 8-40.

TECHNIQUES

     8-100. Subsurface water can be controlled through a combination of techniques. The techniques and
     combinations depend on the conditions existing in the area to be drained. The techniques that follow should
     be considered when planning and designing subsurface drainage.

8-38           TM 3-34.48-1                                         29 February 2016


---

                                Culvert Design

                                     Figure 8-28. Types of subsurface drainage

Depth of Base Course

     8-101. The base course may be built up to a specified depth above the groundwater table. Generally, the
     finished grade must be at least 5 feet above the mean groundwater table level. This technique is feasible
     when—

              A gravity drainage system is impractical.
              The condition to be controlled is limited to a small area, such as a narrow swamp crossing.
              Adequate base-course material is available.

Deep Ditch

     8-102. Where ditches will not interfere with operations or become a hazard to traffic, deep V ditches with
     free outfall may be feasible. Easily built and readily enlarged, these ditches provide positive interception and
     drainage of subsurface water before it reaches the area to be protected. Erosion, maintenance, traffic, and
     right-of-way are factors to be considered before using this solution.

Natural Drainage Channels

     8-103. Where possible and practical, water in existing natural drainage channels should be lowered when
     corresponding effective lowering of the groundwater table will occur. This technique may be particularly
     effective in pervious soil.

Blind Drains

     8-104. French (or blind) drains are constructed by filling a ditch or trench with broken or crushed rock. The
     top surface of the rock may be left exposed so that the trench acts as a combination surface and subsurface
     drain, or the rock may be covered by a relatively impervious soil so that no surface water can penetrate. The
     latter is the general practice. French drains are not recommended for permanent construction because they
     tend to silt up over time. In JOA construction, these drains are often used as a substitute for perforated or
     open-joint pipe or on filter materials used with such piping.

Subsurface Pipe

     8-105. In cases where a V-type or other open-ditch type drainage system is not practical, construction of
     subsurface drainage may be necessary. Failure of the subsurface system stemming from improper control of
     the grade, bedding, pipe placement, placement of filter material, or other installation work gives no warning
     before failure. Such failure is extremely difficult to repair.

     8-106. The most common form of subsurface drainage is perforated pipe. Where the perforations do not
     extend completely around the circumference of the pipe, the pipe is generally laid with the holes down and
     the joints closed. Materials used in manufacturing this type of pipe are corrugated metal, cast iron, vitrified
     clay, nonreinforced concrete, bituminized fiber, and asbestos cement.

8-40                TM 3-34.48-1                                              29 February 2016


---

                                                                                                                                  Culvert Design

     8-107. Bell and spigot pipes can be laid with open joints. If the filter material has been properly designed,
     collars are not needed over the joints. This type of pipe is generally made of vitrified clay, nonreinforced
     concrete, or cast iron.

     8-108. Porous concrete pipe is laid with closed joints. It collects water by seepage through the wall of the
     pipe, and it should not be used where sulfated waters may cause disintegration of the concrete.

     8-109. Farm tile is laid with butt joints slightly separated to permit water collection through the joint.
     Because of its low resistance to high-impact loads, farm tile is not recommended for use on airfields.
     Materials commonly used in manufacturing farm tile are clay or concrete.

Combination Drainage System

     8-110. Combination drains, which attempt to handle both surface runoff and subsurface water in the same
     pipe system, are not recommended. Surface runoff often carries sediment and soil from the drained area into
     the system. This clogs the system and causes flow stoppage. For this reason, subsurface drainage systems
     using some form of piping are generally sealed so that surface runoff cannot enter. The only drainage system
     that will satisfactorily handle surface runoff and subsurface water is the open channel or ditch.

PIPE-LAYING CRITERIA

     8-111. There are essentially four different types of pipe available for subsurface drainage, as previously
     mentioned. They should be laid according to the following specifications:

              The minimum slope for a subdrainage pipe is a 0.15-foot drop in elevation per 100 feet of length.
                  The pipe elevation at a particular location is generally specified by the invert elevation in which
                  the invert is defined as the lowest point in the internal pipe cross section at the location.

              Manholes should be provided at intervals of not more than 1,000 feet with flushing risers between
                  manholes and at dead ends. (See figure 8-27, page 8-38.)

              The pipe should be at least 6 inches in diameter with 6-inch pipe used for drains. Long intercepting
                  lines or extremely severe groundwater conditions may require 8-inch or larger pipe.

              The center of subgrade drains should be located at least 1 foot below the bottom of the base course
                  and not less than 1 foot below the groundwater table. Normally, subgrade drains are required only
                  at the edges of pavement areas where the soil is pervious and drains well. However, local
                  groundwater conditions and base and subgrade soil characteristics may require closer spacing of
                  the drains. When the drain discharges into a culvert or a considerably larger pipe, it should
                  discharge above the water level into the larger pipe. When the drain discharges into a pipe of equal
                  or only slightly larger size, it is generally better to bring the drain in above the receiving drain and
                  make a vertical connection between the two. This prevents the water from backing up in the
                  drainage pipe since these pipes rarely flow full.

              When the impervious layer is at a reasonable depth, intercepting drains should be placed in the
                  impervious layer below the intercepted seepage stratum. The quantity of water collected by an
                  intercepting drain is difficult to determine, but 6-inch pipe is generally sufficient for lengths up to
                  1,000 feet.

VERTICAL WELLS

     8-112. Vertical wells are sometimes constructed to allow trapped subsurface water to pass through an
     impervious soil or rock layer to a lower, freely draining soil layer. If drainage is obstructed, additional wells
     are built or the pocket is drained with an easily maintained lateral subdrain system. Vertical wells are often
     used in northern latitudes where deep freezing is common. They permit fast runoff from melting snow to get
     through the frozen soil and reach a pervious stratum. Under such conditions, the bottoms of these wells are
     treated with calcium chloride or a layer of hay to prevent freezing.

FILTER MATERIAL

     8-113. A layer of filter material approximately 6 inches deep should be placed around subsurface piping
     systems. The selection of the proper filter material is very important since it determines, to a great extent, the

29 February 2016  TM 3-34.48-1  8-41


---

Chapter 8

     success or failure of the drainage system. The improper selection of filter material can cause the drainage
     system to become inoperative in one of the following ways:

              The pipe may become clogged through infiltration of small soil particles.
              Particles in the protected soil may move into or through the filters, causing instability of the

                  surface.
              Free groundwater may not be able to reach the pipe.

     8-114. Criteria have been developed, based on the mechanical-analysis soil curve, to prevent these failures.
     A great deal can be learned about gradation characteristics of a particular soil by observing the soil curves
     on the mechanical analysis chart. Well-graded soils generally have a smooth, grain-size curve with gradual
     changes of slope. Poorly graded, uniform soils generally have a very steep grain-size curve. Skip-graded soils
     have a grain-size curve with a characteristic hump in it. The filter material in skip-graded soil tends to
     segregate during placement. The grain-size curves in figure 8-30 show various gradation characteristics.

grain particles, especially during placement. For the same reason, skip-graded material should not be used.

Selecting Filter Materials

     8-124. Filter material should be selected with a view toward the simplest construction and the lowest cost.
     To further this end, try to use one layer. If several layers of filter material are required, one layer should be
     confined to the region around the pipe openings and another layer placed between it and the protected soil.
     (See figure 8-26.) In this case, the designer selects a filter material for use around the pipe according to the
     filter design formulas. The second filter material is then designed to protect both the inner filter material and
     the surrounding soils. In other words, the design of a multilayer filter for a subdrain system should proceed
     outward from the inside filter material to the subgrade soil being protected.

Geotextiles as a Filter

     8-125. Geotextile fabrics may be used in place of a graded granular filter. To use a geotextile as a filter, line
     the trench with a geotextile filter fabric following the recommendations of the fabric manufacturer. The filter
     fabric should be placed to separate the permeable backfill of the trench from the subgrade or subbase
     materials, but it must not impede the flow of water from the drainage layer to the drainpipe. The filter fabric
     must also protect from the infiltration of fines from surface layers. This is particularly important for drains
     placed outside the pavement area where surface water can enter the drain through a soil surface. The filter
     fabric for the trench will be a nonwoven needle punch fabric. (See table 8-14, page 8-46.)

INSTALLATION OF A SUBDRAINAGE SYSTEM

     8-126. The most efficient and practical type of subdrainage system is one that adequately performs the
     operations for which it was intended and is installed with the care and skill consistent with its purpose.
     Lowering the quality of construction or using a sketchy or inadequate subdrainage system can result in
     disastrous failures. Conversely, installing an elaborate system of underground piping when a simple V ditch
     would serve as well is inadvisable.

                                                 Chapter 9

 Surface Drainage Design in Arctic and Subarctic Regions

         This chapter discusses the problems involved in the design of drainage facilities in
         arctic and subarctic regions. While the design data presented has been developed
         primarily for Alaska, the methods used are generally applicable to other arctic and
         subarctic regions.

ARCTIC AND SUBARCTIC REGIONS

     9-1. Arctic is defined as the northern region. The mean temperature for the warmest month is 50 degrees
     Fahrenheit or less, and the mean annual temperature is below 32 degrees Fahrenheit. In general, the arctic
     coincides with the tundra region north of the limits of trees.

     9-2. Subarctic is defined as the region adjacent to the arctic. The mean temperature is 32 degrees Fahrenheit
     or below for the coldest month, 50 degrees Fahrenheit or above for the warmest month, and there are less
     than four months with a mean temperature above 50 degrees Fahrenheit. In general, the subarctic coincides
     with the circumpolar belt of dominant coniferous forests.

DESIGN CRITERIA FOR COLD CLIMATES

     9-3. In the following section, hydraulic and hydrologic design criteria specific to cold climates are presented
     and discussed.

RAINFALL

     9-4. A study of rainfall intensity-frequency data recorded at arctic stations indicates a considerable variance
     between the average intensity of rainfall for a period of one hour and the average precipitation rates of
     comparable frequency for less than one hour. This is evident when compared with similar rainfall in the
     continental United States. Even within the area of Alaska, there was a noticeable difference between the rains
     at Juneau and Fairbanks. The higher values for rainfall intensity were used to develop design intensity-
     duration (supply) curves. (See figure 9-1, page 9-2.) For design purposes, a minimum rainfall rate of 0.2
     inches per hour is recommended, even maps with an intensity-frequency design storm index. One-hour
     rainfall intensities having various average frequencies of occurrence in the arctic and subarctic regions of
     Alaska are shown on the maps in figure 9-2, page 9-2. This figure, on which rainfall depth curves are
     superimposed, is known as a design storm index. The curves are labeled by the one-hour amounts of rainfall
     that are represented; these, in turn, are coordinated with the intensity-duration or supply curves of figure
     8-2, page 8-4. Figure 9-1 and figure 9-2 provides sufficiently accurate rainfall intensities so that runoff
     computations for any duration may be readily determined.

     9-5. Present information is insufficient to establish quantitative conclusions of the effects of elevation and
     physiographic orientation for all locations. At the time a site is under investigation, it would be helpful to
     obtain a short record of rainfall at a minimum. Such a record may be compared with the concurrent portion
     of a nearby long record and proper frequency values assigned to events in the short record. For example, a
     temporary gauge might have a maximum hourly value of 0.60 inch one summer, and the same storm might
     produce the summer maximum hourly value of 0.40 at a nearby long-record station. Similar comparison of
     other storms for the brief parallel record might confirm the ratio of 6 to 4 as an expression of the difference
     in the orientation, exposure, and elevation of the two stations. This ratio could then be applied to the known
     two-year, 1-hour value of the long-record station to get the estimated two-year, 1-hour value for the short-
     record station. If the long-record station has a two-year, 1-hour value for the construction site, it would be
     6/4 of 0.5 or 0.75. Usually, arrangements can be made to borrow a rain gauge for temporary use from the
     meteorological agency in the area in which the project is located.

INFILTRATION

     9-6. In permafrost areas, infiltration for design purposes should be considered zero. In other areas, a good
     guide may be obtained when test borings are made. Normally, values would not exceed about 0.5 inches per
     hour for coarse sands and gravels and would be as low as 0.1 inches per hour for clayey soils with low
     permeability.

STORM DRAIN DESIGN

     9-7. The type and capacity of the storm-drain facilities required are determined primarily by the promptness
     the design storm runoff must be removed to avoid serious interruption or hazard in the use of important
     operational areas and prevent serious damage to pavement subgrade. It is presumed that site reconnaissance
     phases have been carefully completed and that information that shows topography, natural drainage patterns,
     groundwater conditions, and seasonal frost and permafrost levels is available.

Basic Considerations

     9-8. Even though rainfall magnitudes are small in arctic and subarctic regions, drainage is an important
     factor in selecting an airfield site and planning for construction. The planner should be aware of several
     factors related to drainage to ensure a successful design. These factors include the following:

              Sites should be selected in areas where cuts or the placement of base-course fills will not intercept
                  or block obvious existing natural drainage ways.

              Areas with fine-textured, frost-susceptible soils should be avoided if possible. In arctic and
                  subarctic regions, most soils are of single-grain structure with a very small percentage of clay. As
                  a consequence, cohesive forces between grain particles are very small and the material erodes
                  easily. Frozen, fine-textured soil profiles may also contain large amounts of ice lenses and wedges.

              Design features of a drainage system may be similar to those used in frost regions of the United
                  States if the upper surface of the permafrost layer is deep and if provisions are made for lower
                  temperatures.

              The flow of water in a drainage channel has an accelerating effect on the thawing of frozen ground.
                  This may cause the surface of the permafrost to dip considerably beneath streams or channels that
                  convey water. Bank sloughing and significant changes in channel grades become prominent.
                  Sloughing is often manifested by wide cracks paralleling the ditches. For this reason, drainage
                  ditches should be located as far away from runway and road shoulders as possible.

              Freeing drainage channels of drifted snow becomes a significant task before breakup each spring
                  in many subarctic regions. In these areas, it is advantageous to have ditch shapes and slopes
                  sufficiently wide and flat to accommodate heavy snow-moving equipment. In locations where
                  flow continues year round, narrow, deep ditches are preferable to avoid icings.

29 February 2016  TM 3-34.48-1  9-3


---

Chapter 9

              Large, cut sections should be avoided when planning the drainage layout. Thawed zones or water-
                  bearing strata may be encountered and cause serious icings later. Vegetative cover in permafrost
                  areas should be preserved to the maximum degree practicable. Where disturbed, it should be
                  restored as soon as construction permits.

              Inlets to closed conduits are commonly sealed before freeze-up and opened before breakup each
                  spring.

              Fine-grained soils located immediately above a receding frost zone are very unstable.
                  Consequently, sliding and caving is to be expected on unprotected ditch side slopes.

              Ditches located over areas where permafrost lies on a steep slope should be avoided if possible.
                  Slides may occur because of thawing and consequent wetting of the soil at the interface between
                  frozen and unfrozen ground.

              Maintenance equipment for drainage facilities should include a heavy snow-removing apparatus
                  and a steam boiler with accessories for steam thawing of structures that have become clogged with
                  ice. Pipes for this purpose are often fastened inside the upper portions of culverts before their
                  placement.

Grading

     9-9. Proper grading is an important factor contributing to the success of a drainage system. The
     development of grading and drainage plans must be carefully coordinated. In arctic and subarctic regions, it
     is necessary to eliminate soft, soggy areas.

Temporary Storage

     9-10. Trunk drains and laterals should have sufficient capacity to accommodate the project design runoff.
     Do not consider supplementary ponding above the drain inlets in airfield drainage designs for the arctic and
     subarctic. Formulate plans in sufficient detail to avoid flooding, even during construction.

ICING

     9-11. An icing is an irregular sheet or field of ice with no uniformity as to its shape, thickness, or size. Icings
     are similar with regard to laminated structures, indicating that irrespective of shape, thickness, size, or cause,
     the actual process of formation is the same. Thin films of water traverse over layers of ice or other material
     and, when exposed to the cold air, freeze and form the first or an additional layer of ice. As water flow
     continues, the process is repeated, and an icing with horizontal laminations continues to grow until the water
     supply source is depleted or warmer weather begins.

Types

     9-12. For the purpose of analysis, icings may be divided into three groups, depending largely on the nature
     of the water supply source. River icing is when icing forms along rivers or streams and adjacent areas have
     a water source above or below the riverbed. Ground icing occurs when the source is from groundwater flow
     above permafrost. This term should not be confused with ground ice, which is often encountered in the arctic
     and subarctic as deposits in fine-grained soils. Spring icing occurs when the water source is from
     subpermafrost levels or subpermafrost water under hydrostatic pressure. Spring icings are commonly large
     and thick. Human activity can disturb the ground regime sufficiently enough to cause or accelerate the
     formation of icings.

River

     9-13. Most arctic and subarctic streams carry large loads of sediment that are not fed into the channels in
     uniform quantities. Consequently, the rivers are quite wide and relatively shallow. Many rivers have a braided
     pattern of several smaller streams within the confines of the main channels. These streams frequently shift in
     transverse position and often do so during one period of high flow. Winter flow is ordinarily very small and
     shallow. Freezing penetrates to the bottom of shallow streams quite readily, but the river discharge continues
     as groundwater flow beneath the riverbed. Because of the thermal effects of flowing water, the soil below
     streambeds is unfrozen to greater depths than soil located elsewhere. Consequently, there is a large space for

9-4  TM 3-34.48-1  29 February 2016


---

                                                                     Surface Drainage Design in Arctic and Subarctic Regions

     groundwater storage and flow above the permafrost and below riverbeds. The head motivating ground water
     flow is ordinarily quite large and can result in large pressures above sections where the groundwater flow is
     retarded.

     9-14. Groundwater-flow retardation is a natural process at many river sections because riverbeds are not
     homogeneous in water-carrying capacity. Freezing of the water reduces channel area and capacity in some
     sections more than in others. The formation of anchor ice on the bottom of the streambed results in further
     constriction of the channel cross-section area. The water then finds avenues of escape to the top of the ice
     through weak points, cracks, and fissures. Exposed to the cold atmosphere, the water quickly freezes into
     thin sheets. This action is progressive, and icing continues to increase in thickness until the supply of water
     is exhausted or finds a new outlet or until warmer weather begins. A bridge may shade the streambed and
     prevent the deposition of snow. Freezing would occur more rapidly beneath the bridge than upstream or
     downstream. Subsequent penetrations of frost would diminish groundwater-flow capacity at the bridge
     section and induce the formation of an icing above or at the site. These icings can be of various shapes and
     sizes, depending on the valley topography, the depth of the snow, the intensity of cold, the water supply, and
     other factors.

Ground

     9-15. Ground icings form mounds that have considerable thickness but cover a small area. They also form
     as crustations if groundwater flow is induced to the surface at points that are not of great lateral spacing but
     are of about equal elevation. In addition to a supply of water, there is another requisite to the formation of an
     icing—an area where the water can be exposed to the cold atmosphere. A pavement kept clear of snow offers
     an excellent site over which flowing water can spread out into a thin film and freeze. Icings from groundwater
     above the permafrost are not likely to occur in the arctic, as the permafrost there is too close to the surface to
     permit appreciable storage in the active layer. This occurrence is most severe in the southern zones of the
     subarctic and on slopes that face south. Groundwater flow may be induced to the surface in various ways. It
     is not essential that the seasonal frost reach the permafrost, although this very effectively blocks groundwater
     flow. Partial freezing of the active layer reduces the area through which ground water must pass. The path of
     least resistance may lead to the ground surface through a frost crack, fissure, or holes that have been
     previously made by burrowing animals. Water coming to the surface in this way may flow considerable
     distances down slopes beneath a snow blanket without freezing.

     9-16. Various methods have been tried to prevent the occurrence of such icings. Some of these have met
     with partial success. Russian investigators have advocated the Frost Belt or dam, but this method is effective
     for only a few years. The thawing in summer is accelerated at the site of the frost dam, and eventually the
     permafrost degrades sufficiently to permit groundwater flow below the frost dam. Fences and barriers have
     been used quite effectively under special circumstances.

Spring

     9-17. Icings that occur from artesian, subpermafrost water and springs are ordinarily quite thick and cover a
     considerable area. Reference is often made to the icing in the Momy River Valley of Siberia. The spring icing
     is about 15 miles long and 3 miles wide, with an average thickness of 12 feet. It does not melt and form each
     year. Spring icings can be easily controlled. The temperature of the water emerging from the ground is
     ordinarily quite high and the water does not freeze quickly if confined to a conduit. In some cases, an insulated
     conduit may be required to convey the spring water to locations where the formation of icing will do no
     damage.

Measures Against Icings

     9-18. In the case of river icings, depths to permafrost are ordinarily too large to be blocked effectively by
     accelerated freezing, such as induced by a frost belt or dam. In addition, the subbed river flow is often in
     excess of what can be stored as ice above the location of the bridge to be protected. The control of river icings
     then must be concerned with an insulation of streambeds at the critical section.

     9-19. Ground icings can be controlled to some extent by inducing the ice to form upstream from the site in
     question. This can be accomplished by the installation of frost belts. In open terrain, some success can be

29 February 2016  TM 3-34.48-1  9-5


---

Chapter 9

     achieved by keeping snow removed from a strip crossing the affected area in a direction transverse to
     groundwater flow. Groundwater flow will be blocked by freezing and forced to the surface upstream from
     the cleared area. The snow-free area provides a cold space where surface flow can spread out and freeze. If
     necessary, the depth of stored ice can be increased by erecting some barrier to the flow, such as an ordinary
     wooden-stave snow fence on top of the ice initially formed at the site of the frost belt. Because the process
     employs the removal of snow, it is essential to shift the position of the belt from year to year to not unduly
     influence the depth to permafrost. In timbered regions, it is obviously necessary to maintain the frost belt at
     one location to save the expense of tree removal.

     9-20. If the source of water forming the icing is a spring, then drainage or diversion is necessary to control
     the occurrence. This sometimes requires insulated channels. In the case of springs, flows are ordinarily too
     large to permit a storage of ice at or upstream from the site.
