                                                Chapter 10

                             Soils Trafficability

         Soils trafficability is the capacity of soils to support military vehicles. This chapter
         includes information on operating and maintaining the soil-trafficability test set,
         measuring trafficability with the results of the tests performed by the cone
         penetrometer and remolding equipment, and making trafficability estimates from
         terrain data (topography and soil data) and weather conditions. The procedures in this
         chapter are conservative estimates for field use. Engineers must be cautious as the
         calculated results can vary by 20 percent or more from changes in tire pressure and
         deflection. Plan for the unexpected. This chapter discusses the trafficability of fine-
         and coarse-grained soils; organic soils (muskeg) and snow are not discussed.

BASIC TRAFFICABILITY FACTORS

     10-1. Trafficability is more difficult to assess for fine-grained soils (silts and clays) and sands that contain
     enough fine-grained material to behave like fine-grained soils when wet than coarse-grained soils (clean
     sands). Relationships that describe the soil-vehicle interactions are based on soil shearing-resistance
     measurements made with the cone penetrometer and corrected for soil remolding effects under vehicle traffic
     determined by remolding test procedures.

     10-2. The information discussed in this chapter is limited to problems associated with soils. It does not
     include problems associated with natural or manmade obstacles (forests, ditches) or information on vehicle
     characteristics (such as the maximum tilt or side angle a vehicle can climb without power stall or
     overturning). The basic principles are sound for temperate and tropical climates and for soils that have been
     subjected to freeze-thaw cycles, if they are not frozen at the time of testing or passage of traffic.

     10-3. Originally, this chapter was designed to permit calculations of trafficability by field personnel with a
     hand-held calculator. Performances were estimated for a minimum number of vehicle passes (one pass) or a
     maximum of 50 vehicles in the same ruts (50 passes). Today most relations are used for one pass, and the
     combined effects on vehicle performance of terrain features (soil, vegetation, slope) are determined through
     the use of the computerized Army mobility prediction system contained in the North Atlantic Treaty
     Organization Reference Mobility Model (NRMM). The engineering relationships that produce vehicle speed
     predictions or GO/NO-GO performance based on measured terrain and vehicle characteristics are contained
     in the NRMM. This chapter introduces fundamental relationships, terminologies, and illustrations of this
     computerized, comprehensive mobility evaluation tool. Most military units now have access to NRMM
     relationships through personal computer-based systems that contain the comprehensive NRMM.

SOIL STRENGTH

     10-4. Bearing and traction capacities of soils are the most important soil strength factors effecting
     trafficability, and they are functions of soil shearing resistance. To evaluate the capacity of soils to support
     military vehicle traffic, shearing resistance is measured using a trafficability cone penetrometer. Cone
     penetrometer measurements are expressed in terms of cone index (CI).

29 February 2016  TM 3-34.48-1  10-1


---

Chapter 10

     10-5. Because the strength of fine-grained soils (silts and clays) may decrease when loaded or disturbed,
     remolding tests are used to characterize soil strength. Remolding tests measure the potential for a loss of soil
     strength to occur with vehicle traffic. The results of remolding tests are expressed in terms of the remolding
     index (RI).

     10-6. The soil CI multiplied by the RI produces the rating cone index (RCI) used to denote soil strength
     corrected for remolding effects. The RCI is the principle measure of soil strength used to quantify the
     trafficability of soils.

SLIPPERINESS

     10-7. The effects of soil slipperiness on vehicle performance can be drastic. Excess water or a layer of soft,
     plastic soil (especially clay soil) overlying a firm layer of soil can produce a slippery surface. This is
     especially evident on relatively firm soils after significant rainfall events. Slipperiness is troublesome, even
     when associated with soils that have very high bearing capacities.

     10-8. Slippery soil conditions can cause extreme steering difficulty and degraded traction, especially for
     rubber-tired vehicles. Immobilization can occur when slipperiness is associated with low bearing capacity.
     The adverse effects of slipperiness are more severe on slopes. Sometimes slopes with adequate soil strength
     will not be passable because of slipperiness. Chains on rubber-tired vehicles or removal of rubber track pads
     will usually improve mobility in slippery conditions.

STICKINESS

     10-9. Soil stickiness may pose a problem for vehicles operating in wet soils of low bearing capacity.
     Stickiness occurs in fine-grained soils when they are wet. The greater the plasticity of the soil, the more
     severe the effects of stickiness.

     10-10. Under extreme conditions, sticky soil can accumulate in the vehicle running gear, making travel and
     steering difficult. Although it can adversely affect the speed and control of all vehicles, it usually will not
     cause immobilization except for the smallest tracked vehicles. The worst stickiness is just a nuisance to larger,
     more powerful military vehicles. Removing fenders will reduce stickiness effects on some vehicles.

INSTRUMENTS AND TESTS FOR TRAFFICABILITY

     10-11. This section contains general information regarding the instruments and tests used to measure soils
     trafficability. The specific instruments, operating instructions, and test procedures are described in more
     detail in TM 3-34.48-2. Sieve-analysis tests, plasticity tests, and other field identification tests are described
     in TM 3-34.43/MCRP 3-17-7H/NAVFAC MO 330/AFH 32-1034.

SOIL-TRAFFICABILITY TEST SET

     10-12. Trafficability measurements are made with the soil-trafficability test set. This set consists of one
     canvas carrying case; one cone penetrometer with a 3/8-inch steel shaft, a 5/8-inch aluminum penetrometer
     shaft, a 0.5-square-inch cone, and a 0.2-square-inch cone; one soil sampler; remolding equipment (includes
     a 2 1/2-pound drop hammer and a remolding cylinder with base and pin); and a bag of hand tools. (See
     figure 10-1 for the items shown in their proper locations in the carrying case.) The set is carried on the back.
     (See figure 10-2.) The complete set weighs 19 pounds.

CONE PENETROMETER

     10-13. The primary instrument of the soil-trafficability test set is the cone penetrometer. (See figure 10-3,
     figure 10-4, and figure 10-5.) It is used to determine the shearing strength of low-strength soils for
     trafficability purposes. It is functionally similar to the dynamic cone penetrometer (described in TM 3-34.48-
     2). They are used to measure the shear strength of soils, but the dynamic cone penetrometer is used to
     determine shear strength for relatively high-strength soils (such as subgrade and base course materials for
     roads and airfields) and is not suitable for trafficability measurements.

                                             Figure 10-3. Cone penetrometer

      Figure 10-4. Using a cone penetrometer in the upright position

10-4  TM 3-34.48-1                                                    29 February 2016


---

                                Soils Trafficability

                        Figure 10-5. Using a cone penetrometer in the prone position

     10-14. The cone penetrometer consists of a 30° cone, a 19-inch long penetrometer shaft, a proving ring with
     mounting blocks, a dial indicator, and a handle. When the cone is forced into the ground, the proving ring is
     deformed in proportion to the force applied. The amount of force required to move the cone slowly through
     a given plane per unit area of the base of the cone (0.5 or 0.2 square inch) is indicated on the dial indicator
     inside the proving ring. This force per unit base area is an index of the soils shearing resistance and is called
     the soil CI in that plane.

     10-15. The dial range is 0 to 300 pounds per square inch. The range of loads applied to the cone
     penetrometer for 0 to 300 pounds per square inch on the 0.5 square-inch cone is 0 to 150 pounds. The 3/8-
     inch penetrometer shaft and the 0.5 square-inch cone are used for most measurement applications. The
     0.2-square-inch cone is used with the 3/8-inch penetrometer shaft for sampling in relatively hard soils and
     for remolding tests in remoldable sands. The cone penetrometer cannot be used to measure CI in gravels.
     However, gravels are considered excellent for 50 passes and problems can be determined by visual
     observation. As previously stated, the operating instructions and test procedures for the cone penetrometer
     and the remainder of the soil-trafficability test set are described in greater detail in TM 3-34.48-2.

SOIL MEASUREMENTS FOR TRAFFICABILITY

     10-16. When reconnaissance parties have time to make trafficability measurements, they should obtain data
     for determining the number and type of vehicles that can cross the area and the slopes that they can climb.
     The procedures for measuring soil trafficability data are described in this section.

             Note. The measurements will only be valid for short time periods provided no weather changes
             occur.

CRITICAL LAYER

     10-17. The critical layer is the layer of soil that contributes most significantly to the trafficability of the
     ground for a specific vehicle. The depth of the critical layer varies with the soil type, soil strength profile,
     vehicle type and weight, and number of passes required. Table 10-1, page 10-6, summarizes these variations
     for common types of military vehicles.

RANGE OF CONE INDEX VALUES

     10-18. A CI ranging between 10 and 300 in the critical layer is required to support most military vehicles.
     Except for a few vehicles, a CI below 10 is considered to be a nontrafficable area, and a CI above 300 is
     considered trafficable to most vehicles for 50 passes. These limits usually make it possible, while gathering
     data for a trafficability evaluation, to classify large areas as above or below the critical range without
     extensive testing.

NUMBER OF MEASUREMENTS

     10-19. The number of measurements taken is determined by the time available, the judgment of the range
     of soil strengths, and the general uniformity of the area. Trafficability-measuring instruments are designed
     for rapid observations. The average accuracy for a series of readings increases with the number taken.
     Variations in soft soils require that at least 15 readings be taken to establish a true average CI at a given
     depth. The 15 readings should be distributed throughout a uniform area.

     10-20. If time is not available to take a large number of measurements, use judgment to reduce the number
     according to the following instructions:

              If CI values are between 0 and 150, enough readings should be taken to assure accurate coverage
                  of the area. Readings should be made at enough locations to establish the area boundaries and the
                  average CI within close limits. Four to six sets of readings should be made at each location.
                  Remolding tests (in the case of fine-grained soil and remoldable sand) should be run at a sufficient
                  number of locations to establish the range of RI values. If a tentative route can be selected in the
                  field, penetrometer and remolding measurements should be made at closely spaced intervals to
                  locate any soft spots. Where CI values are less than 10, readings should be limited to the number
                  needed to establish the nontrafficable-area limits. No remolding tests are required.

              If the CI ranges from 150 to 200, select enough locations to verify the area limits. Three or four
                  sets of readings should be made at each location. For fine-grained soils and remoldable sands,
                  remolding tests should be made at the first two or three locations. For RI values of 0.90 or more,
                  additional remolding tests are not needed. If the RI is below 0.90, sufficient remolding tests should
                  be made to establish the range for the area. This can be established with tests at approximately six
                  locations.

              If the CI values are above 200, a few penetrometer readings will usually verify the extent of the
                  area. Two sets of profile readings taken at each location should be adequate. Remolding tests on
                  soil from the critical layer (fine-grained soils and remoldable sands) should be made at the first
                  two or three locations. If these show an RI of 0.80 or more, no additional remolding tests are
                  needed. Sufficient tests should be made to establish the range for the area if the RI is below 0.80.
                  This can be established with tests at approximately four locations.

10-21. Using the sample work sheet in figure 10-6, page 10-8, five tests down to 24 inches were completed
at a selected site. The corresponding penetrometer readings are listed in the blocks for the corresponding
depth and test. For example, in test number 1, the 0-inch reading is 58 and the 6-inch reading is 63. The
readings are then averaged for each depth, as demonstrated in the equation below for the 0-inch depth. The
numbers in the numerator are the readings from each test at that depth. The number in the denominator
represents the number of tests conducted. The resulting quotient is the average CI for that depth. See the
following equation:

𝐴𝐴𝐴𝐴𝐴𝐴𝐴𝐴𝐴𝐴𝐴𝐴𝐴𝐴 𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶 =  58 + 63 + 65 + 72 + 75
                       5 = 66.6 = 66 (round CI values down)

10-22. After calculating the average CI for each depth, the average CI for each 6-inch layer is calculated by
averaging the CI for the top and bottom depths of each layer. If the 0-inch CI is 66 and the 6-inch CI is 71,
the average CI for the 0- to 6-inch layer is 68. The CI is calculated for the 6- to 12-inch, 12- to 18-inch, and
18- to 24-inch layers the same way.

Note. Intermediate values for the 3-, 9-, and 15-inch depths (fine-grained soils and remoldable
sands) can be interpolated when the vehicle types under consideration require them.

10-23. The critical layer for the M929 dump truck for one vehicle and for 50 vehicles is the 9- to 15-inch
layer. Because the readings on the cone penetrometer are taken at the 0-, 6-, 12-, 18-, and 24-inch depths; the
3-, 9-, 15-, and 21-inch readings must be interpolated when necessary.

       Example. To find the average CI for the 3- to 9-inch layer, the average CI for the 0- to 6-inch and
       6- to 12-inch layers are interpolated as shown in the following equation:

                                68 + 73
                                     2 = 70.5 = 70 (always round CI values down)

       Likewise, for the 9- to 15-inch layer, the 6- to 12-inch and 12- to 18-inch layers are interpolated
       as follows:

                                                     73 + 76
                                                         2 = 74.5 = 74

       The resulting average CI for the 9- to 15-inch critical layer is 74.

STRENGTH PROFILE

     10-24. A soil profile is a group of soils with similar characteristics and arrangement of soil horizons in the
     soil profile. For most Army vehicles, in an area with a normal soil profile the critical layer is that between
     six and twelve inches.

Normal Strength Profile in Fine-Grained Soils and Remoldable Sands

     10-25. In a soil with a normal strength profile, the CI readings increase or remain essentially constant with
     each increment of depth. An area with a normal strength profile is shown in table 10-2, page 10-9. CI values
     should be measured at 6-inch increments down to 18 inches in the early stages of area reconnaissance. If
     these measurements consistently reveal that the profile is normal, only readings in the normal critical layer
     need to be recorded. For a tracked vehicle weighing less than 100,000 pounds, such as the M113A3 armored
     personnel carrier, only readings for the 6- and 12-inch depths must be recorded since the critical layer is the
     6- to 12-inch layer. (See table 10-1.)

     10-26. Since a decrease in RI with increasing depth is not common, remolding tests are taken from the
     normal critical layer for the vehicle in question for a normal strength profile. The resulting average RI value
     for the critical layer is multiplied by the average CI value for that layer to determine the average RCI value
     for the critical layer. The RCI for this layer is used as the criterion of trafficability for the particular vehicle.

Abnormal Strength Profile in Fine-Grained Soils and Remoldable Sands

     10-27. An abnormal strength profile has at least one CI reading that is lower than the reading immediately
     above it. An area with an abnormal strength profile is shown in table 10-2. When an abnormal strength profile
     exists, CI readings should be made and recorded at 6-inch increments from the top of the normal critical layer
     (6-inch depth for the M113A3 armored personnel carrier) to 6 inches below the bottom of the normal critical
     layer (18 inches for the M113A3 armored personnel carrier). (See table 10-1, page 10-6.)

     10-28. Similarly, remolding tests must be run on samples from the normal critical layer and from the 6-inch
     layer below it. The lower RCI is used as the trafficability measurement. Low-ground-pressure tracks are an
     exception to this rule. The 3- to 9-inch layer is used as the critical layer for these vehicles.

Chapter 10

Strength Profile in Coarse-Grained Soils

     10-29. The critical layer for most vehicles in coarse-grained soils is the 0- to 6-inch layer. (See table 10-1,
     page 10-6.) Most coarse-grained soils have a normal strength profile with a large increase in strength and
     depth when compared to fine-grained soils. For this reason, CI measurements should be taken at 3- to
     18-inch increments or until the maximum capacity (750 CI) of the penetrometer has been reached.

     10-30. Usually, fewer penetrations are required to establish an average because coarse-grained soil areas
     are generally more uniform than fine-grained soils and remoldable sands. The RI tests are not required.
     Example strength measurements in a coarse-grained soil area are shown in table 10-2, page 10-9.

RATING CONE INDEX

     10-31. As previously defined, the RCI is the CI that will result under traffic. This value can be compared to
     the vehicle cone index (VCI) to determine the trafficability of an area for a specific vehicle.

                                                  Example

 Fine-grained soil areas are investigated for vehicle trafficability with a normal critical layer of 6 to
 12 inches. Because area A has a normal strength profile, a remolding test was run for the 6- to
 12-inch layer. (See table 10-2.) The RCI for area A is 60 (the average of 50 and 70).

                                                          60 × 0.90 = 54
 In area B, an abnormal strength profile was evident. Therefore, remolding tests were necessary for
 both the 6- to 12-inch and 12- to 18-inch layers. In this area, the RCI of the 6- to 12-inch layer is 60
 (the average of 75 and 45).

                                                          60 × 0.90 = 54
 The RCI of the 12- to 18-inch layer is 40.

                                                          40 × 0.90 = 36
 Since the RCI of the 12- to 18-inch layer is less than the RCI for the 6- to 12-inch layer, an RCI of 36
 is the governing value for the trafficability of the vehicles in area B.

                                                  Example

 The critical layer for one or 50 M929 dump trucks is 9 to 15 inches. (See figure
 10-6, page 10-8.) Three remolding samples were collected from the 9- to 15-inch critical layer,
 yielding different RI results. The average of these three remolding results is calculated and this
 number becomes the RI for that layer.

              The RCI values in the critical layer for one vehicle pass (RCI1) and for 50 vehicle passes (RCI50)

     10-33. In other words, the VCI represents the minimum RCI soil strength that is required for a specific
     vehicle to make a specified number of passes through an area without becoming immobilized. The VCI
     concepts are explained in greater detail later in this chapter.

                                                                                                                             Soils Trafficability

     10-34. A mixture of vehicles will usually pass through an area, not a column of one vehicle type. Therefore,
     the VCI and the critical layer RCI values should be determined for the worst case vehicle (the one with the
     highest VCI).

VARIATION OF TRAFFICABILITY WITH WEATHER

     10-35. Changes in weather produce changes in soil trafficability. Trafficability characteristics measured on
     a given date cannot be applied later, unless full allowance is made for potential changes in the state of the
     soil caused by weather effects.

     10-36. Fine-grained soils increase in moisture during rainy periods. This results in slipperiness, stickiness,
     and decreased strength. Dry periods produce the opposite effects. Trafficability on loose sands improves
     during rainy periods due to an increase in cohesion, and sands return to the loose, less trafficable state during
     dry periods.

     10-37. Freezing and thawing conditions cause extreme variations in the trafficability of soils. Several inches
     of frozen soil may carry a large number of extremely heavy vehicles. However, when this same material is
     thawing, it may be impassable to most vehicles. Snow cover can have a significant effect on the depth of
     freezing. The absence of snow allows frost to penetrate deeper into the soil.

     10-38. Techniques have been developed for predicting the effects of weather on soil trafficability. These
     techniques are part of the comprehensive NRMM, but are beyond the scope of this manual.

OTHER TRAFFICABILITY EVALUATION FACTORS

     10-39. Other trafficability evaluation factors include slope, vegetation, and organic-soil areas. Refer to the
     NRMM for procedures beyond the scope of this manual.

     10-40. The steepest slope or ruling grade that must be negotiated should be determined by studying a
     contour map. For travel over slopes, the CI requirements must be increased above the requirements of level
     terrain.

     10-41. The specific effects of vegetation on trafficability are beyond the scope of this manual, but some
     points are worthy of mention. Dense grass, especially if wet, may produce slippery conditions. Additionally,
     soil strength requirements will be greater than normal if small trees or thick brush must be pushed down by
     the vehicle.

     10-42. Much of the terrain in northern latitudes is blanketed with a layer of organic material composed of
     roots, mosses, and other vegetation in various stages of decomposition. Limited testing with military vehicles
     reveals that low-ground-pressure tracked vehicles, such as the M973 small-unit support vehicle, can travel
     50 passes over organic materials that are more than 6 inches thick.

     10-43. Usually, high-ground-pressure vehicles can travel a few passes before they break through and
     become immobilized. Military wheeled vehicles usually cannot travel on most of these organic-soil areas. CI
     measurements denote the relative strength of organic soils. However, the soil-strength vehicle performance
     relations for organic soils are not as well defined as for fine-grained and coarse-grained soils.

     10-44. A complete assessment of the trafficability for a given area must include an evaluation of obstacles
     (such as forests, rivers, boulder fields, ditches, and hedgerows). Obstacle effects on the performance of
     vehicles can be determined using the comprehensive NRMM.

APPLICATION OF TRAFFICABILITY PROCEDURES IN FINE-
GRAINED SOILS AND REMOLDABLE SANDS

     10-45. The procedures presented earlier in this chapter are intended for use in tactical operations. Criteria
     is established so that when the RCI for a given area is equal to or greater than the VCI for one or 50 passes
     of a selected vehicle, sufficient soil strength will be available for the ground to withstand one or 50 passes of
     the same vehicle (or vehicles with lower VCI1 or VCI50) operating at a slow speed in the same ruts (in the
     case of multiple passes) and to permit stopping and resumption of movement, if necessary. The following
     text gives examples for application of trafficability performance criteria for both one and 50 vehicle passes.

Chapter 10

10-46. As previously described, vehicle performance can be significantly degraded when the soil is in a
slippery state (for example, a recent rainfall event on soil with high bearing capacity). Performance curves
that can be used for estimating vehicle performance on slippery soil conditions have been developed, but
using these curves involves complex computation procedures that are beyond the scope of this manual.

       Note. The trafficability techniques in the following text is applicable on slippery surface
       conditions, but the vehicle performance relations provided in this manual are only applicable to
       nonslippery soils.

VEHICLE CONE INDEX

     10-47. The following paragraphs provide information on VCI data, a means of calculating VCI for new or
     unlisted vehicles, and a means to approximate the VCI for less than 50 passes.

Vehicle Cone Index for Typical, Representative Vehicles

     10-48. TM 3-34.48-2 contains a representative listing of typical tracked and wheeled self-propelled military
     vehicles where each vehicle is identified by its standard nomenclature. The purpose of the listing is to provide
     the nominal gross vehicle weights and the associated VCI performance values for one (VCI1) and 50 (VCI50)
     vehicle passes. The listing is segregated based on the type of running gear (tracked or wheeled) and the
     intended vehicle mission. The listing includes other useful information, such as general vehicle
     characteristics that is required for estimating vehicle trafficability performance.

Vehicle Cone Index for New or Unlisted Vehicles

     10-49. For conventional-type vehicles not shown in TM 3-34.48-2, the following procedure can be used to
     calculate the VCI.

     10-50. Calculate VCI by using the NRMM and an axle-by-axle consideration of vehicle characteristics and
     their influence on performance. This is the most accurate method; however, the VCI can also be estimated
     by using assumed equal wheel or track load distributions and nominal highway tire pressures. The NRMM
     accounts for uneven load distributions and differences in tire pressures. The VCI for wheeled vehicles may
     vary over 20 percent due to tire pressure changes alone.

             Note. A reasonable estimate of the improved performance for wheeled vehicles that are equipped
             with central tire inflation systems can be determined by using the formulas below to estimate VCI
             and reduce those estimates by 15 percent to reflect that drivers of vehicles with central tire
             inflation systems will reduce the tire pressures as required.

Self-Propelled, Tracked Vehicles

Self-Propelled, Rear-Wheel-Drive Wheeled Vehicles

     10-53. For rear-wheel-drive vehicles where the first axle is a nondriven axle, a rough approximation for
     VCI can be estimated by using the all-wheel-drive formulas. Convert MI to VCI using figure 10-7, page
     10-13, or table 10-4 and multiply the resulting VCI by 1.4 to account for the effect of the nondriven front
     axle.

Self-Propelled, Half-Tracked Vehicles

    10-54. For half-tracked vehicles, a rough approximation for VCI can be estimated by using the all-wheel-
    drive formulas with the assumption that the vehicle has wheels instead of tracks on the rear end. The notional
    rear wheels are assumed to be the same size and have the same load as the front wheels. A grouser factor of
    1.1 is used to account for increased traction provided by the rear tracks. Use figure 10-7 or table 10-4 to
    convert MI to VCI.

Approximate Vehicle Cone Index for Passes Between One and Fifty

    10-55. To estimate the number of vehicles that can cross an area when the RCI is greater than VCI1, but
    less than VCI50, or to estimate the VCI for less than 50 vehicles, use the following formula:

    where—        (𝑉𝑉𝑉𝑉𝑉𝑉50 − 𝑉𝑉𝑉𝑉𝑉𝑉1) × 𝑛𝑛50 + 𝑉𝑉𝑉𝑉𝑉𝑉1 = 𝑉𝑉𝑉𝑉𝑉𝑉𝑛𝑛 (𝑟𝑟𝑟𝑟𝑟𝑟𝑟𝑟𝑟𝑟 𝑉𝑉𝑉𝑉𝑉𝑉 𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒 𝑢𝑢𝑢𝑢)
    n =     number of vehicles

        Note. VCIn provides a rough estimate for the required minimum RCI for 2 to 49 vehicles. This
        approach involves a linear interpolation simplification. The change in the required RCI soil
        strength is larger for the smaller number of vehicles than it is for the larger number of vehicles,
        but this approach is easier to estimate by hand and produces fair approximations in many cases.

                  Example

Estimate the number of M1A1 tanks that can cross a level area with fine-grained soil. (See TM
3-34.48-2.) Given—

CI  =             65 (critical layer)
                  0.80 (critical layer)
RI  =             58
                  25
VCI50 =
                                                𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅 = 65 × 0.80 = 52
VCI1 =                                     𝑉𝑉𝑉𝑉𝑉𝑉50 − 𝑉𝑉𝑉𝑉𝑉𝑉1 = 58 − 25 = 33

where—                                                  𝑛𝑛
                                                 33 × 50 + 25 = 𝑉𝑉𝑉𝑉𝑉𝑉𝑛𝑛
n   =
                  number of vehicles

To estimate the number of tanks that can cross the area, the number of vehicles is adjusted using
trial and error until VCIn is equal to the RCI or an increase in the number of vehicles will cause VCIn
to exceed the RCI.

If n = 40, then VCIn = 51.4; or if n = 41, then VCIn = 52.1

Since VCI estimates are rounded up, the maximum number of M1A1 tanks that can cross the area
is approximately 40 (a rough estimate).

PERFORMANCE OF VEHICLES ON LEVEL TERRAIN

     10-56. As previously described, a comparison of the RCI with the VCI indicates that a specific vehicle can
     negotiate a given soil condition for a specified number of passes. For example, if a soil has a CI of 120 and

29 February 2016  TM 3-34.48-1                                                                                  10-17


---

Chapter 10

    an RI of 0.60 in its critical layer, the soil strength may be expected to fall to 120 × 0.60, or an RCI of 72
    under traffic. Therefore, this soil is not trafficable for vehicles with a VCI greater than 72.

One-Pass Performance

     10-57. The ability of a vehicle to make one pass when operating at a slow speed in a straight line on level
     terrain is assured if the RCI of the area is greater than the VCI for one pass (VCI1).

                                                  Example

Estimate if an M1A1 tank can complete one pass on a level, fine-grained soil. (Use TM 3-34.48-2, to
determine VCI1.) Given—

CI     =    50 (critical layer)
            0.70 (critical layer)
RI     =    25

VCI1 =

                                   𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅 = 50 × 0.70 = 35

Because the RCI is greater than VCI1 (35 is greater than 25), the M1A1 tank can complete one pass.
Immobilization of a vehicle will likely occur the moment a vehicle enters an area where the RCI is
less than VCI1. Immobilization may occur even when the RCI is slightly greater than VCI1 if water on
the soil surface causes excessive sinkage or slipperiness.

Fifty-Pass Performance

    10-58. The ability of a given vehicle to make 50 passes when operating at a slow speed in a straight line
    through the same ruts (or 50 of the same vehicle type following in straight-line formation) on level terrain is
    assured if the RCI of the area is greater than the VCI for 50 passes (VCI50).

                                                 Example

Estimate if an M923 5-ton cargo truck can complete 50 passes on a level, fine-grained soil. (Use TM
3-34.48-2 to determine VCI50.) Given—

CI     =    80 (critical layer)
            0.82 (critical layer)
RI     =    68

VCI50 =

                        𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅 = 80 × 0.82 = 65.6 = 65 (𝑎𝑎𝑎𝑎𝑎𝑎𝑎𝑎𝑎𝑎𝑎𝑎 𝑟𝑟𝑟𝑟𝑟𝑟𝑟𝑟𝑟𝑟 𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅 𝑣𝑣𝑣𝑣𝑣𝑣𝑣𝑣𝑣𝑣𝑣𝑣 𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑)

Because the RCI is less than VCI50 (65 is less than 68), the M923 truck cannot complete 50 passes.
Immobilization of a vehicle will likely occur before 50 passes when the RCI is less than VCI50.
Immobilization may occur before 50 passes even when the RCI is slightly greater than VCI50 if water
on the soil surface causes excessive sinkage or slipperiness.

PERFORMANCE OF VEHICLES NEGOTIATING SLOPES

     10-59. The performance relations presented herein are applicable for self-propelled tracked and all-wheel-
     drive vehicles.

One-Pass Performance

     10-60. The maximum slope negotiable (expressed in percent grade) and the maximum towing force divided
     by the gross vehicle weight for a given RCI are essentially equal. Therefore, when the RCI is known, the
     maximum slope negotiable by a given vehicle for one pass in a straight line up a slope can be estimated from
     figure 10-8. The differences in the properties of various soils produce some differences in vehicle
     performance, so NRMM actually predicts performance in fine-grained soils based on the specific soil type.
     NRMM accounts for the effects of slipperiness on slopes, but those procedures are beyond the scope of this
     manual.

RCI               vehicle cone index

                                 𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑋𝑋 = 𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅 − 𝑉𝑉𝑉𝑉𝐼𝐼1 = 85 − 25 = 60

Fifty-Pass Performance

     10-61. The maximum slope negotiable (expressed in percent grade) and the maximum towing force divided
     by the gross vehicle weight for a given RCI are essentially equal. Therefore, when the RCI is known, the
     maximum slope negotiable by a specific vehicle for 50 passes (or 50 of the same vehicle type following in
     straight-line formation) can be estimated from figure 10-9. The differences in the properties of various soils
     produce some differences in vehicle performance. NRMM predicts performance in fine-grained soils based
     on the specific soil type. NRMM accounts for the effects of slipperiness on slopes, but those procedures are
     beyond the scope of this manual.

                                                  Example

Estimate the maximum slope that an M1A1 tank can climb for 50 passes where the slope consists
of fine-grained soil. Use TM 3-34.48-2 to determine VCI50. Given—

CI     =    100 (critical layer)
            0.85 (critical layer)
RI     =
                                         𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅 = 100 × 0.85 = 85
                                𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑋𝑋 = 𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅 − 𝑉𝑉𝑉𝑉𝑉𝑉50 = 85 − 58 = 27

Using figure 10-9 the maximum slope (RCIx = 27) is 50 percent. Therefore, the maximum slope the
M1A1 can negotiate for 50 passes under the given conditions is 50 percent.

PERFORMANCE OF VEHICLES TOWING OTHER VEHICLES ON LEVEL TERRAIN

     10-62. The performance relations presented are applicable for self-propelled tracked and all-wheel-drive
     vehicles. The required towing force in soft areas where vehicles are bogged down may equal or exceed the
     weight of the towed vehicle, especially if the towed vehicle has substantial hull or chassis dragging (or
     bulldozing). This may occur when the VCI of the towed vehicle is much higher than the towing vehicle.

One-Pass Performance

     10-63. When the RCI is equal to VCI1, the soil has just enough shear strength for a given vehicle to
     overcome its motion resistance for one pass. If the vehicle is required to tow another vehicle, additional shear

29 February 2016          TM 3-34.48-1                                                                               10-21


---

Chapter 10

    strength is required to produce the necessary thrust to overcome motion resistance (required towing force) of
    the towed vehicle. Thus—

                                                        𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅 − 𝑉𝑉𝑉𝑉𝑉𝑉1 = 𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑋𝑋

    10-64. The equation above provides a measure of the additional shear strength that is available for a vehicle
    to develop a towing force for one pass. Therefore, when the RCI and VCI1 are known, the ability of one
    vehicle to tow another for one pass can be determined.

    10-65. Two one-pass performance curves—one for self-propelled tracked vehicles and one for self-
    propelled wheeled vehicles—are shown in figure 10-8, page 10-19. The maximum towing force (expressed
    as a percentage of the vehicle gross weight) that can be developed by a vehicle on level terrain is related to
    RCIX. A performance curve for vehicles when towed for one pass on level terrain is shown in figure 10-10
    where the required towing force (expressed as a percentage of the vehicle gross weight) is related to RCIX.

PERFORMANCE OF VEHICLES TOWING TRAILERS ON LEVEL TERRAIN AND UP SLOPES

     10-72. The performance of vehicles towing trailers and of tractor-trailer combinations can be predicted
     using the comprehensive NRMM. However, these computations can be reliably made only through the
     integration of complex considerations requiring calculations on an axle-by-axle basis. Therefore, these
     computations are beyond the scope of this manual. Procedures used in the examples for vehicles towing other
     vehicles should not be extended for estimating a single VCI for vehicles towing trailers or for tractor-trailer
     combination vehicles.

OPERATION IN COARSE GRAINED SOILS

     10-73. Coarse-grained soils present trafficability problems different from those encountered in fine-grained
     soils. Some important differences are that—

              Coarse-grained soils do not respond to the remolding test (except for highly saturated sands).
              Wheeled-vehicle performance is affected more by tire-inflation pressure changes on coarse-

                  grained soils than on fine-grained soils.
              Level, coarse-grained soils seldom cause immobilization of tracked vehicles or all-wheel-drive

                  vehicles when operating at low tire-inflation pressures.
              The first pass over a coarse-grained soil area is the most critical, and subsequent passes are usually

                  assured if they are made in first-pass ruts.

     10-74. Coarse-grained soil in the dry state is easily recognizable. It is the round, granular material found on
     most beaches and in sand dunes. When wet, however, it may be confused with remoldable sand or even fine-
     grained soil. Because coarse-grained soils do not remold, there is no need to conduct the remolding test. Use
     RCI for fine-grained soils and CI for coarse-grained soils (assume that RI equals 1.0).

     10-75. Use the following procedures to ensure that the soil in question is coarse-grained. Push the
     penetrometer into the soil. If the color of the soil near the penetrometer immediately becomes lighter, the
     internal drainage is good, which signifies a coarse-grained soil. Another test is to confine a soil sample in the

10-28       TM 3-34.48-1                                                                   29 February 2016


---

                                                                                                                             Soils Trafficability

     remolding cylinder and attempt to penetrate it with the cone penetrometer. If the soil is coarse-grained, it will
     be difficult or impossible to penetrate.

     10-76. The presence of vegetation in coarse-grained-soil areas indicates that the soil is stabilized and is of
     high trafficability. This effect is reflected in high CI readings. Testing to date has not permitted the
     development of CI performance relations for tracked vehicles because tracked vehicles are able to travel on
     level, coarse-grained soils. Furthermore, the effects of soil strength on the performance of a given tracked
     vehicle in coarse-grained soils are minimal.

     10-77. One-pass performance of all-wheel-drive vehicles has been determined. In most cases, the first pass
     is the most critical, and subsequent passes are assured if the first pass is successful.

ALL-WHEEL-DRIVE VEHICLES ON LEVEL TERRAIN

     10-78. The ability of a given vehicle to travel one pass in a straight line over level terrain is generally
     assured if the CI of the area is greater than the VCI. The prediction of the performance of a wheeled vehicle
     in sands is a complex interplay among many vehicle characteristics, including tire size, tire pressure, number
     of tires, tire construction, vehicle characteristics, and the soil condition (soil strength and moisture content).
     Since most natural, sandy soils contain fine-grained materials that cause the soil to behave like a fine-grained
     soil, dry-to-moist, poorly-graded sands are evaluated using the coarse-grained vehicle performance
     relationships contained in the NRMM or other NRMM-based mobility models, such as the Condensed Army
     Mobility Model System.

     10-79. Other sandy soils with appreciable quantities of fine material are treated in the NRMM as fine-
     grained soils. The need to evaluate the interplay among terrain and vehicle characteristics requires that the
     coarse-grained soil predictive relationships be entered into the NRMM. Therefore, these relationships cannot
     be simplified to a point where they could be displayed as figures in this chapter. The relationships do follow
     the trends of the fine-grained relationships, and they compute a minimum soil strength requirement for traffic
     (VCI1), based on measured CI (RI is considered 1.0 for these soils). Speed predictions can then be made for
     these areas.

     10-80. In coarse-grained soils, the performance of wheeled vehicles is affected mostly by tire pressure. To
     optimize vehicle performance, tire pressures should be reduced to mud, sand, and snow pressures at a
     minimum or to the emergency tire pressures if speed is not a requirement. In this manner, vehicle ground
     pressure is decreased from on-road, and vehicle floatation and traction are maximized for the terrain
     conditions encountered.

TRACKED VEHICLES ON LEVEL TERRAIN

     10-81. As a general rule, tracked vehicles are able to travel on level, coarse-grained soils regardless of soil
     strength. Performance predictions in the NRMM are made for two categories of tracked vehicles: flexible
     tracks (found on most military vehicles) or girderized tracks (found on most bulldozer-type vehicles).
     Vehicles with girderized tracks generally produce higher tractive forces on SP soils than do flexible-tracked
     vehicles.

VEHICLE CONE INDEX CALCULATIONS

     10-82. Calculation of a coarse-grained VCI for a vehicle configuration is considered beyond the scope of
     this manual. These predictions are made using the comprehensive NRMM. In general, wheeled vehicles
     operating in sands should use the lowest tire pressures possible and all-wheel-drive for maximum off-road
     performance. Immobilization can easily occur in these soils, especially if the soils are dry and loose. Prepare
     for such emergencies. Tracked vehicles generally do not suffer immobilization on level SP soils.

Chapter 10

TRAFFICABILITY DATA

     10-83. The objective of mapping trafficability data is to provide commanding officers with an estimate of
     an area trafficability before operation. The estimate consists of placing symbols that describe the trafficability
     of a small area at strategic points on existing maps as shown in figure 10-12. The maps produced by the
     techniques described in the following paragraphs are elementary when compared with the complicated and
     comprehensive maps now in production for use with the NRMM.

ESTIMATING

     10-84. Trafficability can be estimated if weather conditions, soils, and area topography are generally
     known. Weather and climatic information are usually available, even for remote areas, from meteorological
     records, climatology textbooks, or interaction with the local population. Soils and topography data may be
     obtained from topographic, soils, and geologic maps; aerial photographs; or interaction with the local
     population.

     10-85. The accuracy of the trafficability estimate depends on the type, quantity, and accuracy of the
     available data. The analyst’s ability to interpret the data is also important, especially if soil types must be
     deduced from geological maps and air photographs.

Weather Conditions

     10-86. For estimating trafficability, consider the general weather conditions: the dry season and the wet
     season.

Dry Season

     10-87. A dry season is defined as a time when climatic and vegetation factors combine to produce low soil
     moistures. For temperate, humid climates (such as the United States east of the Mississippi River), the dry
     season is from about the first of May to the first of November. In this season, evaporation of water from the
     soil is high because of long days, high temperatures, and few clouds. Water is rapidly extracted from the soil
     and transpired into the atmosphere by growing plants. A dry season may also occur at other times of the year
     as a result of long periods of fair weather. Arid climates may be considered to be constantly in a dry season.

     10-88. During the dry season, fine-grained soils and remoldable sands are usually trafficable and, in general,
     are of higher trafficability than dry, coarse-grained soils. The trafficability of dry, coarse-grained soils is
     poorer than that of wet, coarse-grained soils except quicksand. Even in the dry season, a high water table that
     results from underground springs, low-lying and poorly drained soils, or other causes effects trafficability of
     soil types.

Wet Season

     10-89. A wet season is defined as a time when weather conditions combine to produce high soil moistures.
     In temperate, humid climates, the wet season extends from about the first of November to the first of May.
     During the wet season, frequent rains, low temperatures, heavy cloud cover, and the absence of growing
     plants keep soil moisture near a maximum value. Melting snow and ice may produce wet soil conditions.
     Wet seasons may occur at any time as a result of prolonged rains, floods, or irrigation. Adding moisture to
     soil affects the strength of that soil; the effect differs with soil types.

Topography and Classification of Soils

     10-90. The configurations of the soil surface and soil types in a given area are determined from aerial
     photographs, geologic maps, soil maps, and topographic maps.

Aerial Photographs

     10-91. Elevations and slopes can be estimated by personnel who are properly instructed to read (with the
     aid of stereo pairs) and interpret information in aerial photographs. Accurate elevations and slopes can be
     obtained with mechanical equipment by operators trained to use the equipment. Locations for rivers, forests,
     escarpments, and embankments can also be obtained from aerial photographs.

     10-92. The techniques for identifying soils from aerial photographs are so complex that only well-trained
     personnel can fully use aerial photographs for this purpose. However, personnel with minimal training can
     obtain general information. For example, orchards are usually planted in well-drained, sandy soils; vertical
     cuts are evidence of deep loessial (silty) soils; and tile drains in agricultural areas indicate the presence of
     poorly drained soils (silts and clays).

     10-93. In a photograph, light color tones generally indicate higher elevations, sandier soils, and lower soil
     moisture than those signified by dark color tones. However, the same color tone may not signify the same
     conditions in the same photograph and may signify an entirely different condition in another aerial
     photograph. In addition, natural soil tones may be obscured and modified by tones created by vegetation
     (natural and cultivated), plowed fields, and cloud shadows.

Geologic Maps

     10-94. Geologic maps show parent material and age data. With that information and a general knowledge
     of climate, topography, and vegetation, trained analysts can estimate the soil types likely to be found in the
     area.

Soils Maps

     10-95. Trafficability can be estimated rapidly from maps that delineate surface soils according to the USCS,
     although these maps are scarce. The more common types of soils maps are those using an agricultural system
     of soil classification. Information from agricultural maps must be translated into engineering terms before a
     trafficability estimate can be made. No exact method exists for doing this, but analysts familiar with the
     classification systems can usually make good translations. For example, the term loam in the agricultural
     classification system usually includes CL and ML soils in the USCS.

Topographic Maps

     10-96. Physical features (rivers, streams, cultivation, forests, roads) can usually be identified from a
     topographic map. Surface slope estimates can be made from the contour lines (lines passing through points
     of equal elevation).

     10-97. For trafficability classification purposes, topography has been divided into two classes: low
     topography and high topography. Low-topography areas are those at comparatively low elevations with
     respect to the surrounding terrain, and high-topography areas are those at comparatively high elevations.
     Absolute elevation has no significance in identifying the topography class. Low-topography areas are usually
     poorly drained and have water tables occurring within 4 feet of the surface at some time during the year.
     High-topography areas are usually medium-well to well-drained and do not have water tables within 4 feet
     of the surface during the year.

MANUALLY MAPPING SOIL CONDITIONS AND TRAFFICABILITY

     10-98. Although mapping soil conditions and trafficability through manual means is rarely done since the
     development of computerized mobility models, it is important that the procedure be available should the need
     arise. The following paragraphs describe the proper procedure in detail.

     10-99. VCI values vary widely, and it is desirable to present basic terrain data that can be compared directly
     with those values. The four basic terms that describe trafficability are: soil type, RCI, slope, and slipperiness.
     Stickiness effects are not considered significant enough to include on maps.

     10-100. The soil-type condition is shown as A, B, C, or D (defined in table 10-5). The RCI is shown as a
     single number; the slope (in percent grade) is shown as a single number; and slipperiness is shown as N (not

10-32  TM 3-34.48-1  29 February 2016

slippery), P (slippery when wet), or S (slippery). The four factors may be presented in fractional form with
two items in the numerator and two in the denominator as shown in figure 10-12, page 10-31.

10-101. The presentation of trafficability data for strategic purposes is most effective when one vehicle is
used as a standard reference vehicle. For example, if the vehicle selected has a VCI of 49 and the information
on that specific vehicle is presented, trafficability data for that vehicle can be generalized and considered
applicable to vehicles with a VCI of 49 or less. The following are the recommended techniques of mapping
trafficability:

        The base of the map should be a standard topographic map printed in a gray monochrome with
             streams in a strong blue color.

        The four soil-slope combinations should be shown as trafficability symbols, as indicated in table
             10-5. See previous weather conditions.

        Obstacles should be indicated by added numbers in red and circled in red.

        Forests should be indicated by appropriate open-type patterns in strong green.

        The reverse of the trafficability map should contain an inset map of the principle physiographic
             provinces, landforms, geologic areas, and related data used in making the analysis. The inset map
             should show in detail important data on soils, topography, and obstacles that cannot readily be
             shown on the face of the map.

SOIL-TRAFFICABILITY CLASSIFICATION

     10-102. Soil classification of a specific area can be accomplished rapidly for seasonal (high-moisture)
     conditions when the soil has been classified in terms of the USCS, the topography (high or low) has been
     identified, and the VCI for the critical vehicles has been determined using TM 3-34.48-2 or computed, when
     necessary, as previously described.

FINE-GRAINED SOILS

     10-103. The trafficability classification of fine-grained soils is shown in figure 10-13, page 10-36. The
     interpretation of the example shown in the Low Topography, High Moisture Condition graph in the table for
     a level area of MH soil is as follows:

              Vehicles with a VCI50 or VCI1 equal to or greater than 84 will have a less than 50 percent
                  probability of traversing the area.

              Vehicles with a VCI50 or VCI1 equal to or greater than 56, but less than 84, will have a probability
                  equal to or greater than 50 percent, but less than 75 percent, of traversing the area.

              Vehicles with a VCI50 or VCI1 equal to or greater than 18, but less than 56, will have a probability
                  equal to or greater than 75 percent, but less than 90 percent, of traversing the area.

              Vehicles with a VCI50 or VCI1 less than 18 will have a probability equal to or greater than
                  90 percent, but no more than 100 percent, of traversing the area.

COARSE-GRAINED SOILS

     10-104. The trafficability classification of coarse-grained soils can be obtained from figure 10-14, page
     10-37. The classification interpretation is the same as for the trafficability of fine-grained soils from figure
     10-13. To use figure 10-14, identify only the coarse-grained soils (location and origin) and determine the
     VCI values (must use NRMM or other similar mobility models). Figure 10-14 applies to wheeled vehicles.
     The effect of the strength of coarse-grained soils on tracked-vehicle performance is negligible.

                                                Chapter 11

      Maintenance, Repair, and Rehabilitation of Roads,
                          Airfields, and Heliports

         Maintenance is the routine prevention and correction of normal operational damage
         and general deterioration. It is needed to keep road and airfield surfaces and facilities
         in usable condition. Repair is the work necessary to correct damage caused by
         abnormal use, accidents, hostile forces, and severe weather. Repair includes the
         resurfacing of a road or runway when maintenance can no longer accomplish its
         purpose. Based on this manual, rehabilitation is the restoration of captured airfields
         and heliports to usable condition. Rehabilitation resembles war-damage repair except
         that it is accomplished before occupancy

MAINTENANCE AND REPAIR CONSIDERATIONS

     11-1. The purpose of maintenance and repair activities is to keep roads, airfields, and other installation
     surfaces in as usable and as safe a condition as the situation permits. Prompt and adequate maintenance is
     important. Once surface deterioration or destruction has started, it can proceed very rapidly. Postponing
     minor maintenance jobs can result in the development of major repair jobs involving the subgrade, base
     course, and surface.

     11-2. Use the following guidelines when performing maintenance and repair work:
              Ensure that maintenance and repair activities interfere as little as possible with the normal flow of
                  traffic. When feasible, plan and perform maintenance and repair activities to permit at least partial
                  use of the facility. When it is necessary to close the facility to traffic, select alternative facilities
                  or perform repair work at night or during periods of reduced activity. Reopen the facility as soon
                  as practical.
              Remedy the cause before repairing the problem. For example, surface repairs made on a defective
                  subgrade are wasted. Maintenance and repair jobs should include an investigation to find the cause
                  of the damage or deterioration. To ignore the cause invites the reappearance of the damage. Ignore
                  the cause only when making temporary repairs to meet immediate, minimum needs under combat
                  or other urgent conditions.
              Maintain and repair existing surfaces as closely as possible to the original construction in strength,
                  appearance, and texture. Spot strengthening may create differences in wear and traffic impact that
                  can harm adjoining surfaces. Also, uniformity simplifies maintenance and repair operations.
              Prioritize the needed repairs based on tactical requirements, traffic volume, and the hazards that
                  result from complete failure of the facility. For example, roads used for tactical operations support
                  take priority over less essential facilities. One pothole in a heavily used road that is in otherwise
                  excellent condition takes priority over repairs to less heavily used roads in poor condition.

29 February 2016  TM 3-34.48-1  11-1


---

Chapter 11

MAINTENANCE AND REPAIR OPERATIONS

     11-3. Maintenance and repair operations include many tasks besides improving the pavement condition. To
     ensure a comprehensive maintenance and repair operation, incorporate the following tasks:

              Perform routine inspections.
              Stockpile material.
              Perform maintenance and repair of related drainage systems.
              Perform maintenance and repair of the pavement, to include dust and mud control and snow and

                  ice removal.
              Perform miscellaneous tasks, to include maintenance and repair of necessary buildings, structures,

                  and utilities and the operation of necessary utilities.

MAINTENANCE INSPECTIONS

     11-4. The purpose of maintenance inspections is to detect early evidence of defects before actual failure
     occurs. Frequent inspections and effective follow-up procedures prevent minor defects from becoming major
     repair jobs. Inspect surface and drainage systems carefully during rainy seasons, during spring thaws, and
     after heavy storms.

Surface Inspection

     11-5. Surface defects can usually be attributed to excessive loads, inferior surfacing material, poor subgrade
     or base conditions, inadequate drainage, or a combination of these conditions. Surface inspections should
     include a complete inventory of the current pavement defects. Careful investigation of the causes of the
     defects will allow for timely maintenance to prevent the pavement defects from requiring repair. Surface
     defects can be evaluated using UFC 3-270-05 and UFC 3-270-06 for airfield pavements and UFC 3-270-08
     for roads and streets.

Drainage Inspection

     11-6. Ensure that drainage channels and structures are unobstructed. Check culverts and drainage lines for
     structural damage. Inspect check dams for debris and excessive erosion. Investigate water ponding on or
     adjacent to surfaced areas. Inspect the system drainage during or after every storm. Also, thoroughly inspect
     the system in late fall to prepare for winter and in early spring to ensure minimum spring breakup difficulties.
     Inspect subsurface drains at least twice a year.

MATERIALS FOR MAINTENANCE

     11-7. Generally, materials required in the maintenance and repair of roads and airfields are the same as those
     used in new construction. Open pits and prepare stockpiles of sand and gravel; base material; and premixed,
     cold patching materials at convenient places and in sufficient quantities for emergency maintenance and
     repair. Arrange stockpiles for quick loading and transporting to the road or runway. Premixed, cold patching
     material may be prepared as explained in UFC 3-270-01. Maintain small quantities of aggregate in dry storage
     for concrete patching.

DRAINAGE MAINTENANCE

     11-8. Defective or inadequate drainage causes most pavement failures and deterioration. Ponding or delayed
     runoff of surface water allows seepage into the pavement structure unless the surface is tightly sealed.

Surface Drainage

     11-9. Mark areas where ponding occurs on surfaced areas. Correct by filling or raising depressions and by
     providing outlets for water blocked by high shoulders. Control penetration of storm water through pavement
     by sealing joints and cracks. Keep unpaved roads and airfields crowned to prevent water from remaining on
     the road or airfield where it will saturate and weather the surface. Maintain crowns and superelevations with
     graders or drags.

11-2  TM 3-34.48-1  29 February 2016


---

                                             Maintenance, Repair, and Rehabilitation of Roads, Airfields, and Heliports

Shoulders

     11-10. Keep shoulders smooth and graded so that water drains from the surfaced area toward the ditch.
     Replace eroded shoulder material on paved surfaces with new material. Material cleaned out of ditches can
     often be used to rebuild shoulders. Shoulders should be kept bladed flush to, or slightly below, the edges of
     the pavement and should slope away from the pavement to prevent water seepage into the subgrade.

Drainage Ditches

     11-11. Keep drainage ditches clear of weeds, brush, sediment, and other debris that obstruct water flow.
     Maintain line and grade of ditches. Correct sags and minor washouts as they occur. Side ditches can usually
     be maintained with graders.

     11-12. When cleaning and shaping, avoid unnecessary blading or cutting that destroys natural ground cover.
     Where possible, develop dense sod to stabilize open ditches. Where vegetation is not effective because of
     soil or moisture conditions, erosion may be corrected by lining the ditch with riprap, asphalt-coated
     membrane, geosynthetic erosion control materials, or concrete.

     11-13. Inspect check dams in side ditches and clean them regularly. The weir notch of a check dam must
     be kept clean or water will cut into the surfaced area at the edge of the dam. (See figure 11-1.) The aprons of
     check dams must also be maintained, and paving material must be replaced when washed out. Dikes or berms
     may be required along the tops of high-fill slopes to prevent gullies and washes.

                                                   Figure 11-1. Check dam

     11-14. Cut-slope interceptor ditches must be considered for side-hill and through cuts to prevent gully
     washing and erosion from the top of the cuts. If benching or terracing has been used in the design of the cut,
     ensure that the top of each bench is sloped back into the cut to provide for proper drainage. Ensure that each
     bench top is wide enough to maintain that drainage with earthmoving equipment. A good rule of thumb is to
     make benches at least as wide as a dozer blade. Figure 11-2, page 11-4, illustrates proper terraced side-hill-
     cut drainage. For proper design considerations of cut slopes, refer to TM 3-34.64/MCRP 3-17.7G.

Culverts

     11-15. Keep culverts clear of debris and sediment. (See figure 11-3, page 11-4.) This prevents water from
     cutting around or undermining the culverts. Inspect culverts frequently to determine if they are functioning
     properly. Cleaning by hand is usually necessary after heavy rains.

NONPAVED SURFACES

     11-16. Basic maintenance of nonpaved surfaces includes shaping the cross section to maintain adequate
     drainage and a smooth, compacted surface.

            Figure 11-2. Side-hill terracing

                                               Figure 11-3. Culvert entrance

Equipment

     11-17. Most surface maintenance consists of light scraping with grader blades and drags. Multiple-blade
     drags of iron or iron-shod, heavy timber may be used for normal scraping. Drags are frequently used to float
     mud and water off a road and to prevent corrugation or washboarding of the surface. One type of drag is
     shown in figure 11-4.

Materials

     11-18. Materials removed from ditches (other than silt, some clays, and organic soils [OL, OH, Pt]) may be
     used on shoulders and traveled ways. Dispose of silt deposits when removed; they are not suitable for
     construction. After heavy storms and spring thaws, additional material may need to be hauled in.

11-4        TM 3-34.48-1                      29 February 2016
