                           Maintenance, Repair, and Rehabilitation of Roads, Airfields, and Heliports

                  Legend:                       pounds
                  lb                            railroad
                  RR
                           Figure 11-4. Improvised road drag

Procedures

     11-19. Keep traffic areas and shoulders free of potholes, ruts, and irregularities. Light blading will prevent
     corrugation or washboarding. Work from the ditches to the center of the road to ensure good drainage and
     proper road crowning. Since loosened, dry material cannot be compacted. Blading or dragging should be
     done during or soon after rains. For prolonged dry spells or when surface material will not compact, add
     water or moist subsurface material with a rototiller, plow, or scarifier before compaction.

     11-20. Compaction of the graded surface material will reduce maintenance and repair for nonpaved
     surfaces. The type of roller used will vary with the material compacted. The correct moisture content will
     result in the most economical compaction.

     11-21. Soft spots (indicated by rutting or shoving of the surface) are generally caused by excess moisture,
     poor subsurface drainage, or unstable material. Determine the source of excess moisture and correct the
     drainage. On traffic areas, cobbles may be used to stabilize small areas of failure. Where pockets of mulch
     or peat cause surface failures, it may be necessary to remove the objectionable material and replace it with a
     more stable material. When adequate repairs cannot be made, adding crushed rock or clean gravel can
     temporarily reinforce soft spots.

29 February 2016           TM 3-34.48-1                       11-5


---

Chapter 11

     11-22. Keep nonpaved surfaces crowned to prevent water from remaining on the surface and saturating the
     soil. Maintain the crown and superelevation with drags or graders.
     11-23. Dust control may be a problem under some conditions. Spraying with water or a bituminous
     stabilizer is the most commonly used method of controlling dust. Dust control is discussed further in TM
     3-34.48-2. Examples of road repairs are shown in figure 11-5.

                 Figure 11-5. Road maintenance problems and proper corrective action

OILED SURFACES

     11-24. The routine maintenance of oiled surfaces consists of shaping and patching. Shaping is done with
     graders or drags. Patching may be done with a mixture of the soil and oil. Oiling is necessary each year
     because oiled surfaces frequently break up in the spring and become very rough. Thorough scarifying, blading
     (or dragging), and reshaping are necessary before oiling each year.

GRAVEL SURFACES

     11-25. Maintenance procedures for gravel surfaces are similar to those for nonpaved surfaces. Continual
     shaping is needed to maintain a smooth surface and a uniform crown, and the drainage system must be kept
     functioning.

Surface Maintenance

     11-26. Heavily traveled, graveled surfaces require constant attention by maintenance patrols. Intensive
     maintenance is required when the surface is first open to travel. Bumps compacted at this time remain in the
     surface and can be corrected only by scarifying or adding more material. Blade or drag the surface soon after
     rain until ruts and holes are filled. Do not work on a dry surface.

     11-27. Maintain a crown of at least 1/2 inch per foot. Multiple blade drags or sled drags can be used for
     routine maintenance, but graders are necessary for heavy reshaping work.

     11-28. Keep a slight excess of gravel available at the edges of the roadway and blade it uniformly over the
     surface in wet weather. Stockpile additional materials before fall and winter seasons and prolonged wet
     periods. Material added or spread on the surface during warm, dry weather is of little value.

11-6  TM 3-34.48-1  29 February 2016


---

                                             Maintenance, Repair, and Rehabilitation of Roads, Airfields, and Heliports

Repair of Potholes

     11-29. Most potholes are caused by material that was displaced by traffic. Initially, potholes are shallow
     and readily filled by blading when the surface is moist. Deep holes require filling with additional material.
     New material should be moistened and compacted.

Treatment of Corrugations

     11-30. Gravel surfaces tend to develop transverse or nearly transverse waves, called corrugations, which
     may progress into ruts as deep as 4 inches and from 1 1/2 to 3 feet apart. After this stage, they become major
     grooves needing extensive repair.

     11-31. Some blade equipment inherently chatters and causes slight irregularities, especially when the
     operator attempts to move a heavy cut. Corrugations often appear to start from small holes or depressions
     made when the road is wet or from an obstruction, such as a stick or rock. Other contributing factors are soft
     subgrade, poor grading of the gravel, poor binder, and an insufficient amount of binder.

     11-32. Corrugations can be prevented to a considerable extent by frequent maintenance and the careful use
     of maintenance equipment. Once corrugations form, only thoroughly scarifying, reshaping, and compacting
     can remove them. This is called regrading and should begin with a thorough cleaning and reshaping of the
     shoulders and ditches, continuing across the entire roadway.

Use of Calcium Chloride

     11-33. Calcium chloride may be applied to a gravel surface to control or eliminate dust, prevent the loss of
     material under the whipping action of traffic, and aid in maintaining a dense surface. The usual method is to
     apply one pound of calcium chloride per square yard in the late spring and one-half pound per square yard
     twice during the summer season. However, the amount of rain, the volume of traffic, and the character of the
     gravel affect the quantities required. Calcium chloride is corrosive to metal surfaces and may require more
     maintenance for aircraft and vehicles.

     11-34. The best time to apply calcium chloride is following a rain and after necessary blading or dragging
     is completed. If the application cannot be deferred until rain occurs, water the surface before applying the
     calcium chloride. For best results, apply calcium chloride before the traffic area becomes dry and dusty.

PROCESSED MATERIAL SURFACES

     11-35. Traffic areas composed of processed materials (crushed and screened rock, gravel, slag) are
     maintained by methods similar to those used on gravel surfaces. When coarse, processed materials are used,
     surface failures are usually in the form of sharp-edged holes caused by poor drainage. Repairs require
     cleaning the holes down to the solid subgrade and ensuring that no silt, mud, or water remains. Subgrade
     repairs are then made with a well-graded soil aggregate. Surface repairs should consist of a well-tamped or
     rolled-in-place, coarse-graded aggregate of the same gradation as the original surrounding surface.

BITUMINOUS SURFACES

     11-36. The maintenance and repair of bituminous surfaces are discussed in UFC 3-270-01. Some
     considerations applicable to bituminous-surfaced traffic areas follow.

Inspection

     11-37. Maintenance patrols should frequently inspect bituminous pavements for early detection of failures.
     Small defects quickly develop into large ones, resulting in pavement failure unless promptly corrected. Small
     crews using hand tools can quickly make minor repairs with a minimum interruption of traffic. Large,
     bituminous repairs require more time, personnel, and equipment. Such repairs also interfere with traffic. In
     extreme cases, detours may be required to avoid complete traffic stoppage.

29 February 2016  TM 3-34.48-1  11-7


---

Chapter 11

Patches

     11-38. Patches should be trimmed square or oblong with straight, vertical sides running parallel and
     perpendicular to the centerline of the traffic area. (Refer to UFC 3-270-01 for additional information.)

Temporary Repairs

     11-39. Any stable material may be used for temporary repairs in combat areas or where suitable material is
     not available and the traffic area must be patched to keep traffic moving. Good-quality soil and masonry,
     such as concrete rubble, are suitable for this purpose. These patches must be thoroughly compacted and
     constantly maintained with replacement material. More permanent patching should be accomplished as soon
     as possible.

Maintenance of Shoulders

     11-40. Blade shoulders so that water drains from the surface and ruts and washouts are filled. Grade
     shoulder material flush against or slightly below pavement edges to restrict water seepage to the subgrade
     and prevent breaking of the pavement edge caused by traffic driving off the pavement onto the shoulder.
     Replace material displaced from shoulders with material hauled in, as required.

STABILIZED SOIL SURFACES

     11-41. Maintenance of mechanically stabilized soil surfaces and sand-clay surfaces is essentially the same
     as that for nonpaved and gravel surfaces. Procedures described for gravel surfaces are applicable to surfaces
     that contain considerable coarse aggregate. Procedures described for nonpaved surfaces are applicable to
     surfaces that contain little or no coarse aggregate. Bituminous surfaces, soils, and soil-cement may require
     additional maintenance as described in the paragraphs that follow.

Potholes

     11-42. Clean potholes and trim them rectangularly with straight, vertical sides running parallel and
     perpendicular to the centerline. This provides a shoulder against the movement of the patch. Fill the potholes
     with a stabilized mix of the same character as the adjacent sound area. This material should be thoroughly
     compacted in place, one thin layer at a time.

Ravels

     11-43. Edge raveling is caused by water softening the foundation material. Before proceeding with patching
     operations, reconstruct the shoulder or lower the subdrainage so that this condition will not recur. Then, build
     up the foundation. The patching mixture should conform to the surrounding area.

CORAL SURFACES

     11-44. The maintenance of well-built coral traffic areas is relatively simple. Use fresh, raw coral with the
     proper moisture content for the repair material. The best time to perform maintenance is during or after a rain
     storm, while the coral is wet. Fill low spots, ruts, and potholes by shoveling or dumping coral directly from
     a truck onto the low spots. If rolled while wet, these patches will bond onto the original material almost
     without a mark. Salt water is usually available where coral is present, and salt water promotes better bonding
     than fresh water.

     11-45. Occasional blading and rolling are necessary to maintain a proper crown and a smooth surface. In
     dry seasons, sprinkling is necessary to maintain a proper crown, a smooth surface, and high stability and to
     minimize dust. Traffic areas hold up well in wet seasons. An asphalt treatment may be justified in prolonged
     dry seasons if dust and raveling become serious. Careful attention to shoulders and the drainage system is
     essential.

11-8  TM 3-34.48-1  29 February 2016


---

                                             Maintenance, Repair, and Rehabilitation of Roads, Airfields, and Heliports

RIGID PAVEMENTS

     11-46. Maintenance of rigid pavements is covered in UFC 3-270-03 and UFC 3-270-04. Frequently inspect
     concrete pavement to detect early signs of failure, and make prompt repairs to prevent minor defects from
     spreading.

CRATER REPAIR

     11-47. Bombs, shells, land mines, and cratering charges can produce extensive craters in traffic areas.
     Surface damage does not present an unusual repair problem, but explosions may displace or destabilize large
     areas of the subgrade. Drainage may also be disrupted, allowing water penetrating the broken surface to
     accumulate and further soften the subgrade.

     11-48. Satisfactory repairs require the restoration of subgrade stability to support traffic and prevent undue
     surface settling after repairs have been completed. Use the following steps for crater repairs:

              Step 1. Remove surfacing from around the crater edge that is damaged or not firmly bonded to the
                  base course.

              Step 2. Trim the surface and base course to a sound, vertical edge.
              Step 3. Remove water, mud, and debris from the crater.
              Step 4. Fill the crater with successive 6- to 8-inch layers of suitable material to the original level

                  of the subgrade. Compaction is essential; each layer must be thoroughly tamped with hand or
                  pneumatic tamping tools. After the material has reached a suitable level, compaction equipment
                  can be pulled through or driven across the crater.
              Step 5. Repair the base course and wearing surface.

     11-49. Gravel; rock; masonry debris; sandy soil; or other suitable, stable materials can be used to fill craters.
     (See figure 11-6.) Material blown from craters can be used for much of this fill. In an emergency, material
     from the shoulders of roads or airfields may be borrowed and replaced later. When the situation permits and
     where enemy action may be anticipated, stockpiles or material pits should be prepared at convenient sites.
     Alternate layers of sandbags and tamped earth allow good subgrade compaction where other equipment or
     materials are not available. (For a detailed discussion of specific crater repair techniques used in air-base
     damage repair, refer to UFC 3-270-07.)

                                          Figure 11-6. Crater backfill materials

ROAD MAINTENANCE

     11-50. The importance of preventive maintenance and the necessity for prompt maintenance cannot be
     overemphasized. Neglect and delay permit traffic and weather to turn minor defects into major problems.
     Progressive road failure is serious. The more serious a failure is, the more quickly it deteriorates.

29 February 2016  TM 3-34.48-1  11-9


---

Chapter 11

     11-51. In forward areas, extensive repairs are often necessary before roads can be used. Combat engineer
     units usually do expedient work. Under the pressure of combat conditions, temporary repairs are made
     hurriedly using the materials most readily available. Such repairs are intended only to meet immediate
     minimum needs. As the advance units move forward, other engineer units take over the work of additional
     repair and maintenance. Expedient repairs that were previously made are supplemented or replaced by more
     permanent work. Surfaces are brought to a standard that will withstand the required use and maintenance
     becomes routine.

MAINTENANCE PATROLS

     11-52. Adequate maintenance requires a workable maintenance organization. Usually, engineer units
     establish a patrol system that covers the road net they are responsible for. It is desirable to use squads as
     patrols and thus retain unit integrity, with each squad commanded by its squad leader and using its regular
     tables of organization and equipment. The platoon furnishes reinforcements (personnel or equipment) as
     needed.

     11-53. Assign each patrol to a specific area. Organize as many patrols as necessary to adequately cover the
     total area of operations. It is sometimes necessary in forward or heavy-traffic areas to provide enough patrols
     to put the maintenance function on a 24-hour-a-day basis.

Personnel and Equipment

     11-54. Two plans are presented for the organization of maintenance patrols. Consider the merits of each
     plan with respect to the maintenance problems of the situation and the personnel and equipment available for
     the patrols.

     11-55. One patrol consists of a normal squad that is equipped with a dump truck, grader, and hand tools.
     This patrol can handle maintenance and minor repairs normally encountered on a 5- to 15-mile stretch of
     road. The number of people in a squad can be decreased and more miles can be assigned to a patrol expected
     to cover a stretch of permanent pavement in good condition and not heavily traveled. If a patrol is to cover a
     poor dirt road accommodating heavy traffic, more personnel will be furnished by the platoon and fewer miles
     will be assigned.

     11-56. The other plan calls for the assignment of a one to three person patrol, a grader, and hand tools. This
     crew can handle routine maintenance on a 12-mile stretch of average earth, gravel, or water-bound macadam
     road. However, the crew must be supplemented with a truck and repair crew when material must be hauled
     or surface patching is needed.

     11-57. Winter weather; severe storms; heavy, destructive enemy action; and other conditions demand that
     patrols be reinforced with additional personnel and equipment or that the assigned areas be reduced and the
     number of patrols increased. Special conditions often call for special equipment.

Duties

     11-58. The duties of maintenance patrols are as follows:
              Clean out drainage facilities.
              Mow grass and weeds.
              Repair minor washouts and potholes.
              Maintain the road surface (eliminate ruts, potholes, washboards).
              Maintain road shoulders and ditches.
              Make frequent, thorough inspections of road conditions.
              Report the need for repair work more significant than the patrol is equipped or manned to handle
                  to higher headquarters.

11-10  TM 3-34.48-1  29 February 2016


---

                                             Maintenance, Repair, and Rehabilitation of Roads, Airfields, and Heliports

Inspection and Supervision

     11-59. An officer or senior noncommissioned officer is assigned several patrols to supervise, assist, and
     inspect. Normal unit organization should be retained as much as possible. A platoon leader should be
     responsible for the patrols composed of personnel from his command.

REPAIR CREWS

     11-60. The engineer sending out maintenance patrols should keep sufficient equipment and personnel
     available to send out repair crews to handle situations reported by the patrols. The repair crew composition
     will be dictated by the needs of the particular job in terms of equipment and personnel. Frequently, the regular
     maintenance patrol can work with the repair crew, but other maintenance and inspection of the patrol area
     must not be neglected.

MAINTENANCE WITH TRAFFIC

     11-61. Give full consideration to the importance of keeping traffic flowing with a minimum of interference
     or delay. Maintenance of shoulders and ditches can normally be performed without interference from or
     hindrance to traffic. Repairs to other drainage structures may delay traffic or slow other repair work.
     Permanent repairs are often postponed so temporary and emergency repairs can be made to maintain traffic
     flow.

Traffic Control

     11-62. Repairs should be made on one-half of the surface at a time when surface repairs will deny traffic
     the use of sections of the pavement. Block off short sections and post guides to regulate traffic and avoid
     delay.

     11-63. When single-lane traffic must be used, control traffic using the baton method. With this method, a
     flagman is placed at each end of the single-lane traffic section. The flagman at one end of the section has a
     baton or some other distinctive marker. Working under a prepared plan, vehicles traveling in one direction
     are stopped, while those traveling in the opposite direction are permitted to go through. After a suitable time
     interval, the flagman on the open end of the section gives the baton to the driver of the last vehicle permitted
     to go through. Upon arrival at the other end of the section, the driver of the last vehicle gives the baton to the
     flagman. Vehicles are then permitted to travel in the opposite direction until the waiting vehicles have passed
     through and the driver of the last vehicle carries the baton to the other end of the section. This process
     continues as long as necessary.

     11-64. Sometimes two-way traffic can be maintained through blocked-off sections by diverting one stream
     of traffic to the shoulder of the road. Grading and stabilization of the shoulder with gravel or bituminous
     material may be justified in such instances. Repairs to be performed during traffic flow should be carefully
     planned; proper procedures should be selected; and labor, material, and equipment should be on hand to
     complete the work as rapidly as possible.

Bypasses and Detours

     11-65. Bridge or pavement failures or the destruction of part of a roadway by floods or combat action may
     make part or the entire roadway impassable to traffic. In such cases, a bypass or detour around the damaged
     or obstructed area is necessary. The construction of a short bypass around an obstruction may be preferable
     to a longer detour on existing roads. A detour may also be used while a bypass is being constructed. Base the
     decision upon traffic interference, the work involved, and the time available.

     11-66. Conduct reconnaissance to determine the best possible route when establishing a detour. The road
     should be as short as possible and must be in condition, or conditioned, to handle traffic for the period when
     it will be used. Use existing roads when possible. Construct short sections of connecting roads, if necessary.

     11-67. Check and repair bridges or reinforce them with timber or planking. Clean and repair culverts. If the
     need for a detour is anticipated, complete this work beforehand. Detour roads are usually subjected to heavier
     loads and more traffic than their design specifications. Because increased maintenance is usually required to

29 February 2016  TM 3-34.48-1  11-11


---

Chapter 11

     keep detours passable, stockpile surfacing material along the route, carefully plan maintenance operations,
     and keep labor and material constantly available.

     11-68. Direct traffic by placing signs at detour entrances, road intersections, and turns. Post warning signs
     at dangerous points. Place other signs or markings, as required, to ensure minimum traffic delay. Install
     barricades at each end of the road section under repair. Refer to FM 3-34.170/MCWP 3-17.4 for the types
     and posting of road signs.

Safety of Maintenance Personnel

     11-69. Give special attention to the safety of maintenance personnel working where traffic moves past or
     around them. Use restrictive speed and warning signs, barricades, and flagmen to control traffic and lessen
     the danger to maintenance personnel. Instruct crewmembers to avoid stepping into the traveled way and to
     be continually alert to passing traffic. Conspicuously mark maintenance vehicles operating in or on the edge
     of the roadway with red flags, flashing red lights, or similar devices.

WINTER MAINTENANCE

     11-70. Winter weather may present special problems in JOA maintenance. Regions of heavy snowfall
     require special equipment and material to keep pavement and traffic areas in usable condition. Low
     temperatures cause icing on pavement and frost on subgrade structures. Alternate freezing and thawing may
     damage surfaces and block drainage systems with ice. Spring thaws may result in surface and subgrade
     failure. Winter maintenance mainly consists of removing snow and ice, sanding icy surfaces, erecting and
     maintaining snow fences, and keeping drainage systems free from obstruction.

Preparation for Winter

     11-71. Organize snow-removal crews and place equipment in readiness. Stockpile abrasives and chemicals
     in locations where they will be required. Perform late fall maintenance before the winter freeze. Continue
     with routine maintenance of ditches and shoulders as far into the winter as possible so that the drainage
     system will be in the best possible condition for the spring runoff.

     11-72. Keep earth and gravel surfaces smooth and shaped to prevent moisture from entering the subgrade.
     Smoothing and shaping prevent snowplow blades from being obstructed by rough, frozen shoulder and
     surface material. In areas of heavy snowfall, outline bridges, culverts, and narrow places in the road with
     poles that extend above the snow, and mark these locations for maintenance crews.

Snow Fences

     11-73. Conduct reconnaissance before winter to determine where snow fences will be needed to control
     drifting snow. Because it is fine and compacts into a dense mass, drifted snow obstructs traffic more than an
     equal depth of freshly fallen snow. Drifts form when windborne snow is picked up in open spaces, loses
     velocity, and is deposited in sheltered places. Danger spots are roads at ground level or in cuts adjacent to
     large, open areas. Drifts form in the lee (downwind side) of buildings, signboards, and similar wind barriers.
     Similarly, high snowbanks left close to the road by snowplows furnish both the conditions and the material
     for extensive drifting. Snow fences are not normally required near high fills, in wooded or brushy areas, or
     where vegetation prevents snow from drifting on the road.

     11-74. Place snow fences on the windward side of roads according to prevailing winds. (See figure 11-7.)
     The height of the fence determines the distance it is placed from the traveled way. Generally, the proper
     distance is 20 times the height of the fence. This distance is increased where winds are of high velocity.
     According to the above ratio, a 4-foot fence erected 1 foot above the ground should be placed at least 80 feet
     beyond the point where drifting is to be prevented. In extreme cases, a distance as great as 300 feet may be
     necessary.

11-12  TM 3-34.48-1  29 February 2016


---

                  Maintenance, Repair, and Rehabilitation of Roads, Airfields, and Heliports

                                    Figure 11-7. Location of snow fences

11-75. Fences should be as long as possible without any holes or openings. Openings provide for dispersion
of snow on the backside of the fencing. The effect of a snow fence in controlling drifts caused by a road cut
is shown in figure 11-8. Two or more parallel fences may be required, but one tall fence is generally better
than two short fences. If fences are set too far away, they have little or no effect in reducing drifts. If they are
placed too close to the road, drifts to the leeward side of the fence fall on the road.

                           Figure 11-8. Snow fence control of road cut drifts

11-76. Commercial snow fences are commonly used. They consist of metal posts and wooden laths or metal
pickets about 5 feet long, woven together with wire. Such fencing is portable, easily erected and dismantled,
and may be rolled up and stored in the summer. Permanent snow fences include open-board fences on posts
and evergreen or deciduous shrub hedges. Plastic mesh snow fencing is lighter and more efficient than
wooden fencing.

11-77. Other types of snow fencing include wood slats or pressed-steel slats mounted on collapsible
A-frames, worm fences, and brush or branches suspended on wire. Local materials (such as corn stalks, brush,
and coarse grass) anchored in place by wire or wood may be used. Figure 11-9, page 11-14, shows three
types of snow fences.

29 February 2016  TM 3-34.48-1  11-13


---

Chapter 11

                                           Figure 11-9. Types of snow fences

     11-78. Erect a snow fence before the ground is frozen. Drive metal posts into the ground and mount wire
     fencing on the windward side. In regions of heavy snow, use long posts so that fencing may be raised on the
     posts as the season progresses. This will increase snow storage to the leeward side. Install fencing with the
     bottom about 6 inches above ground level to prevent the ends of the pickets from freezing fast and to prevent
     the fence from choking with snow. Frozen ends make it difficult to raise the fence and may cause the pickets
     to break when swayed by the wind. Brace the posts according to the anticipated wind velocities.

     11-79. Inspect snow fences after heavy storms. Repair broken ties and braces, and straighten blown-down
     sections. Raise fences to exceed the height of accumulated snow on the leeward side. Lowering fences may
     be required after midseason thaws or long periods of settling.

     11-80. Remove snow fences in the spring, and repair damaged sections. The fences are frequently stored
     on dunnage at the drift location for use the following winter.

Snow Removal

     11-81. Prompt snow removal is essential to prevent traffic interference and ice formation on the road. Begin
     removal operations when the snow starts. The amount of equipment necessary depends on the intensity of
     the storm. If possible, store equipment at intervals along road sections or road nets that are to receive early
     attention, and operators should be ready to move promptly when a snowstorm arrives.

     11-82. Since snow-removal equipment must frequently be operated on a 24-hour basis during periods of
     heavy storms, provide relief crews. Use snowplows to patrol areas or sections of roads that are subject to
     drifting in windy weather. Standard snow-removal equipment consists of various attachments mounted on
     trucks or similar prime movers. These include one-way, reversible, and rotary-type straight blades; straight
     underbody blades; V-type plows; and rotary snowplows. These items are described in TM 5-624/NAVFAC
     DM MO-102/AFJMAN 32-1040. Graders, dozers, and loaders are also useful in snow removal. Improvised
     equipment, such as drags, may be used in expedient situations.

     11-83. Use comparatively light and fast snow-removal equipment for light snowfalls and at the beginning
     of severe storms. Use heavier equipment to widen traffic lanes and for heavy snowfalls. Continue snow-
     removal operations until the snow has been pushed back, leveled, or hauled to a disposal point. When snow
     removal is delayed or interrupted, the snow may become too deep for available equipment to handle, drifting
     may worsen, or wet snow may freeze.

11-14       TM 3-34.48-1  29 February 2016


---

                                             Maintenance, Repair, and Rehabilitation of Roads, Airfields, and Heliports

     11-84. Trucks with 2 1/2- to 5-ton capacities and equipped with one-way blades are best adapted for long
     stretches of roads. This equipment travels at speeds of 15 to 25 miles per hour, removes snow from the road
     before it is compacted, and provides an open track for traffic.

     11-85. Use 5- to 10-ton trucks equipped with straight or V-shaped blades for heavier snowfalls and to widen
     traffic lanes. This equipment operates at about 15 miles per hour. Use V-shaped plows to break through heavy
     drifts. Use straight or V-shaped plows equipped with side wings to push the snow beyond the shoulder line,
     to prevent drifting, and to provide room for additional snow storage.

     11-86. Trucks used for plowing generally carry abrasives as ballast for better traction. Tractors are
     sometimes required for heavy snows and drifts. Graders are satisfactory for light snow. In areas of very heavy
     snowfall, rotary plows and blowers may be needed.

Surface Ice Control

     11-87. The formation of road ice that results from packed snow, slush, or melting snowbanks is prevented
     if snow removal is effectively performed and drainage is provided. When possible, push snowbanks away
     from pavements so that melted water will not run onto cleared surfaces.

     11-88. Use plows and graders to remove slush from the road to prevent freezing and icing or to remove ice
     that has previously formed. Use care to avoid damaging the pavement. Dry snow compacts under traffic but
     can usually be loosened and bladed off without difficulty. Wet snow or slush, if it is allowed to freeze in
     place, sticks tightly to the pavement and cannot be easily removed without a period of warm weather or the
     use of salts.

     11-89. Various conditions cause icing of road surfaces. Dangerous icing is more likely to occur during the
     late fall and early spring when frequent temperature changes occur. Midday thawing and night freezing is a
     common cause of icing. Rain; sleet; or light, wet snow falling on cold pavement can form ice films too thin
     to be removed by mechanical means and can make long sections of the road hazardous. Curves and grades
     are critical points under icing conditions, and high-crowned roads can become difficult to travel at any point
     when iced over.

Salts

     11-90. At the beginning of a storm, apply sodium chloride or calcium chloride to wet snow and sleet to
     keep it in a slushy condition and prevent it from sticking to the surface. Limit the use of salts on concrete
     pavements to one or two applications per year or the pavement will pit and scale. Salts do not damage
     bituminous surfaces. To prevent blockage of the drains by freezing, place bags of salts at drain inlets or catch
     basins so they do not obstruct flow.

Abrasives

     11-91. Treat icy pavements with abrasives and salts to reduce slipping and skidding. Sand, (treated and
     untreated), cinders, and crushed rock or slag screenings are commonly used. Other materials include pea
     gravel, coal stock, and coke screenings. The choice of materials is based on the availability and the length of
     the haul. Sharp, angular material embeds itself readily, and dark-colored material absorbs the most heat from
     the sun. Untreated materials are fairly effective on compacted snow, but are easily blown or thrown from the
     traveled way.

     11-92. For the most effective use, mix calcium chloride with abrasive material. The calcium chloride causes
     the abrasive to embed in the ice and improves surface traction. Treat abrasives with 40 to 75 pounds of
     calcium chloride per cubic yard for stockpiling, and add another 25 to 50 pounds per cubic yard of calcium
     chloride when applying it to a road. Sodium chloride may be used in place of calcium chloride, but is not
     recommended for temperatures below 10 degrees Fahrenheit.

     11-93. Store abrasive materials where they are quickly available when needed. Establish stockpiles for hand
     application at critical locations, such as steep grades and curves. Make wider distribution with trucks by hand
     or mechanical spreading. Heating an abrasive material before placing it on the road will allow it to melt into
     the ice and prevent it from being forced out by traffic.

29 February 2016  TM 3-34.48-1  11-15


---

Chapter 11

Mechanical Removal

     11-94. Graders can sometimes remove ice that is not tightly bonded to the road surface. Using scarifiers or
     rotary tillers equipped with special teeth can reduce extremely icy conditions. Exercise extreme care so that
     the road surface is not damaged.

Correction of Spring Breakup Problems

     11-95. In regions subject to frost and snow, spring is a critical time in the maintenance of pavement and
     other traffic areas. Abnormal and repetitive traffic loads during the spring breakup period may cause subgrade
     pumping of concrete surfaces and breakthrough of bituminous surfaces. Melting ice and snow, spring rains,
     and frost leaving the ground have a tendency to saturate permeable surfaces. Drainage obstructions may raise
     the water table and make subbases unstable.

     11-96. When the spring thaw begins, open ditches at critical points so that melted water will not flow onto
     the road. Outlets of cuts and road sections next to snowbanks require special attention. As the snow begins
     to melt, snowplows or grading equipment may be required to clear snow from the shoulders to avoid erosion.
     Handwork is usually required to clear the shoulders and open ditch outlets. Remove accumulations of ice in
     culverts and small drainage structures by hand or thaw them with truck-mounted steamers.

     11-97. Frost heaves are indicated by the localized raising of road surfaces and pavements. Damage occurs
     as a result of the heaving of the subgrade soil due to the formation of ice lenses. This expanding subgrade
     causes an upheaval of the surface and subsequent reduction in overall strength. Frost heaves are most
     prevalent in silt and clay subgrades.

     11-98. Frost boils are indicated by the breaking up of a localized section of road surfaces and pavements
     when subjected to traffic. During thawing, the melted water produces a fluid subgrade condition with very
     limited or no supporting capacity. Traffic imposes a force on the pavement and thus to the excess water in
     the subgrade. This in turn exerts an equalizing pressure in all directions. This pressure is relieved through the
     point of least resistance (up through the pavement surface) and produces a small mound similar in appearance
     to an oversized boil.

     11-99. Frost boils are often large and deep enough to make the road impassable until repaired. Repairs may
     be made by one or a combination of the following procedures:

              Bridge soft spots with timber, landing mats, sapling mats, corduroy, or other available material.
                  Store materials in advance at or near load sections where frost boils may occur. Such repairs are
                  temporary; therefore, remove the material when the road thaws and dries.

              Patch soft spots with crushed rock or gravel. Place large rocks in soft spots and cover them with
                  smaller rocks. It is better to remove soft, water-soaked material beforehand, although more time
                  is required.

     11-100. For better results, provide adequate drainage while performing repairs to correct the cause of the
     problem. Remove soft material and dig an outlet ditch to one shoulder. A temporary bridge of planks or other
     material permits traffic to pass. The excavated soft spot and the ditch are backfilled with rock, gravel, or
     other suitable material. Drainage tile may be installed in the ditch before backfilling.

Preventive Maintenance

     11-101. The best maintenance is preventive maintenance. Prohibit traffic during the critical 2- or 3-day
     period on roads prone to frost heaves and boils. Methods to eliminate or minimize the damaging effects of
     frost action are discussed in TM 3-34.48-2.

FORDS AND BRIDGES

     11-102. The approaches and bottoms of fords must be kept smooth and clear of large boulders and debris.
     Replace marking posts that have been knocked down or washed out.

     11-103. Frequently inspect bridge abutments, trestles, piers, and trusses for damage and deterioration. Repair
     defects at the earliest opportunity. The maintenance crew normally obtains help to rebuild or repair the bridge.

11-16  TM 3-34.48-1  29 February 2016

                    Maintenance, Repair, and Rehabilitation of Roads, Airfields, and Heliports

AIRFIELD AND HELIPORT MAINTENANCE

     11-104. Airfield and heliport maintenance is the responsibility of the primary user. At Air Force facilities,
     such maintenance is normally performed by an Air Force civil engineering squadron or similar unit. Army
     engineer units normally maintain Army airfields and heliports. When the repair and rehabilitation
     requirements of Air Force bases exceed the immediate, emergency-damage recovery capability of the air
     base, Army engineer units will be assigned to perform the work.

MAINTENANCE

     11-105. Routine maintenance of hot-mixed asphalt and concrete airfield and heliport pavements can be
     performed during scheduled closures using the methods and materials presented in UFC 3-270-01 (hot-mixed
     asphalt) or UFC 3-270-03 and UFC 3-270-04 (concrete).

     11-106. At expeditionary locations or when scheduled closures are limited, partial-depth spall repairs of
     Portland cement concrete pavements can be accomplished using rapid-set proprietary materials and the
     construction methods of UFC 3-270-03. Acceptable materials are listed in table 11-1.

AIR BASE DAMAGE REPAIR

     11-107. The immediate, emergency-damage recovery of air bases is considered to be the minimum work
     required to permit aircraft to land and take off. The Air Force is primarily responsible for the emergency
     repair of the air base. This includes the emergency repair of paved surfaces, which is called rapid runway
     repair. This is accomplished through the employment of Air Force base civil engineering troop assets, prime
     base engineer emergency forces, and rapid engineering deployable heavy operational repair squadrons
     engineering units. The Army is responsible for semipermanent construction, the beyond-emergency repair of
     the air base and, emergency repairs that exceed Air Force capability upon request.

Chapter 11

Army Responsibilities for Air Base Damage Repair

     11-108. The Army provides engineer support to the Air Force overseas. It ensures that units are equipped,
     manned, and trained to support Air Force needs. This support includes—

              Assisting with the emergency repair of war-damaged air bases where requirements exceed the Air
                  Force organic repair capability.

              Repairing and restoring damaged air bases with beyond-emergency repairs.
              Developing engineer designs, plans, and materials to meet the needs of the Air Force as agreed

                  upon. Where practicable, designs are based on the Army Facilities Component System.
              Supplying construction materials and equipment, except for that provided by the Air Force.
              Assisting within their capabilities with the removal of unexploded ordnance declared safe by

                  explosive ordnance disposal personnel and limited damage assessment operations upon request.
              Managing and supervising the repair and restoration of war damage performed by Army

                  personnel. The Air Force base commander sets the priorities for air base repair.

Air Force Responsibilities for Air Base Damage Repair

     11-109. The Air Force provides military troop engineering support from its resources. The Air Force ensures
     that units are equipped, manned, and trained adequately to support its needs. This support includes—

              Providing emergency repair of war damage to air bases.
              Organizing host nation support (overseas).
              Managing force beddown of units and weapon systems, excluding Army base development

                  responsibilities.
              Providing operation and maintenance of facilities and installations.
              Providing crash rescue and fire suppression.
              Managing force beddown and the emergency repair of war damage.
              Supplying material and equipment to perform its engineering mission.
              Providing logistical support to the Army for supply except classes II, V, VII, and IX.
              Conducting damage assessment and removal of unexploded ordnance.
              Providing chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear collective shelters. Establishing and

                  operating personnel and equipment decontamination sites for the air base and the Army. (There
                  are shortages of these assets on air bases, and support to Army units may be limited.)

     11-110. Air base support agreements may be established in some theaters between the Air Force and the host
     nation where air base damage repair support capability exists. These host nation support agreements may
     include equipment, materials, and manpower assets.

     11-111. For a detailed description of personnel, equipment, and material requirements and critical path
     schedules for repair of runways cratered by high-explosive bombs, refer to UFC 3-270-07. For a further,
     detailed discussion of general air base damage repair, refer to UFC 3-270-07.

TURF SURFACES

     11-112. Plant grass to provide a turf surface on shoulders and graded areas. Turf helps with camouflage,
     reduces dust, and minimizes erosion. Turf surfaces are limited to areas where the climate and soil are
     favorable. (See table 11-2 for the different characteristics of grass.)

MUD CONTROL

     11-113. Mud on the runway creates slippery surfaces that impede takeoff and increase the difficulties and
     dangers of landing. Muddy taxiway and runway surfaces decrease tire life and increase the wear and
     maintenance of brakes. Flying mud particles may damage propellers, rotors, and jet engines. Removing mud
     from wheels, struts, and fuselage is an additional maintenance burden.

    11-114. Mud on airfield and heliport surfaces is deposited by traffic from adjacent muddy areas or caused
    by subgrade failure when excess moisture and mud is pumped to the surface by traffic. Enforce mud
    discipline by limiting taxiway access to service vehicles. Remove mud from vehicle wheels and
    undercarriages before they enter the taxiway. The most satisfactory solution is to provide surfaced service
    roads to hardstands.

Repairs

     11-115. Localized soft or muddy spots in an otherwise satisfactory surface are repaired by replacing the
     unsatisfactory subgrade material with a more suitable one. If the muddy areas are widespread, it may be
     necessary to stop traffic until the surface dries. In extreme conditions, resurfacing may be necessary.

Mud Removal

     11-116. In some instances, surfaces may be kept in operational condition by removing the surface mud.
     Remove mud by hand shoveling, blading, or dragging. Light mud or slush is sometimes removed by hand or
     with rotary brooms.

     11-117. When a grader is used on a landing-mat surface, prevent the blade from tearing the surfacing. One
     method is to bolt a 4- by 12-inch hardwood moldboard over the cutting edge, extending 2 inches below it.
     This provides a scraping edge with sufficient spring to remove the mud from irregularities in the landing mat,
     yet soft enough to protect the mat. A piece of 1/2-inch rubber belting (or the cap from a worn tire) bolted
     between the blade and the moldboard and extending an inch below the cutting edge makes an effective
     squeegee for removing light mud and slush. Grader operations for removing mud and slush from the runway
     are similar to those employed for snow removal. Start in the center of the runway and proceed progressively
     to the edge, overlapping several feet on each pass.

SNOW REMOVAL AND ICE CONTROL

     11-118. Snow removal methods, the order of operations, and the assignment of equipment are established
     before the winter season. Factors to consider when planning the snow-handling program include climatic
     conditions, average snowfall, aircraft to be accommodated, equipment available, and camouflage
     requirements. Aircraft may be equipped with wheels or landing skis. Ski-equipped aircraft operate
     successfully on packed snow. Aircraft with landing wheels cannot operate in more than 3 inches of loose
     snow. This limitation applies to fresh snow on a clear runway, fresh snow on previously packed snow, or
     melting snow previously packed on a runway. For camouflage, it is undesirable to remove all snow from a
     runway when the surrounding terrain is blanketed with snow.

     11-119. Equipment useful for handling snow includes rubber-tired tractors, scoop loaders, graders rotary
     brooms, and band brooms. Supplementary equipment may include single-wing, one-way, and reversible
     snow plows; V type plows; rotary plows; blowers; rollers; and other snow-removal equipment.

11-20                                          TM 3-34.48-1                    29 February 2016


---

                                             Maintenance, Repair, and Rehabilitation of Roads, Airfields, and Heliports

Packing

     11-120. In regions of heavy snowfalls with prolonged cold weather relatively free from sudden thaws, snow
     may be handled by packing. The runway, shoulders, and the adjacent area are packed. Rolling begins when
     3 inches of snow has fallen and continues during the snowfall. Rollers drawn behind a tractor with snow
     treads pack the snow.

     11-121. Smoothing is done with a drag equipped with metal cutting edges on the front and rear or with a
     grader. Usually one tractor is used to pull the drag and the rollers with the drag ahead of the rollers.

     11-122. Rollers are made to a desirable diameter and length with a shell of 10-gauge corrugated steel. The
     shell is supported on an axle by two structural frames (or spiders) at the third points and two steel-plated
     bulkheads at the ends. One plate has a hole to permit filling the roller with sand to increase the weight.

Clearing and Removing

     11-123. Snow clearing and removal are required where climatic conditions prevent packing or snowfalls
     exceed what can be packed on the runway. Remove light snowfalls with a grader or rotary broom. Very light
     snowfalls can be blown off the runway by the prop wash of several aircraft lined up along one edge. Remove
     heavy snowfalls with truck-mounted plows, rotary snowplows, rubber-tired tractors, or scoop loaders. Drifts
     may be opened by a truck or tractor with a V-type blade or by a rotary snowplow.

     11-124. Equip trucks with tire chains and carry ballast for traction while plowing. Keep blades about 1/2 inch
     above the runway surface, especially if the surface is a landing mat. Runners mounted at each end of the
     blade accomplish this clearance.

     11-125. The assignment of plows varies with the condition at each airfield and the type of equipment
     available. Arranging the plows into units simplifies coordination of snow removal with the control tower.
     Ordinarily, one-way, truck-mounted snowplows operate in formation to expedite snow removal. Remove
     snow near landing lights and other obstructions with a blower, if available, or by hand.

     11-126. Do not permit the snow plow moldboard to touch the airfield pavement surface. Use castor wheels
     or shoes to maintain a minimum 1/2-inch clearance. Avoid straddling the centerline with the plow blade,
     since the change in transverse grade across the centerline will reduce or eliminate the clearance between the
     moldboard and the pavement surface, resulting in spalling of the pavement surface.

     11-127. The rapid removal of snow requires a rotary blower, snow loader, or other special equipment. Trucks
     used for hauling snow are equipped with high sideboards. Tractor-drawn sleighs built of lumber may be used
     as an expedient hauling device or to supplement snow-handling trucks.

Abating Ice Conditions

     11-128. Sprinkle ice coatings on runways, taxiways, and hardstands with urea, coarse sand, or cinders.
     Spread by hand or with mechanical spreaders. If practical, heat abrasives before spreading. Remove
     accumulated abrasives in the spring by brooming. Ice conditions on airfields used by jet aircraft are a very
     serious problem because abrasives cannot be used. Do not use sodium chloride and calcium chloride for ice
     control without approval because these salts may promote corrosion of metal aircraft parts.

MAINTENANCE DURING FLYING OPERATIONS

     11-129. Coordinate maintenance and repair work during flying operations, and plan the work for minimum
     interference with air and ground traffic. Maintenance may need to be performed at night or during inclement
     weather so that flying operations are not interrupted.

     11-130. Do not leave equipment hazardous to aircraft on the runway or other areas. Clearly mark construction
     or repair areas on the runway so that they are visible from the air. Mark repairs on taxiways so that they are
     visible to pilots while taxiing.

Chapter 11

REHABILITATION OF CAPTURED AIRFIELDS

     11-131. The decision to rehabilitate a captured enemy airfield and the decision as to the type and construction
     standard of the rehabilitated field are Air Force and Army responsibilities. A combat-heavy engineer battalion
     usually accomplishes the work. Their mission is to convert existing facilities, which are usually damaged, to
     the standard decided on by the Air Force and Army, with a minimum outlay of labor, equipment, and
     materials. Considerable discretion must be exercised in applying standard specifications to captured airfields.
     No large-scale relocation of facilities should be undertaken merely to conform to standard patterns if the
     existing patterns will serve the same purpose in a satisfactory manner. Sensible, existing substitutions and
     deviations from specified arrangements must be recognized and accepted.

     11-132. An appraisal of the damage to a captured field precedes the decision to rehabilitate it. Occasionally,
     it is necessary to expend more effort to restore a badly damaged airfield than to construct a new one. The
     damage includes war damage by our forces in the battle for the airfield and deliberate damage by the enemy
     before yielding the field to our forces. Complete destruction of an airfield is a major undertaking; therefore,
     the enemy will likely resort to one or more of the following less destructive measures:

              Placing delayed-action bombs, mines, and booby traps.
              Demolishing drainage systems and pavements.
              Placing obstacles and debris in the runway.
              Plowing turfed areas.
              Flooding surfaced areas.
              Blowing craters in runways, taxiways, and handstands.
              Demolishing buildings, utilities, and similar installations.

     11-133. When conducting such reconnaissance, assume these damages were inflicted. Use the following
     criteria to prioritize rehabilitation operations for a captured airfield:

              Establish minimum facilities and utilities. Establish a minimum operating strip for immediate
                  operation of friendly aircraft, to include removing unexploded ordnance, delayed-action bombs,
                  mines, and booby traps; clearing debris; and repairing craters on the runway and taxiway surfaces.
                  Promptly repair the drainage system. Concentrate runway work on the minimum operating strip,
                  then on an access route, and finally on other traffic areas. Give early attention to suitable sanitary
                  and water facilities. See TC 5-340 for additional information.

              Improve minimum operational facilities. Restore remaining runways, taxiways, hardstands,
                  parking aprons, access and service roads, and fuel and bomb storage areas before rehabilitating
                  other, less vital facilities.

              Improve other operational facilities. Repair the control tower, operational buildings, crew
                  shelters, communication centers, and other maintenance facilities.

              Final phase of rehabilitation. Camouflage the installation; restore utilities (make use of utility
                  maps and available citizen labor familiar with installation utilities); repair or establish bathing,
                  dining, and recreational facilities; clean up the grounds, to include a complete removal of debris;
                  and seed and sod the installation, as needed.

                                                Chapter 12

                   Road Design and Airfield Layout

         Road selection and design depend on the nature of the subgrade; traffic and drainage
         conditions; the construction time available; the supply of local and imported materials;
         and the engineer equipment, personnel, and expertise available. The completed design
         must meet the requirements for a given load class and allow safe and efficient traffic
         movement. The load-carrying capacity of a road surface depends on continuous, stable
         support furnished by the subgrade. Subgrade stability requires adequate drainage and
         proper load distribution by the surface and base courses. Surface and base courses of
         sufficient thickness and quality to spread the wheel loads over the subgrade are
         necessary so that the applied stress is less than the unit load capacity of the subgrade.
         In areas where seasonal freezing and thawing occur, the load-carrying capacity of
         inadequately designed or improperly constructed roads can be dramatically decreased
         to the extent that failure may occur.

GEOMETRIC DESIGN

     12-1. For safe and speedy traffic movement, the geometric design requirement for road classes must be met.
     In a combat zone, military urgency dictates rough, hasty work designed to meet pressing needs. An improved
     network of well-surfaced, high-quality roads may be required in support areas and near major airfields, ports,
     and supply installations. Road design uses stage construction for the progressive improvement of the road to
     meet increased traffic demands. Road design also uses many technical terms. (See figure 12-1 and figure
     12-2, page 12-2.) UFC 3-250-01FA provides details on the design of bituminous and concrete-surfaced roads,
     UFC 3-250-09FA provides details on the design of aggregate surfaced roads, and UFC 3-250-09FA provides
     details on the geometric design for roads. UFC manuals can be found in the Whole Building and Design
     Guide under Department of Defense criteria.

12-2. The geometric design process begins with good-quality topographic surveys. In most cases, a minimum
5-foot contour interval is required to clearly describe the terrain. EM 1110-1-1005 has information on
topographic surveys. Perform the following steps to complete the design process:

        Step 1. Draw the proposed centerline on the topographic survey.
        Step 2. Plot the centerline on plan and profile paper or with computer-aided design software.
        Step 3. Calculate grades, the degree of curvature of horizontal curves, and curve lengths of vertical

             curves.
        Step 4. Compare these values with the military road specifications stated in table 12-1.
        Step 5. Adjust the centerline, if possible, to reduce any calculated grades and limit horizontal and

             vertical curves that exceed the specifications.
        Step 6. Plot new tangents (straight sections of road) on the plan and profile in those locations

             where horizontal and vertical curves exceed the military road specifications.
        Step 7. Design horizontal and vertical curves for tangent intersections.
        Step 8. Plot newly designed curves on the plan and profile.
        Step 9. Develop a mass diagram for the project. Balance the cuts and fills and optimize ruling

             grade and earthwork volumes.
        Step 10. Design superelevations (curve banking) and widening for horizontal curves.
        Step 11. Draw typical cross sections.
        Step 12. Design the required drainage structures and bridges.

                                                                                                        Road Design and Airfield Layout

SELECTION OF ROAD TYPE

     12-3. Structural characteristics should accommodate traffic volumes throughout the road design life. Table
     12-1, page 12-3, shows four possible road classes. They are based on expected traffic volumes and show the
     values for the design control elements for each road class. The capacities are shown as a range of values.
     Only road Classes B, C, and D apply to JOA construction. If the maximum (or minimum) design value for
     the various criteria is always adhered to, the resulting vehicle capacity of the road will be on the lower side
     of the range. Use discretion by designing the road to the best possible standard in a given road class.

DESIGN CALCULATION

     12-4. The values for each geometric feature must be attained to ensure that the desired road will have a
     capacity equal to or greater than the average daily traffic or design hourly volume shown in table
     12-1, page 12-3. The first step in the design of a road is to estimate the daily or hourly number of vehicles in
     a military organization. If this cannot be done, a conservative estimate is to multiply the number of vehicles
     organic to the units that will use the road by a factor of two. This assumes that each vehicle will use the road
     twice a day (one round-trip).

     12-5. If the anticipated design hourly volume or average daily traffic is known and the sight distance
     restriction can be estimated from preliminary plans, the necessary road type can be determined. (See figure
     12-3 for the relationship between design hourly volume and sight distance restriction.) If average daily traffic
     or design hourly volume and the road type desired are known, sight distance restriction requirements can also
     be determined.

             𝐻𝐻𝐻𝐻𝐻𝐻𝐻𝐻𝐻𝐻𝐻𝐻 𝑣𝑣𝑣𝑣𝑣𝑣𝑣𝑣𝑣𝑣𝑣𝑣 = 500 𝑣𝑣𝑣𝑣ℎ𝑖𝑖𝑖𝑖𝑖𝑖𝑖𝑖𝑖𝑖 𝑝𝑝𝑝𝑝𝑝𝑝 𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑/24 ℎ𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜 𝑝𝑝𝑝𝑝𝑝𝑝 𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑 = 21 𝑣𝑣𝑣𝑣ℎ𝑖𝑖𝑖𝑖𝑖𝑖𝑖𝑖𝑖𝑖 𝑝𝑝𝑝𝑝𝑝𝑝 ℎ𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜
 The calculated design hourly volume of 75 could be met by a Class C road. Therefore, assuming
 that a Class C road is used, plan and profile designs could be drawn and a sight restriction factor
 can be determined from the design.

     12-7. From figure 12-3, page 12-5, a sight distance restriction factor of 62 percent is determined (based on a
     Class C road and a design hourly volume of 75). The maximum sight distance restriction factor for a Class C
     road is 80 percent. This provides a design hourly volume for a Class C road of only 30. Since the sight
     distance restriction factor for the example (62 percent) is less than the maximum of 80, this meets the initial
     requirement of the design hourly volume being greater than or equal to 75. Therefore, the Class C road
     assumption is adequate. If a design hourly volume of 75 could not be handled by the Class C road, it would
     be necessary to construct a Class B road.

ESTIMATING CAPACITY

     12-8. The information in figure 12-3 and table 12-1, page 12-3, is adequate for the geometric design of
     military roads. The information can be used to evaluate the capacity of existing roads by obtaining pertinent
     characteristics and comparing them to the values in table 12-1. If the data does not conform to a given road
     type, estimate the road type and the average daily traffic or design hourly volume that the data best conforms
     to. The volume and capacity values in table 12-1 are for roads that are new or in good condition. As the road
     surface deteriorates, the road is less able to accommodate the traffic for which it was designed. Plan and carry
     out a maintenance program to keep the road in good condition.

GRADE AND ALIGNMENT

     12-9. Before building a road, the engineer must determine the best vertical and horizontal alignment of the
     facility. Design horizontal and vertical alignment to keep sight distance restrictions to a minimum. Define
     the route by a series of straight lines and curves to meet the stated mission and capacity. This provides the
     shortest, most efficient route that requires the least construction effort. Define the route vertically in a series
     of grades and curves that fall within acceptable specifications and requirements. Horizontal and vertical
     alignments are interrelated and must be considered concurrently. However, the principles on each are best
     studied separately. Horizontal and vertical curves are discussed in TM 3-34.55.

HORIZONTAL ALIGNMENT AND HORIZONTAL CURVES

     12-10. Tangents (straight sections of road) should be as long as possible because the shortest distance
     between two points is the connecting straight line. Terrain conditions, however, seldom permit the
     construction of a route between two points in one tangent line. Therefore, to improve route capacity make
     each tangent as long as possible, limit the number of curves, and provide long, straight stretches.

     12-11. Make curves as gentle as possible. Long, gentle curves increase the capacity of the roadway by
     permitting higher speeds. They also provide a safer path of travel for the vehicle. Making gentle, horizontal
     curves will increase the curve length, and decrease the tangent length. However, this reduction in tangent
     length is minor compared to the benefits gained by reducing the total number of curves.

12-6  TM 3-34.48-1  29 February 2016


---

                                                                                                  Road Design and Airfield Layout

12-12. Tangents should intersect other roads and railroads at right angles. Military roads supplement
existing road nets and have intersections at one or both ends of the military road. Operating efficiency usually
is improved when these intersections approach right angles.

12-13. The most common horizontal curves (see figure 12-4) are—

        Simple curve. A simple curve uses the arc of a circle to provide a smooth transition between two
             tangents. This curve is used frequently in the JOA because it fills the needs of the low-speed design
             roads normally used and is easy to construct. A reverse or compound curve can be designed using
             the same basic equations.

        Reverse curve. A reverse curve uses two simple curves that are tangent to a common line at a
             common point. Their centers are on opposite sides of the common line. The radii of the curves
             may not be equal in length.

        Compound curve. A compound curve has two simple curves that are tangent to a common line
             at a common point. The centers of these curves are on the same side of the common line, and the
             curves have radii of different lengths.

        Spiral curve. A spiral curve is a simple curve in the center with parts of a spiral on each end to
             smooth transition to the tangent. The spiral is used only on high-speed roads (Class A and Class
             B). Detailed steps for the design and layout of spiral transition curves are in TM 3-34.55. Low
             design speeds of Class C and Class D roads do not require spiral transition sections.

                  Legend:  radius
                  R

                  Figure 12-4. Types of horizontal curves

ELEMENTS OF A HORIZONTAL CURVE

     12-14. The elements of a simple, horizontal curve (see figure 12-5, page 12-8) are the—
              Point where the curve begins (point of curvature) or leaves tangent A—the tangent nearest the
                  origin of stationing (Station 0 + 00) or start of the project.
              Point where the curve ends (point of tangency) or joins tangent B.
              Intersecting point of two tangents that must be connected by a horizontal curve.
              Tangent distance is the distance from the point of intersection to the point of curvature or from the
                  point of intersection to the point of tangency.
              Radius of curvature is the radius of the circle that forms the curve from point of curvature to point
                  of tangency.

29 February 2016           TM 3-34.48-1                    12-7


---

Chapter 12

              Length of the curve is the distance from point of curvature to point of tangency along the curve,
                  measured as an arc or a series of 100-foot arcs. Railroad engineers measure the length of the curve
                  as a series of 100-foot chords.

              Angle of intersection is the exterior angle at the point of intersection formed by tangents A and B.
                  The central angle, between the radius points at O, is equal to the exterior angle.

              External distance is the distance from the point of intersection to the midpoint of the curve.
              Long chord is the straight-line distance from the point of curvature to the point of tangency.
              Middle ordinate is the distance from the midpoint of the curve to the midpoint of the long chord.

DEGREE OF CURVATURE

     12-15. The connecting curve between two tangents may be short and sharp or long and gentle, depending
     on the properties of the circle chosen. Sharpness is defined by the radius of the circle. For example, a curve
     may be called a 150-foot curve. However, a curve is seldom referred to by its radius because the center of
     the curve is often inaccessible on the long, gentle curves used on modern highways. The more practical and
     common reference term for defining curve sharpness is the degree of curvature. The degree of curvature is
     established as a whole or half degree. The degree of curvature may be stated in terms of the arc or the chord.

Arc Definition

     12-16. The degree of curvature is the angle that subtends a 100-foot arc along the curve. (See figure 12-6.)
     This definition is used by state highway departments and USACE in road design.

12-8           TM 3-34.48-1                                29 February 2016


---

                                                Road Design and Airfield Layout

                  Legend:  degree of curvature
                  D        radius
                  R

                  Figure 12-6. Arc definition for degree of curvature

Chord Definition

     12-17. The degree of curvature is the angle that subtends a 100-foot chord on the curve. (See figure 12-7.)
     This definition results in a slightly larger angle than the arc method, and it is used by the railroad industry
     and USACE in railroad design.

                  Legend:  degree of curvature
                  D        radius
                  R

                  Figure 12-7. Chord definition for degree of curvature

12-18. The difference between the arc and chord definitions is very slight and nearly insignificant
(frequently below 1 percent) for JOA construction. However, because the arc definition is the most widely
used procedure in road design, its definition will be used throughout the rest of the chapter.

EQUATIONS FOR THE SIMPLE, HORIZONTAL-CURVE DESIGN

     12-19. The two methods commonly used to solve horizontal curve problems are the 1° curve method and
     the trigonometric method. These methods may be used with the same degree of accuracy. The 1° curve
     method requires the functions of a 1° curve table (refer to TM 3-34.48-2).

     12-20. Curves of different degrees of curvature can be readily designed because of the proportionality
     between curves and the l° curve. For example, a curve of D = 15° has one-fifteenth the length of the curve,
     external distance, tangent distance, and middle ordinate values as for a 1° curve (D = 1°). The only
     information needed to obtain these values for a 1° curve is the angle of intersection, and the angle of
     intersection is always known at the onset of the design process. The trigonometric method requires a
     calculator with trigonometric functions or trigonometric tables.

Chapter 12

DESIGNING HORIZONTAL CURVES

     12-28. The engineer designing horizontal curves must know two facts about the curve from the preliminary
     survey: the location and station of the point of intersection and the angle between intersecting tangent lines.
     The curves can be designed after this information is obtained.

     12-29. The first step is to determine the desired sharpness of the curve. This is defined by the radius or the
     degree of curvature. Topographic conditions govern the final location of the centerline and sharpness of the
     curve. A maximum or minimum tangent distance may fit the terrain conditions, or there may be a limit on
     the external distance or the middle ordinate. If a restriction exists, solve for the degree of curvature by
     transposing the equations previously given. Where no terrain condition dictates the sharpness of the curve,
     choose a degree of curvature within allowable specifications.

     12-30. When choosing a degree of curvature, remember that gentle curves are more desirable. However,
     these long curves may increase surveying and construction time, materials, and effort required. There is no
     restriction on the length of the curve with respect to a minimum degree of curvature. However, the maximum
     allowable degree of curvature is specified by the road classification. Table 12-1, page 12-3, specifies the
     maximum degree of curvature for each class of road as stated in the row titled Maximum Horizontal
     Curvature.

     12-31. After the degree of curvature is selected, determine the stations of the point of curvature and the
     point of tangency. Next, design the curve except for the calculations needed to locate stationing points of the
     curve between the point of curvature and point of tangency. The following example shows the design of
     horizontal curves using the 1° curve method.

12-37. Horizontal curves are occasionally designed at the site by the surveying team. When this is done,
the route is staked out and stationed progressively along the centerline from the point of origin of the project.
It is not necessary to calculate the station adjustments required by the shortening of the overall centerline

12-38. However, when horizontal curves are designed in an office with the data supplied by the preliminary
survey, the adjustments must be calculated.

12-39. When the preliminary tangent alignment of a route is first determined and stationing along the
tangent lines is accomplished, the station of a point represents its distance from the point of origin as
measured along straight lines only. When a horizontal curve is installed and becomes the centerline of the
route, the stationing distance from the point of curvature to the point of tangency is shortened by 2𝑇𝑇 − 𝐿𝐿 for
each horizontal curve.

12-40. In figure 12-5, page 12-8, the initial centerline distance from the point of curvature to the point of
tangency is measured along the two tangents and is equal to 2𝑇𝑇. When the curve is installed and the new
centerline is created, the final centerline distance from the point of curvature to the point of tangency becomes
the length of the curve. At this point, the centerline stationed ahead would need to be restationed or adjusted.
To prevent restaking the rest of the project centerline, an adjustment is made to the

     second example. Equations are normally shown in the profile section of the plans as a gap in the grade with
     the back and ahead stations written out.

Field Methods of Curve Layout

     12-43. The location and station of the point of curvature and point of tangency of a horizontal curve
     constitute two points on the curve. They do not adequately define the necessary construction. The following
     methods are used in military construction for locating points on the curve:

              Arc method. When the radius of a curve is less than 100 feet and topographic conditions permit,
                  locate the center of the circle and swing an arc to locate a curve or fillet. Curves with a small radius
                  are seldom used except at street intersections and for fillets between hardstands, taxiways, or other
                  operational features of an airfield.

              External-distance method. For short curves where three points are adequate for the construction
                  standard desired, calculate the external distance and locate the center of the curve. This method is
                  not recommended for precise construction or long curves. It is impractical when the terrain on the
                  curve side of the point of intersection is difficult to negotiate and measure.

              Deflection-angle method. This method is usually the fastest and most exact method, particularly
                  for curves with a long radius. In the arc definition, a deflection angle is the angle formed between
                  a tangent line and a chord from the same point. (See figure 12-12.)

Layout Techniques

     12-49. When using the deflection-angle method, set the transit up at the point of curvature. Set zero on the
     vernier, sight the point of intersection (or take a backsight down the centerline), and turn the first deflection
     angle. Measure the subarc distance along the instrument line of sight. To locate the second point on the curve
     (Station 11 + 00), turn the second deflection angle (the angle is measured turning from the point of
     intersection to Station 11 + 00) with the transit still at the point of curvature. Measure the intersection of this
     line of sight and the 100-foot arc from the preceding station to locate Station 11 + 00. Lay out the rest of the
     curve in this manner.

     12-50. If the curve is long so that the transit must be moved or if an obstruction prevents a clear line of
     sight, move the transit to an intermediate station. The same deflection angles previously calculated may be
     used to locate the rest of the curve. (See figure 12-17.)
