                                                                                                        Road Design and Airfield Layout

VERTICAL ALIGNMENT

     12-56. The capabilities of vehicles or aircraft using a particular road or airfield determine the maximum
     allowable grades that should be established. However, other factors may be considered. Excessive grades can
     be installed where speed and capacity are not essential. Whenever possible, grades should be less than the
     prescribed maximum values stated in table 12-1, page 12-3.

     12-57. Within limitations imposed by other criteria, place tangent grade lines so that earthwork is
     minimized. The earthwork required in most road construction projects is usually the largest, single work item.
     Anything that reduces earthwork will improve job efficiency and economy. Attempt to balance earthwork
     operations between cut and fill in an area within the capabilities of available equipment. When drawing the
     grade lines, the engineer can usually do this balancing by inspection, keeping the profile area of cut equal to
     the profile area of fill. These areas are not necessarily proportional to the actual volumes involved, but they
     serve as a basis for comparison. It is impractical to balance a volume of cut with an equivalent volume of fill
     at a distance beyond the hauling capabilities of available equipment.

     12-58. Along any proposed route will be points at which the elevation is already fixed. Intersections with
     existing roads and railroad crossings present predetermined elevations that the engineer must meet when
     locating the tangent grade lines.

     12-59. In addition to the controlling specifications for grades, other criteria may control the placement of
     grade lines. These criteria include the minimum allowable gradients, the maximum allowable change in grade
     at an intersection point, the permissible depth of cut or fill, and the maximum gradients in approaching
     bridges or points of intersection.

PLOTTING A PROFILE VIEW

     12-60. The profile of a road or airfield is a side view of the project. It represents the horizontal distance, or
     stations, as abscissa (x axis) against the elevations at these stations, which are plotted as ordinates (y axis).
     When a horizontal alignment is set and the project stationed, determine the elevation of critical points along
     the centerline. Engineers usually calculate the elevation at half and full stations, point of vertical curvature,
     point of vertical intersection, and high- and low-point elevations.

     12-61. A break point where the prevailing grade makes an appreciable change should be stationed and the
     elevation ascertained. The most common procedure for determining existing terrain elevations is by ground
     survey. However, it is possible to obtain elevations for specific points from a contour map on which the
     proposed horizontal alignment has been plotted. Unless the scale of the contour map is large, this method is
     inaccurate and should be used for preliminary planning and initial location. The centerline profile may not
     represent the typical or prevailing condition across the entire section at a particular point. This error may be
     noticeable when the section is wide, as for an airfield. In such cases, additional profiles may be needed along
     the shoulder line. It is also possible to make a typical profile that represents the average elevation across the
     entire section.

PLOTTING TRIAL GRADE LINES

     12-62. After studying the profile, determine the tangent grade lines. These grade lines serve as the proposed
     final profile of the project. It is possible for rough, pioneer construction to follow existing contours with a
     little smoothing of rough spots. Such a route provides a rough and relatively unsafe roadbed that is not capable
     of carrying a large volume of traffic. A well-designed route has a series of tangent grades with a smooth
     transition between them. These tangent grade lines can be determined with a good profile.

GRADE DETERMINATION

     12-63. The degree of steepness measured longitudinally is normally defined as the percentage of grade. It
     is established as a relationship between vertical rise or fall for each 100-foot horizontal distance and is
     expressed as a percentage (per 100).

VERTICAL CURVES

     12-64. After grade lines are placed, define the route vertically in a series of grade lines (straight segments
     of constant grade) between points of vertical intersection. Design a transition that provides smooth, easy
     movement from one grade line to another at these intersections. The vertical curves used for this transition
     and its pertinent dimensions are easily calculated.

Types of Vertical Curves

     12-65. Two types of vertical curves must be considered: sags and crest. Figure 12-19 shows a typical
     vertical curve installed between two grade lines. The parts of a vertical curve include the following:

              Point of vertical intersection. The point of vertical intersection is the intersection of two grade
                  lines. This station is always read from the profile view.

              Point of vertical curvature. The point of vertical curvature is the point along the first grade line
                  at which the vertical curve begins. The grade line is tangent to the parabolic curve at this point.
                  By convention, the point of vertical curvature is always one-half the length of the vertical curve
                  from the point of vertical intersection, measured horizontally.

              Point of vertical tangency. The point of vertical tangency is the point along the second grade line
                  at which the vertical curve ends. It has the same properties as the point of vertical curvature.

              Percent of grade. The percentage of grade on the grade line nearest the point of origin is called
                  G1, and the other grade line percentage is called G2. These two grade lines, which are tangent to
                  the parabolic curve at the point of vertical curvature and point of vertical tangency, intersect at the
                  point of vertical intersection.

              Length of vertical curve. The length of vertical curve is the horizontal distance from the point of
                  vertical curvature to the point of vertical tangency. The point of vertical intersection is horizontally
                  midway between the point of vertical curvature and point of vertical tangency. Therefore, the
                  distance from the point of vertical curvature to the point of vertical intersection is the length of the
                  vertical curve divided by 2, and the distance from the point of vertical intersection to the point of
                  vertical tangency is also the length of the vertical curve divided by 2.

              Offsets. Offsets are the vertical distances from the grade lines to the vertical curve. The heights
                  of offsets are computed for selected points along the length of the vertical curve. The selected
                  points are usually at every station and half station.

              Maximum offset. The maximum offset is the offset at the point of vertical intersection. It is always
                  the greatest offset along the vertical curve.

Design of Vertical Curves

     12-66. The design of vertical curves includes the following tasks:
              Determine the curve length.
              Calculate the heights of a sufficient number of offsets to adequately define or locate the final grade
                  line.

     12-67. It is possible to design vertical curves to be long and gentle (flat) or short and abrupt. This is done
     by varying the curve length. Depending on the facility to be constructed and the standards of construction
     desired, there are certain limitations on curve length. Minimum lengths are usually specified.

     12-68. The difference in grade between two grade lines is called the change in grade (∆G). This difference
     (symbolized as G) is computed as |G1 – G2|, which represents the absolute value of G1 – G2. The curve
     installed between two grade lines with a large difference in grade, which might occur at the top of a steep
     hill, is longer than the curve required between two grades with a smaller difference in grade.

     12-69. Criteria have been established to ensure that the rate at which the change in gradient is made
     throughout a vertical curve is consistent with the operating characteristics of the vehicles or aircraft using the
     facility. Allowable rate of change (symbolized as r) is expressed as an allowable rate of change of grade for
     a specific horizontal distance. For example, with a criterion of 0.5 percent change in grade over 500 feet, a
     difference in grade of 1.0 percent requires a curve length of 1,000 feet. However, the allowable rate of change
     is usually expressed as the allowable gradient change in 100 feet of length. The allowable rate of change of
     grade is frequently used for airfield vertical curve design.

     12-70. When a crest curve is traversed, the ability of the driver to see down the road or airfield is curtailed.
     If a vertical curve is quite short, the distance that can be seen ahead becomes critically short. Reduced speed
     is required to reduce the safety hazard. Sight distance (symbolized as S) depends on the design speed
     permitted.

     12-71. The vertical-curve-length factor (symbolized as k) is used when determining road vertical curve
     lengths. It is equal to the horizontal distance, in feet, required to effect a 1-percent change in gradient while
     providing the minimum stopping distance.

    Note. The offsets at equal distances from the point of vertical curvature or point of vertical
    tangency are equal. In other words, the offsets are symmetric about the point of vertical
    intersection. This does not mean that the resulting curve is symmetric (unless G1 = G2). The offset
    for only one side of a vertical curve needs to be calculated. Therefore, the above equation can be
    used to calculate the offset at any point within the vertical curve.

12-84. By using the calculated curve elevations and the existing ground elevations, we can determine the
cut or fill values to place on the grade stakes for construction operations. The ground elevations can be
determined from the profile view established from the initial survey. The difference in elevation between the
curve and the ground elevation constitutes the cut or fill value. For example, if the ground elevation at a point
on a curve was 86 feet and the curve elevation at that point was 82 feet, the construction stake would indicate
a cut of 4 feet (86 feet minus 82 feet).

12-89. The design of vertical curves using metric units is the same as English units. The only difference is
the use of meters as units of measurement for elevations and distances. Vertical curves should normally be
staked at 50-foot (every half station) or 10-meter intervals. On extremely rugged terrain, the interval should
be reduced.

CROWNED SECTION

     12-90. The typical cross section of a road is the crowned cross section. The amount of crown provided
     depends on the type of surface used. Normal crown slopes are 2 percent for asphalt and 4 percent for
     aggregate surfaced roads. Figure 12-24 shows a typical cross section for a Class A road. If the road is to be
     surfaced, the subgrade and the finished surface will have the same crown.

Note. A 3 foot shoulder widening is required for guardrails and guideposts.

    12-91. Design slopes to be as flat as is reasonable. Generally, low cuts and fills are economical to construct
    on relatively flat slopes and will enhance aesthetics, safety, and maintenance. Where practical, embankment
    front slopes should be 1V:4H or flatter. Slopes 1V:3H are generally traversable by an errant vehicle that has
    run off the road but do not provide for vehicle recovery. Front slopes steeper than 1V:3H will cause most
    vehicles to overturn. (See table 12-6 for desirable and maximum slope ratios.)

    12-92. Variable slope ratios for cut and fill slopes are desirable to minimize earthwork in high fill areas and
    enhance safety in low fill areas. Avoid using constant slope ratios. When varying slope ratios, a rule-of-
    thumb is at minimum to vary one unit of the horizontal slope ratio over 50 feet of linear roadway distance,

   12-93. Cut and fill slopes steeper than 1V:2H should be avoided in clay and silty soils subject to erosion.
   Loessal soils require special design for cut slopes. Embankment height and side slope are the basic factors
   considered in determining whether a guardrail is needed. Embankment side slopes 1V:3H and flatter do not
   require guardrail. Embankments with a side slope of 1V:2H and a height greater than 6 feet require a
   guardrail.

SUPERELEVATION

   12-94. The outer edge of a road is elevated to balance the overturning forces experienced by a vehicle
   rounding a horizontal curve. The amount of superelevation is governed by the degree of curvature (or the
   curve radius) and the design speed. Detailed information for designing superelevation on curves is in TM
   3-34.55. Table 12-7 lists superelevation rates and appropriate transition lengths to develop the superelevated
   section as a function of the design speed and degree of curvature. Figure 12-25, page
   12-38, shows a Class A road section with a superelevated curve.

   12-95. As a safety factor, the pavement width on the inside lane of a curve is increased. The amount of
   increase is governed by the degree of curvature and the design speed.

Chapter 12

SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS FOR ROADS IN MOUNTAINOUS
TERRAIN

     12-97. There are a number of design and construction elements that should be considered in mountainous
     terrain. The following paragraphs provide guidance on vertical alignments, road prisms or bench cuts, and
     embankments.

VERTICAL ALIGNMENT

     12-98. Divide long grades with relief sections (level or adversely sloped) where possible to prevent heavy
     truck brake overheating and failure. Switchbacks may be necessary in mountainous areas with steep grades.
     Switchbacks are designed with a minimum centerline radius of 60 feet. The roadway width through
     switchback horizontal curves will have to be widened to allow vehicles to negotiate the curve. Where
     practical, reduce the gradient through sharp switchback curves to facilitate braking and vehicle control in the
     vicinity of the switchback. For switchbacks with a curve speed of 20 miles per hour, a maximum gradient of
     4 percent is recommended. For switchbacks with a curve speed of 25 miles per hour, a maximum gradient of
     5 percent is recommended.

ROAD PRISM SELECTION

     12-99. The proper design of the roadway prism can significantly reduce the amount of sediment and debris
     that enters adjacent streams. Often the basic cause of a particular mass failure can be traced to overroading
     or overdesign. Cuts facilitate stability within the roadway by reflecting stability downward.

Sliver Bench Cut

     12-100. Sliver bench construction involves excavating a bench in the existing embankment and using the
     material to construct a sliver fill. A sliver fill is defined as a wedge-shaped fill used to form the road
     embankment.

     12-101. Where the existing sideslopes are 1V:3H or less, the sliver fill may be constructed by sidecasting
     excavated material and compacting in lifts. Existing slopes 1V:4H to 1V:3H should be plowed, stepped, or
     otherwise broken up so that fill material will bond with the existing material.

     12-102. Where the existing sideslopes exceed 1V:3H, the sliver fill should be keyed into the existing
     embankment slope using 2- to 8-foot high benches to allow for a stable joining of new and existing
     embankment material as indicated in figure 12-27. The minimum bench width should be 12 feet to
     accommodate placement and compaction operations and equipment. Construction of sliver fills by simply
     sidecasting excavated soil over the edge of the existing embankment is not recommended. This technique
     does not allow for adequate compaction of the sliver fill.

            max

Full Bench Cut

     12-103. Full bench construction typically involves excavation of the roadbed using a hydraulic excavator.
     (See figure 12-28.) A bench is cut into the rock or soil equal to the width of the road plus the width of the
     ditch, if required. Normally, no material is sidecast, and excavated waste is used to fill low areas along the
     road alignment. Full bench road construction is typically used on steeper sideslopes over 1V:2H. Endhauling
     of excavated material can be expensive, and full bench construction can cost four to seven times more than
     balanced cut and fill methods. Also, full bench roads often result in tall cut slopes. Several rock and soil types
     may not support these large cut slopes.

                                                Figure 12-28. Full bench cut

Fill-Side Retaining Wall

     12-104. Where the existing sideslopes are steeper than 1V:1.5H, the sidefill may have to be contained within
     a suitable retaining wall to avoid long fill slopes. (See figure 12-29.) Suitable retaining wall types include
     reinforced concrete walls, mechanically stabilized earth walls, soil nail walls, and bin walls.

                                          Figure 12-29. Fill-side retaining wall

EARTHEN EMBANKMENTS

     12-105. Embankment benching is designed for construction of embankments on existing ground that is
     sloping by 1V:3H or steeper and for narrow embankments. Cut horizontal benches in the existing slope to a
     sufficient width to accommodate placement and compaction operations and equipment. Bench the slope as

     the embankment is placed and compacted in layers. Begin each bench at the intersection of the original
     ground and the vertical cut of the previous bench. A riprap keyway should be constructed at the base of
     earthen embankments with front slopes of 1V:1.5H as indicated in figure 12-30.

12-106. Place embankment material in horizontal layers not exceeding 12 inches in compacted thickness.
Incorporate oversize boulders or rock fragments into the 12-inch layers by reducing them in size or placing
them individually. Material composed primarily of boulders or rock fragments too large for 12-inch layers
may be placed in layers up to 24 inches thick. Incorporate oversize boulders or rock fragments into the
24-inch layer by reducing them in size or placing them individually. Place sufficient earth and smaller rocks
to fill the voids, and compact.

12-107. Place rock fragments and boulders greater than 24 inches in diameter individually. Reduce rock to
less than 48 inches in the largest dimension. Distribute rock within the embankment to prevent nesting. Place
layers of embankment material around each rock. Fill the voids between rocks. Compact each layer before
placing the next layer.

ROCK EMBANKMENTS

     12-108. Rock embankments may be used where steeper front slopes are required in mountainous terrain.
     Embankment benching is constructed when required for earthen embankments. Embankment benching is
     required for soil and rock foundations. Where rock embankments are being constructed on a soil foundation,
     the bottom layer of riprap should be keyed into the soil to provide a good interlock between the rock and the
     ground. (See figure 12-31.) Where rock embankments are being constructed on a rock foundation, dowels
     should be installed in the existing rock, and the bottom layer of riprap should be grouted. (See figure 12-32.)
     Dowels should be grouted into the existing rock and spaced at 3- to 6-foot intervals.

12-109. The maximum slope of rock embankments constructed with riprap is 1V:1.25H. The rock
embankment can be constructed of placed riprap or keyed riprap. Generally, rock embankments are a
combination of placed and keyed riprap. Placed riprap is rock placed by hand or with a machine to obtain a
dense uniform blanket. Keyed riprap is rock placed on a prepared surface and set into place by impact
pressure. Set the riprap into place by exerting impact pressure with a hydraulic-powered bucket or an
approximate 5,000-pound, 4-foot by 5-foot flat faced mass. Repeated impacts are made until the rock is
firmly seated and forms a reasonably uniform surface without reducing the effective sizes of the rock. The
top portion of rock embankments below the pavement should be covered with geotextile or choked with
smaller rock to prevent pavement subgrade materials from migrating into voids between the riprap.

12-110. The maximum slope of rock embankments constructed with grouted riprap is 1V:1H. Grouted riprap
is rock placed or keyed on a prepared surface, and the voids are filled with grout. Each layer of grouted riprap
should not exceed 5-foot in thickness. (See figure 12-33, page 12-44, and figure 12-34, page 12-44.) After
placing each riprap layer, thoroughly moisten the rocks and wash excess fines from the riprap. Place grout
when the air temperature is no less than 35 degrees Fahrenheit within the near-surface voids of the riprap.
Place the grout in a manner to prevent segregation. Begin placing grout at the lowest elevation of the riprap.

     Fill voids without unseating the rocks. Allow 3 days curing time before adding the next layer of riprap and
     grout. Keep grouted riprap moist for 3 days after the work is completed. Protect the area from freezing for a
     minimum of 7 days after grouting is completed. Keyed riprap may be used behind the grouted riprap in some
     circumstances to reduce the amount of grout that is required.

ROCK CUT SLOPES

     12-111. Discontinuities (joints, foliations, shears, faults) are important factors in the stability of rock slopes.
     The orientation, frequency, persistence, and strength of rock discontinuities are obtained from existing cuts,
     outcrops, or rock cores. The shear strength of rock along the discontinuities that separate the rock mass into
     discrete blocks is a more critical rock slope stability parameter than the strength of the intact rock.
     Groundwater pressure acting with discontinuities can cause significant destabilization by decreasing the shear
     strength due to uplift and increasing the driving forces acting on the block. Typically, the groundwater level
     within a slope can be estimated by observing seepages from and around the rock slope.

     12-112. Some slope construction methods damage the rock so that the finished cut slope has an increased
     likelihood of long-term rockfall. Uncontrolled blasting can cause fracturing and open existing fractures tens
     of feet into the slope. A finished cut slope can be constructed by excavating rock using heavy equipment
     ripping or production blasting techniques, or it can be augmented with controlled blasting methods. The use

12-44           TM 3-34.48-1                          29 February 2016


---

                                                Road Design and Airfield Layout

of controlled blasting, presplitting (preshear) or trim (cushion) blasting, produces a cut slope with
significantly less potential for rockfall. Lightly loaded, aligned, and closely spaced blast holes are used to
form the final cut slope face to minimize the effects of intense detonation gas pressures caused by production
blasting. Controlled blasting is performed before main production blasting is detonated (presplit blasting) or
after production blasting (cushion blasting). In presplit blasting, a row of control blast holes is detonated to
form a break in the slope along the final cut slope, which serves to vent production gas pressure and keep it
from penetrating and damaging the rock that will form the final cut face. In cushion blasting, a row of control
blast holes is detonated last to trim off the rock outside the cut slope. The cushion blasting technique is
normally used in weaker rock conditions or when the rock thickness to be excavated is less than 15 feet.
Controlled blasting is routinely used for rock cuts that are 1V:0.75H or steeper.

12-113. Avoid cut slopes in bedrock dipping down toward the road (downwards out of the slope) because
this type of slope may cave boulders onto the road later. This type of geologic alignment s prone to direct
subsurface drainage toward the road or fill slope. Consider stabilizing uphill slopes by removing perched
boulders and cracked rock faces.

12-114. Rock slope and rockfall issues can often be mitigated by several different options, including fall out
ditches, barriers, catch fences, draped mesh, rock bolting, dowels, shotcrete facing, cable lashing, and
buttresses. Cuts less than 20 feet in height generally do not require a fallout ditch. Rock slopes higher than
30 feet from shoulder grade may require wider fallout ditches.

12-115. When soil or highly weathered rock overlays solid rock, consider designing overburden benches at
the top of the solid rock. The overburden slope should range from 1V:3H to 1V:2H, depending on the type
and depth of overburden and the steepness of the topography. (See table 12-9.)

SPRAY APPLICATIONS AND SURFACE TREATMENTS

     12-116. Surface treatments are the most economical troop-constructed surfaces. They require the fewest
     resources and minimal quality control effort, and they are placed in the shortest period of time. Surface
     treatments range from single, light applications of bituminous material to multiple-surface courses made up
     of bitumen and aggregates. Surface treatments can be divided into two categories: sprayed treatments and
     sprayed bitumen with an aggregate surface.

     12-117. Spray applications, when used as a prime coat or for dustproofing, provide soil or aggregate surfaces
     with the following benefits:

              Waterproofing.
              Dust control.
              Stabilization of the surface.

     12-118. Spray applications are also used for tack coats and fog seals. The tack coat is used when an asphalt
     mixture is placed over an existing paved surface. In this case, a tack coat is applied to the existing surface to

29 February 2016                TM 3-34.48-1                             12-45


---

Chapter 12

bond the two layers together. A tack coat should be used each time an additional layer is placed. The fog seal
is applied to an existing asphalt surface to help seal surface voids and rejuvenate the surface.

12-119. Sprayed bitumen with an aggregate surface provides a waterproof, abrasive, and wear-resistant
surface. The surface treatment provides little additional structural strength over the underlying base course.
Bitumen with aggregate surface treatments will be single-surface or multiple-surface treatment.

12-120. Bituminous materials are emulsified coal tar, asphalt cement, asphalt cutbacks, or asphalt emulsions.
(See table 12-10 for uses of bituminous materials.) Asphalt cement is the heavy material left at the end of the
petroleum distillation process. Crude oil is refined into gasoline, kerosene, diesel, motor oil, asphalt, and
other products. (See figure 12-35.) Asphalt cement may then be further modified by cutting back the asphalt
with a petroleum product (such as naphtha, gasoline, kerosene, or diesel) to form an asphalt cutback. Asphalt
can also be converted into an emulsion by mixing asphalt cement, water, and an emulsifying agent together
with variable-speed pumps to form an asphalt water suspension. Emulsions are anionic (carrying a negative
charge) or cationic (carrying a positive charge). The emulsifying agent determines whether the emulsion is
anionic or cationic and whether it is slow set, medium set, or rapid set.

     12-121. Tars are the residue from high-temperature conversion of coal to coke. (See figure 12-36.) While
     there are tars, cutback tars, and emulsified tars, it is recommended that only emulsified tars be considered for
     use since tar has more environmental issues than asphalt. These tar materials should be used in areas that
     expect to be exposed to petroleum products (gasoline, oil, grease). (See the ASTM on standard specification
     for emulsified refined coal-tar (ready to use, commercial grade) for additional information.) Tars must be
     handled with care when heated because the emissions may irritate the skin. For this reason, the only tar
     discussed in this manual is emulsified coal tar, which can be placed at relatively low temperatures. Tars do
     not dissolve in petroleum products. Tars should be used to seal existing asphalt pavements to provide
     waterproofing and fuel resistant qualities to the pavement.

FIELD IDENTIFICATION

     12-122. Field identification consists of a series of simple tests designed to identify an unknown bitumen
     product in the field. The purpose of these tests is to determine the use of a bituminous material and how to
     use it safely, not the exact specifications that it conforms to. Field-identification procedures are applicable to
     tars and asphalts.

     12-123. Bituminous materials are often stockpiled in unmarked or incorrectly marked containers. This leads
     to confusion and delay during construction because various types and grades of bituminous material are
     manufactured for a specific purpose. Field identification is important to the military engineer because—

              Once the type and grade of material are known, the type of surface that can be constructed can be
                  determined. The safety procedures to be followed also depend on the material identification.

              Once the surface type is known, the construction procedure can be outlined and scheduled for a
                  specific target date.

              Once established, the procedure will determine the proper equipment for the job.

     12-124. Field tests may be performed to identify the bituminous paving material as asphalt cement, asphalt
     cutback, asphalt emulsion, or emulsified coal tar. In addition, it is necessary to identify the viscosity grade of
     the bitumen as close as possible. To distinguish among several asphalt and tar products, it is necessary to
     know something of their origin, physical properties, and the way they are normally used. The identification
     procedure outlined is based on the physical properties of these materials. (See figure 12-37, page 12-50.)

Asphalts and Tars

     12-125. The first procedure in the identification of an unknown bituminous material is to determine if it is
     asphalt or tar. Asphalts and tars may be differentiated by a simple solubility test. To perform the test, attempt
     to dissolve an unknown sample (a few drops if it is liquid or enough to cover the head of a nail if it is solid)
     in any petroleum distillate. Kerosene, gasoline, diesel oil, or jet fuel is suitable for this test. Since asphalt is
     derived from petroleum, it will dissolve in the petroleum distillate. Road tar will not dissolve. If the sample
     is asphalt, the distillate mix will consist of a dark, uniform liquid. If the sample is road tar, the sample will
     be a dark, stringy, undissolved mass in the distillate mix. A check can be made by spotting a piece of paper
     or cloth with the mix. The solubility test provides a positive method of identification.

Grades of Asphalt Cement

     12-126. The various grades of asphalt cement are distinguished by their hardness at designated temperatures.
     Methods for identifying classification of asphalts include penetration, viscosity, and performance graded.
     Most of the United States use performance-graded asphalts, but in other areas of the world the grades might
     be based on viscosity or penetration. A stiffer grade of asphalt resists rutting better, but may result in more
     thermal and fatigue cracking. The selected grade of asphalt will depend on the climate and traffic level. For
     hotter climates or pavements subjected to higher traffic levels, a stiffer grade of asphalt is normally selected.
     When in doubt, use local experience when selecting a grade of asphalt cement to use.

Asphalt Cutbacks

     12-127. The pouring or nonpouring quality is one way to distinguish between asphalt cement and a cutback
     or emulsion. Asphalt cement is cutback with a petroleum distillate to make it more fluid; this is called cutback
     asphalt. If the material does not pour, it is asphalt cement. At 77 degrees Fahrenheit, even the softest asphalt
     cement will not pour or deform noticeably if the container is tilted. If it pours, it is a cutback or emulsion. If
     it is soluble or dilutable in water, it is an emulsion. Also, cutback asphalts have a distinctive gasoline, diesel,
     or other solvent smell.

12-128. To determine if a cutback is a rapid cure or not, a smear test is performed. Smear the substance
uniformly on a piece of glazed paper or another nonabsorbent surface. If volatile materials are present, they
will evaporate. Since rapid cures are cut back with a very volatile substance, most of the volatiles will
evaporate within 10 minutes. The surface of the smear will then become tacky. This is not true of lighter
grades of medium- and slow-curing asphalt cutbacks, which remain fluid and smooth for some time. A
medium cure will not result in a tacky surface for hours, and slow cure will require several days.

12-129. To identify an 800- or 3,000-grade medium-cure or slow-cure cutback, a prolonged smear test is
used. This process is necessary because these grades of medium cure and slow cure contain such small
quantities of cutterstock that they may also become tacky in the 10-minute period specified above. A thin

12-50                                 TM 3-34.48-1                            29 February 2016


---

                                                                                                        Road Design and Airfield Layout

     smear of the material is made on a nonabsorbent surface and left to cure for at least 2 hours. By the end of
     that time, if the material being tested is a rapid cure, the smear will have cured and will be hard or slightly
     sticky. However, if the material being tested is a medium or slow cure, the smear will not be cured and will
     still be quite sticky or fluid-like. If the material is a rapid cure 3,000, it will cure completely in 3 hours, but a
     rapid cure 800 will take about 6 hours. Even after 24 hours, a medium or slow cure will still be sticky.

     12-130. Since medium cures are cutback with kerosene and slow cures are cutback with oil, this may be used
     to differentiate between them. If kerosene is present, heat will produce an odor. It is best to heat the unknown
     sample in a closed container to capture the escaping vapors. Do not apply too much heat. If the sample is a
     medium cure, it will have a strong petroleum or kerosene odor. But if the sample is a slow cure, no kerosene
     or petroleum odor will be detected. It may smell like hot motor oil. The ability to distinguish them from each
     other is perhaps as important as any other part of field identification.

Asphalt Emulsions

     12-131. Another asphalt material used in paving work is an asphalt emulsion, which is a mixture of asphalt,
     water, and an emulsifying agent. It is easy to identify since it is usually distinguished by its dark brown color,
     while other bitumens are black. If mixed with kerosene or some other petroleum distillate, the emulsion can
     be detected by the appearance of small black globules or beads which fall to the bottom of the container. If
     mixed with water, an emulsion will accept the extra water and still remain a uniform liquid. The other
     bitumens will not mix with water. Since an emulsion contains water, a small piece of cloth saturated with it
     will not burn if a flame is applied. The other bitumens will burn or flame. After it has been established that
     the material is an emulsion, it is still important to know if the emulsion is a mixing grade. The best way to
     determine if the emulsion is a mixing grade (slow setting or medium setting) is to try to mix a small amount
     (6 to 8 percent by weight) with damp sand, using a metal spoon. A rapid-setting emulsion cannot be mixed;
     it breaks immediately, gumming up the spoon with the relatively hard original asphalt cement. A slow-setting
     or medium-setting emulsion mixes nicely, coating the sand. Do not add too much emulsion to the sand. This
     will saturate the sand and give inconclusive results. No further identification is necessary since medium-
     setting and slow-setting grades are largely used for the same jobs.

Emulsified Coal Tar

     12-132. If an unknown bituminous material is liquid at 77 degrees Fahrenheit, it is an emulsion or a cutback.
     Add water to the mixture. If the water mixes with the material, it is an emulsion. Add heat to remove the
     water in the emulsified coal tar, and place the material in a petroleum distillate. If the unknown bituminous
     material did not dissolve in the solubility test but formed a stringy mass, the material is tar. If it dissolved, it
     is asphalt.

AGGREGATE IDENTIFICATION

     12-133. Aggregate must also be tested to determine its suitability for bituminous construction. The desirable
     characteristics of an aggregate used in bituminous construction include—

              Angular and rough.
              Tough, hard, and durable.
              Clean and dry.
              Hydrophobic.

     12-134. Available aggregate may not always have desirable characteristics. An aggregate meeting most of
     the requirements is usually selected, unless rejected for other reasons (availability, length of haul, difficulty
     in conducting borrow-pit or quarry operations).

Angular and Rough

     12-135. The aggregate in a pavement must transmit the traffic load to the base, usually by the interlocking
     and surface friction of the different particles. Angular particles with a rough texture are best for this purpose
     since they do not tend to slide past each other. More binder may be required since the angular shaped

29 February 2016  TM 3-34.48-1  12-51


---

Chapter 12

     aggregate does not pack as closely together as a more rounded aggregate, thus requiring more asphalt to fill
     the voids to the proper level.

Tough, Hard, and Durable

     12-136. The aggregate must withstand loads without cracking or being crushed. Resistance to weathering is
     also a function of the durability. The resistance-to-wear of an aggregate can be determined by the Los Angeles
     Abrasion Test, if equipment is available. Equipment and procedures are detailed in the American Association
     of State Highway and Transportation Officials method T96. Equipment for the test is not usually available
     for field testing. The Mohs’ hardness scale may be used to determine the hardness of the aggregate. The
     Mohs’ scale ranges from 1 for talc or mica to 10 for diamond. By trying to scratch the aggregate or the
     common materials and vice versa, it is possible to establish which is harder; from this analysis the hardness
     of the aggregate can be determined. If both materials scratch each other, the hardness of each is the same. Be
     sure to rub the scratch mark to see that it is really a scratch and not a powdering of the softer material. Some
     common materials and their hardness are: fingernail, about 2; copper coin, between 3 and 4; and knife blade,
     nail, and window glass, about 5.5. If the material can be scratched with one of these common items, it is
     considered to be soft. If it cannot be scratched, it is considered to be hard.

Clean and Dry

     12-137. The bituminous binder must penetrate into the pores of the aggregate and adhere to the surface of
     the particles. Coated (with clay or dust) or water-filled aggregate will prevent the penetration or the adherence
     of the binder and result in stripping of the binder. For hot mixes, the aggregate must be hot and dry. If the
     aggregate is not clean, it should be washed as part of the crushing operation or by spreading it on a hard
     surface and hosing it with water. When washing is impractical, dry screening may remove a great deal of
     dust and clay. Hand picking may be necessary if no other method can be used. The aggregate should be made
     as clean as possible with the equipment and manpower available.

Hydrophobic

     12-138. Affinity for water can make an aggregate undesirable. If the aggregate is porous and absorbs water
     easily (hydrophilic), the binder can be forced out of the pores. When this happens, the bond between the
     aggregate and binder weakens, resulting in stripping. Stripping is the loss of the bituminous coating from the
     aggregate particles due to the action of water, leaving exposed aggregate surfaces. The stripping test or the
     swell test can be used to determine the detrimental effect of water on a bituminous mix.

Stripping Test

     12-139. A test sample is prepared by coating a specific amount of aggregate with bituminous material at the
     applicable temperature for the grade of bitumen to be used. The mixture is spread in a loose, thin layer and
     air-cured for 24 hours. A representative sample is placed in a jar (no more than one-half of the jar capacity)
     and covered with water. The jar is closed tightly and allowed to stand 24 hours. At the end of 24 hours, the
     jar with the sample is vigorously shaken for 15 minutes. A visual examination is made to determine the
     percentage of exposed aggregate surface that is reported as percent stripping.

Swell Test

     12-140. Asphalt mixtures containing fines of doubtful quality are sometimes measured for swell as a basis
     for judging the possible effects on a pavement. This test is more frequently used with dense-graded mixtures
     using liquid asphalts. A sample of the mix is compacted in a metal cylinder and cooled to room temperature.
     The specimen and mold are placed in a pan of water and a dial gage is mounted above the sample in contact
     with the surface. An initial reading is taken. The specimen soaks for a specified period (usually 24 hours) or
     until there is no further swelling. Another reading of the dial is taken. The difference is the swell of the
     mixture. Experience has shown that bituminous pavement made with clear, sound stone; slag; or gravel
     aggregate and mineral filler produced from limestone will show test values of less than 1.5 percent.
     Aggregates of doubtful character should be tested for conformance to ASTM tests.

CONSTRUCTION METHODS

     12-141. The following paragraphs describe proper construction methods for three different types of
     bituminous spray applications: prime coat, tack coat, and dust proofing.

PRIME COAT

     12-142. A prime coat is used when a surface treatment or pavement is placed on a soil or aggregate base.
     The prime coat should penetrate the base about 1/4 inch, filling the voids. The prime coat acts as a waterproof
     barrier to prevent moisture from penetrating the wearing surface and reaching the base. Also, the bitumen
     acts as a bonding agent, binding the particles of the base to the wearing surface. Plan priming operations so
     that there will always be an adequate amount of cured, primed base ahead of the surfacing operations, but
     not so far ahead that the base will become dirty or completely cured (dead). To preserve the base, a prime
     coat should be applied as soon as the base is ready; however, the prime coat will lose its effectiveness as a
     bonding agent if the wearing surface is not placed soon after curing. Typically, one should wait at least 48
     hours after priming before material is placed above the primed base.

Base Preparation

     12-143. The base should be well-graded, shaped to the desired cross section, compacted to the specified
     density, well-drained, not too wet but not completely dry, and swept clean. The surface of the base should be
     broomed if it contains excessive loose material (fine or coarse) or dust. Exercise caution when brooming to
     ensure that it does not excessively loosen and remove aggregate particles. Completely cover the base with a
     minimum amount of water and allow it to become dry or almost dry before applying the prime coat so that it
     will absorb the prime material. If the base is too wet, it will not take the prime properly—the moisture may
     come out, particularly in hot weather, and strip the prime from the base during construction. Rain may strip
     the prime from a base that was too wet when primed. Heavy rain may strip a properly primed base to some
     extent, but less than an improperly cured base. However, if a base dries out completely, cracks may develop
     and a heavy rain may cause swelling and loss of density.

Materials

12-144. Bituminous materials used for prime coats will depend on the condition of the soil base and the
climate. In moderate and warm climates, MC-30, MC-70, SS-1, SS-1h, CSS-1 and CSS-1h are satisfactory.
In cold climates, rapid-setting asphalt cutbacks, such as RC-70 and RC-250, are sometimes more satisfactory.
If the climate is damp and cold, the prime coat is sometimes eliminated because it is likely to be extremely
slow in curing. The following formula is used to determine the quantity of prime coat material required:

TACK COAT

     12-145. A tack coat is a sprayed application of a bituminous material that is applied to an existing wearing
     surface of concrete, brick, bituminous material, or binder course before a new bituminous mixture is placed
     over the existing surface. The purpose of the tack coat is to provide a bond between the existing surface and
     the new surface. The tack coat should become tacky within a few hours. A tack coat is not required on a
     primed base unless the prime coat has completely cured and become coated with dust. Figure 12-38 shows
     the sequence of operations for the application of a tack coat.

               Figure 12-38. Tack-coat sequence of operations

prime coat except that the tack coat is generally applied over the proposed width of the pavement. The
following formula is used to determine the quantity of tack coat required:

tachometer chart may be used to establish the rate of application. The usual rate of application varies between

DUSTPROOFING

     12-148. Dustproofing consists of spraying an untreated surface with a diluted, slow-setting asphalt emulsion
     or a low-viscosity cutback. The asphalt and diluent penetrate the fine soil particles and adhere to the dust
     particles.

     12-149. An asphalt cutback is usually sprayed at a rate of 0.1 to 0.5 gallons per square yard. When using an
     emulsion, dilute it with up to five parts of water by volume. Diluted-emulsion dustproofing treatments usually
     require several treatments. The dust stirred by traffic between applications eventually conglomerates and is
     no longer a problem. This is an effective treatment in very dusty areas where one application of cutback
     asphalt is insufficient. Lay a test strip to determine what application rate will be the most effective. Apply
     with an asphalt distributor or something as simple as a common watering can. Dustproofing is usually a
     temporary solution and project plans should include regular inspections and maintenance, as required.

SURFACE TREATMENTS

     12-150. The following paragraphs provide guidance on the proper design and construction of surface
     treatments, which are generally described as a sprayed binder with cover aggregates and commonly referred
     to as chip seals.

SPRAYING ASPHALT WITH COVER AGGREGATE AND SINGLE- AND MULTIPLE-SURFACE
TREATMENTS

     12-151. Sprayed asphalt with a cover-aggregate surface treatment consists of an application of asphalt
     followed by an application of aggregate. If the process is repeated, the resulting surfaces are referred to as
     multiple-surface treatments (double, triple, quadruple), depending on the number of applications.

     12-152. Apply these surface treatments on a primed, unbound base; an asphalt base course; or any type of
     existing pavement. This type of surface treatment, with a good prime coat, provides the lowest-cost

29 February 2016        TM 3-34.48-1                                            12-55


---

Chapter 12

     waterproof covering for a road surface. With good aggregate, this type of surface treatment will economically
     provide a wearing surface to meet the needs of medium and low volumes of traffic.

     12-153. This surface treatment is very useful as a wearing surface on base courses in the staged construction
     of highways pending placement of asphalt-concrete surface courses. There are limitations when this
     application is used. Consider using plant-mix when—

              Weather conditions are unfavorable.
              The surface that the asphalt is going to be sprayed onto is not hard, clean, and dry. (The surface

                  must be hard, clean, and dry for the treatment to adhere properly.)
              The amount and viscosity of the asphalt cannot be balanced with the condition of the underlying

                  material and with the size and amount of cover aggregate to assure proper aggregate retention.
              Heavy, high-speed traffic is likely. (Heavy, high speed traffic may dislodge aggregate from the

                  asphalt. This can be a significant problem, causing broken windshields from flying debris.)

Single-Surface Treatment

     12-154. A single-surface treatment usually consists of a sprayed application of bitumen and an aggregate
     cover one stone deep. Surface treatment may be referred to as a seal coat, armor coat, or carpet coat. A single-
     surface treatment is usually less than 1-inch thick. (See figure 12-39.) Surface treatments serve as an abrasive
     and weather-resistant medium that waterproofs the base. They are not as durable as hot mix asphalt and may
     require frequent maintenance. Although not recommended for airfields (foreign object debris), they may be
     used as an expedient measure. They are particularly suitable for JOA construction because they can be laid
     quickly with a minimum of materials and equipment, constructed in multiple layers with little interference to
     traffic, and used as the first step in stage construction.

     12-155. Surface treatment will not withstand the action of metal wheels on vehicles, tracked vehicles, or
     nonskid chains on vehicle wheels. Do not attempt construction of surface treatments when the temperature
     is below 50 degrees Fahrenheit. The requirements for a surface treatment are as follows:

              The quality of the bitumen must be sufficient enough to hold the stone in place without submerging
                  it in asphalt binder.

              Sufficient aggregate must be used to cover the bitumen.
              The base course that the surface treatment is laid onto must be strong enough to support the

                  anticipated traffic load.

     12-156. Uniformly graded sand or crushed stone, gravel, or slag may be used for surface treatments. The
     purpose of the surface treatment dictates the size of aggregate to be selected. For example, coarse sand may
     be used for sealing a smooth, existing surface. For a badly broken surface, the maximum size of the aggregate
     should be about 3/4 inch. Surface treatments include the following: dust palliatives, prime coats, and sprayed
     asphalt with a cover aggregate (single- and multiple-surface treatments). Rounded aggregates do not provide
     satisfactory performance with surface treatments. Hence, care must be exercised when considering using
     natural sands or poorly crushed gravels.

Material

     12-157. Rapid-cure and medium-cure cutbacks, emulsified tars, rapid-setting emulsions, and asphalt cements
     may be used for surface treatment. Rapid-setting emulsions are the most material. In many places, cutback
     asphalt is not used due to environmental issues. Viscosity grades of the cutbacks or asphalt cements depend
     on the size of aggregate used as cover stone. The larger particles of aggregate require a bitumen of higher
     viscosity so that the bitumen will hold the aggregate. For example, RC-70 or RC-250 may be used with coarse
     sand for a surface treatment to seal cracks in an otherwise satisfactory surface. For resurfacing a badly cracked
     or rough surface, RC-800 or RC-3,000 may be used with 3/4-inch aggregate.

     12-158. To assure uniform distribution, the bitumen should be applied with a bituminous distributor. The
     quantity of the bitumen required is based on the average particle size of the cover stone. The bitumen must
     be sufficient enough to hold the aggregate in place without leaving a sticky surface. The aggregate must not
     be completely submerged in the bitumen. Submerge 1/4-inch aggregate approximately 30 percent, 3/8-inch
     aggregate approximately 32 percent, 1/2-inch aggregate approximately 35 percent, and 3/4-inch aggregate
     approximately 43 percent. Approximately 1 gallon of bitumen is used for 100 pounds of aggregate. The
     recommended rate of bitumen application is given by the following formula:

Multiple-Surface Treatment

     12-160. When a tougher, more resistant surface is desired more than that obtained with a single-surface
     treatment, a multiple-surface treatment may be used. A multiple-surface treatment is two or more successive
     layers of a single-surface treatment. (See figure 12-40.) Smaller particles of aggregate and correspondingly
     less bitumen are used for each successive layer. Although multiple-surface treatments are usually more than
     1-inch thick, they are still considered surface treatments because each layer is usually less than 1 inch and
     the total surface treatment does not add to the load-carrying capacity of the base.

Legend:               gallon
gal                   pounds
lb
                     Figure 12-40. Multiple-surface treatment

12-161. The first layer of a multiple-surface treatment is laid according to the instructions previously given
for a single-surface treatment. Loose aggregate remaining on the first layer must be swept from the surface
so that the layers may bond together. As previously stated, the size of the aggregate and the amount of the
bitumen will decrease for each successive layer. For the second layer, the bitumen will usually be reduced to

29 February 2016     TM 3-34.48-1                                              12-59


---

Chapter 12

one-third or one-half the amount of the first application. The aggregate used in the second application should
be approximately one-half the diameter of that used in the first application. The final application of aggregate
should be swept clean, if necessary, so that an even layer of aggregate will remain. It should also be rolled
with a pneumatic roller so that the aggregate will become embedded in the bitumen. After the surface is rolled
and cured, it is ready for traffic. If the multiple-surface treatment has been laid on an airfield, loose aggregate
must be swept from the surface to minimize the potential for foreign object debris damage to aircraft. Final
sweeping is also recommended for roads.

CONSTRUCTION OF SURFACE TREATMENTS USING SPRAYED ASPHALT WITH COVER
AGGREGATE

     12-162. Surface treatments are widely used because of their low cost and usefulness in light to medium traffic
     roadways and parking areas. These treatments are normally used to seal or waterproof the pavement, provide
     wear resistance, and increase skid resistance. All surface treatments are relatively thin coatings of material
     and do not add structurally to the pavement.

Weather

     12-163. Weather conditions are an important factor for success in the construction of sprayed asphalt with
     cover-aggregate surface treatments and seal coats. For best results in aggregate retention, the pavement
     temperature should be relatively high during the application of the seal coat and some amount of curing
     should be allowed before fast moving and turning traffic is allowed to use the new seal coat. A certain amount
     of curing, or setting, is required even with the heaviest liquid-asphalt materials. This curing takes place best
     when the air temperature is well above 50 degrees Fahrenheit and the relative humidity is low. Every effort
     should be made to plan the work for placement in summer weather. After completion of the surface treatment,
     traffic should be controlled until the surface has cured.

Aggregate

12-164. Once an aggregate has been selected for use based on the desirable characteristics, it is then
necessary to determine what quantity of the aggregate will be required for a specific job. When placing a
surface treatment with an aggregate cover, the quantity of aggregate required can be determined from the
following equation:

12-165. The materials for a multiple-surface treatment are determined by the same method as above except
that the results are multiplied by the number of treatment passes. The aggregate size (not quantity) must be
cut in half for the second layer and each layer thereafter.

Spreading Aggregate

     12-166. Before the application of asphalt begins, an adequate aggregate spreader should be available and
     properly adjusted for the aggregate to be used. The spray-bar width of the bituminous distributor should be
     equal to the width of the aggregate being spread in one pass. Normally, this is the width of one traffic lane.
     An adequate supply of aggregate should be on hand to cover the asphalt that has been spread, without
     interruption, in the shortest practical time after the asphalt hits the surface. In addition, the aggregate spreader
     should be filled, in place, and ready to spread aggregate before commencing the asphalt spray. A common
     fault is to operate the distributor too far ahead of the aggregate spreader.

12-60       TM 3-34.48-1                                             29 February 2016


---

                                                                                                        Road Design and Airfield Layout

     12-167. Aggregate spreaders vary from a simple, controllable gate box attached to the dump truck, to very
     efficient, self-propelled units that apply the larger-size aggregate on the bottom and the finer-size on the top.
     The more efficient, self-propelled units are most desirable.

Standard, Hopper-Type Aggregate Spreaders
     12-168. The standard aggregate spreader can handle aggregate, which ranges from sand to 1 1/2-inch gravel.
     (See figure 12-41.) The rate and depth of application depend on the gate opening. The width of the spread
     may be varied from 4 to 8 feet in 1-foot increments. Depending on the manufacturer, the spreader has two or
     four wheels. It hooks on the rear of a 5-ton dump truck and the truck backs up. This allows the aggregate to
     be spread on the bitumen ahead of the truck tires, thus preventing pickup of the bitumen. As a safety
     precaution, no one should be allowed to stand on the aggregate, in the truck, or on the spreader at any time.

                             Figure 12-41. Typical hopper-type aggregate spreader

Rolling

     12-169. Pneumatic-tire rollers should be used for surface-treatment construction. Steel-wheeled rollers are
     not recommended for rolling, unless that is the only equipment available. The rollers should not be heavy
     enough to crush the aggregate particles. Vibratory rollers should not be used.

     12-170. Pneumatic-tire rollers are essential to firmly embed the aggregate into low areas or graded
     deformities that would normally be bridged over by using steel-wheel rollers. Pneumatic-tire rollers produce
     conformity across the width of the roadway, particularly over the outer quarters of the surface where there is
     the least traffic. The rollers should be heavy enough to properly imbed the aggregate, but rolling should be
     stopped as soon as crushing becomes evident. When double or triple surface treatments are used, each course
     should be rolled before subsequent applications of asphalt. When an asphalt fog seal is used, it should be
     applied after the rolling is complete.

Traffic Control

     12-171. It is important that traffic be controlled to prevent loss of aggregate. One method of controlling
     traffic is to form a single line of traffic behind a pilot vehicle with a red flag between stops at each end of the
     work area.

Asphalt Distributor

     12-172. The asphalt distributor is the key piece of equipment in the construction of surface treatments. It
     consists of a truck (or a trailer) equipped with a mounted, insulated tank with a heating system that is usually
     oil-burning, with direct heat from the flue passing through the tank. It is supplied with a power-driven pump
     that is suitable to handle products ranging from light, cold-application liquid asphalt to heavy asphalt cements

29 February 2016  TM 3-34.48-1  12-61


---

Chapter 12

     heated to spraying viscosity. Attached to the back end of the tank is a system of spray bars and nozzles
     through which the asphalt is forced under pressure onto the construction surface. The construction of the
     spray bars should provide full circulation of the asphalt through the bar when not spraying. These spray bars
     should have a minimum application width of 8 feet. On larger equipment, the spray bars will cover as much
     as a 24-foot width in one pass when equipped with a suitable capacity pump. The height of the spray bar
     determines the type of coverage: single lap, double lap, or triple lap. (See figure 12-42.) Normally a double
     or triple lap application is desired. A suitable thermometer should be installed in the tank to readily ascertain
     the temperature of the contents. A connection should be available to attach a hose for a single- or double-
     nozzle outlet to cover areas not reached by the spray bars or as a means of forcing a stream of asphalt to a
     desired point as in subsealing rigid, slab pavements. Distributors are made in sizes that range from 800 to
     4,000 gallons. Some maintenance distributors as small as 400 gallons are available.

                                            Figure 12-42. Spray bar coverage

     12-173. It is essential that the distributor be capable of distributing the asphalt uniformly over the surface
     being treated. For best results in surface treatments—

              Maintain uniform pressure and temperature on the spray nozzles. The fan of the spray from each
                  nozzle must be uniform and set at the proper angle with the spray bar (according to manufacturer
                  instructions) so that the spray fans do not interfere with each other.

              Maintain the spray bar at the proper height above the road surface (according to manufacturer
                  instructions) to provide complete and uniform overlap of the spray fans.

              Ensure that the distributor road speed is uniform.
              Check the spread of the distributor spray bar before beginning. The valve action should be

                  instantaneous, in opening and closing. The spraying operation should be inspected frequently to
                  ensure that the nozzles are the proper height from the road surface and working fully. An otherwise
                  good job may be spoiled if one or more spray nozzles are clogged.

MAINTENANCE AND REPAIR OF BITUMINOUS SURFACES

     12-174. Maintenance patrols frequently inspect bituminous pavements for early detection of failures. Small
     defects quickly develop into larger ones under the effects of weather and traffic and may result in pavement
     failure unless promptly corrected. Minor repairs are quickly made with small crews and hand tools, with a
     minimum interruption of traffic. Larger bituminous repairs require more time, personnel, and equipment; it
     may result in interference with traffic or, in extreme cases, require construction of detours to avoid a complete
     stoppage.

     12-175. Patches should be trimmed square or oblong with straight, vertical sides running parallel and
     perpendicular to the centerline of the traffic area. Stable material can be used for temporary repairs in combat
     areas or where suitable material is not available and the traffic area must be patched to keep traffic moving.
     Good-quality soil and masonry or concrete rubble are suitable for this purpose. These patches must be
     thoroughly compacted and constantly maintained with replacement material. More permanent patching
     should be accomplished as soon as possible.

12-62  TM 3-34.48-1  29 February 2016


---

                                                                                                  Road Design and Airfield Layout

12-176. Shoulders are bladed to facilitate drainage of rainwater from the surface. Ruts and washouts are
filled. Shoulder material is kept graded flush against pavement edges to restrict the seepage of water to the
subgrade and to prevent breaking of the pavement edge by traffic driving off the pavement onto the shoulder.
Material displaced from shoulders is replaced with new material, as required.
